Computational optimization is essential to many subdomains of engineering, science, and business such as design, control, operations, supply chains, game theory, data science/analytics, and machine learning.

This course provides a practical introduction to models, algorithms, and modern software for large-scale numerical optimization, especially for decision-making in engineering and business contexts. Topics include (nonconvex) nonlinear programming, deterministic global optimization, integer programming, dynamic optimization, and stochastic programming. Multi-objective optimization, optimization with embedded machine learning models as constraints, optimal experiment design, optimization for statistical inference, and mathematical programs with complementarity constraints may be covered based on time and student interests. The class is designed for advanced undergraduate/graduate engineering, science, mathematics, business, and statistics students who wish to incorporate computation optimization methods into their research. The course begins with an introduction to modeling and the Python-based Pyomo computational environment. Optimization theory and algorithms are emphasized throughout the semester.

A superstructure represents the candidate units, streams and configurations considered in a design problem. Discrete variables select units or connections; continuous variables size and operate them. A structure omitted from this search space cannot be selected by optimization. Including an option does not guarantee its physical feasibility: balances, performance and specifications still have to be imposed.

BGW (1997), Example 15.2, pp. 500–502, considers three ammonia-process choices: tubular versus multibed-quench reactor, flash condensation versus absorption/distillation for product separation, and membrane versus no hydrogen recovery. Choosing exactly one option at each of three independent stages gives 2^3=8 combinations. A tree lists those combinations; a network superstructure shares units and can represent recycle and simultaneous routes. BGW’s network may represent combinations beyond the eight tree leaves if multiple paths are allowed. Exactly-one assumptions must therefore be written as constraints, rather than inferred from the drawing.

A general mixed-integer nonlinear program is\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\quad\text{s.t. }\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\le\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{x}\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n,\quad \mathbf{y}\in Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^t.

Here \mathbf{x} is continuous and \mathbf{y} is integer. Binary variables restrict Y to a subset of \{0,1\}^t. Both variable types can enter every function, including the equality constraints. In the linear special case the model is a MILP; if all its decision variables are integer it is an IP. An integer domain alone does not make nonlinear functions linear. Biegler (2010), Eq. (1.1), p. 3 and p. 4, gives the binary form and the class distinctions.

The reactor problem below is a compact superstructure with two parallel candidates. The two-reactor power-law NLP permits zero flows instead of explicit build switches; fixed charges will make selection a separate binary decision.

Reference: Example 15.3 from Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997). 

See handout

Assume that we have the choice of selecting two reactors (shown below) for the reaction A \rightarrow B. Reactor I has a higher conversion (80%) but it is more expensive; reactor II has a lower conversion (66.7%) but is cheaper. The cost of feed A is $5/kmol. Which process alternative (reactor I, reactor II, or both) has the minimum costs to make 10 kmol/hr of product B?

Let x_r be the feed flowrate into reactor r. Its cost contribution, including feed, isC_r=a_r(x_r/x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{0.6}+c_f x_r,\quad x_{\mathrm{ref}}=1~\mathrm{kmol/hr},\quad c_f=5~\mathrm{\$/kmol}.

The reactor cost coefficients are rates in dollars per hour; the reference scale makes the power-law base dimensionless.

With n=|\mathcal R| reactors, the expanded model declares 1+2n continuous variables and n+2 linear equalities: one split, n conversions and one mixer. The original NLP has 1+2n lower-bounded variables and no upper bounds. Its objective is nonlinear even though its constraints are linear.

These equality rows are independent when every \theta_r>0. In a linear combination of rows, the coefficient of x_0 first forces the splitter multiplier to zero; the coefficient of each x_r then forces its conversion multiplier to zero, and the z_r coefficients force the mixer multiplier to zero. Thus the affine equality solution space has dimension (1+2n)-(n+2)=n-1. For P>0 it contains strictly positive reactor flows, so nonnegativity leaves a feasible set of that relative dimension. At its endpoints the bounds restrict the feasible directions. Counting rows alone would not establish rank or feasibility in a different model.

For two reactors this gives 5 variables, 4 independent equalities and one independent split choice.

The MILP below retains those 5 continuous variables and 4 equalities, and adds 2 binaries and 2 big-M inequalities. Its code also declares upper bounds of 20 on x_0,x_1,x_2: 2 lower-only continuous variables and 5 variables bounded on both sides, including the binaries. The formulation without those explicit upper bounds has the same feasible set here: positive conversions and the production equality already imply x_1\le12.5, x_2\le15 and x_0\le15. A declared bound is still counted even when redundant.

The NLP demonstration later replaces the two reactor-feed lower bounds by 

10-6 to avoid singular derivatives. This slightly changes its feasible set; its output approximates the zero-flow endpoints.

The coefficients a_r=5.5,4.0 are specified in dollars per hour when the numerical flow is measured in kmol/hr. With those coefficient units, a_r x_r^{0.6} does not have units of dollars per hour. A dimensional power is possible if its coefficient carries the corresponding compensating units; that is not how these coefficients are declared.

Write the implicit reference scale explicitly:C_r=a_r(x_r/x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{0.6},\qquad x_{\mathrm{ref}}=1~\mathrm{kmol/hr}.

Now the exponent acts on a dimensionless ratio and C_r has units of dollars per hour. The numerical objective is unchanged in the chosen units. If flow units change, convert x_{\mathrm{ref}} too; changing only the numerical unit changes the fitted correlation. assert_units_consistent checks dimensional consistency, not physical adequacy, feasibility or optimality.

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.environ import units as u
from pyomo.util.check_units import assert_units_consistent

# Pyomo's unit library has kmol and hr but no money, so declare a currency.
u.load_definitions_from_strings(["USD = [currency]"])

nlp = pyo.ConcreteModel()

## Define sets
nlp.REACTORS = pyo.Set(initialize=range(1, 3))

## Define parameters (data)

# Cost coefficient of reactor r, a_r [USD/hr]
cost_coefficient = {1: 5.5, 2: 4.0}
nlp.reactor_cost = pyo.Param(
    nlp.REACTORS, initialize=cost_coefficient, units=u.USD / u.hr
)

# Required product rate, P [kmol B/hr]
nlp.product_flowrate = pyo.Param(initialize=10.0, units=u.kmol / u.hr)

# Conversion of reactor r, theta_r [kmol B/kmol A]
reactor_conversion = {1: 0.8, 2: 2 / 3}
nlp.conversion = pyo.Param(nlp.REACTORS, initialize=reactor_conversion)

# Price of feed A, c_f [USD/kmol]
nlp.feed_cost = pyo.Param(initialize=5.0, units=u.USD / u.kmol)

# Reference flowrate for the economy-of-scale term, x_ref [kmol/hr]
nlp.flowrate_ref = pyo.Param(initialize=1.0, units=u.kmol / u.hr)


## Define variables

# Total feed of A, x_0 in the notes [kmol/hr]
nlp.feed_flowrate = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr)

# Feed into reactor r, x_r in the notes [kmol/hr]
nlp.reactor_feed = pyo.Var(
    nlp.REACTORS, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr
)

# Effluent leaving reactor r, z_r in the notes [kmol B/hr]
nlp.reactor_effluent = pyo.Var(
    nlp.REACTORS, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr
)

## Define constraints





# Add your solution here






## Define objective


# Total cost [USD/hr]. The exponent 0.6 is the economy-of-scale factor beta,
# applied to the flowrate scaled by x_ref so that the power is dimensionless.
@nlp.Objective()
def cost(b):
    return (
        sum(
            b.reactor_cost[r] * (b.reactor_feed[r] / b.flowrate_ref) ** (0.6)
            for r in b.REACTORS
        )
        + b.feed_cost * b.feed_flowrate
    )



# Inspect the model
nlp.pprint()

# Raises UnitsError if any constraint or the objective is dimensionally inconsistent
assert_units_consistent(nlp)

print("Units are consistent.")



Click to see the solution to the activity# Mass balance over the splitter [kmol/hr]
@nlp.Constraint()
def inlet_split(b):
    return b.feed_flowrate == sum(b.reactor_feed[r] for r in b.REACTORS)


# Reactor conversion, z_r = theta_r * x_r [kmol B/hr]
@nlp.Constraint(nlp.REACTORS)
def reactor_performance(b, r):
    return b.reactor_effluent[r] == b.conversion[r] * b.reactor_feed[r]


# Mass balance over the mixer meets product requirements [kmol B/hr]
@nlp.Constraint()
def mixer(b):
    return b.product_flowrate == sum(b.reactor_effluent[r] for r in b.REACTORS)

def initialize(model, reactor_choice=1):
    """Initialize all of the variables in the model to demonstrate local solutions

    Arguments:
        model: Pyomo model
        reactor_choice: 1 or 2

    Returns:
        nothing

    Action:
        initializes model

    """

    # Guess 20 kmol/hr feed of A
    model.feed_flowrate = 20.0

    # Either assign all of the feed to reactor 1 or 2
    if reactor_choice == 1:
        model.reactor_feed[1] = 20.0
        model.reactor_feed[2] = 0
    elif reactor_choice == 2:
        model.reactor_feed[1] = 0
        model.reactor_feed[2] = 20.0
    else:
        raise ValueError("Argument reactor_choice needs value 1 or 2.")

    # Based on the feed assignments, calculate effluent flowrate
    for r in model.REACTORS:
        model.reactor_effluent[r] = model.reactor_feed[r]() * model.conversion[r]


initialize(nlp, reactor_choice=1)
nlp.pprint()



Solve the current model and inspect its termination condition.

from pyomo.common.errors import ApplicationError

solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
try:
    results = solver.solve(nlp, tee=True)
except ApplicationError as error:
    # This failure is intentional: the next cell explains the singular derivative.
    print(f"Expected solver failure: {type(error).__name__}: {error}")













What happened? 

00.6 is fine --- it is 0. The derivative is not: \frac{d}{dx}x^{0.6} = 0.6\,x^{-0.4} \to \infty as x \to 0, and Ipopt needs it. Read the message again: can't evaluate pow'(0,0.6) --- note the prime. Work around? Let’s set the lower bound to something really small:

small_number = 1e-6
for r in nlp.REACTORS:

    # Set lower bound
    nlp.reactor_feed[r].setlb(small_number)

    # Adjust initial point if needed
    nlp.reactor_feed[r] = max(nlp.reactor_feed[r](), small_number)

nlp.pprint()



Now let’s resolve:

solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
results = solver.solve(nlp, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)



Now we can print the variable names and values:

def print_solution(model):
    """Print variable names and values

    Arguments:
        model: Pyomo model

    """

    print("Variable Names\t\tValue")
    for c in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var):
        print(c.name, "\t\t", pyo.value(c))

    print("\nObjective Name\t\tValue")
    for c in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Objective):
        print(c.name, "\t\t", pyo.value(c))


print_solution(nlp)



# Full returned variable vector, reported compactly for the handout.
print(f"x0={pyo.value(nlp.feed_flowrate):.10f}, "
      f"x1={pyo.value(nlp.reactor_feed[1]):.10f}, "
      f"x2={pyo.value(nlp.reactor_feed[2]):.3e}")
print(f"z1={pyo.value(nlp.reactor_effluent[1]):.10f}, "
      f"z2={pyo.value(nlp.reactor_effluent[2]):.3e}; "
      f"C={pyo.value(nlp.cost):.8f} USD/hr")

Eliminating z_1,z_2,x_0,x_1 givesx_1(t)=\frac{10-(2/3)t}{0.8},\qquad 0\le t=x_2\le15,C(t)=5.5\,x_1(t)^{0.6}+4t^{0.6}+5[x_1(t)+t],

where numerical flows use kmol/hr and the reference flow is 1 kmol/hr. On the open segment, each positive power-law term is strictly concave; the feed term is affine. Thus C is strictly concave and continuous on the closed segment. For 0\le\lambda\le1 and t=15\lambda, concavity givesC(t)\ge(1-\lambda)C(0)+\lambda C(15)\ge\min\{C(0),C(15)\}.

Comparing endpoints therefore proves the global optimum of this particular model: reactor I only, x_1=12.5,x_2=0, costing about 87.53 dollars/hr. Reactor II alone costs about 95.31 dollars/hr. The interior maximum is at x_2\approx11.26; BGW’s sketch labels it 11.4. These values use the exact conversion 2/3, rather than the rounded 0.67 in the printed equations.

Concavity alone does not make both endpoints local minima. Here the incoming unused-reactor cost has a positive h^{0.6} term that dominates the O(h) change in the active reactor and feed. Near t=0, C(t)-C(0)=4t^{0.6}+O(t)>0; near t=15, C(15-h)-C(15)=5.5(5h/6)^{0.6}+O(h)>0. Hence both endpoints are strict local minima relative to the feasible segment.

The derivative of x^{0.6} is singular at zero. The usual differentiable KKT theorem cannot be applied at these exact endpoints. The notebook instead solves the slightly perturbed model with reactor-feed lower bounds 

10-6. Its two initializations demonstrate two local returns; there is no general rule that a local solver selects the nearest endpoint, and an optimal termination message alone does not prove the global result. The endpoint comparison above supplies that proof.

The analytic curve is owned by figures/plots/reactor-concave-local-minima.py; it is not a second implementation of solver output. Source: BGW (1997), Example 15.3, pp. 509–511.

Replace the power-law equipment cost by a fixed charge plus a constant marginal cost. This gives a different cost approximation whose resulting model is a MILP. A globally solved MILP certifies that approximation; it does not certify an arbitrary original nonlinear cost model. The on/off link below imposes an upper capacity when a reactor is selected. It does not impose a positive minimum operating flow.

For each reactor introduce y_r\in\{0,1\} and impose 0\le x_r\le M_r y_r. Its equipment cost is \bar b_r y_r+\bar a_r x_r, with (\bar b_1,\bar b_2)=(7.5,5.5) dollars/hr and (\bar a_1,\bar a_2)=(1.4,1.0) dollars/kmol. Add the feed cost 5x_0. A one-time capital expense must be annualized or otherwise put on the same time basis before combining it with a rate in dollars/hr.

The link proves y_r=0\Rightarrow x_r=0, or equivalently x_r>0\Rightarrow y_r=1. It permits y_r=1,x_r=0: a selected unit can be idle. With a positive fixed charge and no other reason to retain an idle unit, minimization switches it off. A positive minimum throughput would require the additional row L_r y_r\le x_r for a justified L_r>0.

After minimizing over a free switch for one unit, its cost as a function of flow is piecewise:\widehat C_r(x_r)=\begin{cases}0,&x_r=0,\\\bar b_r+\bar a_r x_r,&0<x_r\le M_r.\end{cases}

This is a discontinuous function of x_r alone. The binary gives it a linear mixed-integer representation; it is not correct to say no such scalar function exists. The plotted zero-cost point represents an unbuilt unit, and the positive-flow branch represents a selected unit.

The shared analytic figure contains equipment-only and equipment-plus-feed panels and an origin inset. The separate exploratory cell below lets you change the two total-cost lines. It plots the selected-unit branch at zero as well; the shared figure distinguishes that branch from the unbuilt zero-cost point. Both implementations serve these stated, different roles.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

feed = np.linspace(0, 20, 101)

# Price of feed A, c_f [USD/kmol] -- the same for both reactors

    cost_linearized = c_linear * feed + c_fixed

        color=color,

    )

        color=color,
        linestyle="--",

y_r = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if reactor } r \text{ is selected} \\

x_r \leq 20 y_r, \quad \forall r \in \mathcal{R}

Thus if y_r = 0, then x_r = 0

Finally, we can define the new linearized reactor cost model:\begin{align*}
\text{Reactor I:} \quad & 7.5 y_1 + 1.4 x_1 \\
\text{Reactor II:} \quad & 5.5 y_2 + 1.0 x_2
\end{align*}

Recall that x_0 = x_1 + x_2. Thus, the feed cost is 5x_0 = 5 x_1 + 5 x_2.

Putting this all together gives the following MILP optimization problem:\begin{align*}
\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \quad & C = 7.5 y_1 + 6.4 x_1 + 5.5 y_2 + 6.0 x_2 \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & 0.8 x_1 + (2/3) x_2 = 10 \\
& x_1 - 20 y_1 \leq 0 \\
& x_2 - 20 y_2 \leq 0 \\
& x_1, x_2 \geq 0, \quad y_1, y_2 \in \{0, 1\}
\end{align*}

The marginal costs per unit of product, including feed, are 6.4/0.8=8 for reactor I and 6/(2/3)=9 for reactor II. Thus, when both are selected, all production still uses I. The cheapest feasible row proves the global optimum of this two-reactor MILP. Its agreement in reactor choice with the nonlinear model is specific to these data; their objective values differ.

With t binary choices, exhaustive enumeration has 2^t assignments: 1,024 at t=10 and 1,073,741,824 at t=30. General integer variables need their own finite bounds before exhaustive enumeration is finite. Practical methods discard groups using valid bounds rather than solving every assignment. The complete branch-and-bound algorithm is taught in the course’s MINLP Algorithms guide; this section supplies the modeling example. Source: BGW (1997), pp. 512–513.

milp = pyo.ConcreteModel()

## Define sets
milp.REACTORS = pyo.Set(initialize=range(1, 3))

## Define parameters (data)

# Big-M throughput limit, M [kmol/hr]

For a nonnegative flow, x_r\le M_r y_r is valid only when M_r is at least the largest feasible value of x_r in the intended physical model. With \theta_r>0, x\ge0 and \sum_r\theta_r x_r=P, every term is at most P, sox_r\le P/\theta_r;\qquad M_1=12.5,\quad M_2=15

are valid individual bounds here. The common value 20 is valid but weaker. A bound of 10 excludes the feasible reactor-I-only design. Bounds must be re-derived if conversion, production requirements, additional reactions or flow signs change.

Relaxing a binary switch gives 0\le y_r\le1. At x_1=12.5, the link requires y_1\ge12.5/M_1. With common M=20, the smallest switch is 0.625; with 20,000 it is 0.000625. The physical production equality already bounds both flows, so increasing this valid logical bound does not add new integer designs in this particular example. It does allow the LP to pay a smaller fraction of the fixed charge. The scalar switch picture below omits the reactor production equality and explicit physical caps so its mechanism is visible.

For fixed M_r, the single-unit set \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):0\le x\le M_r\} has convex hull 0\le y\le1, 0\le x\le M_r y. If y>0, any relaxed point equals (1-y)(0,0)+y(x/y,1); the y=0 case is (0,0). This proof concerns one switch. Intersecting many such hulls with balances does not generally give the convex hull of the whole process.

For minimization the relaxed feasible set contains every integer-feasible point, so its globally optimal value is a lower bound on the MILP optimum, provided the same objective is used. The table computed below solves the complete reactor model, not just the scalar picture. The common bound of 20 gives 84.6875 dollars/hr; 20,000 gives 80.0046875; the individual production bounds give 87.5 and close the objective gap for these data. This is not a general integrality guarantee.

Source: BGW (1997), Eqs. (15.10)–(15.12), p. 512, and Appendix A, §A.3.2, pp. 758, 760–761. The production-bound and convex-combination arguments are supplied here in full.

# Count declared rows and bounds, rather than subtracting rows from variables.
def declared_counts(model):
    variables = list(model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var))
    rows = list(model.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True))
    return dict(
        continuous=sum(v.is_continuous() for v in variables),
        binary=sum(v.is_binary() for v in variables),
        linear_equalities=sum(c.equality and c.body.polynomial_degree() in (0, 1) for c in rows),
        linear_inequalities=sum(not c.equality and c.body.polynomial_degree() in (0, 1) for c in rows),
        lower_only=sum(v.lb is not None and v.ub is None for v in variables),
        both_bounds=sum(v.lb is not None and v.ub is not None for v in variables),
    )

A common special MINLP form is\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{y}+f(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{s.t. }\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\le\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{x}\in X,\quad \mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^t.

Here fixed charges are linear in \mathbf{y} and binaries enter the coupling inequalities linearly. The matrix \mathbf{A} contains signed coefficients; it is not the positive scalar upper bound M. This is BGW problem (P1), p. 513, a specialization of the general form above. Binaries can enter nonlinear equalities in the general form, so \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}) is not a restriction to impose on all MINLPs.

Operation

Result

Fix all binaries to a specified assignment

continuous NLP subproblem; it can be infeasible

Relax binaries to their bounds 0\le\mathbf{y}\le1

continuous NLP relaxation

Use affine objective and constraint expressions, retaining binaries

MILP

Start with a MILP and fix or relax every integer variable

LP subproblem or LP relaxation

Replacing a nonlinear cost by an affine approximation changes the model; it is not an exact identity. For a general nonlinear relaxation, a local returned objective need not be a lower bound: the lower-bound statement requires the globally minimized relaxation.

Scheduling and planning use binaries for assignments, operating campaigns and facility locations. Unit commitment uses start/on decisions with continuous output; nonlinear heat-rate functions lead to MINLP, while suitable linear data/formulations lead to MILP. Discrete equipment design can select tray numbers, feed-tray location, exchanger connections or catalog sizes. Biegler (2010), Table 1.1, p. 6 and Exercise 6, p. 16, gives engineering examples. Further worked MO-book models: 

workforce shift scheduling, 

machine scheduling, 

facility location, 

dinner seating, and 

exam-room scheduling.

For a signed regression coefficient \gamma_j\in[L_j,U_j], with valid L_j\le0\le U_j, a selection binary can imposeL_j y_j\le\gamma_j\le U_j y_j.

Both sides matter: y_j=0 then forces \gamma_j=0. The nonnegative reactor’s one-sided switch does not apply unchanged to a coefficient that can be negative. A cardinality budget \sum_jy_j\le k limits selected terms. The bound validity and choice of k are additional modeling decisions.

Some nonsmooth functions have continuous reformulations: positive absolute-value penalties and max epigraphs can be LPs, as developed in the 

continuous formulation reference. Exact nonconvex graph relations or logical alternatives may require binaries. It is incorrect to claim that every absolute value or maximum introduces integer variables.

Broader modeling and theory references: H. P. Williams, Model Building in Mathematical Programming, 5th ed., Wiley, 2013; G. L. Nemhauser and L. A. Wolsey, Integer and Combinatorial Optimization, Wiley, 1988.

A bounded integer q\in\{L,\ldots,U\} can be represented by q=L+\sum_{k=0}^{b-1}2^k z_k, z_k\in\{0,1\}, with b=\lceil\log_2(U-L+1)\rceil and the additional restriction \sum_k2^kz_k\le U-L. The restriction excludes unused binary codes when the range size is not a power of two. The case U=L needs no binary. This represents a bounded integer domain; it does not linearize a nonlinear function of that integer.

Sets

Click to expand\mathcal{F} = \{\text{take away, veggies, bread}\}\mathcal{N} = \{P, C, F, V\}

Parameters

Click to expand

\pi_i: price for food option i \in \mathcal{F}

r_j: nutrition requirement for nutrient j \in \mathcal{N}

D_{ij}: nutrition info for food i \in \mathcal{F} and nutrient j \in \mathcal{N}

Variables

Click to expand

x_i: amount of food i \in \mathcal{F} eaten/purchased

Objective and Constraints

Click to expand

Minimize:

\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}} x_i \cdot \pi_i \quad \text{(cost)}

Subject to:

\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}} D_{ij} \cdot x_i \geq r_j \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{N} \quad \text{(be healthy)}

Bounds:

x_i \geq 0 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{F}

Full Model

Let’s put all of the components together into the full model written in compact notation.\begin{align*}
\min_{\mathbf{x}} \quad & \sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}} x_i \cdot \pi_i & \text{(cost)} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}} D_{ij} \cdot x_i \geq r_j, \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{N} & \text{(be healthy)} \\
& x_i \geq 0, \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{F} & \text{(non-negative bounds)}
\end{align*}

Degree of Freedom Analysis

We will later learn more about how to factor inequality constraints into degree of freedom analysis. For now, please count the number of equality and inequality constraints separately.

Click to expand

Continuous variables: 3

Inequality constraints: 4

Bounds: 3

Question: Why is it okay to have more inequality constraints than variables?

Answer: Not all inequality constraints may be active at a time.

Problem size

Let N_f represent the number of food options and N_n represent the number of nutrients.

Click to expand

Continuous variables: N_f. One serving variable x_i per food option.

Integer/discrete variables: 0. Every variable is declared NonNegativeReals. Servings are
divisible in this model --- half a loaf of bread is allowed.

Equality constraints: 0. The model contains only >= constraints. Nothing forces the diet to
hit a requirement exactly.

Inequality constraints: N_n, from C1 --- one per nutrient.

Variable bounds: N_f, all lower-only. x_i \geq 0 for every food option, and there is no
upper bound. As above, bounds are counted separately from the inequality constraints, and split
into lower-only, upper-only and both --- here it is entirely lower-only.

Parameters: N_f N_n + N_f + N_n. The nutrition table D_{i,j} alone has N_f N_n entries,
plus N_f prices and N_n requirements. The data grows as the product while the model grows
only as the sum: adding a hundred food options adds a hundred variables but four hundred numbers to
look up. In practice the data, not the solve, is the expensive part of scaling this model up.

Classify the problem

Is this an LP, QP, NLP, MILP or MINLP? Is it convex? What does that buy you?

Click to expand

Linear program (LP).

The objective \sum_i \pi_i x_i is linear in x --- the prices are data, not variables.

Every constraint \sum_i D_{i,j} x_i \geq r_j is linear in x, for the same reason.

Every variable is continuous (NonNegativeReals), so nothing is integer and it is not a
MILP.

It is convex, because a linear objective over a polyhedral feasible set is convex. Two things
follow, and they are the reason we care about the classification at all:

Every local minimum is a global minimum. A solver reporting “optimal” has found the
answer, not an answer.

Specialized algorithms apply. Simplex and interior-point methods exploit linearity directly,
and an LP with thousands of variables is routine. We use Ipopt below --- a general nonlinear
solver --- only because we want the KKT multipliers it reports. An LP solver can never be used
on an NLP; an NLP solver can always be used on an LP, and usually should not be.

Aside: two ways to write a constraint rule

records.content:
The “be healthy” constraint is our first indexed constraint: one inequality for every nutrient
j \in \mathcal{N}. Pyomo builds an indexed constraint from a rule --- a function of the model and
the index --- which it calls once per index. There are two ways to hand Pyomo that rule, and they build
exactly the same model.

The older form defines the function, then attaches it with the rule= keyword:def diet_min_rule(m, n):
    return sum(m.food_info[f, n] * m.food_eaten[f] for f in m.FOOD) >= m.needs[n]


m.diet_min = pyo.Constraint(m.NUTRIENTS, rule=diet_min_rule)

The decorator form attaches the function as it is defined:@m.Constraint(m.NUTRIENTS)
def diet_min(b, n):
    return sum(b.food_info[f, n] * b.food_eaten[f] for f in b.FOOD) >= b.needs[n]

This course uses the decorator from here on, and so does our


Pyomo style guide. Two reasons: the name is written once instead of three
times (function name, _rule suffix, component name), so the component name cannot drift away from the
function that defines it; and the lines are shorter, which matters when the model goes into a handout.
Note the first argument is the block Pyomo is building, so we call it b rather than m.

You still need to be able to read the rule= form. It is what the Pyomo textbook uses and what you will
meet in most existing research code. When you see rule=some_function, translate it into the decorator in
your head. This is the only place in the course notes where we write a constraint both ways.

m.price = pyo.Param(m.FOOD, initialize=price, units=u.USD / u.serving)

## Define variables
m.food_eaten = pyo.Var(
    m.FOOD, initialize=1.0, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.serving
)


## Define constraints
# Be healthy: sum_i D_ij * x_i >= r_j [nutrient]
@m.Constraint(m.NUTRIENTS)
def diet_min(b, n):
    return sum(b.food_info[f, n] * b.food_eaten[f] for f in b.FOOD) >= b.needs[n]


## Define objective
# Total cost of the diet, sum_i pi_i * x_i [USD]
@m.Objective(sense=pyo.minimize)
def cost(b):
    return sum(b.food_eaten[f] * b.price[f] for f in b.FOOD)


# Print model
m.pprint()

A bulk distributor supplies custom milk blends to several customers. Each customer specifies a minimum fat content, pays a fixed price per unit, and will buy no more than a stated maximum. The distributor sources raw milk from local farms, each producing milk of known fat content at a known cost.

The distributor has found cheaper raw milk at some remote farms. But it owns only one truck with a single tank for the remote route, so milk from the remote farms must be mixed in that tank before transport. That creates a pool of uniform composition, which is then blended with local milk to meet each customer’s requirement.

Three options:

Business as usual --- local farms only.

Buy a second truck --- keep each remote farm’s milk separate, so everything blends freely.

Pool the remote farms --- one truck, one tank, one composition.

Options 1 and 2 are linear programs. Option 3 is not, and that is the point of the example.

The rest of the notebook follows the course’s five-step procedure --- mathematical model, model-size analysis, Pyomo implementation, analysis of the results --- and works all three options through each step side by side.

Note

The source data does not name the physical unit of milk. Amounts are in unnamed “units”, costs and prices are per unit, and fat content is a mass fraction. The units below are annotated as such.

The objective measures operating profit. No truck purchase price, transport cost, tank capacity, or supplier limit is included. Comparing equipment investments requires those additional data and a common time horizon.

It is tempting to write three models. Do not. All three options are the same model under different restrictions, and only one question changes between them:

Which farms can we buy from, and which of those must share the single tanker?

Sets. \mathcal{L}, the farms whose milk blends freely; \mathcal{R}, the farms that must share one tanker; \mathcal{S} = \mathcal{L} \cup \mathcal{R}, every farm we buy from; \mathcal{K}, the customers.

Parameters. \phi_s, the fat fraction of farm s’s milk [dimensionless]; \kappa_s, its cost per unit [USD/milk]; \pi_k, the price customer k pays [USD/milk]; d_k, its maximum demand [milk]; \phi^{\min}_k, the minimum fat fraction it accepts [dimensionless].

The three subsections below write out each option in that notation. Read them together: Options 1 and 2 are the same equations over different farm sets, and Option 3 is those equations with a pool bolted on.

Only the local farms, and nothing is pooled: \mathcal{L} is the local farms and \mathcal{R} = \emptyset. The one decision variable is z_{l,k}, the amount of milk from farm l blended into the delivery to customer k [milk].\begin{align}
\max_{\mathbf{z}} \quad & \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\pi_k - \kappa_l) z_{l,k} && \text{profit} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} z_{l,k} \leq d_k && \forall k \in \mathcal{K} \quad \text{demand} \\
& \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} \phi_l z_{l,k} \geq \phi^{\min}_k \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} z_{l,k} && \forall k \in \mathcal{K} \quad \text{blend quality} \\
& z_{l,k} \geq 0
\end{align}

The blend quality constraint is the only one worth pausing on. It says the fat delivered to customer k is at least the fraction \phi^{\min}_k of the milk delivered to customer k, which is a linear statement even though “average fat fraction” is a ratio: multiplying through by the denominator clears it. Every term is linear, so this is a linear program.

A second truck means each remote farm’s milk travels in its own tank, so it blends freely exactly like the local milk. Nothing is pooled, so \mathcal{R} is still empty --- the remote farms simply move into \mathcal{L}:\mathcal{L} = \{\text{Farm A}, \text{Farm B}, \text{Farm C}, \text{Farm D}\}, \qquad \mathcal{R} = \emptyset .

The equations are the ones written for Option 1, unchanged. It is still a linear program, and it is a relaxation of Option 3: everything Option 3 can do, Option 2 can do too, by sending the same milk down four separate tanks instead of one. So Option 2’s profit is an upper bound on Option 3’s.

Only one truck is available for the remote route, so purchases from the remote farms are combined into a single pool of uniform composition, transported, and then blended with local milk. Now \mathcal{L} is the local farms and \mathcal{R} the remote ones.

This is the p-parameterization of the pooling problem: the pool composition is itself a decision variable, p.

Variables. z_{l,k}, local milk shipped from l \in \mathcal{L} to customer k; x_r, milk bought from remote farm r; y_k, pooled milk delivered to customer k; and p, the fat fraction of the pool.\begin{align}
\max_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}, p} \quad & \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\pi_k - \kappa_l) z_{l,k} + \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \pi_k y_k - \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \kappa_r x_r && \text{profit} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} z_{l,k} + y_k \leq d_k && \forall k \in \mathcal{K} \quad \text{demand} \\
& \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} x_r = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} y_k && \text{pool balance} \\
& \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \phi_r x_r = \underbrace{p \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} x_r}_{\textbf{bilinear}} && \text{pool fat balance} \\
& \underbrace{p\, y_k}_{\textbf{bilinear}} + \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} \phi_l z_{l,k} \geq \phi^{\min}_k \Big( \sum_{l \in \mathcal{L}} z_{l,k} + y_k \Big) && \forall k \in \mathcal{K} \quad \text{blend quality}
\end{align}

Every variable is nonnegative, y_k \leq d_k, and p is bounded below and above by the smallest and largest fat fractions among the remote farms --- a pool cannot be richer than its richest input.

The pool fat balance can be written either as p \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} x_r, as above and as the Pyomo code below does, or as p \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} y_k. The two agree on the feasible set, because the pool balance constraint immediately above forces \sum_{r} x_r = \sum_{k} y_k.

The last two constraints contain bilinear terms: a product of the composition variable p with a flow variable. A bilinear term is smooth and differentiable everywhere. The feasible set of this particular model is nonconvex, as the explicit midpoint counterexample below proves. A product in a formula alone does not prove that every instance has a nonconvex feasible set or exclude all possible reformulations.

This is the model, and Options 1 and 2 are inside it. Set \mathcal{R} = \emptyset: there is no tanker, so \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} and p are never declared, the pool balance and pool fat balance disappear, the p\,y_k term in the blend quality constraint is zero, and what is left is exactly the linear program of Option 1. A nonempty remote set activates the bilinear block; the data and constraints determine its feasible geometry. The model class in the table above is a consequence of the restriction, not an independent choice.

Note

Notation warning: p here is a composition, not a search direction. The symbol is the pooling literature’s own and is worth keeping, but elsewhere in this course p is a step.

The short add_pool_block helper is called by this builder; it is the actual pool implementation used in every solve below. There is no second model builder. Farms in local blend freely; farms in pooled share one tanker. If pooled is empty the pool variables are never declared and Pyomo is handed a linear program --- the code reduces the same way the mathematics did in Step 1.

Units. Milk here is measured in generic units, so the notebook declares a milk
unit and a USD currency and hangs them on every Param and Var. Fat content stays
dimensionless, because it is a mass fraction. The builder ends with
assert_units_consistent, which is the part that earns the declaration: it is what
would catch a price or a cost mixed into a constraint that balances amounts of
milk. It cannot catch everything: fat content is dimensionless, so a fat balance
and a milk balance carry the same units.

The optional fat_data argument supplies a new farm-assay dictionary for sensitivity experiments; omitting it uses the original data. def add_pool_block(m):
    """Add the shared-composition block to the already declared farm/customer data."""
    # Amounts use the same milk unit as customer demands.
    m.x = pyo.Var(m.R, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.milk)
    m.y = pyo.Var(m.K, bounds=lambda b, k: (0, b.demand[k]), units=u.milk)
    m.p = pyo.Var(bounds=(min(pyo.value(m.fat[r]) for r in m.R),
                         max(pyo.value(m.fat[r]) for r in m.R)))
    @m.Constraint()
    def pool_balance(b):
        return sum(b.x[r] for r in b.R) == sum(b.y[k] for k in b.K)
    # Using sum_R x or sum_K y here agrees because of pool_balance.
    @m.Constraint()
    def pool_quality(b):
        return sum(b.fat[r] * b.x[r] for r in b.R) == b.p * sum(b.x[r] for r in b.R)



def create_milk_model(local, pooled, fat_data=None):
    """Create the milk blending/pooling model in Pyomo

    One model covers all three options. The only thing that changes is which
    farms are reachable, and which of them must share the single tanker:

        Option 1  local=local_farms, pooled=[]            business as usual
        Option 2  local=all_farms,   pooled=[]            a second truck
        Option 3  local=local_farms, pooled=remote_farms  one truck, one pool

    Farms in `local` blend freely: their milk reaches each customer as its own
    stream z_{l,k}. Farms in `pooled` share one tanker, so their milk is first
    mixed into a single stream of composition p and only then blended. If
    `pooled` is empty there is no tanker, the pool variables are never
    declared, and every remaining term is linear -- the model is an LP.

    Arguments:
        local: list of farm names whose milk blends freely
        pooled: list of farm names whose milk must share one tanker

    Returns:
        m: Pyomo concrete model
    """
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel("Milk blending and pooling")

    # Freely blended farms, L in the notes
    m.L = pyo.Set(initialize=local)

    # Pooled farms, R in the notes. Empty for Options 1 and 2.
    m.R = pyo.Set(initialize=pooled)

    # All farms sourced from, L union R
    m.S = pyo.Set(initialize=list(local) + list(pooled))

    # Customers, K in the notes
    m.K = pyo.Set(initialize=customer_names)

    # Fat fraction of the milk from farm s, phi_s [dimensionless]
    fat_values = fat if fat_data is None else fat_data
    m.fat = pyo.Param(m.S, initialize={s: fat_values[s] for s in m.S})

    # Purchase cost per unit from farm s, kappa_s [USD/milk]
    m.cost = pyo.Param(m.S, initialize={s: cost[s] for s in m.S}, units=u.USD / u.milk)

    # Price paid per unit by customer k, pi_k [USD/milk]
    m.price = pyo.Param(m.K, initialize=price, units=u.USD / u.milk)

    # Maximum demand of customer k, d_k [milk]
    m.demand = pyo.Param(m.K, initialize=demand, units=u.milk)

    # Minimum fat fraction customer k accepts, phi_min_k [dimensionless]
    m.min_fat = pyo.Param(m.K, initialize=min_fat)

    # Freely blended milk from farm l to customer k, z_{l,k} [milk]
    m.z = pyo.Var(m.L, m.K, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.milk)

    # Only pooled options contain the shared-composition variables and rows.
    if len(m.R) > 0:
        add_pool_block(m)

    # Helper expressions, written so the constraints below read the same way
    # whether or not a pool exists.
    def pooled_milk(b, k):
        return b.y[k] if len(b.R) > 0 else 0.0

    def pooled_fat(b, k):
        return b.p * b.y[k] if len(b.R) > 0 else 0.0

    # Maximize profit [USD]
    @m.Objective(sense=pyo.maximize)
    def profit(b):
        revenue_and_cost_local = sum(
            (b.price[k] - b.cost[l]) * b.z[l, k] for l in b.L for k in b.K
        )
        if len(b.R) == 0:
            return revenue_and_cost_local
        return (
            revenue_and_cost_local
            + sum(b.price[k] * b.y[k] for k in b.K)
            - sum(b.cost[r] * b.x[r] for r in b.R)
        )

    # Deliveries cannot exceed each customer's demand [milk]
    @m.Constraint(m.K)
    def demand_limit(b, k):
        return sum(b.z[l, k] for l in b.L) + pooled_milk(b, k) <= b.demand[k]

    # Each delivery meets its fat spec. BILINEAR when a pool exists. [milk]
    @m.Constraint(m.K)
    def blend_quality(b, k):
        fat_delivered = pooled_fat(b, k) + sum(b.fat[l] * b.z[l, k] for l in b.L)
        milk_delivered = sum(b.z[l, k] for l in b.L) + pooled_milk(b, k)
        return fat_delivered >= b.min_fat[k] * milk_delivered

    # Raises UnitsError if any constraint or the objective is inconsistent
    assert_units_consistent(m)

    return m




def model_size(m, label):
    """Count declared rows and bound sides; do not infer local dimension from counts."""
    variables = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Var, active=True))
    rows = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True))
    linear = lambda row: row.body.polynomial_degree() in (0, 1)
    print(label)
    print(f"  continuous variables      {len(variables):3d}")
    print(f"  linear equality rows      {sum(c.equality and linear(c) for c in rows):3d}")
    print(f"  nonlinear equality rows   {sum(c.equality and not linear(c) for c in rows):3d}")
    print(f"  linear inequality rows    {sum(not c.equality and linear(c) for c in rows):3d}")
    print(f"  nonlinear inequality rows {sum(not c.equality and not linear(c) for c in rows):3d}")
    print(f"  lower bound sides         {sum(x.lb is not None for x in variables):3d}")
    print(f"  upper bound sides         {sum(x.ub is not None for x in variables):3d}\n")




# The farm partition selects the physical transport restriction.
m1 = create_milk_model(local_farms, [])
m2 = create_milk_model(all_farms, [])
m3 = create_milk_model(local_farms, remote_farms)
model_size(m1, "Option 1: local farms only")
model_size(m2, "Option 2: all farms, one truck each")

The pool block is the only part of the builder that Options 1 and 2 skip. Its two equality constraints are exactly the two that Step 2 counted.

model_size(m3, "Option 3: remote farms pooled")

One model uses one report function. The pool rows appear only when a pool exists. Using Ipopt throughout holds the solver family fixed, while model restrictions and initialization can still change the returned point. LP and nonlinear results need feasibility and termination checks; global certification requires an appropriate bound or proof.

solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")


def solve_and_report(m, title, opt=None):
    """Solve one option and print the supplier and customer tables.

    Arguments:
        m: a Pyomo concrete model from create_milk_model
        title: heading printed above the tables
        opt: solver to use; defaults to Ipopt with no options set

    Returns:
        the operating profit at the returned point
    """
    opt = solver if opt is None else opt
    results = opt.solve(m)
    assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), f"Solve failed for {title}"

    pooled = len(m.R) > 0

    print(f"{title}")
    if pooled:
        print(f"  pool composition p = {pyo.value(m.p):6.4f}")
    print(f"  profit             = {pyo.value(m.profit):,.2f}\n")

    # One row per farm: what its milk cost, and where it went.
    rows = []
    for s in m.S:
        row = {"fat": pyo.value(m.fat[s]), "cost": pyo.value(m.cost[s])}
        for k in m.K:
            row[k] = pyo.value(m.z[s, k]) if s in m.L else 0.0
        if pooled:
            row["Pool"] = pyo.value(m.x[s]) if s in m.R else 0.0
        rows.append(row)
    print("  Supplier report")
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows, index=list(m.S)).round(4))

    # One row per customer: what was delivered, and at what fat fraction.
    rows = []
    for k in m.K:
        row = {"min_fat": pyo.value(m.min_fat[k]), "demand": pyo.value(m.demand[k])}
        for l in m.L:
            row[l] = pyo.value(m.z[l, k])
        total = sum(pyo.value(m.z[l, k]) for l in m.L)
        fat_out = sum(pyo.value(m.z[l, k]) * pyo.value(m.fat[l]) for l in m.L)
        if pooled:
            row["Pool"] = pyo.value(m.y[k])
            total += pyo.value(m.y[k])
            fat_out += pyo.value(m.y[k]) * pyo.value(m.p)
        row["Total"] = total
        row["fat delivered"] = fat_out / total if total > 0 else np.nan
        rows.append(row)
    print("  Customer report")
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows, index=list(m.K)).round(4))

    return pyo.value(m.profit)

profit_1 = solve_and_report(m1, "Option 1, local farms only")









Both local farms are used. All three blend-quality constraints bind in the reported baseline. The LP solution is checked numerically; its convexity permits a global certificate when the necessary feasibility and dual conditions hold. A solver name or termination message alone is not that certificate.

profit_2 = solve_and_report(m2, "Option 2, all farms, one truck each")









Sourcing from the remote farms is worth a great deal --- but Option 2 needs a second truck to keep the two remote supplies separated in transit. Note also that the local farms are displaced entirely, and that Customer 2 is delivered milk richer than it requires. That is product giveaway: the optimizer hands over quality because the alternative costs more.

This is the only one of the three that is hard, and the rest of this step is about why.

nlp_solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")

nlp_solver.options["bound_frac"] = 0.01
profit_3 = solve_and_report(m3, "Option 3, pooled, bound_frac = 0.01", nlp_solver)









Solve it twice.

Ipopt’s bound_frac sets a relative interior distance for initial bound adjustment, together with the absolute-distance option bound_push. It can change the initial values of several variables without changing the model. Solve with two values and compare the returned feasible plans. See the 

official Ipopt initialization options.

nlp_solver.options["bound_frac"] = 0.5
m3_alt = create_milk_model(local_farms, remote_farms)
profit_3_alt = solve_and_report(
    m3_alt, "Option 3, pooled, bound_frac = 0.5", nlp_solver

ActivitySame model, same solver, same tolerances. One option changed, and it only affects where the solver starts. Which of the two answers is right, and how would you know?

Why: fix p and look.

Fixing p makes every remaining term linear. The sweep solves an LP at each sampled composition. Three labeled peak candidates occur at 0.033, 0.040, and 0.045; a finite grid by itself is not a proof that it found every local or global optimum.

The profile can jump at p=0.045. Below that value, Customer 1 cannot receive pooled milk: its minimum fat is 0.045, the richest local farm has exactly that fraction, and every other available stream is leaner. At p=0.045, pooled milk can serve Customer 1. The code computes the left-branch limit by fixing p=0.045 while retaining y_1=0, and separately records the near-left sample at 0.045-10^{-7}. These are different quantities, and solver tolerances matter near the switch.

Do not predict the returned solution from the closest scalar p_0. The full initial point has twelve coordinates. The max_iter=0 probes below report the bound-adjusted p for two settings; the main runs report where the solver ends. Reproduce the complete initialization and settings when comparing basins.

# ---------- SOLVE ----------------------------------------------------------
# Fix p and every remaining term is linear: what is left is an LP, one per
# value of p. Build the Pyomo model ONCE and re-fix p between solves --
# rebuilding it at every grid point costs far more than the solves do.
#
# The grid is split at the two customer fat requirements that fall strictly
# inside the range of p, so a sampled curve does not join across a possible switch. Each
# segment stops just short of its right-hand breakpoint, so nothing draws a
# line across a jump that is not there.

# The model's own bounds on p: a pool is no richer than its richest input and
# no leaner than its leanest.
p_lo = min(fat[r] for r in remote_farms)  # 0.033
p_hi = max(fat[r] for r in remote_farms)  # 0.050

# Derived from the data, not hard-coded, so the sweep follows the instance if
# the instance ever changes.
breaks = sorted({v for v in min_fat.values() if p_lo < v < p_hi})  # 0.040, 0.045

m_sweep = create_milk_model(local_farms, remote_farms)


def profit_at_fixed_p(p_value):
    """Solve the pooling model with the pool composition p fixed. This is an LP."""
    m_sweep.p.fix(p_value)
    status = solver.solve(m_sweep)
    if not pyo.check_optimal_termination(status):
        return np.nan
    return pyo.value(m_sweep.profit)


eps = 1e-7
edges = [p_lo] + breaks + [p_hi]
segments = []
for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
    grid = np.linspace(lo, hi - eps, 400)
    segments.append((grid, np.array([profit_at_fixed_p(p) for p in grid])))

# The right-hand end of the last segment IS attained, so include it.
grid, vals = segments[-1]
segments[-1] = (np.append(grid, p_hi), np.append(vals, profit_at_fixed_p(p_hi)))

# Three peak candidates: the lower bound on p and each breakpoint.
maxima = [(p, profit_at_fixed_p(p)) for p in [p_lo] + breaks]

# Keep the near-left sample separate from the left-branch limiting LP.
near_left_sample = profit_at_fixed_p(breaks[-1] - eps)
# For p < Customer 1's minimum, every permitted stream is too lean
# except local Farm A, so pooled delivery to Customer 1 must be zero.
m_sweep.p.fix(breaks[-1])
m_sweep.y["Customer 1"].fix(0)
left_status = solver.solve(m_sweep)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(left_status)
jump_limit = pyo.value(m_sweep.profit)
m_sweep.y["Customer 1"].unfix()


# Where did the two Ipopt runs above START? `bound_frac` pushes every variable
# off its bounds before the first iteration; read that pushed-in point back by
# solving with max_iter = 0. Pyomo warns that the solve did not converge --
# it was never meant to.
def initial_p(bound_frac):
    """Ipopt's pushed-in initial value of p, for a given bound_frac."""
    probe = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
    probe.options["bound_frac"] = bound_frac
    probe.options["max_iter"] = 0
    m = create_milk_model(local_farms, remote_farms)
    probe.solve(m)
    return pyo.value(m.p)


ipopt_runs = [
    {
        "label": "bound_frac = 0.01",
        "bound_frac": 0.01,
        "p_start": initial_p(0.01),
        "p_land": pyo.value(m3.p),
        "profit_land": profit_3,
    },
    {
        "label": "bound_frac = 0.5",
        "bound_frac": 0.5,
        "p_start": initial_p(0.5),
        "p_land": pyo.value(m3_alt.p),
        "profit_land": profit_3_alt,
    },
]

print(f"{sum(len(g) for g, _ in segments) + 5} LP solves (including the separate left-branch limit)")
for p_star, f_star in maxima:
    print(f"  peak candidate at p = {p_star:.3f}:  profit = {f_star:12,.2f}")
for run in ipopt_runs:
    print(
        f"  {run['label']:<20} starts at p = {run['p_start']:.6f}"
        f" and lands at p = {run['p_land']:.4f}"
    )

results = {

        pd.DataFrame(maxima, columns=["p", "profit"])
    ),
    # The value approached from the left at the jump, and never attained.
    "jump_limit": {"p": float(breaks[-1]), "profit": float(jump_limit)},
    "near_left_sample": {"p": float(breaks[-1] - eps), "profit": float(near_left_sample), "epsilon": float(eps)},

}

# figures/results/pooling-profit-vs-p.json, committed to the repo, so a change

    description="Profit of the milk pooling model as a function of the pool "

# The PLOTTING function: it takes the extracted results, not the Pyomo model.
#
# This cell is tagged `figure:pooling-profit-vs-p`, which makes it the single
# source of the figure in the lecture handout. See figures/README.md;
# figures/render_from_notebook.py re-runs exactly this cell against the
# archived JSON when the house style changes, so there is no second copy of the
# plotting code anywhere.


def plot_pooling_profit_vs_p(results):
    """Profit against the pool composition p: three labeled peak candidates and a branch switch.

    Two things the usual phrasing -- "three local maxima near 0.033, 0.040 and
    0.045" -- does not say, and the figure shows:

    * The BEST of the three sits ON the lower bound of p. It is not found by
      setting a derivative to zero.
    * The profit is neither smooth nor even continuous. The kink at p = 0.040
      is Customer 3's minimum fat fraction and the JUMP at p = 0.045 is
      Customer 1's: at p = 0.045 the pool on its own can finally satisfy the
      largest, best-paying customer, and 6,000 units of demand become servable
      in one step. It is drawn as a discontinuity -- two segments, an open
      circle for the limit from the left, a filled one for the value attained
      -- because joining them with a line would draw a claim that is false.

    The two Ipopt runs are marked where they START, on the axis. The second
    starts nearer the maximum at 0.040 than the one at 0.045 and walks to
    0.045 anyway: the starting point is twelve numbers, not one.

    Greyscale: the profit curve is the only series. Nothing is keyed by colour.
    """
    segments = [helper.as_dataframe(t) for t in results["segments"]]
    maxima = helper.as_dataframe(results["maxima"])
    runs = helper.as_dataframe(results["ipopt_runs"])
    p_lo = results["bounds"]["p_lo"]
    p_hi = results["bounds"]["p_hi"]
    jump = results["jump_limit"]

    blue = "#0072B2"  # Okabe-Ito

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.6))

    for seg in segments:
        ax.plot(seg["p"], seg["profit"], color=blue, linestyle="-", linewidth=2.4)

    # --- the three local maxima -------------------------------------------
    for _, row in maxima.iterrows():
        ax.plot([row["p"]], [row["profit"]], marker="o", markersize=9,
                color="black", zorder=5, linestyle="none")

    # Open circle: the limit from the left at the jump, which is NOT attained.
    ax.plot([jump["p"]], [jump["profit"]], marker="o", markersize=9,
            markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor="black",
            markeredgewidth=1.6, linestyle="none", zorder=5)

    # --- direct labels on the maxima --------------------------------------
    label_offsets = [(10, 4), (-4, 14), (8, 4)]
    label_align = ["left", "center", "left"]
    for (_, row), (dx, dy), ha in zip(maxima.iterrows(), label_offsets, label_align):
        ax.annotate(
            # {,} rather than a bare comma: mathtext sets a bare comma as
            # punctuation and inserts a space, giving "$102, 833".
            f"$p = {row['p']:.3f}$\n$\\${row['profit']:,.0f}$".replace(",", "{,}"),
            xy=(row["p"], row["profit"]),
            xytext=(dx, dy),
            textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=11,
            ha=ha,
            va="bottom",
            linespacing=1.05,
        )

    ax.annotate(
        "the best of the three is\non the LOWER BOUND of $p$",
        xy=(p_lo, maxima["profit"].iloc[0]),
        xytext=(0.05, 0.60),
        textcoords="axes fraction",
        fontsize=11,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="black", linewidth=1.1,
                        shrinkB=8.0),
    )

    # --- where the two Ipopt runs started, and where they went -------------
    y_lo, y_hi = ax.get_ylim()
    tick = y_lo + 0.035 * (y_hi - y_lo)
    for _, run in runs.iterrows():
        ax.plot([run["p_start"]], [tick], marker="^", markersize=8,
                color="black", linestyle="none", clip_on=False, zorder=6)
        ax.annotate("$p_0$", xy=(run["p_start"], tick), xytext=(0, 9),
                    textcoords="offset points", fontsize=10, ha="center",
                    va="bottom")
    ax.annotate(
        "starts here $\\rightarrow$ lands at $0.045$,\n"
        "though $0.040$ is nearer",
        xy=(runs["p_start"].iloc[1], tick),
        xytext=(0.05, 0.30),
        textcoords="axes fraction",
        fontsize=11,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="black", linewidth=1.1,
                        shrinkB=6.0),
    )

    # Headroom at the top for the two labels that sit above their markers.
    y_lo2, y_hi2 = ax.get_ylim()
    ax.set_ylim(y_lo2, y_hi2 + 0.13 * (y_hi2 - y_lo2))

    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(
        plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _pos: f"{v:,.0f}")
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("pool composition $p$")
    ax.set_ylabel("profit [\\$]")
    ax.set_xlim(p_lo - 0.0004, p_hi + 0.0004)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0.033, 0.0501, 0.003))

    fig.tight_layout()
    ax.tick_params(colors="black")
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_color("black")
    return fig

hierarchy.lvl2: Feasible-plan proof of the profit ordering
Feasible-plan proof of the profit ordering

records.content:
Let V_i^* denote the best achievable operating profit in Option i, under the same prices, assays, demands and available farms, with disjoint local/remote sets and a nonempty remote set. There are no additional investment costs, stream capacities or transport penalties. ThenV_1^*\le V_3^*\le V_2^*.

Option 1 into Option 3. Retain every local delivery and set \mathbf x=\mathbf y=\mathbf0. Choose any p within its assay bounds. Both pool balances hold and the objective is unchanged. Thus every Option 1 plan has an equally profitable pooled realization.

Option 3 into Option 2. Given a feasible pooled plan, put Q=\sum_r x_r=\sum_k y_k. If Q>0, replace its remote shipments byz_{r,k}=\frac{x_r y_k}{Q}.

The remote-farm totals are \sum_k z_{r,k}=x_r, and each customer’s remote quantity is \sum_r z_{r,k}=y_k. Pool fat balance gives \sum_r\phi_r x_r=pQ, so\sum_r\phi_r z_{r,k}=p y_k.

Each customer’s amount and fat delivery stay unchanged, as do remote purchase cost and sales revenue. The original local shipments remain. This constructs a feasible Option 2 plan with the same profit. If Q=0, nonnegativity forces all x_r,y_k to zero; take all new remote shipments zero and do not divide by Q.

These embeddings compare optimal values, not every pair of local-solver results. They also explain what would break the proof: an extra farm-to-customer capacity, different costs, or a changed investment objective must be checked again.

Use only Customer 2, whose demand is 2,500 and minimum fat is 0.030; set all local shipments and other deliveries to zero.

Hence the original feasible set is nonconvex. This is a proof about these equations and data; it does not assert that every model with a product is nonconvex or that every conceivable reformulation is impossible.

The reported pooled candidate improves on the local baseline by 21,833.33, about 52.7% of the 41,441.18 gain available in the separate-stream LP. The separate-stream plan exceeds that pooled candidate by $19,607.84. This last difference is a comparison of reported plans; it equals the global value gap only if the pooled optimum is independently certified. None of these numbers subtracts a truck purchase price. A capital decision needs equipment and transport costs on the same time horizon.

For L=40, K=500, R=2, the pooled formulation has LK+R+K+1=20,503 variables. The LK shipment block dominates for this stated modest remote-farm count. Aggregating customers reduces both K and LK; grouping farms reduces LK. An averaged customer specification need not meet every original customer’s quality requirement. Keep disaggregation and validation in the workflow.

Fat assays, prices and demands are measured or forecast inputs. Change an assay through fat_data, rebuild, and solve with recorded starts; then check the resulting plan against the original and perturbed requirements. A change in a local-solver result can reflect both changed data and a different basin. A scenario comparison or multistart is not automatically a robust guarantee, an expected-value policy, or a global sensitivity derivative.

For a systematic upper bound, the existing 

global-optimization guide derives the McCormick relaxation, runs the bound and candidate calculations, and explains the remaining gap. The complete model and original data stay here.

Declared model size

For n=|\mathcal C|, the mathematical model has 2+2n continuous variables, 4n linear inequality rows, \binom n2 nonlinear inequality rows, and the two simple lower bounds on A,B. For n=3, that is 8 variables, 12 linear rows, 3 nonlinear rows, and 2 lower bound sides.

The actual builder also declares PositiveReals domains for all x_i,y_i, adding 2n redundant lower bounds. They are implied by x_i,y_i\ge R_i>0. Thus the implementation has 8 lower bound sides for three circles. Count bound sides separately from general inequality rows. Counts alone neither prove feasibility nor give the local dimension of a constrained feasible set.

First, we will define a function that builds the model.

def create_circle_model(circle_radii):
    """Create circle optimization model in Pyomo

    Arguments:
        circle_radii: dictionary with keys=circle name and value=radius (float)

    Returns:
        model: Pyomo model
    """
    model = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    # Ordered circle identifiers; radii and coordinates use metres.
    model.CIRCLES = pyo.Set(initialize=circle_radii.keys())
    model.R = pyo.Param(model.CIRCLES, domain=pyo.PositiveReals,
                        initialize=circle_radii, units=pyo.units.m)
    model.box_height = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.PositiveReals, units=pyo.units.m)
    model.box_width = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.PositiveReals, units=pyo.units.m)
    model.x = pyo.Var(model.CIRCLES, domain=pyo.PositiveReals, units=pyo.units.m)
    model.y = pyo.Var(model.CIRCLES, domain=pyo.PositiveReals, units=pyo.units.m)
    model.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=2 * (model.box_height + model.box_width),
                          sense=pyo.minimize)

    # One indexed rule creates one row per circle; b is the model.
    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def left_x_con(b, c):
        """Keep circle c inside the left edge of the box."""
        return b.x[c] >= b.R[c]

    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def left_y_con(b, c):
        """Keep circle c above the bottom edge of the box."""
        return b.y[c] >= b.R[c]

    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def right_x_con(b, c):
        """Keep circle c inside the right edge of the box."""
        return b.x[c] <= b.box_width - b.R[c]

    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def right_y_con(b, c):
        """Keep circle c below the top edge of the box."""
        return b.y[c] <= b.box_height - b.R[c]

    # Skip self-pairs and reversed duplicate pairs.
    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES, model.CIRCLES)
    def no_overlap_con(b, c1, c2):
        """Separate each distinct pair of circles."""
        if c1 < c2:
            return ((b.x[c1] - b.x[c2]) ** 2 + (b.y[c1] - b.y[c2]) ** 2
                    >= (b.R[c1] + b.R[c2]) ** 2)
        else:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
    return model




Next, we will define a function that initializes the model. Notice this is separate from the function above: the model and the initial point are two different things, and for a nonconvex problem the initial point is part of the specification of what you solved.

def initialize_circle_model(model, height_init=25, width_init=25, spread=10):
    """Initialize the x and y coordinates using uniform distribution

    Arguments:
        model: Pyomo model
        height_init: initial value for box_height (default=25)
        width_init: initial value for box_width (default=25)
        spread: width of the uniform window the centers are drawn from
            (default=10)

    Returns:
        Nothing. But per Pyomo scoping rules, the input argument `model`
        can be modified in this function.

    """
    # Initialize
    model.box_height = height_init
    model.box_width = width_init

    for i in model.CIRCLES:
        # Adding circle radii ensures the circle remains in the >0, >0 quadrant
        model.x[i] = random.uniform(0, spread) + pyo.value(model.R[i])
        model.y[i] = random.uniform(0, spread) + pyo.value(model.R[i])



Next, we will create a dictionary containing the circle names and radii values.

PositiveReals excludes zero, although the writer exposes a zero lower bound to a continuous solver. Positive radii and the containment inequalities force feasible coordinates and box dimensions strictly positive. Solver bound adjustment is separate from the stored Pyomo initialization.

Next we define the function that draws an arrangement of circles. Two things about
it are worth copying into your own work.

It takes extracted results, not the Pyomo model. extract_circles turns the model
into plain Python; plot_circles draws that plain Python and never sees the model. So
you can fiddle with the picture as many times as you like without calling Ipopt again,
and the picture cannot quietly show you something other than what you solved. The
handout figure further down is built the same way.

It is drawn in the course house style, the same style the lecture notes use: the box
carries its two dimensions A and B (those are the objective), each circle is
labelled with its radius, and the starting arrangement can be drawn underneath as a
dotted outline. The three circles are also given three different hatch textures, so the
figure still reads when it is printed in black and white.

# ---------- EXTRACT, then PLOT --------------------------------------------
# Two functions, deliberately separate -- see the note above.


def extract_circles(m):
    """Pyomo model -> plain Python. After this, nothing needs the model again.

    Arguments:
        m: Pyomo concrete model, solved or merely initialized

    Returns:
        dict with the box dimensions `A` and `B`, the `radii`, and the `centers`
    """
    return {
        "A": pyo.value(m.box_height),
        "B": pyo.value(m.box_width),
        "radii": {i: pyo.value(m.R[i]) for i in m.CIRCLES},
        "centers": {i: (pyo.value(m.x[i]), pyo.value(m.y[i])) for i in m.CIRCLES},
    }


# The house hatch sequence, copied from figures/plots/_house.py as a LITERAL:
# that module is not on disk on Colab, so it must not be imported here. The
# first three entries are three different texture FAMILIES -- lines, dots,
# crosses -- so every pair of circles differs in kind rather than in the sign
# of a slope, which is the cue that survives greyscale printing.
HATCHES = ("///", "...", "xxx", "|||", "---", "\\\\\\")
SHADE_ALPHA = 0.18
OKABE_BLUE = "#0072B2"  # Okabe-Ito; the only color in the figure


def plot_circles(results, start=None, title=None, ax=None, span=None):
    """Draw one arrangement of circles in a box, in the course house style.

    Arguments:
        results: dict from `extract_circles` -- the arrangement to draw solid
        start: optionally, another such dict, drawn dotted and unfilled
            underneath to show where the solver started
        title: text above the panel
        ax: draw into an existing axes instead of creating a figure
        span: force the axis range instead of computing it from the content.
            Pass the same value to several panels when their sizes are meant
            to be compared by eye -- otherwise each panel is scaled to fit and
            two boxes of different size look identical.

    Returns:
        The matplotlib Axes.
    """
    A, B = results["A"], results["B"]
    radii, centers = results["radii"], results["centers"]

    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
    hatch_colour = plt.rcParams["hatch.color"]

    # Axis limits from the CONTENT, not from the box: at a loose initial point
    # a circle can stick out well past the walls, and clipping it hides the
    # very thing the picture is being drawn to show.
    extent = []
    for d in (results, start):
        if d is not None:
            extent += [d["A"], d["B"]]
            for i in d["radii"]:
                cx, cy = d["centers"][i]
                extent += [cx + d["radii"][i], cy + d["radii"][i]]
    span = max(extent) if span is None else span
    pad = 0.14 * span

    # Where the solver started: dotted, unfilled, underneath everything else.
    if start is not None:
        ax.add_patch(
            mpatches.Rectangle(
                (0, 0), start["B"], start["A"], facecolor="none",
                edgecolor="0.72", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5, zorder=1,
            )
        )
        for i in start["radii"]:
            cx, cy = start["centers"][i]
            ax.add_patch(
                mpatches.Circle(
                    (cx, cy), start["radii"][i], facecolor="none",
                    edgecolor="0.72", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5, zorder=1,
                )
            )

    # The circles: a pale hatch that survives greyscale, a blue outline, and
    # the radius written in the middle. Circle i is labelled R_i, exactly as
    # the model indexes it.
    for k, i in enumerate(radii):
        cx, cy = centers[i]
        ax.add_patch(
            mpatches.Circle(
                (cx, cy), radii[i], facecolor="0.55", alpha=SHADE_ALPHA,
                hatch=HATCHES[k % len(HATCHES)], edgecolor=hatch_colour,
                linewidth=0.0, zorder=2,
            )
        )
        ax.add_patch(
            mpatches.Circle(
                (cx, cy), radii[i], facecolor="none", edgecolor=OKABE_BLUE,
                linewidth=2.4, zorder=3,
            )
        )
        # The label sits half a radius ABOVE the center, not on it. At a loose
        # initial point two circles can be nearly concentric -- the circles
        # overlap, because an initial point need not be feasible -- and two
        # labels on the same spot are unreadable. Offsetting by a fraction of
        # each circle's OWN radius separates them, because the radii differ.
        # The white box keeps the text legible over the hatching.
        ax.annotate(
            f"$R_{{{i}}}$", xy=(cx, cy + 0.5 * radii[i]), fontsize=13,
            ha="center", va="center", zorder=6,
            bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.75, pad=1.0),
        )

    # The box, with its two dimensions written on it: A and B ARE the objective.
    ax.add_patch(
        mpatches.Rectangle((0, 0), B, A, facecolor="none", edgecolor="black",
                           linewidth=2.6, zorder=4)
    )
    off = -0.5 * pad
    ax.annotate("", xy=(off, 0), xytext=(off, A),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="black", lw=1.3))
    ax.annotate(f"$A = {A:.2f}$", xy=(off, 0.5 * A), fontsize=12.5, ha="center",
                va="center", rotation=90,
                bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0))
    ax.annotate("", xy=(0, off), xytext=(B, off),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="black", lw=1.3))
    ax.annotate(f"$B = {B:.2f}$", xy=(0.5 * B, off), fontsize=12.5, ha="center",
                va="center", bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0))

    ax.set_xlim(-pad, span + 0.5 * pad)
    ax.set_ylim(-pad, span + 0.5 * pad)
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$ [m]")
    ax.set_ylabel("$y$ [m]")
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=13.5)
    if start is not None:
        ax.annotate("dotted: where the solver started", xy=(0.02, 0.98),
                    xycoords="axes fraction", fontsize=11, ha="left", va="top",
                    color="0.40")
    return ax


# Keep the initial point: we want to draw it again underneath the solution.
first_start = extract_circles(model)
plot_circles(first_start, title="Initial point")
plt.show()

# Specify the solver
solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")

# Solve the model
results = solver.solve(model, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)



Next, we can inspect the solution. Because Pyomo is a Python extension, we can use Python (for loops, etc.) to programmatically inspect the solution.

# Print variable values
print("Name\tValue")
for c in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var):
    print(c.name, "\t", pyo.value(c))

# Plot the solution, with the initial point dotted underneath
plot_circles(
    extract_circles(model), start=first_start, title="Solution from the first start"

plt.show()
