The 

temperature control lab is an Arduino-based hands-on experiment for teaching dynamic modeling and process control developed by Prof. John Hedengren. At Notre Dame, we restructured our core 

undergraduate process control class around six hands-on laboratory assignments with the TCLab.

The TCLab board contains two heater plus temperature sensor assemblies. Using Python (or MATLAB), students can independently manipulate the electrical power to the heaters and measure the temperatures.

For simplicity, we will develop a mathematical single heater and temperature sensor assembly. However, this workshop example also supports modeling both assemblies.

We will define two states:

T_{H,1} is the temperature of the heater/fin assembly (°C)

T_{S,1} is the temperature of the sensor (°C)

Assumptions:

The two bodies are uniform temperature, i.e., we are neglecting any temperature gradients in the fin.

The sensor exchanges heat only with the heater, and heat transfer to the surroundings is dominated by the heat sink attached to the heater.

Heat capacities C_p are constant.

Radiative heat transfer is negligible.

We define the manipulated variable:

u_1 is the power sent to the heater (% of max)

This motivates the following model:\begin{align}
C^H_p\frac{dT_{H,1}}{dt} & = U_a(T_{amb} - T_{H,1}) + U_b(T_{S,1} - T_{H,1}) + \alpha P_1u_1\\
C^S_p\frac{dT_{S,1}}{dt} & = U_b(T_{H,1} - T_{S,1}) 
\end{align}

The model has the following unknown parameters:

C^H_p is the heat capacity of the heater/fin assembly (J / °C)

C^S_p is the heat capacity of the sensor (J / °C)

U_a is the heat transfer coefficient from the heater/fin to ambient (W / °C)

U_b is the heat transfer coefficient from the heater/fin to the sensor (W / °C)

And the following known parameters:

\alpha P_1 are constants for the TCLab (W / %)

T_{amb} is the ambient temperature (°C)

Let’s start by defining some model coefficients:

# parameters
# alpha * P converts heater command (%) to power (W), so alpha*P must be W / %.
# Percent is dimensionless, so W / % is just W.
alpha = 0.00016 * units.W  # W per (unit of P * percent of u1)
P = 200  # dimensionless scale factor for the heater
Ua = (
    0.050 * units.W / units.kelvin
)  # heat transfer coefficient from heater to environment
CpH = 2.2 * units.J / units.kelvin  # heat capacity of the heater (J/deg C)
CpS = 1.9 * units.J / units.kelvin  # heat capacity of the sensor (J/deg C)
Ub = 0.021 * units.W / units.kelvin  # heat transfer coefficient from heater to sensor
Tamb_C = 21.0  # ambient temperature in deg C
Tamb = units.convert_temp_C_to_K(Tamb_C) * units.kelvin  # ambient temperature

We will start by simulating our TCLab model. In other words, we will solve the following optimization problem with zero degrees of freedom:\begin{align*}
\max{}~~ & 0 \\
\mathrm{s.t.}~~ & C_p^H \frac{dT_H}{dt} = U_a (T_{amb} - T_H) + U_b (T_S - T_H) + \alpha P u(t) \\
 & C_p^S \frac{dT_S}{dt} = - U_b (T_S - T_H) \\
 & T_H(t_0) = T_{amb} \\
 & T_S(t_0) = T_{amb} \\
 & u(t) = u_{ramp} = 50\%, \quad \forall t \in [t_0, t_f]
\end{align*}

Here “s.t.” means “subject to”, i.e., the constraints.

# Final time [seconds].
#
# Why no units here? A ContinuousSet cannot carry units. This is Pyomo issue
# #1790, still open: https://github.com/Pyomo/pyomo/issues/1790
# It is also the reason we must check units BEFORE discretizing -- see the
# section below and ./units_and_pyomo_dae.md
tf = 200

# control input [%]
u = 50.0

# Create a Pyomo model
m = pyo.ConcreteModel("TCLab Heater/Sensor")

# Define time domain
m.t = dae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, tf))

# Define the state variables as a function of time
m.Th = pyo.Var(m.t, units=units.kelvin)
m.Ts = pyo.Var(m.t, units=units.kelvin)

# Define the derivatives of the state variables.
#
# DerivativeVar defaults to DIMENSIONLESS -- it does not inherit units from the
# state variable. Here m.t is time in seconds, so dT/dt is K/s. Say it explicitly.
m.dTh = dae.DerivativeVar(m.Th, units=units.kelvin / units.s)
m.dTs = dae.DerivativeVar(m.Ts, units=units.kelvin / units.s)


# Define the first differential equation
@m.Constraint(m.t)
def heater1(m, t):
    return (
        CpH * m.dTh[t]
        == Ua * (Tamb - m.Th[t]) + Ub * (m.Ts[t] - m.Th[t]) + alpha * P * u
    )


# Define the second differential equation
@m.Constraint(m.t)
def sensor1(m, t):
    return CpS * m.dTs[t] == Ub * (m.Th[t] - m.Ts[t])


# Set the initial conditions
m.Th[0].fix(Tamb)
m.Ts[0].fix(Tamb)

# Check dimensional consistency NOW, while the model is still continuous.
# After discretization this same call raises InconsistentUnitsError -- see below.
assert_units_consistent(m)
print("Units are consistent (continuous model, before discretization).")

# Apply a finite difference formula to numerically integrate the differential equations
pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference").apply_to(m, nfe=100, wrt=m.t)

# Call our nonlinear optimization/equation solver, Ipopt
results = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt").solve(m)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)

# Plot the results
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=True)

# Plot 1: Temperature
ax[0].plot(m.t, [units.convert_temp_K_to_C(m.Th[t]()) for t in m.t], label="Th")
ax[0].plot(
    m.t, [units.convert_temp_K_to_C(m.Ts[t]()) for t in m.t], label="Ts", linestyle="--"
)
ax[0].legend()
ax[0].set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax[0].grid()

# Plot 2: Heater Power
ax[1].axhline(u, label="Power")
ax[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax[1].set_ylabel("Heater Power (%)")
ax[1].grid()
plt.show()

hierarchy.lvl3: Why the units check comes before TransformationFactory
Why the units check comes before TransformationFactory

records.content:
The cell above called assert_units_consistent(m) immediately before discretizing.
The order is not cosmetic.

Warning

Run the same check after TransformationFactory("dae.finite_difference") and it
fails, on a model that is dimensionally correct:InconsistentUnitsError: Error in units found in expression:
  dTh[2.0] - 0.5*(Th[2.0] - Th[0]): kelvin / second not compatible with kelvin.

dae.collocation fails the same way. So does every other model in this section whose
time domain is measured in seconds.

Here is what happened. A backward difference for \frac{dT_H}{dt} at time t_i is\dot{T}_{H,i} \approx \frac{T_{H,i} - T_{H,i-1}}{\Delta t},

and Pyomo writes it out with 1/\Delta t already evaluated to a number:dTh[2.0] == 0.5*(Th[2.0] - Th[0])

That 0.5 is 1/\Delta t, and it should carry units of \mathrm{s}^{-1}.
It does not. A ContinuousSet stores plain Python floats and cannot hold units, which
is exactly why tf = 200 above has its units only in a comment. Pyomo therefore reads
the right-hand side as a temperature and the left-hand side as a temperature rate,
and reports -- correctly, given what it can see -- that they disagree.

This is 

Pyomo issue #1790, still
open. Nothing is wrong with our model and nothing is wrong with the finite-difference
arithmetic; the units container simply has nowhere to record what the time domain is
measured in.

The practical rule is short:

Declare units on everything, then assert_units_consistent at the end of your
model-building function, before any discretization.

You give up nothing by checking early. The discretization equations are generated by
Pyomo, not written by you, so they are not where your modeling errors hide. Checking
the continuous model checks every equation you actually typed.

Run the cell below to see the failure for yourself.

# Reproduce the failure. The model `m` above has already been discretized, so
# asserting on it now raises -- even though the SAME model passed the check moments
# before `TransformationFactory` was applied.

try:
    assert_units_consistent(m)
    print("Units are consistent -- unexpected!")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
    print(e)







Note

Two things assert_units_consistent does not check: Var bounds and values passed
to .fix(). Both m.u = pyo.Var(m.t, bounds=(0, 100)) and m.Th[0].fix(Tamb) would
pass even if the bare numbers were in the wrong units. Units are a strong check on your
equations and no check at all on your numbers.

The related trap in this notebook: m.dTh = dae.DerivativeVar(m.Th) -- with no
units= -- defaults to dimensionless, not to K/s. DerivativeVar never infers
units from its state variable. Written that way, assert_units_consistent fails on the
continuous model, before any discretization, withjoule / kelvin not compatible with watt

because CpH * m.dTh[t] collapses to J/K instead of J/s. Compare that with the
post-discretization message in the warning above (kelvin / second not compatible with kelvin): the two failures read quite differently, which is how you tell a missing
declaration from issue #1790.

See 

Units in Pyomo.dae Models for the whole picture, including the one modeling
choice that sidesteps issue #1790 (scaling time onto a dimensionless interval, as in


Pyomo.DAE Example: Race Car).

The code below to access and print results from the Pyomo model:

for i, t in enumerate(m.t):
    # Only print every 10 timesteps
    if i % 10 == 0:
        print(
            "Th=",
            round(pyo.value(m.Th[t]), 2),
            "K and Ts=",
            round(pyo.value(m.Ts[t]), 2),
            "K at time",
            round(t, 2),
            "seconds.",
        )



Uncomment and run the code below to see the details of the Pyomo model:

# m.pprint()

Modify the code above to find the value for u that causes Th to reach 60 °C at the final time. In others words, we are using trial and error to solve the following optimization problem:\begin{align*}
\min_{u_{ramp}} ~~ & ||~ T_{H}(t_f) - 60 ~||^2 \\
\mathrm{s.t.}~~ & C_p^H \frac{dT_H}{dt} = U_a (T_{amb} - T_H) + U_b (T_S - T_H) + \alpha P u(t) \\
 & C_p^S \frac{dT_S}{dt} = - U_b (T_S - T_H) \\
 & T_H(t_0) = T_{amb} \\
 & T_S(t_0) = T_{amb} \\
 & u(t) = u_{ramp}, \quad \forall t \in [t_0, t_f]
\end{align*}

An optimal control policy minimizes the differences\begin{align*}
\min_{u} \int_{t_0}^{t_f} \|~SP(t) - T_H(t)~\|^2\,dt \\
\end{align*}

subject to constraints\begin{align*}
C_p^H \frac{dT_H}{dt} & = U_a (T_{amb} - T_H) + U_b (T_S - T_H) + \alpha P u(t)\\
C_p^S \frac{dT_S}{dt} & = - U_b (T_S - T_H)  \\
\\
\text{control limits}\qquad0 \leq u(t) & \leq 100.0
\\
\text{initial condition}\qquad T_H(t_0) & = T_{amb} \\
\text{initial condition}\qquad T_S(t_0) & = T_{amb}
\end{align*}

This is different than our example above because we allow u to have a unique value for each timestep.

Note that pyomo.dae has an Integral object to help with these situations.

# Set point, deg C
SP = units.convert_temp_C_to_K(60.0) * units.kelvin

# Create a Pyomo model
m = pyo.ConcreteModel("TCLab Heater/Sensor")

# Define time domain
m.t = dae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, tf))

# Define the state variables as a function of time
m.Th = pyo.Var(m.t, units=units.kelvin)
m.Ts = pyo.Var(m.t, units=units.kelvin)

# Define the derivatives of the state variables (K/s -- state it explicitly)
m.dTh = dae.DerivativeVar(m.Th, units=units.kelvin / units.s)
m.dTs = dae.DerivativeVar(m.Ts, units=units.kelvin / units.s)

# Define the control variable (heater power, % of max) as a function of time.
# Percent is dimensionless; alpha * P carries the W / % conversion.
m.u = pyo.Var(m.t, bounds=(0, 100))


# Define the integral of the squared error
@m.Integral(m.t)
def ise(m, t):
    return (SP - m.Th[t]) ** 2


# Define the first differential equation
# Notice we are defining the equation using the decorator syntax
@m.Constraint(m.t)
def heater1(m, t):
    return (
        CpH * m.dTh[t]
        == Ua * (Tamb - m.Th[t]) + Ub * (m.Ts[t] - m.Th[t]) + alpha * P * m.u[t]
    )


# Define the second differential equation
@m.Constraint(m.t)
def sensor1(m, t):
    return CpS * m.dTs[t] == Ub * (m.Th[t] - m.Ts[t])


# Set the initial conditions
m.Th[0].fix(Tamb)
m.Ts[0].fix(Tamb)


# Define the objective function
@m.Objective(sense=pyo.minimize)
def objective(m):
    return m.ise


# Units, again checked on the continuous model before discretizing.
#
# Note that m.ise comes out in K**2, not K**2 * s. pyomo.dae builds the Integral
# as a weighted sum whose quadrature weights are dimensionless -- the same
# consequence of issue #1790. The objective is still internally consistent, so
# the check passes.
assert_units_consistent(m)
print("ise units:", units.get_units(m.ise))

# Apply a collocation method to numerically integrate the differential equations
pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation").apply_to(m, nfe=200, wrt=m.t)

# Call our nonlinear optimization/equation solver, Ipopt
results = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt").solve(m)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)


# We are going to repeat plotting two more times,
# so let's define a function
def plot_results(m):
    """
    Plot results from Pyomo optimization

    Arguments:
    m: Pyomo model

    Returns:
    Nothing

    """

    # Plot the results
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1)

    ax[0].plot(m.t, [units.convert_temp_K_to_C(m.Th[t]()) for t in m.t], label="Th")
    ax[0].plot(
        m.t,
        [units.convert_temp_K_to_C(m.Ts[t]()) for t in m.t],
        label="Ts",
        linestyle="--",
    )
    ax[0].legend()
    ax[0].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
    ax[0].set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
    ax[0].grid()

    ax[1].plot(m.t, [m.u[t]() for t in m.t], label="u")
    ax[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
    ax[1].set_ylabel("H. Power (%)")
    ax[1].grid()


plot_results(m)

Now let’s consider optimizing the control input u(t) to track a more sophisticated time-varying setpoint signal SP(t).

Python function r(t) uses numpy.interp to compute values of the reference trajectory at any point in time.

import numpy as np

dt = 2
n = round(tf / dt)
t_grid = np.linspace(0, tf, n + 1)

 & T_H(t_0) = T_{amb} \\
 & T_S(t_0) = T_{amb}
\end{align*}

# Create a Pyomo model
m = pyo.ConcreteModel("TCLab Heater/Sensor")

# Define time domain
m.t = dae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, tf))

# Define the state variables as a function of time
m.Th = pyo.Var(m.t, units=units.kelvin)
m.Ts = pyo.Var(m.t, units=units.kelvin)

# Define the derivatives of the state variables (K/s -- state it explicitly)
m.dTh = dae.DerivativeVar(m.Th, units=units.kelvin / units.s)

# Define the control variable (heater power) as a function of time
m.u = pyo.Var(m.t, bounds=(0, 100))


# Define the integral of the squared error

def ise(m, t):

# Define the first differential equation
@m.Constraint(m.t)
def heater1(m, t):

        CpH * m.dTh[t]

# Define the objective function

assert_units_consistent(m)

hierarchy.lvl2: Problem Statement and Optimal Control Formulation
Problem Statement and Optimal Control Formulation

records.content:
You are a race car driver with a simple goal. Drive distance L in the minimal amount of time but come to a complete stop at the finish line.

Mathematically, you want to solve the following optimal control problem:\begin{align*}
\min_{u,t_f} \quad & t_f \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & \frac{dx}{dt} = v \\
& \frac{dv}{dt} = u - R v^2 \\
& x(t=0) = 0, ~~ x(t=t_f) = L \\
& v(t=0) = 0, ~~ v(t=t_f) = 0 \\
& -3 \leq u \leq 1
\end{align*}

where u is the acceleration/braking (your control variable) and R is the drag coefficient (parameter).

For the numerical runs, L=100 m and R=0.001 m^{-1}; u is the applied acceleration in m/s^2, so Rv^2 has the same units. The code bounds 0\le x\le150 m and v\ge0, and requires t_f\ge0.001 s. These bounds are part of the stated model, not implicit consequences of time normalization.

hierarchy.lvl2: Problem Statement and Optimal Control Formulation
Problem Statement and Optimal Control Formulation

records.content:
Let t = \tau \cdot t_f where \tau \in [0,1]. Thus dt = t_f d\tau. The optimal control problem becomes:\begin{align*}
\min_{u,t_f} \quad & t_f \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & \frac{dx}{d\tau} = t_f v \\
& \frac{dv}{d\tau} = t_f (u - R v^2) \\
& x(\tau = 0) = 0, ~~ x(\tau = 1) = L \\
& v(\tau = 0) = 0, ~~ v(\tau = 1) = 0 \\
& -3 \leq u \leq 1
\end{align*}

This change of variables assumes t_f>0. For a nonzero fixed start time use t=t_0+(t_f-t_0)\tau and multiply by the duration t_f-t_0. Any explicit physical-time argument in the model must change too.

We can use Pyomo.dae to automatically formulate the collocation equations (i.e., add constraints that numerically integrate the ODE model).

def create_model1():

    # Define the  model
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

    # Define the model parameters
    m.R = pyo.Param(initialize=0.001, units=1 / units.m)  # Friction factor
    m.L = pyo.Param(initialize=100.0, units=units.m)  # Final position

    # Define time
    m.tau = dae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, 1))  # Dimensionless time set
    m.tf = pyo.Var(initialize=1, bounds=(1e-3, None), units=units.s)  # Final time

    # Define remaining algebraic variables
    m.x = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, m.L + 50 * units.m), units=units.m)  # Position
    m.v = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, None), units=units.m / units.s)  # Velocity
    m.u = pyo.Var(
        m.tau, bounds=(-3.0, 1.0), initialize=0, units=units.m / units.s / units.s
    )  # Acceleration

    # Define derivative variables.
    #
    # Units MUST be given explicitly: DerivativeVar defaults to dimensionless and
    # does NOT inherit units from the state variable. Because tau is dimensionless,
    # d/dtau has the SAME units as the state itself.
    m.dx = dae.DerivativeVar(m.x, units=units.m)
    m.dv = dae.DerivativeVar(m.v, units=units.m / units.s)

    # Declare the objective (minimize final time)
    m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.tf)

    # Define the constraints
    # position
    @m.Constraint(m.tau)
    def ode1(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        return m.dx[i] == m.tf * m.v[i]

    # velocity
    @m.Constraint(m.tau)
    def ode2(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        return m.dv[i] == m.tf * (m.u[i] - m.R * m.v[i] ** 2)

    # Define the initial/boundary conditions
    def _init(m):
        yield m.x[0] == 0
        yield m.x[1] == m.L
        yield m.v[0] == 0
        yield m.v[1] == 0

    m.initcon = pyo.ConstraintList(rule=_init)

    # Check dimensional consistency HERE, on the continuous model, BEFORE the
    # discretization equations are added. See ./units_and_pyomo_dae.md and
    # https://github.com/Pyomo/pyomo/issues/1790
    assert_units_consistent(m)

    return m


m = create_model1()



Now let’s inspect the model.

m.pprint()

Notice where assert_units_consistent(m) sits in create_model1 above: at the very
end of the model-building function, before any discretization is applied.

Warning

For a Pyomo.dae model, assert_units_consistent can pass on the continuous model
and then fail after discretization. The discretization equations that Pyomo
writes for you multiply state variables by a numerical reciprocal-\Delta t
coefficient, and that coefficient is dimensionless because a ContinuousSet cannot
carry units. This is 

Pyomo issue #1790,
which documents this class of unit-checking limitation.

Check the continuous model before discretizing. Then inspect any transformed-unit failure to distinguish a dimensionless mesh coefficient from an actual modeling error. Generated equations and your scaling assumptions still need verification; checking units does not certify the transformation or the numerical solution.

Two details in the code above are worth pausing on.

DerivativeVar does not inherit units. It defaults to dimensionless. A model
can look thoroughly annotated and still fail the very first check. Before this
notebook declared units= on m.dx and m.dv, assert_units_consistent failed
immediately with dimensionless not compatible with meter -- even though every
Var and Param had units.

The units of dx/d\tau are metres, not metres per second. We scaled time, so
\tau is dimensionless and the derivative carries the same units as the state.

That second point has a pleasant consequence, explored in the cell below.

See 

Units in Pyomo.dae Models for the full story, including what the check does
not look at (Var bounds and .fix() values are never checked).

# The time-scaling trick has a side benefit: because tau is DIMENSIONLESS, the
# finite-difference/collocation coefficients really are dimensionless, so this model
# passes the units check BEFORE and AFTER discretization.
#
# Do not generalize from this! It is a happy accident of scaling time to [0, 1].
# A model whose ContinuousSet is time-in-seconds fails after discretization --
# see notebooks/3/PyomoDAE_TCLab.ipynb for that case.

m_demo = create_model1()  # assert_units_consistent already ran inside
print("Before discretization: units are consistent.")

pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation").apply_to(
    m_demo, nfe=15, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU", ncp=3
)

try:
    assert_units_consistent(m_demo)
    print("After discretization:  units are STILL consistent (tau is dimensionless).")
except Exception as e:
    print("After discretization:  FAILED ->", e)

Pyomo.dae writes the collocation equations for us. This experiment varies nfe, the number of finite elements, while holding three Radau stages per element and one control per element fixed. Changing stage count, control parameterization or mesh locations is a separate experiment. We solve the same model on
two meshes and compare.

Notice what tee=True prints before the iteration table -- Ipopt reports how
many variables and equality constraints the collocation equations produced.
That count, not the size of the ODE, is what the solver actually sees.

# COARSE mesh: N = 10 finite elements.
#
# N = 10 is chosen, not arbitrary. The optimal control here is bang-bang: full
# throttle (u = +1) until one switching time, then full braking (u = -3) to the
# line. At N = 10 that switching time falls strictly INSIDE a finite element,
# and because reduce_collocation_points holds u constant across an element, the
# only way the discretized problem can say "switch part-way through this
# element" is to give the WHOLE element an intermediate value. Watch for it
# below: one element sits at u = -0.52 m/s^2 for 1.7 s -- a braking level the
# true optimal control never uses. That is an artifact of the mesh, not physics.

NFE_COARSE = 10

m_coarse = create_model1()

# Declare the discretizer
discretizer = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation")
discretizer.apply_to(m_coarse, nfe=NFE_COARSE, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU", ncp=3)

# force piecewise constant controls (acceleration) over each finite element
m_coarse = discretizer.reduce_collocation_points(
    m_coarse, var=m_coarse.u, ncp=1, contset=m_coarse.tau
)

# Solve. tee=True prints Ipopt's own log: first the problem-size block -- how
# many variables and equality constraints the collocation equations produced --
# and then the iteration table.
solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
solve_status = solver.solve(m_coarse, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(solve_status), (
    f"Solve failed: status={solve_status.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={solve_status.solver.termination_condition}"
)

print("final time = %6.2f seconds" % (pyo.value(m_coarse.tf)))

Does the intermediate braking force go away if we consider a finer time
discretization?

# FINE mesh: N = 100 finite elements.
#
# The same problem on a mesh ten times finer. Nothing about the model changes;
# only nfe does. The switching element is still there -- it always is, because
# the switch almost never lands exactly on an element boundary -- but it is now
# 0.16 s wide instead of 1.7 s, so the control profile looks like the bang-bang
# solution it is approximating, and the objective stops moving.

NFE_FINE = 100

m_fine = create_model1()

# Declare the discretizer
discretizer = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation")
discretizer.apply_to(m_fine, nfe=NFE_FINE, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU", ncp=3)

# force piecewise constant controls (acceleration) over each finite element
m_fine = discretizer.reduce_collocation_points(
    m_fine, var=m_fine.u, ncp=1, contset=m_fine.tau
)

# Solve. tee=True prints Ipopt's own log: first the problem-size block -- how
# many variables and equality constraints the collocation equations produced --
# and then the iteration table.
solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
solve_status = solver.solve(m_fine, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(solve_status), (
    f"Solve failed: status={solve_status.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={solve_status.solver.termination_condition}"
)

print("final time = %6.2f seconds" % (pyo.value(m_fine.tf)))

Both solves are done, so pull the trajectories out of the two models and
archive them. Separating “solve” from “analyze” is a habit worth keeping: the
plotting cells below then depend only on results, and can be re-run without a
solver.

def extract_race_car_results(m, nfe):
    """Pull the solved trajectories out of a Pyomo model into plain lists.

    Arguments:
        m: solved, discretized race-car model
        nfe: number of finite elements used, for the label

    Returns:
        dict of JSON-safe values -- everything the figures need and nothing else

    The time axis is rebuilt here: the model is written in dimensionless time
    tau in [0, 1], so physical time is t = tau * t_f, and t_f is itself a
    decision variable. Two meshes therefore have DIFFERENT final times, which
    is the number the mesh-refinement argument turns on.
    """
    tf = pyo.value(m.tf)
    tau = sorted(m.tau)
    return {
        "label": f"N = {nfe}",
        "nfe": nfe,
        "tf": tf,
        "t": [i * tf for i in tau],  # time [s]
        "x": [pyo.value(m.x[i]) for i in tau],  # position [m]
        "v": [pyo.value(m.v[i]) for i in tau],  # velocity [m/s]
        "u": [pyo.value(m.u[i]) for i in tau],  # acceleration [m/s^2]
        # Element boundaries in physical time, so a figure can show WHERE the
        # control is allowed to change value.
        "elements": [b * tf for b in m.tau.get_finite_elements()],
        "element_u": [pyo.value(m.u[b]) for b in m.tau.get_finite_elements()[1:]],
    }


results = {
    "meshes": [
        extract_race_car_results(m_coarse, NFE_COARSE),
        extract_race_car_results(m_fine, NFE_FINE),
    ],
    "u_lower": -3.0,  # [m/s^2]
    "u_upper": 1.0,  # [m/s^2]
    "L": 100.0,  # [m]
}

for mesh in results["meshes"]:
    print(f"{mesh['label']:>8}:  t_f = {mesh['tf']:.4f} s")

DESCRIPTION = (
    "Minimum-time race car (m = 1, L = 100 m, drag R = 0.001 1/m, "
    "-3 <= u <= 1), solved with Pyomo.dae LAGRANGE-RADAU collocation, ncp = 3, "
    "with the control reduced to piecewise constant on each element. Two "
    "meshes: N = 10, coarse enough that the bang-bang switch is trapped inside "
    "one element and that element takes an intermediate braking value, and "
    "N = 100, where the switch is resolved."
)

for figure_name in ("race-car-control", "race-car-states"):
    helper.save_results(
        figure_name,
        results,
        notebook="notebooks/3-dev/PyomoDAE_car.ipynb",
        source_tag="handout:race-car-model",
        description=DESCRIPTION,
        solver="Ipopt 3.13.2 (IDAES build, linear solver ma27)",
        source_cells=[("notebooks/3-dev/PyomoDAE_car.ipynb", tag) for tag in
                      ("handout-output:race-car-coarse", "handout-output:race-car-fine",
                       "numeric:race-car-extract")],
    )

This is where the two meshes disagree.

# This cell is tagged `figure:race-car-control', which makes it the single
# source of the control-profile figure the Lecture 7 handout prints.
# figures/render_from_notebook.py re-runs exactly this cell against the archived
# JSON when the house style changes, so there is no second copy of the plotting
# code. That driver binds `np', `plt' and `helper' for the cell, so it imports
# nothing and uses no name defined in an earlier cell except `results'.


def plot_race_car_control(results):
    """The control profile on both meshes, and what the coarse mesh gets wrong.

    THE FIGURE'S POINT is the flat step at u ~ -0.5 in the coarse profile. The
    exact solution is bang-bang -- it takes only the two bound values -- so any
    element sitting between them is the discretization confessing that it put
    the switching time inside an element and had to average across it. On the
    fine mesh the same element is a tenth as wide and the profile reads as the
    step function it approximates.

    STEPS AT ELEMENT EDGES. The control is piecewise constant on each finite
    element. stairs(values, edges) places every jump at the element boundary;
    stepping through collocation times would shift a jump into the next element.

    ⚠ tau = 0 IS DROPPED from the control series. u[0] is not a control the
    solver uses -- the reduced control is indexed by element, and the first
    element's value lives at its first collocation point -- so plotting u[0]
    puts a spurious step from its initialize=0 value at the left edge.

    ELEMENT RULES, coarse mesh only. The light vertical lines are the finite
    element boundaries: the control is constant between two of them by
    construction, so the rules explain the staircase rather than decorating it.
    Drawing them for N = 100 would be a grey block.

    GREYSCALE. Two series, each taking colour AND linestyle together from the
    house prop_cycle (figures/dowling.mplstyle pairs the two element-wise),
    plus different line widths, plus a direct label beside each curve. Any one
    of those is enough on a photocopy.
    """
    meshes = results["meshes"]
    coarse = meshes[0]
    u_lo, u_hi = results["u_lower"], results["u_upper"]
    t_max = max(m["tf"] for m in meshes)
    colors = plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 4.2))

    # Element boundaries FIRST, so they sit under the data.
    for b in coarse["elements"]:
        ax.axvline(b, color="0.85", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)

    for u_bound in (u_hi, u_lo):
        ax.axhline(
            u_bound, color="0.55", linewidth=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 3)), zorder=1
        )

    for k, mesh in enumerate(meshes):
        # Radau stores an element's constant control at its right endpoint.
        # The jump belongs at the shared element boundary, not at the next
        # element's first interior collocation point.
        ax.stairs(mesh["element_u"], mesh["elements"], baseline=None,
                  linewidth=3.2 if k == 0 else 1.8, zorder=3-k,
                  linestyle="-" if k == 0 else "--", color=colors[k])

    # The defect, called out where it happens. Exactly one coarse element sits
    # strictly between the bounds; find it rather than hard-coding a time.
    tol = 1e-3
    trapped = [
        (t, u)
        for t, u in zip(coarse["t"][1:], coarse["u"][1:])
        if u_lo + tol < u < u_hi - tol
    ]
    if trapped:
        t_bad = trapped[len(trapped) // 2][0]
        u_bad = trapped[0][1]
        ax.annotate(
            "the switch is trapped inside one element:\n"
            f"the solver can only average across it, {u_bad:+.2f} m/s$^2$\n"
            f"held for the element's full {coarse['tf'] / coarse['nfe']:.1f} s",
            xy=(t_bad, u_bad),
            xytext=(0.13, 0.30),
            textcoords="axes fraction",
            ha="left",
            va="center",
            fontsize=11,
            arrowprops=dict(
                arrowstyle="->",
                linewidth=1.1,
                color="0.25",
                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.25",
            ),
        )

    # DIRECT LABELS, not a legend: the two profiles coincide for most of the
    # horizon, so a legend box would sit somewhere the eye has to travel to.
    # They go ABOVE the engine-limit line -- headroom made by the ylim below,
    # because every other corner of these axes has a curve or a rule in it.
    for k, mesh in enumerate(meshes):
        ax.annotate(
            f"{mesh['label']},   $t_f$ = {mesh['tf']:.2f} s",
            xy=(0.985, 0.95 - 0.09 * k),
            xycoords="axes fraction",
            ha="right",
            va="center",
            fontsize=12.5,
            color=colors[k],
        )

    ax.annotate(
        "engine limit,  $u = +1$",
        xy=(0.4, u_hi - 0.12),
        ha="left",
        va="top",
        fontsize=10.5,
        color="0.35",
    )
    ax.annotate(
        "brake limit,  $u = -3$",
        xy=(0.4, u_lo + 0.14),
        ha="left",
        va="bottom",
        fontsize=10.5,
        color="0.35",
    )
    ax.annotate(
        f"vertical rules: the {coarse['nfe']} finite element boundaries",
        xy=(0.4, u_lo - 0.62),
        ha="left",
        va="bottom",
        fontsize=10.5,
        color="0.45",
    )

    ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"acceleration $u$ (m/s$^2$)")
    ax.set_xlim(0, t_max * 1.02)
    ax.set_ylim(u_lo - 0.8, u_hi + 1.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


fig = plot_race_car_control(results)

# Write media/figures/race-car-control.{png,pdf} -- what the lecture handout
# \includegraphics. A no-op on Colab, where there is no repo to write to.
helper.save_figure(fig, "race-car-control")

And this is where they agree -- which is the trap.

# Tagged `figure:race-car-states': the single source of the state-trajectory
# figure in the Lecture 7 handout. Same contract as the cell above -- it uses
# only `results', `plt' and `helper', and defines its own figsize.


def plot_race_car_states(results):
    """Position and velocity on both meshes.

    WHY THIS FIGURE SITS BESIDE THE CONTROL FIGURE. That one shows where the
    coarse discretization goes wrong; this one shows how little of it reaches
    the states. Position is visually identical on the two meshes, and the coarse
    solution still lands exactly on x = L with v = 0 -- because those are
    constraints, and a constraint holds on any mesh. What the coarse mesh gets
    wrong is the OBJECTIVE. A student reading only these two panels would
    conclude N = 10 was fine.

    THE VELOCITY PANEL IS WHERE THE DEFECT IS VISIBLE. The trapped element's
    weak braking rounds the peak of the coarse velocity curve where the fine one
    turns sharply, and the coarse car then brakes at the limit for longer to
    still stop on the line.

    GREYSCALE. Colour and linestyle move together from the house prop_cycle,
    the line widths differ, and the labels are direct rather than a legend.
    """
    meshes = results["meshes"]
    colors = plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"]
    t_max = max(m["tf"] for m in meshes)

    fig, (ax_x, ax_v) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.0, 4.0))

    ax_x.axhline(
        results["L"], color="0.55", linewidth=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 3)), zorder=1
    )
    for k, mesh in enumerate(meshes):
        style = dict(linewidth=3.2 if k == 0 else 1.8, zorder=3 - k)
        ax_x.plot(mesh["t"], mesh["x"], **style)
        ax_v.plot(mesh["t"], mesh["v"], **style)

    ax_x.annotate(
        f"finish line, $L$ = {results['L']:.0f} m",
        xy=(0.4, results["L"] - 3),
        ha="left",
        va="top",
        fontsize=10.5,
        color="0.35",
    )

    # Both labels go in the empty upper-left wedge of the velocity panel, above
    # the acceleration ramp and left of the peak.
    for k, mesh in enumerate(meshes):
        ax_v.annotate(
            f"{mesh['label']},   $t_f$ = {mesh['tf']:.2f} s",
            xy=(0.03, 0.93 - 0.09 * k),
            xycoords="axes fraction",
            ha="left",
            va="center",
            fontsize=12.5,
            color=colors[k],
        )

    ax_v.annotate(
        "stopped on the line:\n$v(t_f) = 0$ is a constraint,\nso it holds on both meshes",
        xy=(meshes[0]["tf"], 0.0),
        xytext=(0.42, 0.30),
        textcoords="axes fraction",
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        fontsize=10.5,
        color="0.35",
        arrowprops=dict(
            arrowstyle="->",
            linewidth=1.0,
            color="0.45",
            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.2",
        ),
    )

    ax_x.set_xlabel("time (s)")
    ax_x.set_ylabel("position $x$ (m)")
    ax_v.set_xlabel("time (s)")
    ax_v.set_ylabel("velocity $v$ (m/s)")
    for ax in (ax_x, ax_v):
        ax.set_xlim(0, t_max * 1.02)
    ax_v.set_ylim(0, max(max(m["v"]) for m in meshes) * 1.30)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


fig = plot_race_car_states(results)
helper.save_figure(fig, "race-car-states")

The transcribed endpoint constraints hold to the solver tolerance on both meshes. They do not certify the continuous trajectory or control-switch location. Compare final time, control values, the mesh, and a separately integrated trajectory. The moving-element experiment below supplies an independent bang-bang reference.

The bounded-duration model uses final time at least 0.001 seconds. The reproducible experiment below uses 15 elements, three Radau points, and controls free at every collocation point, so its results are not directly comparable with the piecewise-constant-control mesh runs. It records the initial duration, duration bound, final time and solver iterations. Iteration counts depend on the software and linear solver; a poor guess is not a guaranteed failure.

For harder problems, bound physical durations, initialize from simulation when possible, and solve coarse before refining.

The deliberately out-of-bounds zero-duration starting value tests how Ipopt projects an invalid guess into the stated positive-duration domain. It does not relax that bound. All rows use the same formulation.

An initial value that makes a logarithm, reciprocal, or other model expression undefined can prevent even the first residual evaluation. Stiffness and poor variable or residual scaling can also make the first local model unhelpful. The present experiment alone does not identify why recovery succeeds; calling the model “nearly linear” is not an explanation of every nonlinear solve. Fix controls at a nominal profile and use a successful simulation to initialize the states when possible. Simulator(m).initialize_model() supplies that pattern; the 

temperature-control lab example gives the full workflow. Check that the model and simulator support the intended DAE before relying on it.

The original model, coefficients, state bounds and control bounds are retained. This explicit Radau transcription makes physical element lengths decision variables, with nominal length 1.65 s and a 45 percent movement band: 0.9075 to 2.3925 s. Their sum is the final time. Position and velocity remain continuous; one control value belongs to each element.

For stage j in element i, use a_{jk} obtained by integrating the three-point Radau derivative basis:x_{ij}=x_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k a_{jk}v_{ik},\qquad
v_{ij}=v_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k a_{jk}(u_i-Rv_{ik}^2).

The last Radau stage is the endpoint. Warm-start from the uniform ten-element solution. The control switch can then move onto a shared element boundary; this is a different formulation from changing only the nfe option in Pyomo.DAE.

Biegler, Section 10.3.1, equations (10.20)-(10.22), pp. 296-298.

More generally, Biegler’s movement band is h_i\in[(1-\gamma)\bar h_i,(1+\gamma)\bar h_i], with positive nominal lengths and 0\le\gamma<1/2. These bounds prevent collapse and limit mesh movement. This experiment uses \bar h_i=1.65 s and \gamma=0.45. For normalized fractions, use \sum_i\eta_i=1 and h_i=t_f\eta_i instead of applying the duration twice. Fix the lengths for the first solve before releasing them.

Setting u_{ij}=u_i removes within-element control oscillations and reduces the control dimension. It is a modeling restriction, not a universal cure for singular controls: it can also prevent a switch inside an element. Moving boundaries and increasing the element count address that restriction in different ways.

import numpy as np
from numpy.polynomial import Polynomial

def radau_three_coefficients():
    c = np.array([(4-np.sqrt(6))/10, (4+np.sqrt(6))/10, 1.0])
    A = np.zeros((3, 3))
    for k in range(3):
        basis = Polynomial([1.0])
        for j in range(3):
            if j != k:
                basis *= Polynomial([-c[j], 1.0]) / (c[k]-c[j])
        integral = basis.integ()
        A[:, k] = integral(c)-integral(0.0)
    assert np.allclose(A.sum(axis=1), c)
    assert np.isclose(A[-1].sum(), 1.0)
    return c, A

def create_variable_element_car(nfe=10, nominal=1.65, gamma=0.45):
    c, A = radau_three_coefficients()
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    m.I = pyo.RangeSet(1, nfe)
    m.J = pyo.RangeSet(0, 2)
    m.B = pyo.RangeSet(0, nfe)
    m.R = pyo.Param(initialize=0.001, units=1/units.m)
    m.L = pyo.Param(initialize=100.0, units=units.m)
    m.h = pyo.Var(m.I, bounds=((1-gamma)*nominal, (1+gamma)*nominal),
                  initialize=nominal, units=units.s)
    m.tf = pyo.Var(bounds=(1e-3, None), initialize=nfe*nominal, units=units.s)
    m.x = pyo.Var(m.I, m.J, bounds=(0, m.L+50*units.m), units=units.m)
    m.v = pyo.Var(m.I, m.J, bounds=(0, None), units=units.m/units.s)
    m.u = pyo.Var(m.I, bounds=(-3, 1), units=units.m/units.s**2)
    m.xb = pyo.Var(m.B, bounds=(0, m.L+50*units.m), units=units.m)
    m.vb = pyo.Var(m.B, bounds=(0, None), units=units.m/units.s)
    m.xb[0].fix(0); m.vb[0].fix(0)
    m.xb[nfe].fix(100); m.vb[nfe].fix(0)
    @m.Constraint()
    def horizon(m):
        return sum(m.h[i] for i in m.I) == m.tf
    @m.Constraint(m.I, m.J)
    def position(m, i, j):
        return m.x[i,j] == m.xb[i-1] + m.h[i]*sum(A[j,k]*m.v[i,k] for k in m.J)
    @m.Constraint(m.I, m.J)
    def velocity(m, i, j):
        return m.v[i,j] == m.vb[i-1] + m.h[i]*sum(
            A[j,k]*(m.u[i]-m.R*m.v[i,k]**2) for k in m.J)
    @m.Constraint(m.I)
    def position_end(m, i):
        return m.xb[i] == m.x[i,2]
    @m.Constraint(m.I)
    def velocity_end(m, i):
        return m.vb[i] == m.v[i,2]
    m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.tf)
    assert_units_consistent(m)
    # A feasible physical shape from the already solved uniform mesh.
    old = extract_race_car_results(m_coarse, NFE_COARSE)
    initial_edges = np.arange(nfe+1)*nominal
    for i in m.B:
        time = initial_edges[i]/initial_edges[-1]*old["tf"]
        m.xb[i].set_value(np.interp(time, old["t"], old["x"]))
        m.vb[i].set_value(np.interp(time, old["t"], old["v"]))
    # Reset fixed endpoints exactly after interpolation.
    m.xb[0].fix(0); m.vb[0].fix(0)
    m.xb[nfe].fix(100); m.vb[nfe].fix(0)
    for i in m.I:
        m.u[i].set_value(old["element_u"][min(i-1,len(old["element_u"])-1)])
        for j in m.J:
            time = (initial_edges[i-1]+nominal*c[j])/initial_edges[-1]*old["tf"]
            m.x[i,j].set_value(np.interp(time, old["t"], old["x"]))
            m.v[i,j].set_value(np.interp(time, old["t"], old["v"]))
    return m

m_variable = create_variable_element_car()
variable_status = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt").solve(m_variable, tee=True,

For this model the bang-bang reference accelerates at a=1 until speed v_s, then brakes at -b=-3. Integrating dx/dv=v/(u-Rv^2) givesx_a=-\frac{\log(1-Rv_s^2/a)}{2R},\quad
x_b=\frac{\log(1+Rv_s^2/b)}{2R}.

Solve x_a+x_b=L with 0<v_s<\sqrt{a/R}. The two durations aret_a=\frac{\operatorname{atanh}(v_s\sqrt{R/a})}{\sqrt{aR}},\qquad
t_b=\frac{\arctan(v_s\sqrt{R/b})}{\sqrt{bR}}.

These formulas come from the continuous ODE, independently of collocation. They define a reference candidate, not a general global-optimality certificate for arbitrary nonlinear control problems.

The next cell also integrates each computed piecewise-constant control on its actual intervals using a tight-tolerance ODE solve, restarting exactly at each control change. This checks the continuous terminal residual separately from the collocation constraints.

On a uniform mesh, a boundary where the control first changes sign is not a true bang-bang switch if an intermediate-control element remains. Read that interval and its control value. The moving-element run must put controls at the acceleration/braking bounds on either side before its boundary can be compared with the one-switch reference. Several length allocations within a constant-control arc can be nearly equivalent, so do not interpret the reported mesh as unique.

from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import scipy, pyomo, platform

R, acceleration, braking, distance = 0.001, 1.0, 3.0, 100.0
v_switch = brentq(lambda v: (-np.log1p(-R*v*v/acceleration)
                 +np.log1p(R*v*v/braking))/(2*R)-distance,
                 0, np.sqrt(acceleration/R)*(1-1e-12))
t_switch = np.arctanh(v_switch*np.sqrt(R/acceleration))/np.sqrt(acceleration*R)
t_brake = np.arctan(v_switch*np.sqrt(R/braking))/np.sqrt(braking*R)
reference = {"switch_speed":v_switch,"switch_time":t_switch,"final_time":t_switch+t_brake}

uniform = [extract_race_car_results(m_coarse,NFE_COARSE),
           extract_race_car_results(m_fine,NFE_FINE)]
edges = np.r_[0.0,np.cumsum([pyo.value(m_variable.h[i]) for i in m_variable.I])]
variable = {"label":"N = 10, moving","nfe":10,"tf":pyo.value(m_variable.tf),
            "elements":edges.tolist(),
            "element_u":[pyo.value(m_variable.u[i]) for i in m_variable.I]}
comparisons = []
for mesh in uniform+[variable]:
    state = np.array([0.0,0.0])
    for left,right,control in zip(mesh["elements"][:-1],mesh["elements"][1:],mesh["element_u"]):
        simulation = solve_ivp(lambda t,y:[y[1],control-R*y[1]**2],
                     (left,right),state,rtol=1e-11,atol=1e-12,method="DOP853")
        assert simulation.success and np.isclose(simulation.t[-1],right)
        state = simulation.y[:,-1]
    switches = [mesh["elements"][j] for j in range(1,len(mesh["element_u"]))
                if mesh["element_u"][j-1]>0 and mesh["element_u"][j]<0]
    comparisons.append({**mesh,"simulated_x_final":float(state[0]),
                        "simulated_v_final":float(state[1]),
                        "switch_boundaries":switches})
moving_check = comparisons[-1]
assert all(min(abs(u-acceleration),abs(u+braking))<1e-6 for u in variable["element_u"])
assert len(moving_check["switch_boundaries"])==1
assert abs(moving_check["switch_boundaries"][0]-reference["switch_time"])<1e-5
assert abs(moving_check["tf"]-reference["final_time"])<1e-5
assert abs(moving_check["simulated_x_final"]-distance)<1e-5
assert abs(moving_check["simulated_v_final"])<1e-6
comparison_results = {"meshes":comparisons,"reference":reference,"R":R,"L":distance,
                      "u_lower":-3.0,"u_upper":1.0,
                      "environment":{"pyomo":pyomo.__version__,"scipy":scipy.__version__,
                                     "python":platform.python_version()}}
for row in comparisons:
    print(f'{row["label"]:>16}: tf={row["tf"]:.8f}, '
          f'continuous dx={row["simulated_x_final"]-distance:+.3e}, '
          f'continuous v={row["simulated_v_final"]:+.3e}, '
          f'switch boundaries={row["switch_boundaries"]}')
print("Independent reference:",reference)
helper.save_results("race-car-variable-elements",comparison_results,
    notebook="notebooks/3-dev/PyomoDAE_car.ipynb",
    source_tag="handout:race-car-model",
    source_cells=[("notebooks/3-dev/PyomoDAE_car.ipynb",tag) for tag in
                  ("handout-output:race-car-coarse","handout-output:race-car-fine",
                   "numeric:race-car-extract","numeric:race-car-variable",
                   "numeric:race-car-independent")],
    description="Uniform10/100 and optimized10-element car controls, with independent bang-bang and continuous-integration checks.",
    solver="Ipopt3.13.2/ma27; DOP853 independent trajectory check")
results = comparison_results

Another modeling option is to define an extra differential equation to compute time. The normalized-time formulation is unchanged: tau remains the fixed independent variable on [0,1], and tf remains a decision variable. The additional state is useful when physical time must be available along the trajectory; otherwise, recover it after solving as t=\tau t_f.\begin{align*}
\min_{u} \quad & t_f \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & \frac{dx}{d\tau} = t_f v \\
& \frac{dv}{d\tau} = t_f (u - R v^2) \\
& \frac{dt}{d\tau} = t_f \\
& x(\tau = 0) = 0, ~~ x(\tau = 1) = L \\
& v(\tau = 0) = 0, ~~ v(\tau = 1) = 0 \\
& t(\tau = 0) = 0 \\
& -3 \leq u \leq 1
\end{align*}

def create_model2():

    # Define the  model
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

    # Define the model parameters
    m.R = pyo.Param(initialize=0.001, units=1 / units.m)  # Friction factor
    m.L = pyo.Param(initialize=100.0, units=units.m)  # Final position

    # Define time
    m.tau = dae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, 1))  # Dimensionless time set
    m.time = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, None), units=units.s)  # Time
    m.tf = pyo.Var(initialize=1, bounds=(1e-3, None), units=units.s)  # Final time

    # Define remaining algebraic variables
    m.x = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, m.L + 50 * units.m), units=units.m)  # Position
    m.v = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, None), units=units.m / units.s)  # Velocity
    m.u = pyo.Var(
        m.tau, bounds=(-3.0, 1.0), initialize=0, units=units.m / units.s / units.s
    )  # Acceleration

    # Define derivative variables. tau is dimensionless, so d/dtau carries the
    # same units as the state. DerivativeVar does not infer these -- say them.
    m.dtime = dae.DerivativeVar(m.time, units=units.s)
    m.dx = dae.DerivativeVar(m.x, units=units.m)
    m.dv = dae.DerivativeVar(m.v, units=units.m / units.s)

    # Declare the objective (minimize final time)
    m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.tf)

    # Define the constraints
    # position
    @m.Constraint(m.tau)
    def ode1(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        return m.dx[i] == m.tf * m.v[i]

    # velocity
    @m.Constraint(m.tau)
    def ode2(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        return m.dv[i] == m.tf * (m.u[i] - m.R * m.v[i] ** 2)

    # time
    @m.Constraint(m.tau)
    def ode3(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        return m.dtime[i] == m.tf

    # Define the initial/boundary conditions
    def _init(m):
        yield m.x[0] == 0
        yield m.x[1] == m.L
        yield m.v[0] == 0
        yield m.v[1] == 0
        yield m.time[0] == 0

    m.initcon = pyo.ConstraintList(rule=_init)

    # Units are checked on the continuous model, before discretization.
    assert_units_consistent(m)

    return m


m = create_model2()



# Declare the discretizer
discretizer = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation")
discretizer.apply_to(m, nfe=15, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU", ncp=3)

# force piecewise constant controls (acceleration) over each finite element
m = discretizer.reduce_collocation_points(m, var=m.u, ncp=1, contset=m.tau)

# Solve
solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
results = solver.solve(m, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)

print("final time = %6.2f seconds" % (pyo.value(m.tf)))

You are a race car driver with a simple goal. Drive distance L in the minimal amount of time but come to a complete stop at the finish line.

Mathematically, you want to solve the following optimal control problem:\begin{align*}
\min_{u} \quad & t_f \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & \frac{dx}{dt} = v \\
& \frac{dv}{dt} = u - R v^2 \\
& x(t=0) = 0, ~~ x(t=t_f) = L \\
& v(t=0) = 0, ~~ v(t=t_f) = 0 \\
& -3 \leq u \leq 1
\end{align*}

where u is the acceleration/braking (your control variable) and R is the drag coefficient (parameter).

Let t = \tau \cdot t_f where \tau \in [0,1]. Thus dt = t_f d\tau. The optimal control problem becomes:\begin{align*}
\min_{u} \quad & t_f \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & \frac{dx}{d\tau} = t_f v \\
& \frac{dv}{d\tau} = t_f (u - R v^2) \\
& x(\tau = 0) = 0, ~~ x(\tau = 1) = L \\
& v(\tau = 0) = 0, ~~ v(\tau = 1) = 0 \\
& -3 \leq u \leq 1
\end{align*}

# Define the  model
m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

# Define the model parameters
m.R = pyo.Param(initialize=0.001, units=1 / units.m)  # Friction factor
m.L = pyo.Param(initialize=100.0, units=units.m)  # Final position

# Define time. The ContinuousSet cannot carry units -- it holds plain floats.
# Here that costs us nothing, because tau really IS dimensionless.
m.tau = dae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, 1))  # Dimensionless (scaled) time
m.time = pyo.Var(m.tau, units=units.s)  # Physical time
m.tf = pyo.Var(units=units.s)  # Final time

# Define remaining algebraic variables
m.x = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, m.L + 50 * units.m), units=units.m)  # Position
m.v = pyo.Var(m.tau, bounds=(0, None), units=units.m / units.s)  # Velocity
m.u = pyo.Var(
    m.tau, bounds=(-3.0, 1.0), initialize=0, units=units.m / units.s**2
)  # Acceleration

# Define derivative variables.
#
# DerivativeVar defaults to DIMENSIONLESS -- it does not inherit units from the
# state variable. And because tau is dimensionless, d/dtau carries the SAME
# units as the state, not the state's units per second.
m.dtime = dae.DerivativeVar(m.time, units=units.s)
m.dx = dae.DerivativeVar(m.x, units=units.m)
m.dv = dae.DerivativeVar(m.v, units=units.m / units.s)

# Declare the objective (minimize final time)
m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.tf)


# Define the constraints
# position
@m.Constraint(m.tau)
def ode1(m, i):
    if i == 0:
        return pyo.Constraint.Skip
    return m.dx[i] == m.tf * m.v[i]


# velocity
@m.Constraint(m.tau)
def ode2(m, i):
    if i == 0:
        return pyo.Constraint.Skip
    return m.dv[i] == m.tf * (m.u[i] - m.R * m.v[i] ** 2)


# time
@m.Constraint(m.tau)
def ode3(m, i):
    if i == 0:
        return pyo.Constraint.Skip
    return m.dtime[i] == m.tf


# Define the inital/boundary conditions
def _init(m):
    yield m.x[0] == 0
    yield m.x[1] == m.L
    yield m.v[0] == 0
    yield m.v[1] == 0
    yield m.time[0] == 0


m.initcon = pyo.ConstraintList(rule=_init)

# Check units NOW, before the next cell discretizes the model.
# See ./units_and_pyomo_dae.md and https://github.com/Pyomo/pyomo/issues/1790
assert_units_consistent(m)
print("Pyomo.dae model: units are consistent (before discretization).")



Warning

The assert_units_consistent(m) call sits at the end of the model declaration above,
before the discretization in the next cell. That order matters for every
Pyomo.dae model: the discretization equations Pyomo generates multiply states by a
numerical reciprocal-\Delta t coefficient that carries no units, because a
ContinuousSet cannot hold any. This is


Pyomo issue #1790, still open.

This particular model happens to survive the check afterwards too, since \tau is
genuinely dimensionless -- but do not rely on that. See


Units in Pyomo.dae Models, and 

Pyomo.DAE Example: Temperature Control Lab for a model whose time
domain is in seconds and which therefore fails.

The quadrature rule approximates the integral I with weighted sum of function evaluations:I := \int_{-1}^{1} f(x) dx \approx \underbrace{\sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l f(x_l)}_{\text{quadrature rule}}

where:

x_l are nodes (also known as abscissas)

w_l are weights

L number of nodes and weights

Central questions:

How does this choice impact approximation error?

Let f(x) = a_{2L-1} x^{2L-1} + a_{2L-2} x^{2L-2} + ... + a_{1} x^1 + a_{0}

Exactness through degree 2L-1 imposes 2L moment equations (one for each monomial 1,x,\ldots,x^{2L-1}). These match the 2L unknown node and weight values in an L-point rule. This count motivates the attainable degree; orthogonal-polynomial theory supplies the nodes and proves exactness.

One way to derive the Gauss-Legendre quadrature rules is by looking at the integral generic monomials of degree 0 up to 2L-1 and setting each equal to the L point Gauss-Legendre quadrature rule:\begin{align*} \int\limits_{-1}^{1} dx\, a_0 x^0 &=  a_0\sum_{l=1}^L w_l x_l^0, \\
\int\limits_{-1}^{1} dx\, a_1 x^1 &= a_1\sum_{l=1}^L w_l x_l^1, \\
& ~~ \vdots \\
\int\limits_{-1}^{1} dx\, a_{2L-1} x^{2L-1} &= a_{2L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L w_l x_l^{2L-1}.
\end{align*}

Notice that the a_i constants cancel out of each equation so they do not matter. This system is 2L equations with L weights, w_l, and L nodes, x_l. We could solve these equations to get the weights and nodes, though this is not how it is done in practice generally---this is accomplished by using the theory of orthogonal polynomials.

records.content:
As a simple demonstration of the Gauss-Legendre quadrature, let’s show that it integrates polynomials of degree 2L-1 exactly.  Consider the integral\int\limits_{-1}^1 (x+1)^{2L-1}\,dx = \frac{2^{2 L-1}}{L}.

We can use the GLQuad function to evaluate the error.

L = np.arange(1, 12)
for l in L:

    # Create f
    f = lambda x: (x + 1) ** (2 * l - 1)

    # Evaluate exact (analytic) solution
    integral = 2 ** (2 * l - 1) / l

    # Evaluate quadrature rule
    GLintegral = GLQuad(f, l)

    # Print results
    print(
        "L =",
        l,
        "\t Estimate is",
        GLintegral,
        "Exact value is",
        integral,
        "\nAbs. Relative Error is",
        np.abs(GLintegral - integral) / integral,
    )

records.content:
We are generally interested in integrals not just over the domain x\in [-1,1].  We’ll now make a function that does Gauss-Legendre quadrature over a general range using the formula\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \frac{b-a}{2} \int_{-1}^1 f\left(\frac{b-a}{2}z + \frac{a+b}{2}\right)\,dz.

def generalGL(f, a, b, L):
    """Compute the Gauss-Legendre Quadrature estimate
    of the integral of f(x) from a to b
    Inputs:
    f:   name of function to integrate
    a:   lower bound of integral
    b:   upper bound of integral
    L:   Number of quadrature nodes (see GLQuad)
    Returns:
    G-L Quadrature estimate"""

    # Set bound on L
    assert L >= 1

    # Define a re-scaled f
    f_rescaled = lambda z: f(0.5 * (b - a) * z + 0.5 * (a + b))

    # Define the integral
    integral = GLQuad(f_rescaled, L)

    # Calculate the G-L quadrature estimate
    return integral * (b - a) * 0.5



Let’s show that this version integrates polynomials of degree 2L-1 exactly.  Consider the integral\int\limits_{-3}^2 (x+1)^{2L-1}\,dx = \frac{9^L-4^L}{2 L}.

L = np.arange(1, 12)

# Loop over L to calculate the integral and the G-L estimate
for l in L:
    # Define a lambda function
    f = lambda x: (x + 1) ** (2 * l - 1)
    # Calculate the integral
    integral = (9**l - 4**l) / (2 * l)
    # Calculate the estimate
    GLintegral = generalGL(f, -3, 2, l)
    # Print statement for the error comparison
    print(
        "L =",
        l,
        "\t Estimate is",
        GLintegral,
        "Exact value is",
        integral,
        "\nAbs. Relative Error is",
        np.abs(GLintegral - integral) / integral,
    )

records.content:
Sometimes we desire either:

The first node is at the beginning of the interval, i.e., x_1 = -1 or

The last node is at the end of the interval, i.e., x_{L} = 1.

This is known as Gauss-Radau quadrature. The remaining nodes and weights are chosen optimally; thus, Radau quadrature exactly integrates all polynomials of degree 2L-2 or less. Specifying one of the nodes leaves only 2L-1 degrees of freedom.

More info: 

https://​mathworld​.wolfram​.com​/RadauQuadrature​.html

records.content:
Consider solving the differential equation\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(t,\mathbf{x}), \quad \mathbf{x}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}_0,

to determine \mathbf{x}(t_f). This can be expressed as an integral:\mathbf{x}(t_f) = \int_{t_0}^{t_f} \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} dt + \mathbf{x}_0 = \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t_f} \mathbf{f}(t, \mathbf{x}(t)) dt}_{\text{quadrature rule}} + \mathbf{x}_0

Thus, Runge-Kutta methods can be interpreted as a quadrature rule.

A collocation method approximates the state with a polynomial and enforces the differential and algebraic equations at selected collocation points. The resulting finite system of algebraic equations can be solved directly or embedded in an optimization problem.

records.content:
Derivations are followed from Section 10.2 of Biegler (2010).

Consider the following multiperiod dynamic optimization problem (8.5).\begin{align*}
\min & \sum_{l=1}^{N_T} \Phi^l\left(\mathbf{z}^l\left(t_l\right), \mathbf{y}^l\left(t_l\right), \mathbf{u}^l\left(t_l\right), \mathbf{p}^l\right) \\
\text { s.t. } & \frac{d \mathbf{z}^l}{d t}=\mathbf{f}^l\left(\mathbf{z}^l(t), \mathbf{y}^l(t), \mathbf{u}^l(t), \mathbf{p}^l\right), \quad \mathbf{z}^l\left(t_{l-1}\right)=\mathbf{z}_0^l, \\
& \mathbf{g}^l\left(\mathbf{z}^l(t), \mathbf{y}^l(t), \mathbf{u}^l(t), \mathbf{p}^l\right)=\mathbf{0}, \\
& \mathbf{u}_L^l \leq \mathbf{u}^l(t) \leq \mathbf{u}_U^l, \\
& \mathbf{p}_L^l \leq \mathbf{p}^l \leq \mathbf{p}_U^l, \\
& \mathbf{y}_L^l \leq \mathbf{y}^l(t) \leq \mathbf{y}_U^l, \\
& \mathbf{z}_L^l \leq \mathbf{z}^l(t) \leq \mathbf{z}_U^l, \quad t \in\left(t_{l-1}, t_l\right], l=1, \ldots, N_T, \\
& \mathbf{h}\left(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{z}_0^1, \mathbf{z}^1\left(t_1\right), \mathbf{z}_0^2, \mathbf{z}^2\left(t_2\right), \ldots, \mathbf{z}_0^{N_T}, \mathbf{z}^{N_T}\left(t_{N_T}\right)\right)=\mathbf{0}
\end{align*}

Each physical period l may contain many finite elements. Period junctions use the coupling function \mathbf h; finite-element boundaries within a period use state continuity. The decision variables include the nodal states, control coefficients and any free parameters. A running cost can be included by adding an accumulator state, \dot q=L(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t), and minimizing q(t_f) plus terminal cost.

This source-controlled course schematic was re-authored from the mathematical layout of Biegler (2010), Figure 10.1; it is not a reproduction of the textbook artwork.

records.content:
The collocation method can be developed by solving the differential equation ( dz/dt ) at specific time points. For example, Figure 10.1 shows the state variable approximation for a single finite element:\begin{align}
\mathbf{z}^K(t) = \boldsymbol\alpha_0 + \boldsymbol\alpha_1t + \cdots + \boldsymbol\alpha_Kt^K 
\end{align}

The coefficients \boldsymbol\alpha_j are vectors when the state is a vector. A power basis is mathematically valid, but nodal Lagrange coefficients are directly interpretable as state values. This profile can also be represented as a Lagrange interpolation polynomial. For Gauss-Legendre or right Radau, choose K+1 distinct interpolation points within element i, the state can be represented as:\begin{align}
& t = t_{i-1} + h_i\tau , \\
& \mathbf{z}^K(t) = \sum_{j=0}^K \ell_j(\tau)\mathbf{z}_{ij} , \\
& \text{for } t \in [t_{i-1},t_i] \text{ and } \tau \in [0,1] , \\
& \text{where } \ell_j(\tau) = \prod_{\substack{k=0 \\ k\neq j}}^K \frac{(\tau-\tau_k)}{(\tau_j-\tau_k)} \\
& \tau_0=0 \\
& \tau_j<\tau_{j+1}, \\
& j=0,...,K-1 , \\
& \text{and } h_i \text{ is the length of element } i. \\
\end{align}

The key property of this polynomial is that
 z^K(t_{ij})=z_{ij}  where  t_{ij}=t_{i-1} + \tau_j h_i .

At \tau=\tau_k, every \ell_j with j\ne k contains a zero numerator; \ell_k(\tau_k)=1. Thus \mathbf z^K(t_{ik})=\mathbf z_{ik}. The basis also satisfies \sum_j\ell_j=1: both sides interpolate the constant polynomial at K+1 distinct nodes. These identities justify interpreting coefficients as nodal values.

Why change coordinates? Power coefficients are not nodal states, so componentwise bounds on those coefficients do not directly impose physical state bounds. Monomial Vandermonde systems can also become poorly conditioned as the degree grows or the time interval is badly scaled; nearly dependent columns make coefficients sensitive even when the represented profile changes little. Normalizing each element and using nodal coordinates makes the variables easier to interpret. It does not remove every conditioning problem, and nodal bounds still need the between-node check below.

Bounds are nodal. Imposing \mathbf z_L\le\mathbf z_{ij}\le\mathbf z_U does not bound the whole polynomial. Lagrange basis functions can be negative between nodes. Check additional points, extrema of the interpolation polynomial, or the independently integrated trajectory. For a continuous path constraint, mesh refinement and a residual check are part of validation.

The counterexample below uses p(\tau)=4.2\tau(1-\tau) at the initial point and three right-Radau nodes. Every nodal value lies in [0,1], but p(1/2)=1.05.

radau = np.array([(4-np.sqrt(6))/10,(4+np.sqrt(6))/10,1.0])
nodes = np.r_[0.0,radau]
values = 4.2*nodes*(1-nodes)
assert np.all((values>=0)&(values<=1))
assert np.isclose(4.2*0.5*(1-0.5),1.05)
print("Nodal values:",values,"; value at tau=1/2:",1.05)

records.content:
Let K distinct derivative nodes be c_j. Define\bar\ell_j(\tau)=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{\tau-c_k}{c_j-c_k},\qquad
\Omega_j(\tau)=\int_0^\tau\bar\ell_j(s)\,ds.

The derivative polynomial has degree at most K-1; integrating it with the initial value gives\mathbf z^K(t_{i-1}+h_i\tau)=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_{k=1}^K\Omega_k(\tau)\mathbf v_{ik}.

Here \mathbf v_{ik} denotes the physical-time derivative, not the state. Differentiating cancels the factor h_i, and \bar\ell_k(c_j)=\delta_{kj} gives d\mathbf z^K/dt(t_{ij})=\mathbf v_{ij}. The factor arises from dt=h_i\,d\tau.

For a semi-explicit DAE, enforce\mathbf v_{ij}=\mathbf f(\mathbf Z_{ij},\mathbf Y_{ij},\mathbf U_{ij},\mathbf p,t_{ij}),\qquad
\mathbf0=\mathbf g(\mathbf Z_{ij},\mathbf Y_{ij},\mathbf U_{ij},\mathbf p,t_{ij}).

Evaluating the state at the stages and endpoint gives\begin{aligned}
\mathbf Z_{ij}&=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k a_{jk}\mathbf f_{ik},&a_{jk}&=\Omega_k(c_j),\\
\mathbf z_i&=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k b_k\mathbf f_{ik},&b_k&=\Omega_k(1).
\end{aligned}

These are the Runge-Kutta stage and update equations. For a state-only ODE they are standard RK; for a DAE the algebraic stage equations are additional. A degree-K state polynomial is fixed by its initial value and its derivative at K distinct points, so this derivative representation is equivalent to the state-coordinate equations when the state interpolation nodes are distinct.

Not every node set is implicit. For one node c, a_{11}=c and b_1=1. The choices c=0,1/2,1 give forward Euler, implicit midpoint and backward Euler. Standard Gauss, Radau IIA and Lobatto IIIA are implicit families (the first Lobatto stage is an explicit evaluation). For Lobatto the derivative nodes include zero; do not append a duplicate zero to the K+1-point state formula.

Partition of unity gives stage times. Since \sum_k\bar\ell_k=1, \sum_k\Omega_k(\tau)=\tau. Hence \mathbf A\mathbf1=\mathbf c and \mathbf b^T\mathbf1=1. For dt/dt=1 this reproduces t_{ij}=t_{i-1}+h_ic_j and t_i=t_{i-1}+h_i. With normalized local coordinate, dt/d\tau=h_i, not 1. Always use b_k for the endpoint update; the last row of \mathbf A equals \mathbf b^T only when the last node is 1.

records.content:
The incoming value on element i+1 equals the endpoint reconstructed on element i:\mathbf z_{i+1,0}=\mathbf z_i=\sum_{j=0}^K\ell_j(1)\mathbf z_{ij}
=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k b_k\mathbf v_{ik}.

The state remains continuous when its derivative has a finite jump. Right Radau has c_K=1, so its endpoint is the last stage. Gauss-Legendre has c_K<1; it needs the endpoint evaluation, which generally differs from the last stage.

Controls may be piecewise constant and jump at a boundary. Do not impose continuity unless the physical actuator or chosen approximation requires it. Algebraic variables require a separate check. If \mathbf g(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t)=0 defines a unique regular local branch \mathbf y=\mathbf Y(\mathbf z,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t) and its inputs are continuous, then \mathbf y is continuous. Index 1 alone does not ensure this if \mathbf u jumps. In \dot z=y, 0=y-u, switching u from 1 to 2 makes y jump while z stays continuous. At a discontinuity, distinguish the left and right values at the shared time.

For the common degree-(K-1) control and algebraic profile representations, use the K-node derivative basis:\mathbf u_i^K(\tau)=\sum_{j=1}^K\bar\ell_j(\tau)\mathbf U_{ij},\qquad
\mathbf y_i^K(\tau)=\sum_{j=1}^K\bar\ell_j(\tau)\mathbf Y_{ij}.

These profiles need not match across elements. A lower-order control parameterization can instead set all \mathbf U_{ij} equal on an element. For a regular algebraic branch, an endpoint algebraic value may also be recovered by solving \mathbf g=0 from the endpoint differential state and the appropriate left/right control; this does not justify equating both sides when the control jumps. Nodal bounds on either interpolated profile still need a between-node check.

For one differential state, fixed mesh and prescribed controls/parameters, an expanded derivative transcription has:

Quantity

Count

stage states Z_{ij}

NK

stage derivatives v_{ij}

NK

boundary states z_0,\ldots,z_N

N+1

stage reconstruction equations

NK

stage ODE equations

NK

endpoint update equations

N

There are N(2K+1)+1 variables and N(2K+1) equations before fixing z_0. The initial condition removes the remaining degree of freedom. Each regular algebraic stage variable adds a variable and its equation. Free controls, parameters, durations and terminal constraints change the count. Pyomo may eliminate boundary/stage duplicates or use a different derivative representation; its raw counts need not equal this pedagogical expanded formulation. A square count is necessary for a regular simulation, but does not prove independence or numerical accuracy.

records.content:
Let \Delta t=t_f-t_0>0 and \sigma=(t-t_0)/\Delta t\in[0,1]. Then\frac{d\mathbf z}{d\sigma}=\Delta t\,\mathbf f(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t_0+\Delta t\sigma),\qquad
0=\mathbf g(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t_0+\Delta t\sigma).

The transformed derivative is with respect to \sigma. The duration multiplies every physical-time right-hand side, and any explicit time argument must also be transformed. Minimize t_0+\Delta t for minimum arrival time with fixed t_0. In Biegler’s notation p_f is this duration; the car code calls it tf because t_0=0.

Normalization fixes the domain on which Pyomo creates points; it does not impose a positive duration. Add a physically meaningful lower bound, initialize within the bounds, and use units to check both sides. The car example uses tf >= 0.001 s. For moving normalized mesh fractions \eta_i>0, require \sum_i\eta_i=1 and use physical lengths h_i=\Delta t\eta_i; do not multiply by the duration twice. Alternatively optimize physical h_i with \sum_i h_i=\Delta t.

records.content:
For Gauss-Legendre, the K nodes are the roots of the shifted degree-K Legendre polynomial. The corresponding quadrature integrates all degrees through 2K-1. The orthogonality proof and its assumptions are in 

Numeric Integration for DAEs.

Right Radau adds the endpoint 1 to the roots of a degree-(K-1) polynomial orthogonal with weight 1-\tau. Lobatto adds 0 and 1 to the roots of a degree-(K-2) polynomial orthogonal with weight \tau(1-\tau). These are free-node Jacobi constructions, with the fixed endpoints added afterward. Exact symbolic tables and verification are in 

Collocation Points and Runge-Kutta Coefficients.

For a sufficiently smooth ODE, the standard Gauss, Radau IIA and Lobatto IIIA endpoint orders are 2K, 2K-1 and 2K-2. An order-p method has an unnormalized one-step defect O(h^{p+1}), or normalized local truncation error O(h^p). Stage errors and DAE algebraic-variable errors need not have that same order. Quadrature moment tests alone do not prove every nonlinear Runge-Kutta order condition.

Gauss and Radau IIA are A-stable and algebraically stable. Algebraic stability implies AN-stability; the converse applies for distinct abscissas. Radau IIA also has homogeneous stiff decay. A-stability bounds amplification for left-half-plane eigenvalues; it does not ensure accurate transient decay or convergence of the nonlinear stage solve. Gauss large-step oscillations can be reduced by refining the mesh until the transient is resolved. For a very stiff problem, that can require far more elements than a method with stiff decay.

See Biegler, Section 10.2.2, pp. 290–293; Ascher & Petzold, pp. 101–104 and Exercise 4.13, p. 119. See the numerical-integration guide for the formal stability definitions, rather than treating their names as interchangeable.

A practical choice. Start with right Radau for a stiff model when damping fast homogeneous transients matters. For a smooth nonstiff problem, compare Gauss-Legendre: it has one higher endpoint order at the same stage count. That is a reason to measure error and work, not a universal speed ranking. Gauss oscillations can be resolved by sufficiently fine elements. Lobatto is useful for understanding endpoint choices but is not supplied by Pyomo.DAE.

records.content:
Order the variables by element. A collocation row involves stages in its own element, the incoming boundary state, that element’s control coefficients, and any shared parameters. Continuity connects neighboring elements. The Jacobian therefore has local blocks and a border for shared parameters or a free final time. It need not be a plain banded matrix. A stage derivative can couple every state component, so a block can itself be dense. Sparse NLP solvers exploit the incidence pattern and compute derivatives of the transcribed equations.

A simultaneous NLP iterate can violate the dynamic equations. At a converged point it satisfies the discrete residual tolerance, which still leaves a discretization error. In a sequential architecture, successful integration supplies a dynamic trajectory for a trial control; it does not automatically enforce path constraints, state bounds or terminal conditions. The architecture comparison is taught in 

Differential Algebraic Equations (DAEs).

records.content:
Free element lengths add products of h_i with stage derivatives. They let a discontinuity align with an element boundary, but require positive lengths and sensible movement bounds. Inactive pieces can make many meshes nearly equivalent, leaving weak curvature in the mesh variables. See the executed 

moving-element car example, and Biegler, pp. 296–298.

Scale both variables and residuals. A typical-state scale changes \mathbf z=\mathbf z_{\rm ref}+\mathbf S_z\hat{\mathbf z}; a residual scale changes the nonlinear solver’s numerical balance. Preserve units before choosing either. A duration bound is a physical domain constraint, not a substitute for scaling.

An index-1 semi-explicit DAE has locally nonsingular \partial\mathbf g/\partial\mathbf y. Higher-index DAEs and active path constraints can require differentiated consistency conditions or index reduction; general smooth-ODE order claims cannot be transferred unchanged. Biegler, Section 10.4.5, pp. 317–322, develops high-index path constraints.

Spatial semi-discretization can generate a stiff ODE or DAE. The discretization, boundary equations and constraint index determine which integrator assumptions apply; the fact that the result is finite-dimensional is insufficient. See the 

heat-conduction guide.

records.content:
Prepared by: Prof. Alexander Dowling (2026)

This notebook is the PDE companion to Lecture 7. We take one transient conduction problem,
write it for three geometries at once, discretize space with the method of lines, and solve
the resulting differential-algebraic system with Pyomo.dae.

The physical problem and the idea of indexing the three geometries with a single shape parameter
are adapted from J. C. Kantor,


ND Pyomo Cookbook,
notebook 5.03 “Heat Conduction in Various Geometries”. The derivation, the code and the numerical
experiments below are our own.

AI-drafted prose, not yet reviewed by Prof. Dowling.

records.content:
A solid body, initially at uniform temperature T_0, is dropped at t=0 into a bath held at
T_\infty. The surface reaches the bath temperature immediately, and we want the temperature
everywhere inside as a function of time.

With constant positive thermal conductivity k, density \rho and heat capacity C_p, no source term, and no axial or angular temperature variation,
the energy balance is\rho C_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot \left( k \nabla T \right) = k \nabla^2 T .

Divide by \rho C_p and define the thermal diffusivity \alpha = k / (\rho C_p), which has units
of length^2/time:\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \nabla^2 T .

records.content:
The three classical bodies -- an infinite slab of half-thickness R, an infinite cylinder of
radius R, and a sphere of radius R -- are all one-dimensional: temperature depends on a single
space coordinate r measured from the center. In each case the Laplacian of a radially symmetric
field is\nabla^2 T = \frac{1}{r^{s}} \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left( r^{s} \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \right)
            = \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial r^2} + \frac{s}{r} \frac{\partial T}{\partial r},

where the shape index s is

Geometry

r measured from

Surface at

Slab (infinite plate, half-thickness R)

the midplane

r = R

Cylinder (infinite, radius R)

r = R

Sphere (radius R)

r = R

For the slab, s=0 and the extra term vanishes -- Cartesian coordinates. For s = 1 and s = 2
the geometry contributes the \tfrac{s}{r}\partial T/\partial r term, which is singular at the
center. That singularity is the interesting part of this notebook, so hold onto it.
