In the following cell, we define a function to define and return the Pyomo model for the kinetic model to be used for parameter estimation.

import pyomo.contrib.parmest.parmest as parmest
from pyomo.contrib.parmest.experiment import Experiment


def reaction_kinetics_model(data):

    # define Pyomo model
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    m.T = data["T"][0]  # K
    m.CA0 = data["CA0"][0]  # mol/L
    m.R = 8.31446261815324  # J / K / mol

    # # define 'experimental' data timesteps as Pyomo set
    m.t = pyo.Set(initialize=data["time"].tolist())

    # Kinetic parameters to be fitted defined as Pyomo variables
    # Initialized by 'true' values
    m.A1 = pyo.Var(initialize=200, bounds=(100, 300))  # 1/hr
    m.A2 = pyo.Var(initialize=400, bounds=(300, 500))  # 1/hr
    m.E1 = pyo.Var(initialize=10, bounds=(1, 20))  # kJ/mol
    m.E2 = pyo.Var(initialize=15, bounds=(1, 30))  # kJ/mol

    # Concentration variables indexed by time
    m.CA = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=m.CA0)  # mol/L
    m.CB = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=0)  # mol/L
    m.CC = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=0)  # mol/L

    # kinetic rate constants from Arrhenius equation
    m.k1 = pyo.Expression(rule=m.A1 * pyo.exp(-m.E1 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T)))  # 1/hr
    m.k2 = pyo.Expression(rule=m.A2 * pyo.exp(-m.E2 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T)))  # 1/hr

    # Constraints to change concentrations based on kinetics
    @m.Constraint(m.t)
    def CA_rate(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        else:
            return m.CA[i] == m.CA0 * pyo.exp(-m.k1 * i)

    @m.Constraint(m.t)
    def CB_rate(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        else:
            return m.CB[i] == m.k1 * m.CA0 / (m.k2 - m.k1) * (
                pyo.exp(-m.k1 * i) - pyo.exp(-m.k2 * i)
            )

    @m.Constraint(m.t)
    def CC_rate(m, i):
        if i == 0:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip
        else:
            return m.CC[i] == m.CA0 - m.CA[i] - m.CB[i]

    return m




# The Experiment contract: get_labeled_model() is the only method Pyomo
# insists on. Everything else here is ours. The labels below are what make one
# model usable by two tools -- parmest reads three of them, Pyomo.DoE reads a
# fourth (experiment_inputs, the design). Each tool reads what it needs and
# ignores the rest; that is the point of the abstraction, not an inconsistency.
class ReactionKineticsExperiment(Experiment):

    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.model = None

    def create_model(self):
        self.model = m = reaction_kinetics_model(self.data)
        return m

    def finalize_model(self):
        m = self.model

        # Initial Conditions

        m.CA[0].fix(m.CA0)
        m.CB[0].fix(0.0)
        m.CC[0].fix(0.0)

        return m

    def label_model(self):
        m = self.model

        # experiment_outputs: the measured responses y_i -- what the model
        # predicts and the experiment observed, paired value by value.
        m.experiment_outputs = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.experiment_outputs.update(
            (m.CA[t], self.data["CA"][ind]) for ind, t in enumerate(self.data["time"])
        )
        m.experiment_outputs.update(
            (m.CB[t], self.data["CB"][ind]) for ind, t in enumerate(self.data["time"])
        )
        m.experiment_outputs.update(
            (m.CC[t], self.data["CC"][ind]) for ind, t in enumerate(self.data["time"])
        )

        # unknown_parameters: theta, the quantities being estimated. The value
        # stored with each is its current guess, used to initialize the solve.
        m.unknown_parameters = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.unknown_parameters.update(
            (k, pyo.value(k)) for k in [m.A1, m.A2, m.E1, m.E2]
        )

        # measurement_error: sigma_i, the standard DEVIATION of the noise on
        # each measurement -- not the variance, and not a weight. It is what
        # builds the covariance matrix used to weight the residuals. Pyomo 6.10
        # requires this suffix before cov_est() will run. The value is
        # `stdev_m_error` from the Parmest-generate-data notebook: the noise
        # actually added when these data files were generated.
        m.measurement_error = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.measurement_error.update((k, 0.1) for k in m.experiment_outputs)
        return m

    def get_labeled_model(self):
        m = self.create_model()
        m = self.finalize_model()
        m = self.label_model()
        return m

Here, we will estimate parameters A_1, A_2, E_1, and E_2 using data generated for a batch ‘experiment’ at 250 K with an inlet concentration of 0.5 mol/L of A.

The parameter estimation problem is solved with the least squares optimization scheme
$$\begin{align}
\begin{split}
    \min_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \quad & \sum_{i}^{} (y_i - f(\mathbf{x}_i,\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}))^2\\
    \textrm{s.t.} \quad & \mathrm{bounds \ on} \ \boldsymbol{\theta}\\
    & \mathrm{other \ physical \ constraints}\\
\end{split}
\end{align}

$
where i is used to index the datapoints in a dataset and \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ is the optimal set of parameter values that minimizes the prediction error.

In contrast to the approach above, we will now try to solve the model without the analytic solution for the concentrations using Pyomo.DAE.  To recap, the concentrations in a batch reactor evolve with time per the following differential equations:\frac{d C_A}{dt} = r_A = -k_1 C_A\frac{d C_B}{dt} = r_B = k_1 C_A - k_2 C_B\frac{d C_C}{dt} = r_C = k_2 C_B

This is a linear system of differential equations. Assuming the feed is only species A, i.e.,C_A(t=0) = C_{A0} \quad C_B(t=0) = 0 \quad C_C(t=0) = 0

In the following cell, we define a function to define and return the Pyomo DAE model (dynamic mode) for the kinetic model to be used for parameter estimation.  In this model, the rate equations are presented in terms of linear differential equations.

Note

With CasADi 3.7.2, Pyomo’s Simulator(..., package="casadi") emits a CasADi warning about legacy integrator time-grid options. The call is inside Pyomo 6.10.1 rather than this notebook, and the simulation and fitted values remain reproducible. Recheck this note when either dependency is upgraded.

Note

A note on units. This pyomo.dae model records its units in comments
(# 1/hr, # mol/L, # kJ/mol) rather than with Pyomo’s units= argument, unlike
the dynamic optimization notebooks in


Units in Pyomo.dae Models. That is a deliberate scope decision, not an
oversight: the model is consumed by parmest, which builds the sum-of-squares
objective and clones the model per experiment, and m.T is assigned as a plain Python
attribute rather than a Pyomo Param. Annotating it properly means annotating the
experiment data columns too.

It is worth seeing what the comments are hiding, though. The Arrhenius expression ism.k1 = pyo.Expression(rule=m.A1 * pyo.exp(-m.E1 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T)))

That bare 1000 is a hand-rolled unit conversion: E1 is in kJ/mol and R is in
J/(K·mol), so the activation energy must be multiplied by 1000 to reach joules. Nothing
in the code says so. Get the factor wrong -- or drop it when you refactor -- and the
model still runs, still converges, and returns confidently wrong kinetic parameters.

This is precisely the class of error assert_units_consistent exists to catch. If E1
carried units.kJ / units.mol and R carried units.J / units.K / units.mol, Pyomo
would do the conversion itself and the 1000 would disappear.

The exponent’s argument must also come out dimensionless, which is a free check on
the whole expression:\frac{[\mathrm{kJ}/\mathrm{mol}] \cdot 1000}
     {[\mathrm{J}/(\mathrm{K}\cdot\mathrm{mol})] \cdot [\mathrm{K}]}
= \frac{\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{mol}}{\mathrm{J}/\mathrm{mol}} = 1 .

And note the same ContinuousSet limitation as everywhere else: m.t is initialized
from data["time"] in hours, and there is nowhere to record that. See


Pyomo issue #1790.

import pyomo.contrib.parmest.parmest as parmest
from pyomo.contrib.parmest.experiment import Experiment


def reaction_kinetics_model_dae(data):

    # define Pyomo model
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    m.T = data["T"][0]  # K
    m.CA0 = data["CA0"][0]  # mol/L
    m.R = 8.31446261815324  # J / K / mol

    # # define 'experimental' data timesteps as Pyomo set
    m.t = dae.ContinuousSet(initialize=data["time"].tolist(), bounds=(0, 1))

    # Kinetic parameters to be fitted defined as Pyomo variables
    # Initialized by 'true' values
    m.A1 = pyo.Var(initialize=200, bounds=(100, 300))  # 1/hr
    m.A2 = pyo.Var(initialize=400, bounds=(300, 500))  # 1/hr
    m.E1 = pyo.Var(initialize=10, bounds=(1, 20))  # kJ/mol
    m.E2 = pyo.Var(initialize=15, bounds=(1, 30))  # kJ/mol

    # Concentration variables indexed by time
    m.CA = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=m.CA0)  # mol/L
    m.CB = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=0)  # mol/L
    m.CC = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=0)  # mol/L

    # Derivatives of concentration
    m.dCA = dae.DerivativeVar(m.CA, wrt=m.t)
    m.dCB = dae.DerivativeVar(m.CB, wrt=m.t)
    m.dCC = dae.DerivativeVar(m.CC, wrt=m.t)

    # kinetic rate constants from Arrhenius equation
    m.k1 = pyo.Expression(rule=m.A1 * pyo.exp(-m.E1 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T)))  # 1/hr
    m.k2 = pyo.Expression(rule=m.A2 * pyo.exp(-m.E2 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T)))  # 1/hr

    # Constraints to change concentrations based on kinetics
    @m.Constraint(m.t)
    def CA_rate(m, i):

        return m.dCA[i] == -m.k1 * m.CA[i]

    @m.Constraint(m.t)
    def CB_rate(m, i):

        return m.dCB[i] == m.k1 * m.CA[i] - m.k2 * m.CB[i]

    @m.Constraint(m.t)
    def CC_rate(m, i):

        return m.dCC[i] == m.k2 * m.CB[i]

    return m


class ReactionKineticsExperiment_dae(Experiment):

    def __init__(self, data):  # , experiment_number):
        self.data = data
        self.model = None

    def create_model(self):
        self.model = m = reaction_kinetics_model_dae(self.data)
        return m

    def finalize_model(self):
        m = self.model

        # Initial Conditions
        m.CA0 = self.data["CA0"][0]
        m.T = self.data["T"][0]

        m.CA[0].fix(m.CA0)
        m.CB[0].fix(0.0)
        m.CC[0].fix(0.0)

        # Initialize the model with simulator
        sim = dae.Simulator(m, package="casadi")
        tsim, profiles = sim.simulate(numpoints=100, integrator="idas")

        sim.initialize_model()

        # Discretize model using collocation
        discretizer = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation")
        discretizer.apply_to(m, wrt=m.t, nfe=20, ncp=4, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU")

        return m

    def label_model(self):
        m = self.model

        m.experiment_outputs = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.experiment_outputs.update(
            (m.CA[t], self.data["CA"][ind]) for ind, t in enumerate(self.data["time"])
        )
        m.experiment_outputs.update(
            (m.CB[t], self.data["CB"][ind]) for ind, t in enumerate(self.data["time"])
        )
        m.experiment_outputs.update(
            (m.CC[t], self.data["CC"][ind]) for ind, t in enumerate(self.data["time"])
        )

        m.unknown_parameters = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.unknown_parameters.update(
            (k, pyo.value(k)) for k in [m.A1, m.A2, m.E1, m.E2]
        )

        return m

    def get_labeled_model(self):
        m = self.create_model()
        m = self.finalize_model()
        m = self.label_model()

        return m

parmest estimates the local parameter covariance from the reduced Hessian:cov = pest.cov_est(method="reduced_hessian")

In Pyomo 6.10, covariance is a separate calculation; do not pass the deprecated calc_cov=True argument to theta_est(). The matrix describes local uncertainty near the fitted parameters. It does not diagnose model-form error or make a poorly informative experiment informative. See 

Kang et al. (2019) for the reduced-Hessian approach.

# run parmest

exp_list = []

for i in range(
    16
):  # making a list of different experiments, each exp has corresponding data
    df = pd.read_csv(file_name_generic.format(i + 1), index_col=0)
    # print(df.head())
    exp_list.append(ReactionKineticsExperiment(df))

pest = parmest.Estimator(exp_list, obj_function="SSE")

obj, theta = pest.theta_est()

# Pyomo 6.10: the calc_cov/cov_n arguments to theta_est() are deprecated;
# the covariance matrix is now computed by a separate method.
cov = pest.cov_est(method="reduced_hessian")
# print(cov)

# print(theta)


print("===  Parameter values  ===")
print("A1 = {:0.3f} 1/hr".format(theta["A1"]))
print("A2 = {:0.3f} 1/hr".format(theta["A2"]))
print("E1 = {:0.3f} kJ/mol".format(theta["E1"]))
print("E2 = {:0.3f} kJ/mol".format(theta["E2"]))

The Fisher information matrix, \mathbf{FIM}, is calculated as the inverse of the parameter covariance matrix:
\mathbf{FIM} = {(\mathbf{Cov}.)}^{-1}

Because the FIM is real and symmetric, its eigendecomposition is \mathbf{FIM} = \mathbf{v} \boldsymbol{\lambda} \mathbf{v}^T, where the columns of \mathbf{v} are orthonormal eigenvectors and \boldsymbol{\lambda} is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. Each eigenvector component corresponds to a fitted parameter in the order used by theta_names. Its magnitude shows how strongly that parameter participates in the eigenvector’s direction.

The eigenvector corresponding to the smallest FIM eigenvalue is the direction of least information and greatest local covariance variance, since the covariance eigenvalues are the reciprocals of the FIM eigenvalues. A parameter with a large component in this direction is therefore weakly identified (or sloppy): locally, changes along this combined parameter direction have the least effect on model fit. This is a local linearized conclusion, not a guarantee that fixing one parameter leaves the nonlinear model unchanged. See 

Laky et al. (2026), Section 2.2, equations (12)--(14).

# Fisher information matrix can be computed using the inverse of the reduced Hessian
# defining the names of the parameters in a list
theta_names = ["A1", "A2", "E1", "E2"]

fim = np.linalg.inv(cov)

# Eigen decomposition of the Fisher information matrix
# The Fisher information matrix is symmetric, so use eigh: it guarantees real
# eigenvalues, whereas the general-purpose eig returns a complex dtype.
eig_values, eig_vectors = np.linalg.eigh(fim)

for i, eig in enumerate(eig_values):
    print("***************************************************************")
    print("\nEigen value: {:0.3e}\n".format(eig))
    print("=== Eigen vector elements with corresponding parameter names ===\n")
    print("------------------------------")
    print("| Vector element | Parameter |")
    print("------------------------------")
    # Column i of eig_vectors is the eigenvector for eig_values[i], so the
    # element belonging to theta_names[j] is eig_vectors[j, i], not [i, j].
    for j, theta_name in enumerate(theta_names):
        if eig_vectors[j, i] < 0.0:
            print("|   {:0.3e}   |    {}     |".format(eig_vectors[j, i], theta_name))
        else:
            print("|   {:0.3e}    |    {}     |".format(eig_vectors[j, i], theta_name))
    print("\n")



The eigenvector for the smallest eigenvalue is dominated by A2 and then A1. Thus the locally least-informed combined direction primarily trades off those two parameters. This suggests that A2 and A1 participate most strongly in the weakly identified direction; it does not, by itself, define an invariant ranking of individual-parameter identifiability.

Bootstrap resampling approximates sampling variability without relying only on the local quadratic covariance approximation:

resample the experiments with replacement;

refit the parameters for each resample; and

summarize the empirical parameter distribution.

Use a fixed seed for reproducibility. The 

Pyomo ParmEst guide documents theta_est_bootstrap() and the companion plotting tools.

# create Estimator object

pest = parmest.Estimator(exp_list, obj_function="SSE", tee=False)

### Parameter estimation with bootstrap resampling

# seed= makes the resampling reproducible (Pyomo style guide, section 8)
bootstrap_theta = pest.theta_est_bootstrap(10, seed=1234)
print(bootstrap_theta.head())



Once the parameter estimates are generated through bootstrap resampling, we can visualize the estimates using the pairwise_plot() function as follows:

pyomo.contrib.parmest.graphics.pairwise_plot(
    bootstrap_theta, title="Bootstrap theta estimates"
)



Confidence regions can be plotted around the bootstrap estimates for various distributions with confidence \alpha.

# plot bootstrap parameter estimates with confidence intervals
pyomo.contrib.parmest.graphics.pairwise_plot(
    bootstrap_theta,
    theta,
    0.8,
    ["MVN", "KDE", "Rect"],
    title="Bootstrap theta with confidence regions",
)

A likelihood-ratio region retains parameter vectors whose loss is not significantly worse than the optimum. Unlike the reduced-Hessian ellipse, it can reveal curvature and asymmetry in a nonlinear estimation problem.

Here we evaluate the objective at candidate parameter vectors, apply likelihood_ratio_test(), and plot the accepted region.

from itertools import product

### Likelihood ratio test

# generate arrays of parameter values
A1 = np.arange(180.0, 190.0, 1.0)
A2 = np.arange(395.0, 405.0, 1.0)
E1 = np.arange(5.0, 15.0, 1.0)
E2 = np.arange(10.0, 20.0, 1.0)

# format parameter values into a pandas dataframe to be provided as input to calculate
# corresponding objective function values
# theta_vals = pd.DataFrame(list(product(A1, A2, E1, E2)), columns=theta_names)
theta_vals = bootstrap_theta
obj_at_theta = pest.objective_at_theta(theta_vals)
print(obj_at_theta.head())



LR = pest.likelihood_ratio_test(obj_at_theta, obj, [0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95])
print(LR.head())



The likelihood ratio test results with confidence \alpha can be visualized as follows:

pyomo.contrib.parmest.graphics.pairwise_plot(
    LR, theta, 0.8, title="LR results within 80% confidence region"
)

records.content:
Consider two chemical reactions that convert molecule A to desired product B and a less valuable side-product C:A \overset{k_1}{\rightarrow} B \overset{k_2}{\rightarrow} C

Goal:

Design a large-scale continuous reactor that maximizes the production of B.


The rate laws for these two chemical reactions are:r_A = -k_1 C_Ar_B = k_1 C_A - k_2 C_Br_C = k_2 C_B

Here, C_A, C_B, and C_C are the concentrations of each species.

The rate constants k_1 and k_2 depend on temperature as follows:k_1 = A_1 \exp \left({\frac{-1000 E_1}{R T}} \right)k_2 = A_2 \exp \left({\frac{-1000 E_2}{R T}}\right)

where:

A_1 [\mathrm{hr}^{-1}], A_2 [\mathrm{hr}^{-1}], E_1 [kJ/mol], and E_2 [kJ/mol] are fitted model parameters.

R [J/mol K] is the ideal-gas constant.

T [K] is absolute temperature.

Objective:

Using the Pyomo ecosystem, we would like to perform uncertainty quantification and design of experiments on a small-scale batch reactor to infer parameters A_1, A_2, E_1, and E_2.

records.content:
The concentrations in a batch reactor evolve with time and are modeled by the following differential equations:\frac{d C_A}{dt} = r_A = -k_1 C_A(t)\frac{d C_B}{dt} = r_B = k_1 C_A(t) - k_2 C_B(t)\frac{d C_C}{dt} = r_C = k_2 C_B(t)

We have now established a linear system of differential equations. Next we can write our initial conditions where we assume the feed is only species A such that:C_A(t=0) = C_{A0}, \quad C_B(t=0) = 0, \quad C_C(t=0) = 0

When k_1 and k_2 are at constant temperature, we have the following analytic solution:C_A(t) = C_{A0} \exp(-k_1 t)C_B(t) = \frac{k_1}{k_2 - k_1} C_{A0} \left[\exp(-k_1 t) - \exp(-k_2 t) \right]C_C(t) = C_{A0} - \frac{k_2}{k_2 - k_1} C_{A0} \exp(-k_1 t) + \frac{k_1}{k_2 - k_1} \exp(-k_2 t) C_{A0} = C_{A0} - C_{A}(t) - C_{B}(t)

See the following for more information on batch reactors:

Batch Reactor: 

AIChE / 

Wikipedia

This mathematical model is comprised of a system of differential algebraic equations (DAEs). This system will be solved using Pyomo.DAE.

See the following notebooks from CBE 60499 regarding Pyomo.DAE:

Dynamic Optimization Overview

Dynamic Optimization Example

The experiment class follows Pyomo’s Experiment interface:

create_model() builds the equations and variables.

finalize_model() fixes nominal parameters, applies collocation, and completes the square simulation model.

label_model() attaches the four required suffixes: experiment inputs, experiment outputs, unknown parameters, and measurement errors.

get_labeled_model() returns the finished model to Pyomo.DoE.

The suffix values have specific meanings. Unknown-parameter values are nominal values, and measurement_error stores the measurement standard deviation, not its variance or a least-squares weight. Here each concentration measurement has standard deviation 0.01 mol/L.

class ReactorExperiment(Experiment):
    def __init__(
        self,
        t_control=None,
        control_val=None,
        t_range=None,
        CA_init=5,
        C_init=None,
        theta_pe=None,
        NFE=32,
        ncp=3,
    ):
        """
        Arguments:
        ---------
        t_control: time-dependent design (control) variables, a list of control timepoints
        control_val: control design variable values T at corresponding timepoints
        t_range: time range, h
        CA_init: time-independent design (control) variable, an initial value for CA
        C_init: An initial value for C
        theta_pe: optimized parmest parameters for the arrhenius kinetic equations
        NFE: number of finite elements in the discretizer
        ncp: number of collocation points per finite element in the discretizer
        """
        if t_control is None:
            t_control = [0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.375, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75, 0.875, 1]
        if control_val is None:
            control_val = [500, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300]
        if t_range is None:
            t_range = [0, 1]
        if C_init is None:
            C_init = [5, 0, 0]
        if theta_pe is None:
            theta_pe = {"A1": 85, "A2": 370, "E1": 8, "E2": 15}

        self.t_range = t_range
        self.CA_init = CA_init
        self.C_init = C_init
        self.NFE = NFE
        self.ncp = ncp
        self.t_control = t_control
        self.control_val = control_val
        self.theta_pe = theta_pe
        self.model = None

    def create_model(self):
        # model build
        m = self.model = pyo.ConcreteModel()

        # concentration intialization
        m.CA_init = self.CA_init

        # Time-independent design variable
        m.t0 = pyo.Set(initialize=[0])
        m.CA0 = pyo.Var(
            m.t0, initialize=self.CA_init, bounds=(0, 5.0), domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals
        )  # mol/L

        # parameters
        m.R = pyo.Param(mutable=False, initialize=8.314)

        # variables
        m.t = ContinuousSet(bounds=(self.t_range[0], self.t_range[1]))

        # Parameter list
        para_list = ["A1", "A2", "E1", "E2"]
        m.para_list = para_list
        # Define parameters as Param
        m.A1 = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
        m.A2 = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
        m.E1 = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
        m.E2 = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)

        # Concentration variables under perturbation
        m.C_set = pyo.Set(initialize=["CA", "CB", "CC"])
        m.CA = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=self.C_init[0], domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
        m.CB = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=self.C_init[1], domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
        m.CC = pyo.Var(m.t, initialize=self.C_init[2], domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)

        # Time derivatives
        m.dCAdt = DerivativeVar(m.CA, wrt=m.t)
        m.dCBdt = DerivativeVar(m.CB, wrt=m.t)
        m.dCCdt = DerivativeVar(m.CC, wrt=m.t)

        # Time-dependent design variable, initialized with the first control value
        m.t_control = self.t_control
        # Control time points
        m.t_con = pyo.Set(initialize=m.t_control)
        # Controls
        controls = {}
        for i, t in enumerate(self.t_control):
            controls[t] = self.control_val[i]

        def T_initial(m, t):
            if t in m.t_con:
                return controls[t]
            else:
                # count how many control points are before the current t;
                # locate the nearest neighbouring control point before this t
                j = -1
                for t_con in m.t_con:
                    if t > t_con:
                        j += 1
                neighbour_t = m.t_control[j]
                return controls[neighbour_t]

        m.T = pyo.Var(
            m.t, initialize=T_initial, bounds=(300, 700), domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals
        )

        m.kp1 = pyo.Var(m.t, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
        m.kp2 = pyo.Var(m.t, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)

        @m.Constraint(m.t)
        def kp1_cons(m, t):
            return m.kp1[t] == m.A1 * pyo.exp(-m.E1 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T[t]))

        @m.Constraint(m.t)
        def kp2_cons(m, t):
            return m.kp2[t] == m.A2 * pyo.exp(-m.E2 * 1000 / (m.R * m.T[t]))

        @m.Constraint(m.C_set, m.t)
        def dCdt_rule(m, y, t):
            """
            Calculate CA in Jacobian matrix analytically

            Arguments:
            y: CA, CB, CC
            t: timepoints

            Return:
            m: Pyomo model
            """
            if y == "CA":
                return m.dCAdt[t] == -m.kp1[t] * m.CA[t]
            elif y == "CB":
                return m.dCBdt[t] == m.kp1[t] * m.CA[t] - m.kp2[t] * m.CB[t]
            elif y == "CC":
                return m.dCCdt[t] == m.kp2[t] * m.CB[t]

        @m.Constraint(m.t)
        def alge(m, t):
            """
            The algebraic equation for mole balance

            Arguments:
            t: time

            Return:
            m: Pyomo model
            """
            return m.CA[t] + m.CB[t] + m.CC[t] == m.CA0[0]

    def finalize_model(self):
        m = self.model

        # fix Arrhenius parameters (any changes necessary will be done automatically by pyomo- this is necessary to ensure that the model DoF is 0)
        m.A1.fix(self.theta_pe["A1"])
        m.A2.fix(self.theta_pe["A2"])
        m.E1.fix(self.theta_pe["E1"])
        m.E2.fix(self.theta_pe["E2"])

        # fix the starting concentration value (similar to Arrhenius parameters, though not strictly necessary in the same way)
        m.CA0.fix(self.CA_init)

        # Boundary Conditions
        m.CB[0.0].fix(0.0)
        m.CC[0.0].fix(0.0)

        @m.Constraint(m.t)
        def T_control(m, t):
            """
            T at interval timepoint equal to the T of the control time point at the beginning of this interval
            Count how many control points are before the current t;
            locate the nearest neighbouring control point before this t

            Arguments:
            m: model
            t: time

            Return:
            m: Pyomo model
            """
            if t in m.t_con:
                return pyo.Constraint.Skip
            else:
                j = -1
                for t_con in m.t_con:
                    if t > t_con:
                        j += 1
                neighbour_t = m.t_control[j]
                return m.T[t] == m.T[neighbour_t]

        # Discretization
        discretizer = pyo.TransformationFactory("dae.collocation")
        discretizer.apply_to(m, nfe=self.NFE, ncp=self.ncp, wrt=m.t)
        for t in m.t:
            m.dCdt_rule["CC", t].deactivate()

    def label_model(self):
        m = self.model

        # Concentration measurement labels
        m.experiment_outputs = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.experiment_outputs.update((m.CA[t], None) for t in m.t_control)
        m.experiment_outputs.update((m.CB[t], None) for t in m.t_control)
        m.experiment_outputs.update((m.CC[t], None) for t in m.t_control)

        # measurement values
        m.measurement_error = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.measurement_error.update((m.CA[t], 0.01) for t in m.t_control)
        m.measurement_error.update((m.CB[t], 0.01) for t in m.t_control)
        m.measurement_error.update((m.CC[t], 0.01) for t in m.t_control)

        # Design variables
        m.experiment_inputs = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.experiment_inputs.update((m.CA0[t], None) for t in m.t0)
        m.experiment_inputs.update((m.T[t], None) for t in m.t_control)

        # unkown parameter labels
        m.unknown_parameters = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
        m.unknown_parameters.update((k, pyo.value(k)) for k in [m.A1, m.A2, m.E1, m.E2])

    def get_labeled_model(self):
        if self.model is None:
            self.create_model()
            self.finalize_model()
            self.label_model()
        return self.model

Recall the unknown model parameters, \boldsymbol{\theta} = (A_1, A_2, E_1, E_2).

Our goal is to maximize the precision of \boldsymbol{\theta} by measuring the model outputs called \mathbf{y} for the initial conditions at each time point such that \mathbf{y}(t)=(C_A(t), C_B(t), C_C(t)).

The code block below generates an experiment and then runs the DOE module on the generated experiment class. It uses a relative perturbation of 0.001 and central differences. Central differences are second-order accurate for a smooth response, but 0.001 is a starting value rather than a universal choice: a sensitivity check should confirm that truncation and roundoff errors are acceptably balanced for this model.

experiment = ReactorExperiment()
doe_obj = DesignOfExperiments(
    experiment=experiment,
    fd_formula="central",
    step=1e-3,
    objective_option=ObjectiveLib.determinant,
    scale_constant_value=1.0,
    scale_nominal_param_value=True,
    improve_cholesky_roundoff_error=True,
    tee=False,
)

The DesignOfExperiments object now holds the labeled experiment, finite-difference settings, scaling convention, objective, and solver options. We will first inspect the FIM at the nominal design, then explore the design space, and optimize only once at the end.

The design variables are the initial concentration and the piecewise-constant temperature profile. Pyomo.DoE will maximize the selected FIM criterion subject to the dynamic model and design bounds.

This is a local design: the sensitivities and FIM are evaluated near the nominal Arrhenius parameters supplied to the experiment.

records.content:
The next section connects the software output to determinants, eigenvalues, and the FIM. Useful refreshers are:

determinants and eigenvalues in this course; and

linear algebra in Data and Computing.

Objective:

The FIM measures the information content for the unknown parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} from the model output y_i such that:y_i=f(\boldsymbol{\psi}_i, \boldsymbol{\theta})

In order to quantify the uncertainty of the estimated parameters for parameter estimation, consider the covariance matrix for the parameters:\mathbf{V}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\psi}) = \left[\sum_{r}^{N_{r}}\sum_{r'}^{N_{r}} \tilde{\sigma}_{(r,r')}\mathbf{Q}_{r}^{T}\mathbf{Q}_{r'}+\mathbf{V}_{\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{-1}\right]^{-1}

where:

\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}: estimated parameters.

\tilde{\sigma}: element in the inverse of the observational covariance matrix.

r, r': measurements.

\mathbf{Q}: dynamic sensitivity.

\mathbf{V}_{\theta}: prior information.

The inverse of \mathbf{V} estimates the FIM such that: \mathbf{V}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\psi}) = [\mathbf{M}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\psi})]^{-1}

where:

\boldsymbol{\psi}: design vector from a DAE system 

For sequential design of experiments, consider prior information such that after N_e experiments, the FIM is calculated by:\mathbf{M}= \sum_{k=1}^{N_e-1}\mathbf{M}_k+\mathbf{M}_{N_e}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\psi}_{N_e}) = \mathbf{K}+\mathbf{M}_{N_e}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\psi}_{N_e})

where:

N_e - 1: previous experiments

\mathbf{K}: constant matrix encoding information from all N_e - 1

Key Takeaways:
In regards to parameter estimation,

A large FIM value denotes more information about \boldsymbol{\theta} is gained from the model.

See the following notebook from CBE 60258 for more information on FIM:

Computing FIM
This method computes a FIM-based MBDoE optimization problem with no degrees of freedom.

In our results, we will use the five optimality conditions below:

Optimality Condition

Definition

Computation

Geometry

D-Optimality

Maximizes the determinant of \mathbf{M} or minimizes the determinant of \mathbf{V}

Determinant

Minimizes the volume of the  confidence ellipsoid

A-Optimality

Minimizes the trace of \mathbf{V}, equivalently \mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{M}^{-1}) = \sum_i 1/\lambda_i

Trace of the inverse

Reduces average marginal variance and emphasizes poorly informed directions

Pseudo-A-Optimality

Maximizes the trace of \mathbf{M}, i.e. \sum_i \lambda_i. Not equivalent to A-optimality

Trace

Dominated by the largest eigenvalue; a numerically cheap surrogate

E-Optimality

Maximizes \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{M}), equivalently minimizing the largest covariance eigenvalue

Minimum eigenvalue

Reduces uncertainty in the least-informed parameter combination and the confidence ellipsoid’s major axis

Modified E-Optimality

Minimizes \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{M})/\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{M})

Condition number

Reduces directional imbalance (ellipsoid eccentricity) without necessarily increasing total information

Note on A-optimality. Maximizing \mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{M}) is not the same as A-optimality, although it is often identified as such. A-optimality minimizes \mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{M}^{-1}) = \sum_i 1/\lambda_i, which is dominated by the smallest eigenvalue, so it prioritizes poorly-informed directions. Maximizing \mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{M}) = \sum_i \lambda_i is dominated by the largest eigenvalue and is called pseudo-A-optimality; it is cheap because it needs no inversion or eigenvalues. See Laky, Lilonfe, Martin, Klise, Nicholson, Siirola & Dowling, Optimal experimental design using eigenvalue-based criteria with Pyomo.DoE, Digital Discovery (2026), DOI 10.1039/d6dd00160b, Table 1 and eqns (12) and (18).

See the following notebooks from CBE 60499 and CBE 60258 for more information on condition numbers:

Condition Number: 

CBE 60499 / 

CBE 60258

For additional information on condition number and trace:

Wikipedia: 

Condition Number / 

Trace

Now that our analysis is complete, we can take a further look at our results.  First, the initial FIM matrix, with only the diagonal populated.

doe_obj.fim_initial



Next, let’s take a look at a single FIM matrix.  After the experiment is run, the FIM is populated with values showing that the experiment has yielded information about the 4 Arrhenius parameters.

records.content:
A full-factorial sweep evaluates the FIM on a design grid before continuous optimization. It helps us:

see whether the criterion has multiple attractive regions;

check whether an optimizer’s result is plausible; and

understand the computational cost of adding design dimensions.

For readability, vary only the initial concentration and the first temperature checkpoint here.

# Make design ranges to compute the full factorial design
design_ranges = {"CA0[0]": [0.5, 5, 10], "T[0]": [300, 700, 9]}



Evaluate the grid sequentially. Each grid point requires a square simulation and sensitivity calculation, so this step is more expensive than evaluating the response model alone.

# Compute the full factorial design with the sequential FIM calculation
doe_obj.compute_FIM_full_factorial(design_ranges=design_ranges, method="sequential")



Why do this?  It is useful to get an idea of the optimum values for the design variables, but by evaluating each over a range and filling in a full rectangle of results, we get an idea of the shape of the optimization surface.  We also get an idea of what directions of optimization work on each of the optimalities, and whether the overall optimal solution performs badly at any of the metrics.

    sensitivity_design_variables=["CA0[0]", "T[0]"],

    },
    title_text="Reactor Example",

As an example, the reactor-case D-optimality figure shows:

The most informative region is around C_{A0}=5.0 \ \text{M}, T=500.0 \ \text{K}.
The least informative region is around C_{A0}=0.5 \ \text{M}, T=300.0 \ \text{K}.

This can be a lot to take in at once, but think of each square within each plot as a unique experiment.  To know what the optimality values are for an experiment set at an initial A concentration of 2.5 M and a temperature of 700 K, merely requires finding that location on the plots.

The power of viewing multiple experiments at once is that it gives a more contextualized view of the design space.  Viewing one value is also possible, but it tells less of a complete story out of the surrounding space’s context.

# Keep solver output compact for the course website.

# Notice we specified the "determinant" objective when creating the DesignOfExperiments object
doe_obj.run_doe()

Next, we can summarize the FIM.

def results_summary(result):
    """Summarize the results of the experiment design
    Arguments:
    ----------
    result: The FIM matrix from the optimized experiment

    Returns:
    --------
    None

    Note: Taken from https://github.com/dowlinglab/pyomo-doe/blob/main/notebooks/tclab_pyomo.py

    """
    # The FIM is symmetric, so use eigh: it guarantees real eigenvalues in
    # ascending order, whereas the general-purpose eig returns a complex dtype.
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(result)

    min_eig = min(eigenvalues)

    print("======Results Summary======")
    print("Four design criteria log10() value:")
    # NOTE: trace(FIM) is PSEUDO-A-optimality, not A-optimality.
    # A-optimality is min trace(FIM^-1). See Laky et al., Digital Discovery (2026),
    # Table 1, eqns (12) and (18).
    print("Pseudo-A-optimality:", np.log10(np.trace(result)))
    print("D-optimality:", np.log10(np.linalg.det(result)))
    print("E-optimality:", np.log10(min_eig))
    print("Modified E-optimality:", np.log10(np.linalg.cond(result)))
    print("\nFIM:\n", np.array(result))

    print("\neigenvalues:\n", eigenvalues)

    print("\neigenvectors:\n", eigenvectors)

def plot_experiment_results(model):
    """
    Plot the results of the experiment design

    Arguments:
    ----------
    model: The Pyomo model

    Returns:
    --------
    None
    """
    # Extract the timepoints
    time = np.array([pyo.value(t) for t in model.t])

    # Extract the concentrations
    CA = np.array([pyo.value(model.CA[t]) for t in model.t])
    CB = np.array([pyo.value(model.CB[t]) for t in model.t])
    CC = np.array([pyo.value(model.CC[t]) for t in model.t])
    T = np.array([pyo.value(model.T[t]) for t in model.t])

    # Create the plot
    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()

    # Plot concentrations on the left y-axis
    # Okabe-Ito colours paired with distinct linestyles (see figures/README.md):
    # blue/green/purple alone collapse to nearly the same grey in print.
    ax1.plot(time, CA, label="$C_A$", color="black", linestyle="-")
    ax1.plot(time, CB, label="$C_B$", color="#0072B2", linestyle="--")
    ax1.plot(time, CC, label="$C_C$", color="#E69F00", linestyle="-.")
    ax1.set_xlabel("Time (h)")
    ax1.set_ylabel("Concentration (mol/L)")
    ax1.legend(loc="upper left")

    # Create a second y-axis for temperature
    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
    ax2.plot(time, T, label="$T$", color="#D55E00", linestyle=":")
    ax2.set_ylabel("Temperature (K)", color="#D55E00")
    ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#D55E00")

    # Add legend for the temperature line
    ax2.legend(loc="upper right")

We can interpret Newton-type methods for unconstrained optimization as root finding of \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}.

At iteration k, we assemble an approximation to f(\mathbf{x}) using a Taylor series expansion:f(\mathbf{x}^k + \mathbf{p}^k) \approx f(\mathbf{x}^k) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^k)^T \mathbf{p}^k + \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p}^k)^T (\mathbf{B}^k) \mathbf{p}^k

Set the gradient of this quadratic model to zero, \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^k)+\mathbf{B}^k\mathbf{p}^k=\mathbf{0}. For nonsingular \mathbf{B}^k, the resulting linear solve gives:\mathbf{p}^k = -(\mathbf{B}^k)^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^k)

The choice of \mathbf{B}^k determines the algorithm classification:

Pure Newton Method, \mathbf{B}^k = \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^k)

Steepest Descent, \mathbf{B}^k = \frac{1}{\alpha} \mathbf{I}, where scalar \alpha is sometimes known as the dampening factor

Levenberg-Marquardt, \mathbf{B}^k = \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^k) + \delta \mathbf{I}, where scalar \delta is chosen to ensure \mathbf{B}^k is positive definite.

Broyden Methods, \mathbf{B}^{k} is approximated using history of gradient evaluations, i.e., \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^0), ... \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^k). We will study the SR1 and BFGS formulas in this family of methods.

This section explores how choosing \mathbf{B}^k impacts the shape of the approximation and calculated step.

Define a function that:

Computes the i. Newton, ii. Levenberg-Marquardt and iii. Steepest Descent Step for a given starting point x_0

Plots the step in terms of f(x) and f'(x)

Why does f(x) increase for all of the steps?

Explain Newton-type method in the context of root finding for \nabla f(x) = 0 using the second plot.

For \mathbf{p}^k=-(\mathbf{B}^k)^{-1}

Thus \mathbf{p}^k is a descent direction whenever 
abla f(\mathbf{x}^k)
e\mathbf{0}. A line search still chooses a step length that produces sufficient decrease. (Biegler, Eqs. 3.2--3.5, p. 41.)
Excerpts from Section 3.4 in Biegler (2010).

Let f\in C^1(D) on an open D, with \mathbf{x}\in D. At a fixed direction, define \phi(\alpha)=f(\mathbf{x}+\alpha\mathbf{p}) and d=\phi'(0)=\nabla f(\mathbf{x})^T\mathbf{p}<0. For fixed 0<\eta<1, the Armijo condition for a feasible positive length \alpha is\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+\eta\alpha d.

Here feasible means that the trial point lies in the objective domain. The condition requires a fraction of the initial linear-model decrease.

Why short steps pass. Differentiability along the ray gives \phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)=\alpha d+r(\alpha), where r(\alpha)/\alpha\to0 as \alpha\downarrow0. Put c=-(1-\eta)d>0; positivity follows from \eta<1 and d<0. By the remainder limit, there is \bar\alpha>0 such that |r(\alpha)|\le c\alpha/2 for 0<\alpha<\bar\alpha. Openness of D lets us reduce \bar\alpha so every trial in that interval is feasible. Subtract the Armijo right-hand side:\phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)-\eta\alpha d
=(1-\eta)\alpha d+r(\alpha)
=-c\alpha+r(\alpha)\le-\frac{c\alpha}{2}<0.

Thus every sufficiently short positive step along this descent direction passes Armijo. The test also permits unnecessarily small steps if the selection rule has no lower-size control.

Use 0<\eta<1/2 for the Goldstein--Armijo conditions, which add the lower value bound:\phi(0)+(1-\eta)\alpha d\le\phi(\alpha)\le\phi(0)+\eta\alpha d.

Near zero the actual curve initially drops faster than the lower line, so that line excludes very short steps. For the profile \phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)=-\alpha+\alpha^2/2, \eta=1/4, the positive accepted interval is [1/2,3/2].

Alternatively, choose \eta<\zeta<1. Wolfe combines Armijo with \phi'(\alpha)\ge\zeta d; strong Wolfe combines it with |\phi'(\alpha)|\le\zeta|d|. These require a directional derivative at a trial point. Goldstein uses function values. On a nonconvex ray the accepted set need not be one connected interval; the brackets in a particular figure describe that example.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eqs. (3.31)--(3.34), pp. 47--48, with the ordering correction in the errata; Nocedal and Wright (2006), Eqs. (3.4), (3.6)--(3.7), (3.11), pp. 33--36. The general Armijo range is 0<\eta<1; the strict \eta<1/2 choice also supplies the margin used in the unit-step result below.

hierarchy.lvl3: Global convergence: gradient norms and the descent angle
Global convergence: gradient norms and the descent angle

records.content:
Use Euclidean vector norms and their induced matrix norm. Consider a nonterminated sequence of descent steps, with f bounded below and continuously differentiable, and its gradient uniformly Lipschitz on an open set containing the initial sublevel set. Lipschitz continuity means that some L>0 satisfies \|\nabla f(\mathbf{u})-\nabla f(\mathbf{v})\|\le L\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\| for every pair \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} in that open set. The acceptance parameters are fixed across the sequence. Writed_k=(\mathbf{g}^k)^T\mathbf{p}^k<0,\qquad
\cos\vartheta_k=\frac{-d_k}{\|\mathbf{g}^k\|\|\mathbf{p}^k\|}.

For Goldstein--Armijo steps, the Zoutendijk sum is finite:\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\cos^2\vartheta_k\|\mathbf{g}^k\|^2<\infty.

Here is the value-based proof. Fix an iteration and let \beta be the first positive crossing of the Goldstein lower line before the accepted \alpha. Such a crossing exists because the curve starts below that line and the accepted value lies at or above it. On [0,\beta], the curve lies below that line and therefore within the initial sublevel set. The gradient Lipschitz bound gives\phi(\beta)-\phi(0)\le\beta d+\frac{L}{2}\beta^2\|\mathbf{p}\|^2.

At the crossing the left side is (1-\eta)\beta d, so\alpha\ge\beta\ge\frac{2\eta(-d)}{L\|\mathbf{p}\|^2}.

Armijo now suppliesf(\mathbf{x}^k)-f(\mathbf{x}^{k+1})
\ge\eta\alpha_k(-d_k)
\ge\frac{2\eta^2}{L}\cos^2\vartheta_k\|\mathbf{g}^k\|^2.

Summing telescopes the actual decreases, and f has a lower bound. The resulting sum is finite. Biegler’s mean-value proof uses a looser constant; the conclusion is the same. A Wolfe proof instead compares the directional derivatives at the two endpoints, yielding the analogous Zoutendijk result.

For \mathbf p=-\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf g, let m=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf B)>0 and M=\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf B). The inverse Rayleigh bound gives \mathbf g^T\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf g\ge\|\mathbf g\|^2/M. The induced norm gives \|\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf g\|\le\|\mathbf g\|/m. Substituting the numerator’s lower bound and the denominator’s upper bound gives\cos\vartheta
=\frac{\mathbf g^T\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf g}{\|\mathbf g\|\|\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf g\|}
\ge\frac{\|\mathbf g\|^2/M}{\|\mathbf g\|^2/m}
=\frac mM=\frac1{\kappa(\mathbf B)}.

A uniform condition-number bound supplies a fixed c>0 with \cos\vartheta_k\ge c for every iteration. Put a_k=\cos^2\vartheta_k\|\mathbf g^k\|^2\ge0. The Zoutendijk result says \sum_k a_k<\infty. Terms of a convergent nonnegative series satisfy a_k\to0, so0\le c^2\|\mathbf g^k\|^2\le a_k\longrightarrow0.

The squeeze theorem and fixed c>0 give \|\mathbf g^k\|\to0.

Hence \|\mathbf g^k\|\to0. For an accumulation point in the differentiability domain, continuity of the gradient then gives stationarity. This does not by itself prove convergence of the whole iterate sequence, second-order conditions, or global optimality.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Theorem 3.3 and Eqs. (3.35)--(3.42), pp. 48--49; Nocedal and Wright (2006), Theorem 3.2, p. 38, for Wolfe steps. The eigenvalue/norm estimates have their existing home in 

Quasi-Newton Methods; they are applied here to the search angle.

hierarchy.lvl3: Armijo backtracking and the actual visualization code
Armijo backtracking and the actual visualization code

records.content:
The standard reference procedure starts with a descent direction, tries \alpha=1, and, while Armijo fails, replaces \alpha by \rho_{\mathrm{ls}}\alpha, with fixed 0<\rho_{\mathrm{ls}}<1. It accepts the first trial that passes Armijo. The local argument above ensures finite termination along a descent ray. The previous rejected trial prevents uncontrolled overshrinking by the selection rule. If contractions vary, safeguard them between fixed positive lower and upper bounds below one.

This is not a rule to keep shrinking until both Goldstein bounds pass. For \phi(\alpha)-\phi(0)=-\alpha+10\alpha^2, \eta=0.1, Goldstein--Armijo accepts [0.01,0.09]. Halving from one first passes Armijo at 1/16. A contraction by 

10-3 jumps to 0.001, below the Goldstein interval; every further contraction remains below it. To require Goldstein or Wolfe, use a suitable bracketing/selection method that can increase a trial when the lower-size test fails.

The function plot_alpha below is a graphical experiment: it evaluates a finite, linearly spaced grid, scans it downward, exempts its initial full trial from the Goldstein check, and reports a lower-bound failure on later trials. It is not the geometric backtracking algorithm just stated or a general Wolfe solver. Its deliberate ascent-direction and restricted-grid failures remain part of the exercise.

A condition-number bound alone is sufficient in the Goldstein theorem above, but is not sufficient for a unit-step-capped Armijo method: directions can shrink summably even with condition number one. A conventional global Armijo result also controls the scale of the direction, for example by uniform positive lower and upper eigenvalue bounds on \mathbf{B}^k.

Sources: Nocedal and Wright (2006), Algorithm 3.1 and discussion, p. 37; Dennis and Schnabel (1996), Algorithm 6.3.5, p. 126; Biegler (2010), Algorithm 3.2 and the additional Goldstein discussion, p. 50. Safeguarded quadratic/cubic interpolation is detailed below.

Recovery of the fast local rate

Suppose f\in C^2(D) on an open neighborhood D of the limit, and a nonterminated descent sequence with nonzero directions converges to \mathbf{x}^*, \nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*)=\mathbf{0}, and \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^*)\succ0. Use fixed Wolfe parameters 0<\eta<1/2 and \eta<\zeta<1. Let the directions satisfy\frac{\|\mathbf{g}^k+\mathbf{G}^k\mathbf{p}^k\|}{\|\mathbf{p}^k\|}\to0,\qquad
\mathbf{G}^k=\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^k).

For Newton-type solves this is the Dennis--Moré directional condition. Nondegeneracy and the residual condition imply \mathbf{p}^k\to0. They also give d_k=(\mathbf{g}^k)^T\mathbf{p}^k\le-c\|\mathbf{p}^k\|^2 eventually, for some c>0.

Taylor expansion and the small residual givef(\mathbf{x}^k+\mathbf{p}^k)-f(\mathbf{x}^k)
=\frac12d_k+o(\|\mathbf{p}^k\|^2),\qquad
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^k+\mathbf{p}^k)^T\mathbf{p}^k=o(\|\mathbf{p}^k\|^2).

Thus Armijo has negative slack (1/2-\eta)d_k+o(\|\mathbf{p}^k\|^2) when 0<\eta<1/2; the curvature condition also passes for fixed \eta<\zeta<1. Unit steps are eventually admissible. The search must try and accept them to obtain the superlinear rate. Admissibility alone does not force that selection.

The endpoint \eta=1/2 has no Taylor-error margin. For f(x)=x^2+x^3, x<0 near zero, exact Newton gives p=-(2x+3x^2)/(2+6x). Its unit step fails endpoint Armijo, but its half step satisfies Wolfe with \zeta=0.9 for sufficiently small negative x. The half-step recurrence isx^+=\frac{x(2+9x)}{4+12x},\qquad \frac{|x^+|}{|x|}\to\frac12.

It stays negative near zero and converges only linearly despite zero Newton directional residual. We therefore use the conservative strict parameter bound in the handout/reference. The whole-iterate versus directional-error equivalence has its existing full proof in 

Quasi-Newton Methods; the local Newton error proof is in 

Newton Methods.

Sources: Nocedal and Wright (2006), Theorems 3.6--3.7, pp. 46--47; Biegler (2010), Theorem 3.4, p. 50, with nondegeneracy explicit. The endpoint example is an independently derived illustration.

cover -- including one where the line search fails.

Goal: Visualize Armijo and Goldstein conditions for an example.

def plot_alpha(xk, eta_ls=0.25, algorithm="newton", alpha_max=1.0):
    """
    Calculate step and visualize line search conditions

    Arguments:
        xk : initial point (required)
        eta_ls : eta in Goldstein-Armijo conditions
        algorithm : either "newton" or "steepest-descent"
        alpha_max : plots alpha between 0 and alpha_max

    Returns:
        Nothing

    Creates:
        Plot showing function value and line search conditions as a function of alpha
    """

    fxk = f(xk)
    dfxk = df(xk)

    if algorithm == "newton":
        pk = -dfxk / ddf(xk)
    elif algorithm == "steepest-descent":
        pk = -dfxk
    else:
        raise ValueError(
            "algorithm argument must be either 'newton' or 'steepest-descent'"
        )

    print("Considering xk =", xk, "and f(xk) = ", fxk)
    print("Step with", algorithm, "algorithm:")
    print("pk = ", pk)
    print("With full step, xk+1 =", pk + xk, "and f(xk+1) =", f(xk + pk))

    n = 100
    alpha = np.linspace(0, alpha_max, n)
    fval = np.zeros(n)

    for i in range(0, n):
        fval[i] = f(xk + alpha[i] * pk)

    fs = 18
    plt.figure()

    # Evaluate f(x^{k+1}) for different alpha values.
    # Color and linestyle match figures/plots/line-search-conditions.py, the
    # static version of this figure in the course pack: house cycle in order,
    # black solid, blue dashed, orange dash-dot. The linestyles are what make
    # the three series separable in greyscale.
    plt.plot(alpha, fval, color="black", linestyle="-", label=r"$f(x^{k+1})$")

    # Armijo condition
    arm = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(0, n):
        arm[i] = fxk + eta_ls * alpha[i] * dfxk * pk

    plt.plot(alpha, arm, color="#0072B2", linestyle="--", label="Armijo")

    # Goldstein condition
    gold = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(0, n):
        gold[i] = fxk + (1 - eta_ls) * alpha[i] * dfxk * pk

    plt.plot(alpha, gold, color="#E69F00", linestyle="-.", label="Goldstein")

    # Apply backtracking linestep (starting with alpha = alpha_max)
    i = n - 1
    flag = True
    failed = False
    while flag:

        if i < n - 1 and fval[i] < gold[i]:
            flag = False
            print(
                "Line search failed. Goldstein conditions violated. Consider increasing alpha_max."
            )
            failed = True

        # Armijo condition
        if fval[i] < arm[i]:
            flag = False
        else:
            i = i - 1

        if i < 0:
            print("Line search failed. Try decreasing alpha_max.")
            failed = True
            # Stop here. Without this, the loop keeps going with a negative
            # index, which wraps around to the end of the array and reports a
            # second, contradictory diagnosis.
            flag = False

    if not failed:
        print(
            "alphak =",
            alpha[i],
            "with backtracking line search starting at alpha =",
            alpha_max,
        )
        print("f(xk + alphak*pk) =", fval[i])

        plt.scatter(
            alpha[i],
            fval[i],
            marker="x",
            color="black",
            label=r"$\alpha^{k}$ for line search",
        )

    # Labels
    plt.xlabel(r"$\alpha^k$", fontsize=fs)
    plt.ylabel(r"$f(x^k + \alpha^k p^k)$", fontsize=fs)
    plt.grid()
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

plot_alpha(-3, eta_ls=0.25, algorithm="newton", alpha_max=1.5)





Discussion

Why did the backtracking line search stop at \alpha^k =  alpha_max?

Is it possible to find a larger improvement in f(x) with \alpha^k > 1?

plot_alpha(-3, eta_ls=0.25, algorithm="steepest-descent", alpha_max=1e-1)





Discussion

Why did the line search stop where the Armijo conditions are satisfied?

Why not further decrease \alpha^k to achieve a greater improvement in the objective?

plot_alpha(0, eta_ls=0.25, algorithm="newton", alpha_max=1.0)





Discussion

Why does the line search fail?

How could we modify Newton’s method to improve robustness?

plot_alpha(0, eta_ls=0.25, algorithm="steepest-descent", alpha_max=5e-1)





Discussion

How does the region where the Armijo and Goldstein conditions are satisfied change for different values of eta_ls?
Excerpts from Section 3.5 in Biegler (2010).

At iteration k, with \Delta^k>0, the closed ball is \overline B(0,\Delta^k)=\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb R^n:\|\mathbf p\|\le\Delta^k\}. A line search instead restricts its nonzero fixed direction to \{\alpha\mathbf p:\alpha>0\}. With symmetric \mathbf{B}^k, use the Euclidean-ball subproblem\min_{\mathbf{p}}\ m^k(\mathbf{p})=(\mathbf{g}^k)^T\mathbf{p}
+\frac12\mathbf{p}^T\mathbf{B}^k\mathbf{p},
\qquad \|\mathbf{p}\|\le\Delta^k,\quad \Delta^k>0.

The constant f(\mathbf{x}^k) is omitted because it changes neither the minimizer nor the predicted reduction. Weierstrass states that a continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum and maximum; its existing existence discussion is in 

Unconstrained Optimality Conditions. A continuous quadratic therefore attains a minimum on this compact ball even when \mathbf{B}^k is indefinite.

The radius is updated by comparing actual objective reduction with predicted model reduction. Source: Biegler (2010), Eq. (3.49), p. 53; Nocedal and Wright (2006), pp. 68--70.

Choose 0<\kappa_1<\kappa_2<1, 0<\gamma<\min\{1/4,\kappa_1\}, and 0<\Delta^0\le\bar\Delta. Evaluate the current gradient before testing it; a small gradient reports a stationary candidate. For a nonterminated iteration:

Compute a feasible, sufficiently model-reducing step \mathbf{p}^k. Report stagnation together with the gradient norm if its movement is too small.

Compute \operatorname{pred}=m^k(0)-m^k(\mathbf{p}^k)>0. A nonpositive prediction signals a failed subproblem step; do not form a meaningless ratio.

Evaluate \operatorname{ared}=f(\mathbf{x}^k)-f(\mathbf{x}^k+\mathbf{p}^k) and \rho^k=\operatorname{ared}/\operatorname{pred}.

If \rho^k<\kappa_1, set \Delta^{k+1}=\kappa_1\|\mathbf{p}^k\|. If \rho^k>\kappa_2 and the step reaches the boundary, set \Delta^{k+1}=\min(2\Delta^k,\bar\Delta). Otherwise retain the radius.

Accept the trial iterate only if \rho^k>\gamma; otherwise retain the old iterate and recompute a step with the new radius.

Acceptance and radius change have different thresholds. With prediction 10, actual decrease 1.5, \gamma=0.1, \kappa_1=0.25, and step norm 2, the ratio is 0.15: accept the step but shrink the next radius to 0.5. A good interior step need not enlarge the radius because the current bound did not restrict it.

Source: Biegler (2010), Algorithm 3.3, p. 53, adapted to test evaluated quantities and report failed diagnostics. Nocedal and Wright’s Algorithm 4.1, p. 69, uses the closely related shrink rule \Delta^{k+1}=\Delta^k/4, rather than Biegler’s step-norm rule; do not silently mix the two.

Why order the thresholds? Every rejected trial has \rho\le\gamma<\kappa_1, so it triggers a radius decrease. The strict inequality also handles \rho=\gamma. Biegler’s usual choice \kappa_1=1/4 with 0<\gamma<1/4 has this property. His more general parameter list in Algorithm 3.3 does not explicitly state the ordering; the following independently derived example shows why that broader list needs qualification for this update rule.

Consider f(x)=19x^2/20, starting at x=1, with exact gradient g=19/10, model curvature B=1, and radius \Delta=2. The exact model minimizer is the interior step p=-19/10, giving\operatorname{pred}=\frac{361}{200},\qquad
\operatorname{ared}=\frac{361}{2000},\qquad
\rho=\frac1{10}.

Choose \gamma=1/5, \kappa_1=1/20, and \kappa_2=3/4. The trial is rejected because \rho<\gamma, but the radius is retained because \rho\ge\kappa_1 and the expansion condition fails. Reusing the same model repeats the identical rejected step indefinitely, with gradient 19/10. The objective is smooth and bounded below, the model matrices are bounded, and the exact step gives sufficient model reduction. Thus those assumptions alone do not establish stationarity when the thresholds allow rejected steps to keep the radius. This example motivates the strict ordering used above; it does not alter the numerical activity’s default parameters.

The Levenberg--Marquardt path varies a multiplier continuously; dogleg uses straight segments connecting the origin, Cauchy step, and Newton step.

\mathbf{p}^C: Cauchy step

\mathbf{p}^N: Newton step

Let \mathbf B=\mathbf B^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, \mathbf g\in\mathbb R^n, and \Delta>0. A feasible vector \mathbf{p}^* is a global minimum of the quadratic model over the ball if and only if some \delta\ge0 satisfies(\mathbf{B}+\delta\mathbf{I})\mathbf{p}^*=-\mathbf{g},\qquad
\delta(\Delta-\|\mathbf{p}^*\|)=0,\qquad
\mathbf{B}+\delta\mathbf{I}\succeq0.

Feasibility \|\mathbf{p}^*\|\le\Delta is essential. If \delta>0, the boundary is active. The converse fails: a Newton minimum may lie exactly on the boundary with \delta=0. At a singular shifted matrix, use the linear system and an appropriate null-space component, not an undefined inverse.

For sufficiency, put \mathbf h=\mathbf v-\mathbf p^*, where \mathbf v is any feasible comparison point. First expand the quadratic at \mathbf p^* and substitute the shifted stationarity equation \mathbf g+\mathbf B\mathbf p^*=-\delta\mathbf p^*:m(\mathbf v)-m(\mathbf p^*)
=(\mathbf g+\mathbf B\mathbf p^*)^T\mathbf h+\frac12\mathbf h^T\mathbf B\mathbf h
=-\delta(\mathbf p^*)^T\mathbf h+\frac12\mathbf h^T\mathbf B\mathbf h.

Next expand \|\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf p^*+\mathbf h\|^2 and rearrange:2(\mathbf p^*)^T\mathbf h=\|\mathbf v\|^2-\|\mathbf p^*\|^2-\|\mathbf h\|^2.

Substituting this identity into the linear term and combining the quadratic terms givesm(\mathbf v)-m(\mathbf p^*)=
\frac12\mathbf h^T(\mathbf B+\delta\mathbf I)\mathbf h
+\frac{\delta}{2}(\|\mathbf p^*\|^2-\|\mathbf v\|^2)\ge0.

The first term is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. The second is zero if \delta=0; otherwise complementarity puts the candidate on the boundary and feasibility bounds the comparison norm. This certifies the model minimum, not a global minimum of the actual objective. The converse characterization is proved in Nocedal and Wright, pp. 89--91.

Sources: Nocedal and Wright (2006), Theorem 4.1, p. 70; Biegler (2010), Theorem 3.6 and Eq. (3.50), p. 54, with the missing feasibility condition supplied.

For \mathbf{g}\ne\mathbf{0}, the Cauchy point minimizes the quadratic on the feasible steepest-descent ray. Write q=\mathbf{g}^T\mathbf{B}\mathbf{g}. Then\mathbf{p}^C=-\tau_C\mathbf{g},\qquad
\tau_C=\begin{cases}
\min\{\|\mathbf{g}\|^2/q,\Delta/\|\mathbf{g}\|\},&q>0,\\
\Delta/\|\mathbf{g}\|,&q\le0.
\end{cases}

If q\le0, the ray model keeps decreasing, so its best feasible point is the boundary. With q>0, the unconstrained ray minimum is used only when it fits. Define that untruncated vector as \mathbf{p}^U=-\|\mathbf{g}\|^2\mathbf{g}/q.

Biegler Eq. (3.52) calls the untruncated positive-curvature vector a Cauchy step and clips it in the later dogleg rule. Nocedal and Wright’s Cauchy point is already clipped. The formulas above distinguish these roles explicitly.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eq. (3.52), p. 54; Nocedal and Wright (2006), Eqs. (4.11)--(4.12), p. 72.

For \mathbf{B}\succ0, calculate \mathbf{p}^N=-\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{g} by a solve, and let \mathbf{p}^U be the untruncated ray minimum:

If \|\mathbf{p}^N\|\le\Delta, take the full model minimum.

Otherwise, if \Delta\le\|\mathbf{p}^U\|, take \Delta\mathbf{p}^U/\|\mathbf{p}^U\|, the first-leg boundary point.

Otherwise take \mathbf{p}^U+\theta\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{p}^N-\mathbf{p}^U and the second segment intersects the boundary.

The intermediate condition gives 0<\theta<1. Expanding the norm constraint produces\|\mathbf{d}\|^2\theta^2+2\mathbf{d}^T\mathbf{p}^U\theta+
\|\mathbf{p}^U\|^2-\Delta^2=0.

The applicable root is\theta=\frac{-\mathbf{d}^T\mathbf{p}^U+
\sqrt{(\mathbf{d}^T\mathbf{p}^U)^2+
\|\mathbf{d}\|^2(\Delta^2-\|\mathbf{p}^U\|^2)}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|^2}.

This avoids a scalar iteration. In the shared figure, \mathbf{B}=\operatorname{diag}(1,10), \mathbf{g}=(-2,-6)^T, and \Delta=1.5. The inputs give \mathbf{p}^N=(2,0.6)^T, \mathbf{p}^U=\mathbf{p}^C=(20/91,60/91)^T, and \theta\approx0.6434961. The dogleg boundary point and the exact L--M boundary point generally differ; the former approximates the full subproblem.

Both norm growth and model decrease along this path rely on positive definiteness. An indefinite exact Hessian needs a method that can use negative curvature, as detailed in the hard-case reference below.

Sources: Biegler (2010), §3.5.1 and Figure 3.4, p. 55; Nocedal and Wright (2006), Eqs. (4.15)--(4.16), p. 74, and Lemma 4.2, p. 75. The generated picture and numerical implementation have one source in the course figure pipeline.

For f(x)=x^2, x^0=2, the sequence x^k=(-1)^k(1+2^{-k}) has decreasing objective values but two limit points, -1 and 1. Its displacement stays large while the actual decrease tends to zero. Let p_k=x^{k+1}-x^k and take \alpha_k=1. These are descent directions, but their predicted linear decrease has a nonzero asymptotic magnitude. Thus any fixed positive Armijo fraction eventually rejects them.

For x^k=1+2^{-k}, use p_k=-1 and \alpha_k=2^{-(k+1)}. Direct subtraction verifies the recurrence, and the geometric series totals one. The iterates reach the nonstationary limit 1. Actual decrease relative to the initial directional derivative tends to one, so Armijo permits these arbitrarily small steps, while Goldstein or Wolfe eventually rejects them.

The second exponent corrects the inconsistent printed step sequence in Dennis and Schnabel, p. 118. It follows from subtracting consecutive displayed iterates, rather than adopting an index convention silently.

Sources: Dennis and Schnabel (1996), §6.3 and Figure 6.3.2, pp. 117--118; Biegler (2010), §3.4, pp. 47--48.

Write \phi_0=\phi(0), d=\phi'(0)<0, and suppose the positive trial a_1 fails Armijo. Fitq_2(a)=\phi_0+da+Aa^2,\qquad
A=\frac{\phi(a_1)-\phi_0-da_1}{a_1^2}.

If A>0, its minimizer is a_q=-d/(2A). This uses only the initial value/slope and one rejected value. If the fit has no useful positive minimum, use a contraction instead.

After two distinct positive rejected trials, definer_i=\frac{\phi(a_i)-\phi_0-da_i}{a_i^2},\quad
B=\frac{r_1-r_2}{a_1-a_2},\quad A=r_1-Ba_1.

The cubic fit q_3(a)=\phi_0+da+Aa^2+Ba^3 satisfies both values. Solve d+2Aa+3Ba^2=0, selecting a positive stationary point with positive second derivative. If B=0, use the quadratic formula above; a negative discriminant or unusable minimum calls for fallback.

Do not accept a point merely because it minimizes an interpolant. Safeguard the next trial, for example within [0.1a_{\mathrm{current}},0.5a_{\mathrm{current}}], evaluate the actual objective there, and test Armijo again. Safeguards avoid almost unchanged trials and extremely small jumps caused by a poor fit. The two distinct trial values are essential; equal nodes do not define this cubic fit.

A Goldstein/Wolfe search has different lower-size logic: a trial that is too short must be increased or bracketed, not contracted forever. The reference backtracking experiment in the handout with -a+10a^2 demonstrates this distinction.

Sources: Dennis and Schnabel (1996), §6.3.2, pp. 126--128; Biegler (2010), Algorithm 3.2, p. 50, and Exercise 4, p. 61; Nocedal and Wright (2006), §3.5, pp. 56--60.

First suppose \mathbf{B}\succ0, \mathbf{g}\ne\mathbf{0}, and the Newton model minimum lies outside the radius. For \delta\ge0, solve(\mathbf{B}+\delta\mathbf{I})\mathbf{p}(\delta)=-\mathbf{g}.

The norm r(\delta)=\|\mathbf{p}(\delta)\| decreases strictly from its outside value to zero. Solve r(\delta)=\Delta, preferably via the reciprocal secular functionh(\delta)=\frac1{r(\delta)}-\frac1\Delta.

Differentiating the solve gives \mathbf{p}'=-(\mathbf{B}+\delta\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{p}. A second solve (\mathbf{B}+\delta\mathbf{I})\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p} yieldsh'(\delta)=\frac{\mathbf{p}^T\mathbf{q}}{\|\mathbf{p}\|^3}>0.

The same Cholesky factor can serve both solves. Establish a bracket with h(\delta_{\mathrm{lo}})<0<h(\delta_{\mathrm{hi}}), increasing the upper trial until it is large enough. A Newton proposal \delta-h/h' must remain in the admissible bracket; otherwise use a bracketed fallback. Stop at the accuracy appropriate for the model-reduction/feasibility requirement, rather than forcing unnecessary multiplier digits.

The reciprocal form is often nearly linear in the large-shift regime because r(\delta)\sim\|\mathbf{g}\|/\delta. Biegler’s two-or-three-iteration observation concerns a useful approximate root; it is not an iteration bound for every model.

For an indefinite matrix, the positive-definite solve domain starts above \max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}\}. A root may fail to exist in that open domain: the hard case requires the singular endpoint and a null-space correction. Repeatedly increasing a shift cannot repair that missing component.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eq. (3.51), p. 54; Nocedal and Wright (2006), §4.3 and Algorithm 4.3, pp. 85--87.

For symmetric \mathbf{B}\ne0, \mathbf{g}\ne0, use Euclidean/induced norms and lett_0=\min\{\Delta,\|\mathbf{g}\|/\|\mathbf{B}\|\},\qquad
\mathbf{p}_0=-t_0\mathbf{g}/\|\mathbf{g}\|.

Feasibility and comparison. Since \|\mathbf p_0\|=t_0\le\Delta, this trial is feasible and lies on the ray -t\mathbf g. The Cauchy point minimizes over that feasible ray, hence m(\mathbf p^C)\le m(\mathbf p_0).

Substitute into the model. Using \mathbf p_0=-t_0\mathbf g/\|\mathbf g\| givesm(0)-m(\mathbf p^C)\ge m(0)-m(\mathbf p_0)
=t_0\|\mathbf g\|-\frac12\mathbf p_0^T\mathbf B\mathbf p_0.

Bound the quadratic term. The induced norm yields |\mathbf p_0^T\mathbf B\mathbf p_0|\le\|\mathbf B\|\|\mathbf p_0\|^2=\|\mathbf B\|t_0^2. Also t_0\le\|\mathbf g\|/\|\mathbf B\|, som(0)-m(\mathbf p_0)\ge t_0\|\mathbf g\|-\frac12\|\mathbf B\|t_0^2
\ge\frac12t_0\|\mathbf g\|.

Together these inequalities give the same lower bound for the Cauchy reduction. Any step at least as good as Cauchy therefore suppliesm(0)-m(\mathbf{p})\ge\frac12\|\mathbf{g}\|
\min\{\Delta,\|\mathbf{g}\|/\|\mathbf{B}\|\}.

If \mathbf{B}=0, the feasible boundary ray gives reduction \Delta\|\mathbf{g}\| directly; do not divide by its zero norm. If \mathbf{g}=0, first-order stopping/classification is separate, and an indefinite model may still have a negative-curvature reduction.

Exact model minima satisfy the bound. Positive-definite dogleg steps do too, because the chosen point is at least as good as the feasible Cauchy point. A fixed positive fraction of this bound is enough in the general convergence framework.

With bounded model norms, an objective bounded below on the initial sublevel set and globally Lipschitz gradient, the standard trust-region iteration stated above with the ordered thresholds 0<\gamma<\min\{1/4,\kappa_1\} and 0<\kappa_1<\kappa_2<1 and feasible steps satisfying a fixed positive fraction of the displayed Cauchy reduction bound gives \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^k)\|\to0. This is a first-order conclusion; positive-definite approximations do not classify the true limiting Hessian.

Under that Lipschitz hypothesis, for an exact gradient and \|\mathbf{B}\|\le\beta, the model mismatch obeys|\operatorname{ared}-\operatorname{pred}|
\le\frac{L+\beta}{2}\|\mathbf{p}\|^2.

If \|\mathbf{g}\|\ge\varepsilon>0 and the radius is small enough for the radius branch of the sufficient-reduction bound, then|\rho-1|\le\frac{(L+\beta)\Delta}{2c_1\varepsilon}.

Thus an accurate smooth model becomes relatively reliable at sufficiently small radii while the gradient stays large. Persistent collapse suggests inaccurate/noisy derivatives or values, a failed subproblem solve, or a numerically meaningless ratio when prediction is tiny. The ideal smooth proof does not apply unchanged to such errors. Stopping on a tiny radius or step should report the gradient norm, not label a minimum.

Near a nondegenerate minimum, fast local trust-region behavior requires stronger assumptions. Biegler Theorem 3.11 assumes Lipschitz Hessian, convergence to a point satisfying second-order sufficiency, model matrices converging to the limiting Hessian, and asymptotically exact subproblem solves with at least Cauchy reduction. Under that framework the radius bound eventually becomes inactive; it is not an unconditional noncollapse promise.

Sources: Nocedal and Wright (2006), Lemma 4.3, p. 78, and §4.2, pp. 77--84; Biegler (2010), Theorems 3.7--3.8, pp. 55--56, and Theorem 3.11, p. 58.

Suppose \mathbf B is symmetric, \lambda_{\min}<0, and let \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^T. In the positive-definite shifted domain,\mathbf{p}(\delta)=-\sum_i
\frac{\mathbf{v}_i\mathbf{v}_i^T\mathbf{g}}{\lambda_i+\delta},
\qquad \delta>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}\}.

If the gradient has a component in the most-negative eigenspace, the norm can grow without bound as the shift approaches its lower endpoint. If the gradient is orthogonal to that entire eigenspace, the limit can be finite. Orthogonality alone is not enough to say every radius is unreachable: compare the limiting norm with the required radius. The hard case arises when the boundary cannot be reached by a nonsingular shifted solve.

At \delta=-\lambda_{\min}, solve for the component perpendicular to the singular eigenspace and add a vector in that null space. For a simple most-negative eigenvalue, one may write\mathbf{p}^*=\widehat{\mathbf{p}}+\tau\mathbf{v}_{\min},\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{p}}=-(\mathbf{B}-\lambda_{\min}\mathbf{I})^\dagger\mathbf{g}.

Here the dagger is the pseudoinverse, the base solution is perpendicular to the null space, and \tau is chosen to reach the radius. There is no ordinary inverse at that singular endpoint. For repeated most-negative eigenvalues, use the corresponding null space, not an arbitrarily chosen unrelated eigenvector.

For \mathbf{B}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,2), \mathbf{g}=(0,1)^T, \Delta=1, nonsingular shifts give \mathbf{p}(\delta)=(0,-1/(2+\delta))^T, whose limiting norm is 1/3. At \delta=1, the base solution is (0,-1/3)^T. The two boundary solutions are\mathbf{p}^*=(\pm\sqrt{8/9},-1/3)^T,\qquad m(\mathbf{p}^*)=-2/3.

They satisfy feasibility, shifted stationarity, complementarity and positive semidefiniteness. The added negative-curvature direction improves the base model value from -2/9 to -2/3.

A pure positive-definite correction may suppress this useful curvature. For larger problems, truncated conjugate-gradient trust-region methods detect nonpositive curvature or a boundary crossing and truncate there, avoiding a full eigenvalue decomposition. This is a different mechanism from using an arbitrary indefinite Newton direction in a line search.

Sources: Nocedal and Wright (2006), §4.3, pp. 87--88, Eq. (4.45), and §7.1, pp. 169--175; Biegler (2010), Eqs. (3.54)--(3.55) and Algorithm 3.4, pp. 56--57.

# Load the numerical tools and the course's shared figure style.
import sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mpmath as mp
from scipy import linalg
from matplotlib import cm
if 'google.colab' in sys.modules:
    import urllib.request
    urllib.request.urlretrieve('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndcbe/optimization/main/notebooks/helper.py', 'helper.py')
else:
    sys.path.insert(0, '../')
import helper
helper.set_plotting_style()

For a real symmetric \mathbf B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, considerf(\mathbf x)=c+\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x+\tfrac12\mathbf x^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf x.

The symmetric spectral theorem gives \mathbf B=\mathbf V\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}, with \mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V=\mathbf I and \boldsymbol\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n). Define the coordinates \mathbf z=\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x and the transformed function q(\mathbf z)=f(\mathbf V\mathbf z). The function value is preserved; the coordinate vector changes. Write \bar{\mathbf a}=\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\mathbf a. Then\begin{aligned}
q(\mathbf z)&=c+\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V\mathbf z
 +\tfrac12\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V\mathbf z\\
&=c+\bar{\mathbf a}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf z+\tfrac12\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf z
=c+\sum_j\bar a_j z_j+\tfrac12\sum_j\lambda_j z_j^2.
\end{aligned}

Each column of \mathbf V supplies a coordinate direction. Diagonal \boldsymbol\Lambda removes cross terms. See Biegler (2010), §2.2.2, Eqs.(2.8)–(2.10), pp.22–23.

Stationarity requires \bar a_j+\lambda_j z_j=0 for every j. Let J_0=\{j:\lambda_j=0\}. A stationary point exists exactly when \bar a_j=0 for every j\in J_0. In that casez_j^*=-\bar a_j/\lambda_j\quad(j\notin J_0),\qquad
z_j^*\text{ is arbitrary}\quad(j\in J_0),\qquad \mathbf x^*=\mathbf V\mathbf z^*.

Setting the free coordinates to zero selects one representative; it does not establish uniqueness. If a null coordinate has \bar a_j\ne0, moving along that coordinate makes the affine term arbitrarily positive or negative.

For every j\notin J_0, the full square completion is\tfrac12\lambda_j z_j^2+\bar a_jz_j
=\tfrac12\lambda_j\left(z_j+\frac{\bar a_j}{\lambda_j}\right)^2
 -\frac{\bar a_j^2}{2\lambda_j}
=\tfrac12\lambda_j(z_j-z_j^*)^2-\frac{\bar a_j^2}{2\lambda_j}.

Consequently, with \bar c=c-\sum_{j\notin J_0}\bar a_j^2/(2\lambda_j),q(\mathbf z)=\bar c+\sum_{j\in J_0}\bar a_jz_j
 +\tfrac12\sum_{j\notin J_0}\lambda_j(z_j-z_j^*)^2.

This formula also describes the case with no stationary point: the null-coordinate linear term remains. It avoids dividing by a zero eigenvalue.
