The helper below requires an explicitly symmetric real matrix and uses the symmetric eigensolver. Its relative threshold identifies numerically small eigenvalues. It analyzes the thresholded model and prints the residual in the original stored system. Neither thresholding nor a small residual proves the exact rank of a nearly singular matrix. If the thresholded stationarity equations are incompatible, the code draws the surface about a plotting center and does not mark that center as a stationary point.

def quad_analyze(c, a, B):
    """Plot a real symmetric quadratic and report a numerical stationary candidate.

    Returns a dictionary with the eigenpairs, threshold, residual, and candidate.
    A None candidate means the thresholded stationarity equations are incompatible;
    exact rank and compatibility near the threshold require further analysis.
    """
    if np.iscomplexobj(c) or np.iscomplexobj(a) or np.iscomplexobj(B):
        raise ValueError('The quadratic coefficients must be real')
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=float)
    B = np.asarray(B, dtype=float)
    if a.ndim != 1 or B.shape != (a.size, a.size) or a.size == 0:
        raise ValueError('a must be a nonempty vector and B a matching square matrix')
    if not np.isfinite(c) or not np.all(np.isfinite(a)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(B)):
        raise ValueError('All coefficients must be finite')
    if not np.array_equal(B, B.T):
        raise ValueError('B must be symmetric; form the symmetric part explicitly if intended')
    eigenvalues, V = linalg.eigh(B)
    abar = V.T @ a
    scale = float(np.max(np.abs(eigenvalues)))
    threshold = a.size * np.finfo(float).eps * scale
    small = np.abs(eigenvalues) <= threshold
    rhs_tolerance = a.size * np.finfo(float).eps * np.linalg.norm(a)
    compatible = bool(np.all(np.abs(abar[small]) <= rhs_tolerance))
    zcenter = np.zeros(a.size)
    zcenter[~small] = -abar[~small] / eigenvalues[~small]
    center = V @ zcenter
    residual = a + B @ center
    candidate = center.copy() if compatible else None
    print('B =\n', B, '\na =', a, '\nc =', c)
    print('eigenvalues =', eigenvalues, '\neigenvectors (columns) =\n', V)
    print('transformed linear coefficient =', abar)
    print('near-zero threshold =', threshold)
    print('numerically small eigenvalues =', eigenvalues[small])
    if candidate is None:
        print('Thresholded stationarity equations are incompatible; no stationary marker is drawn.')
        print('Plot center =', center)
    else:
        print('Numerical stationary candidate =', candidate)
        if np.any(small):
            print('Free coordinates in the thresholded model are set to zero for this representative.')
    print('gradient at center =', residual)
    print('gradient 2-norm =', np.linalg.norm(residual))
    if a.size == 2:
        grid = np.linspace(-5., 5., 81)
        X1, X2 = np.meshgrid(center[0] + grid, center[1] + grid)
        F = c + a[0]*X1 + a[1]*X2 + .5*(B[0,0]*X1**2 + 2*B[0,1]*X1*X2 + B[1,1]*X2**2)
        fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
        ax = fig.add_subplot(projection='3d')
        ax.plot_surface(X1, X2, F, cmap=cm.viridis, linewidth=0)
        if candidate is not None:
            value = c + a @ candidate + .5*candidate @ B @ candidate
            ax.scatter(*candidate, value, marker='o', color='#D55E00', edgecolor='black', s=65,
                       label='numerical stationary candidate')
            ax.legend(fontsize=10)
        ax.set(xlabel='$x_1$', ylabel='$x_2$', zlabel=r'$f(\mathbf{x})$')
        plt.show()
    return dict(eigenvalues=eigenvalues, eigenvectors=V, transformed_linear=abar,
                threshold=threshold, small_eigenvalues=small,
                candidate=candidate, plot_center=center, gradient=residual)

c = 0
a = np.array([1, 1])
B = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])

quad_analyze(c, a, B)

hierarchy.lvl3: Balls, neighborhoods, interior, boundary and closure
Balls, neighborhoods, interior, boundary and closure

records.content:
For \bar{\mathbf x}\in\mathbb R^n and r>0, the open and closed balls are\mathcal B(\bar{\mathbf x},r)=\{\mathbf x:\|\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x}\|<r\},\qquad
\overline{\mathcal B}(\bar{\mathbf x},r)=\{\mathbf x:\|\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x}\|\le r\}.

A set S is open if every \mathbf x\in S has a ball \mathcal B(\mathbf x,r)\subseteq S. A neighborhood of a point is an open set containing that point. In particular, an open ball is a neighborhood; a neighborhood need not be a ball.

For S\subseteq\mathbb R^n:

\mathbf x is an interior point if some ball about it is contained in S; the interior is \operatorname{int}S.

\mathbf x is a boundary point if every ball about it meets both S and its complement; the boundary is \partial S.

\mathbf x is in the closure \operatorname{cl}S if every ball about it meets S.

Thus \operatorname{cl}S=S\cup\partial S. The interior is the largest open subset of S; the closure is the smallest closed set containing S. A boundary point need not belong to S: for S=(0,1), the boundary is \{0,1\} and the closure is [0,1].

See Nocedal & Wright (2006), pp.620–621. The empty set and the whole space are both open and closed; these properties are not opposites.

A sequence assigns a point \mathbf x^k\in\mathbb R^n to each positive integer k. It converges to \bar{\mathbf x} if\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists K\ \forall k\ge K:\quad\|\mathbf x^k-\bar{\mathbf x}\|<\epsilon.

A subsequence has indices k_1<k_2<\cdots. A limit point of a sequence is the limit of one of its subsequences. A convergent sequence has exactly one limit point. The nonconvergent sequence \mathbf x^k=((-1)^k,1/k)^{\mathsf T} has the two limit points (1,0)^{\mathsf T} and (-1,0)^{\mathsf T}, obtained from the even and odd subsequences. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), pp.617–618.

A set is closed if its complement is open. Equivalently, it contains every limit of every convergent sequence of its points.

Proof that closed sets contain such limits. Suppose \mathbf x^k\in S, \mathbf x^k\to\bar{\mathbf x}, and \bar{\mathbf x}\notin S. The open complement contains a ball \mathcal B(\bar{\mathbf x},r) disjoint from S. Convergence puts every sufficiently late iterate in the smaller ball of radius r/2, hence in both S and its complement, a contradiction. Therefore \bar{\mathbf x}\in S.

Converse. If \bar{\mathbf x}\in\operatorname{cl}S, choose \mathbf x^k\in S\cap\mathcal B(\bar{\mathbf x},1/k). This sequence converges to \bar{\mathbf x}. A set containing all such limits therefore contains its closure and is closed. This also proves the sequence characterization of closure. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), pp.620–621.

S\subseteq\mathbb R^n is bounded if some M>0 satisfies \lVert\mathbf x\rVert\le M for every \mathbf x\in S. It is compact if every sequence in S has a subsequence converging to a point of S. In \mathbb R^n, compactness is equivalent to being closed and bounded. The finite-dimensional hypothesis matters. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), pp.620–621.

hierarchy.lvl3: Weierstrass theorem and a minimizing sequence
Weierstrass theorem and a minimizing sequence

records.content:
A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set S\subseteq\mathbb R^n attains a minimum and a maximum. See Rapcsák, “Smooth Nonlinear Nonconvex Optimization,” in Encyclopedia of Optimization, 2nd ed. (2009), p.3623. The cited statement gives the minimum; applying it to the negative function gives the maximum.

Here is the complete sequential argument. Write m=\inf_{\mathbf x\in S}\phi(\mathbf x).

If m is finite, choose \mathbf x^k\in S with m\le\phi(\mathbf x^k)<m+1/k. If m=-\infty, choose \phi(\mathbf x^k)<-k. These choices are permitted by the definition of infimum.

Compactness supplies a subsequence \mathbf x^{k_i}\to\hat{\mathbf x}\in S. Continuity implies \phi(\mathbf x^{k_i})\to\phi(\hat{\mathbf x}), a finite real number.

The m=-\infty alternative contradicts that finite limit. Hence m is finite, and the same subsequence has function values tending to m. Uniqueness of a real limit gives \phi(\hat{\mathbf x})=m.

The maximum follows from the minimum of -\phi. This is a compactness-plus-continuity proof, not a derivative test.

Without the hypotheses the conclusion can fail. The function \phi(x)=x on (0,1) has no minimum; e^x on \mathbb R has infimum zero but no minimizer. Compactness alone is insufficient: on [0,1], define \phi(0)=1 and \phi(x)=x for x>0. Its infimum is zero, is not attained, and the function is discontinuous at zero.

hierarchy.lvl3: Limits and continuity on a domain
Limits and continuity on a domain

records.content:
Let \phi:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R. At an accumulation point \bar{\mathbf x} of D, the limit is \ell if\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0:\quad
\mathbf x\in D,\ 0<\|\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x}\|<\delta
\ \Longrightarrow\ |\phi(\mathbf x)-\ell|<\epsilon.

The function is continuous at \bar{\mathbf x}\in D if the same implication, with \ell=\phi(\bar{\mathbf x}), holds for all \mathbf x\in D with \|\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x}\|<\delta. It is continuous on D when it is continuous at every point of D. The domain is part of the definition. See Biegler (2010), Def.2.9, p.25; Nocedal & Wright (2006), Eq.(A.38), p.623.

The formula 1/x is continuous on \mathbb R\setminus\{0\}, and in particular on (0,\infty). It is undefined at zero. Since |1/x| is unbounded near zero, no assigned finite value at zero gives a continuous extension. This does not make the function discontinuous at a point outside its stated domain.

\phi:D\to\mathbb R is Lipschitz continuous on N\subseteq D if one finite constant L>0 satisfies|\phi(\mathbf x)-\phi(\mathbf y)|\le L\|\mathbf x-\mathbf y\|
\qquad\text{for every }\mathbf x,\mathbf y\in N.

The constant is selected before the pair of points. It may depend on the set N. Local Lipschitz continuity at an interior point means that such a neighborhood N exists. This uses Nocedal & Wright (2006), Eq.(A.42), p.624; the quantifier order in Biegler’s Def.2.10, p.25, does not impose a single constant on the set.

The continuous function \sqrt{x} is not Lipschitz on [0,\infty). Setting x=0 and y=a>0 would require \sqrt a\le La, hence L\ge1/\sqrt a for every a>0, which is impossible. On [1,\infty),|\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}|=\frac{|x-y|}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}\le\tfrac12|x-y|.

Thus L=1/2 works there. The derivative 1/(2\sqrt{x}) becomes unbounded toward zero, consistent with the first result.

More generally, a differentiable scalar function with \|\nabla\phi\|\le L along every segment in a convex set is Lipschitz there, provided the function is continuous on each segment and differentiable in its interior. Apply the scalar mean value theorem along the segment and Cauchy–Schwarz. Conversely, where an L-Lipschitz function is differentiable, taking directional limits gives |\nabla\phi^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p|\le L\|\mathbf p\|. Lipschitz continuity does not require differentiability everywhere; |x| is an example.

hierarchy.lvl3: Derivatives, gradients, Hessians and level sets
Derivatives, gradients, Hessians and level sets

records.content:
For a scalar function, \phi'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}[\phi(a+h)-\phi(a)]/h when the limit exists; the second derivative is the derivative of \phi'. For \phi:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R at an interior point, the coordinate partial derivatives are\partial_i\phi(\mathbf x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\phi(\mathbf x+h\mathbf e_i)-\phi(\mathbf x)}{h},\qquad
\partial_i\partial_j\phi=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x_j}\right).

The gradient is the column of first partials and the Hessian collects second partials:\nabla\phi=(\partial_1\phi,\ldots,\partial_n\phi)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
[\nabla^2\phi]_{ij}=\partial_i\partial_j\phi.

Differentiability at \mathbf x means that the linear model has a remainder negligible relative to the step:\phi(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)=\phi(\mathbf x)+\nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p+o(\|\mathbf p\|)
\quad(\mathbf p\to\mathbf0).

Existence of all coordinate partials alone does not imply this property. A function is C^1 if its first partials exist and are continuous, and C^2 if its second partials exist and are continuous. For a differentiable function, the two-sided directional derivative is\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\phi(\mathbf x+h\mathbf p)-\phi(\mathbf x)}{h}
=\nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p.

A real C^2 function has a symmetric Hessian. This permits real eigenvalues, an orthogonal eigenbasis and symmetric factorizations. Cholesky additionally requires positive definiteness; symmetry alone is insufficient. Symmetry also permits storing one triangle, containing n(n+1)/2 entries rather than n^2; the factor tends to one half as n grows. See Biegler (2010), Defs.2.11–2.12, pp.25–27; Nocedal & Wright (2006), pp.626–628.

For \alpha\in\mathbb R, a level set is \{\mathbf x\in D:\phi(\mathbf x)=\alpha\} and a sublevel set is \{\mathbf x\in D:\phi(\mathbf x)\le\alpha\}. At a regular point with nonzero gradient, differentiate \phi(\mathbf x(t))=\alpha to obtain \nabla\phi^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x'(t)=0. This proves the normal-direction statement; a zero gradient does not specify a normal direction.

hierarchy.lvl3: Mean value and implicit function theorems
Mean value and implicit function theorems

records.content:
If \phi is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with a<b, then\phi(b)-\phi(a)=\phi'(\xi)(b-a)\qquad\text{for some }\xi\in(a,b).

For a C^1 scalar-valued function on a neighborhood of a segment from \mathbf x to \mathbf x+\mathbf p, apply this theorem to g(t)=\phi(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p). Then g'(t)=\nabla\phi(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), Eqs.(A.54)–(A.55), p.629.

There need not be one common mean-value point for a vector-valued function. For \mathbf g(t)=(t^2,t^3)^{\mathsf T} on [0,1], the two components would require 2\xi=1 and 3\xi^2=1, respectively. Those values of \xi differ. The integral form used for gradients 

below avoids that claim.

Implicit function theorem. Let \mathbf h:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n be C^1 near (\mathbf z^*,\mathbf0), with \mathbf h(\mathbf z^*,\mathbf0)=\mathbf0 and nonsingular \nabla_{\mathbf z}\mathbf h there. Then product neighborhoods exist on which the nearby roots are exactly the graph of a unique C^1 function \mathbf z(\mathbf t) with \mathbf z(\mathbf0)=\mathbf z^*. Using the course’s derivative arrays, whose row indexes the input component,[\nabla_{\mathbf z}\mathbf h]_{ij}=\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_i},\quad
[\nabla_{\mathbf t}\mathbf h]_{ij}=\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial t_i},\quad
\nabla\mathbf z=-\nabla_{\mathbf t}\mathbf h\,[\nabla_{\mathbf z}\mathbf h]^{-1}.

The dimensions are n\times n, m\times n and m\times n, respectively; evaluate the derivative arrays at (\mathbf z(\mathbf t),\mathbf t). The formula follows by differentiating \mathbf h(\mathbf z(\mathbf t),\mathbf t)=\mathbf0. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), Thm.A.2, p.631.

For h(z,t)=z^2+t-1 near (1,0), h_z=2\ne0, so the local branch is z(t)=\sqrt{1-t} and z'(0)=-h_t/h_z=-1/2. There is another branch near (-1,0); local uniqueness near z=1 does not assert a unique root globally. At (0,1) the nonsingularity hypothesis fails.

hierarchy.lvl3: Convex combinations, hulls, half-spaces and polyhedra
Convex combinations, hulls, half-spaces and polyhedra

records.content:
A convex combination of \mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_m is \sum_i\theta_i\mathbf x_i with \theta_i\ge0 and \sum_i\theta_i=1. Their convex hull is the set of all these combinations. A set S is convex if\theta\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf x_b\in S
\quad\text{for every }\mathbf x_a,\mathbf x_b\in S,\ \theta\in[0,1].

The convex hull is convex: a convex combination of two combinations has nonnegative coefficients summing to one. Any convex set containing all the original points contains every finite convex combination, by induction. Hence the hull is the smallest convex set containing them. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), p.621; Nesterov (2018), pp.141–142.

For \mathbf a\ne\mathbf0, a hyperplane is \{\mathbf x:\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x=b\}. The two closed half-spaces use \le b and \ge b. The normal \mathbf a is perpendicular to the hyperplane. A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many half-spaces and hyperplanes, equivalently \{\mathbf x:\mathbf A\mathbf x\le\mathbf b\} after writing an equality as two inequalities. A polyhedron can be empty or unbounded.

Proof for a half-space. If \mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_a\le b and \mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_b\le b, then\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}(\theta\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf x_b)
=\theta\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_b
\le\theta b+(1-\theta)b=b.

A hyperplane uses the same computation with equality. Applying the inequality row by row proves the polyhedron is convex. Lecture 2 is the primary handout home for the half-space and intersection convexity proofs. The existing 

Introduction to Constrained Nonlinear Optimization guide collects the general intersection proof and convex-program formulation checklist. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), p.8; Nesterov (2018), Def.3.1.4, p.159.

Using the positive-scaling convention, the ray through \mathbf d\ne\mathbf0 is \{\tau\mathbf d:\tau>0\}. A cone C satisfies\mathbf d\in C\ \Longrightarrow\ \tau\mathbf d\in C\qquad\text{for every }\tau>0.

This convention does not require the origin. A convex cone is also a convex set. The generated set \{\sum_i\tau_i\mathbf d_i:\tau_i\ge0\} contains the origin and is a convex cone: nonnegative scaling and convex combinations preserve nonnegative coefficients. The set \{(x_1,x_2):x_1\ge0\text{ or }x_2\ge0\} is a cone but is not convex; the points (1,-2) and (-2,1) have a midpoint outside it. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), Eq.(A.36) and pp.621–622.

hierarchy.lvl3: A convex half-space need not be a cone
A convex half-space need not be a cone

records.content:
Convex combinations keep a point in a half-space, but positive scaling can leave it. ForH=\{\mathbf x:x_1+2x_2\le4\},\qquad \mathbf x_b=(2,1/2)^{\mathsf T},

we have \mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_b=3\le4 for \mathbf a=(1,2)^{\mathsf T}, whereas \mathbf a^{\mathsf T}(2\mathbf x_b)=6>4. Thus H is convex and is not a cone.

More generally, for \mathbf a\ne\mathbf0, the closed half-space H_b=\{\mathbf x:\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x\le b\} is a cone under the positive-scaling definition exactly when b=0. If b=0, multiplying the inequality by any \tau>0 preserves it. If b\ne0, choose the boundary point \mathbf x_b=b\mathbf a/\|\mathbf a\|_2^2. For b>0, 2\mathbf x_b has functional value 2b>b; for b<0, \mathbf x_b/2 has value b/2>b. Either case violates positive-scaling closure. This argument also applies under the convention that permits a cone to exclude the origin.

hierarchy.lvl3: Convex functions and the first-order characterization
Convex functions and the first-order characterization

records.content:
Let D\subseteq\mathbb R^n be convex. A function \phi:D\to\mathbb R is convex if for all \mathbf x_a,\mathbf x_b\in D and \theta\in(0,1),\phi(\theta\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf x_b)
\le\theta\phi(\mathbf x_a)+(1-\theta)\phi(\mathbf x_b).

It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict whenever \mathbf x_a\ne\mathbf x_b. On an open convex domain, a differentiable function is convex exactly when\phi(\mathbf y)\ge\phi(\mathbf x)+\nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\mathbf x)
\qquad(\mathbf x,\mathbf y\in D).

Strict convexity is equivalent to the strict first-order inequality for distinct points. The excluded equal-point case matters: equality always holds at \mathbf y=\mathbf x. See Biegler (2010), Def.2.13, p.27, with the distinct-point qualification in Nocedal & Wright (2006), p.8; Nesterov (2018), Thm.2.1.2, pp.62–63.

hierarchy.lvl3: First-order inequality implies the chord inequality
First-order inequality implies the chord inequality

records.content:
Set \mathbf x_c=\theta\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf x_b. Apply the first-order inequality twice, both times based at \mathbf x_c:\begin{aligned}
\phi(\mathbf x_a)&\ge\phi(\mathbf x_c)+\nabla\phi(\mathbf x_c)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf x_a-\mathbf x_c),\\
\phi(\mathbf x_b)&\ge\phi(\mathbf x_c)+\nabla\phi(\mathbf x_c)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf x_b-\mathbf x_c).
\end{aligned}

Multiply these inequalities by \theta and 1-\theta, both positive, and add. The gradient term is zero because\theta(\mathbf x_a-\mathbf x_c)+(1-\theta)(\mathbf x_b-\mathbf x_c)
=\theta\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf x_b-\mathbf x_c=\mathbf0.

The remaining inequality is precisely the chord inequality. Strict first-order inequalities give the strict chord inequality for distinct endpoints.

hierarchy.lvl3: Chord inequality implies the first-order inequality
Chord inequality implies the first-order inequality

records.content:
Fix \mathbf x,\mathbf y\in D and write \mathbf p=\mathbf y-\mathbf x.

Convexity gives \phi(\mathbf x+\theta\mathbf p)\le(1-\theta)\phi(\mathbf x)+\theta\phi(\mathbf y).

Subtract \phi(\mathbf x) and divide by the positive \theta:\frac{\phi(\mathbf x+\theta\mathbf p)-\phi(\mathbf x)}{\theta}
\le\phi(\mathbf y)-\phi(\mathbf x).

Let \theta\downarrow0. Differentiability at \mathbf x makes the left side tend to \nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p. A weak inequality survives the limit, giving the first-order inequality. Continuity of the gradient is not needed for this step.

A strict inequality does not automatically survive a limit. For the strict result, first obtain the weak supporting inequality just proved. At a distinct pair, strict convexity and that support bound imply\phi(\mathbf x)+\theta\nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p
\le\phi(\mathbf x+\theta\mathbf p)
<(1-\theta)\phi(\mathbf x)+\theta\phi(\mathbf y).

Subtract and divide by \theta>0 to get the strict first-order inequality. These arguments also explain why negating a first-order inequality at one pair of points does not justify applying the failure at two prescribed directions.

For a C^2 function on an open convex domain, convexity is equivalent to \nabla^2\phi(\mathbf x)\succeq0 everywhere. Necessity follows by applying the supporting inequality to \mathbf x\pm h\mathbf p, adding, dividing by h^2 and taking h\to0. This gives \mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\phi(\mathbf x)\mathbf p\ge0 for every \mathbf p.

For sufficiency, the exact integral Taylor remainder is\phi(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)-\phi(\mathbf x)-\nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p
=\int_0^1(1-t)\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\phi(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p)\mathbf p\,dt.

A positive-semidefinite Hessian makes the integral nonnegative. Pointwise positive definiteness makes it positive for \mathbf p\ne\mathbf0, so it is sufficient for strict convexity. It is not necessary: x^4 is strictly convex but has second derivative zero at zero.

A differentiable function on a convex domain is m-strongly convex, m>0, if\phi(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)\ge\phi(\mathbf x)+\nabla\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p+\tfrac m2\|\mathbf p\|^2

for every segment in its domain. In the C^2 case this is equivalent to the uniform bound \nabla^2\phi(\mathbf x)\succeq m\mathbf I. A positive-definite Hessian at every point alone does not supply one uniform m. For example, e^x has positive second derivative everywhere on \mathbb R, but the infimum of its second derivative is zero as x\to-\infty. See Nesterov (2018), Def.2.1.3 and Thm.2.1.11, pp.74–75; this corrects the pointwise-Hessian condition in Biegler’s Def.2.13.

A function is quasi-convex if each sublevel set is convex. Every convex function is quasi-convex: if \phi(\mathbf x_a),\phi(\mathbf x_b)\le\alpha, convexity yields\phi(\theta\mathbf x_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf x_b)
\le\theta\phi(\mathbf x_a)+(1-\theta)\phi(\mathbf x_b)\le\alpha.

See Nesterov (2018), Lemma2.2.5, p.101. The converse fails. For \phi(x)=1-e^{-x^2}, the sublevel set for 0\le\alpha<1 is[-\sqrt{-\ln(1-\alpha)},\sqrt{-\ln(1-\alpha)}].

It is empty for \alpha<0 and all of \mathbb R for \alpha\ge1. Every case is convex, but \phi''(x)=(2-4x^2)e^{-x^2}<0 when |x|>1/\sqrt2. In contrast, x^4-2x^2 is not quasi-convex: at level -1/2 its sublevel set is two disjoint intervals, with |x| between \sqrt{1-1/\sqrt2} and \sqrt{1+1/\sqrt2}.

On \mathbb R, x^2, x^4, x, and 1-e^{-x^2} distinguish the nested classes strongly convex, strictly convex, convex and quasi-convex, respectively.

Suppose the entire segment \mathbf x+t\mathbf p, 0\le t\le1, lies in a neighborhood where f is C^1. Then some t_1\in(0,1) satisfiesf(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)=f(\mathbf x)+\nabla f(\mathbf x+t_1\mathbf p)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p.

If f is C^2 there, some t_2\in(0,1) satisfiesf(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)=f(\mathbf x)+\nabla f(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p
 +\tfrac12\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(\mathbf x+t_2\mathbf p)\mathbf p.

The two points need not be the same. Both statements are exact. To prove them, apply the corresponding one-dimensional theorem to g(t)=f(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p), using g'(t)=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p and g''(t)=\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f\,\mathbf p. Componentwise fundamental theorem of calculus gives the exact vector identity\nabla f(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)-\nabla f(\mathbf x)
=\int_0^1\nabla^2f(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p)\mathbf p\,dt.

Integrating the scalar derivative twice also givesf(\mathbf x+\mathbf p)=f(\mathbf x)+\nabla f(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p
+\int_0^1(1-t)\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p)\mathbf p\,dt.

For the first formula, differentiate each component of \nabla f(\mathbf x+t\mathbf p) and integrate from zero to one. For the second, integrate the change in g'(t), then interchange the order over the triangular region 0\le s\le t\le1. Neither argument asserts a common vector mean-value point.

For the symmetric quadratic, \nabla f=\mathbf a+\mathbf B\mathbf x and \nabla^2f=\mathbf B, so the second-order Taylor model is exact with no remainder. The integral of 1-t is 1/2, recovering the quadratic term directly.

If each function evaluation has absolute error bounded by \eta, the evaluation contribution is at most 2\eta/h for a one-sided formula and \eta/h for central differences, before accounting for arithmetic and argument-rounding errors. Subtracting nearby computed function values can expose those errors. In particular, a floating-point sum a+h can round back to a.

A useful scale model isE(h)\approx C h^p+\frac{D\eta}{h},\qquad
h_*\approx\left(\frac{D\eta}{pC}\right)^{1/(p+1)}\quad(C,D,\eta>0).

Differentiate the model to obtain pC h^{p-1}-D\eta/h^2=0. The orders are h_*\sim\eta^{1/2} for one-sided differences and h_*\sim\eta^{1/3} for central differences, with best modeled errors of orders \eta^{1/2} and \eta^{2/3}. Constants depend on function/derivative scales. When the evaluation scale is order one and \eta is of unit-roundoff size, these suggest steps around 

10-8 and 

10-5.3 in binary64. They are scale estimates, not universal optimal steps or exact measured minima.

For a full gradient in n variables, a reused base value gives n+1 evaluations for forward differences; central differences use 2n. This cost comparison concerns gradients built by finite differences, not every derivative-free algorithm.

records.content:
The cells below evaluate f(x)=e^x at a=1 and a=10 with binary64 function calls and arithmetic. The derivative reference e^a is evaluated at 100 decimal digits and checked at 160. Thus the reported error compares the actual stored derivative approximation with the analytic derivative, not with a rounded binary64 reference. The plot is built one curve at a time; the final figure and archived data are also used by the lecture notes.

The step grid is h=10^{-16},10^{-15.75},\ldots,10^0, four points per decade including both endpoints. Measured minima are restricted to this finite grid and can vary with the numerical library. The table prints every formula’s minimizing grid step and error for both evaluation points.

def finite_difference_experiment(point):
    """Measure binary64 exp differences against a converged high-precision derivative."""
    steps = np.power(10., np.arange(-16., .25, .25))
    base = float(np.exp(point))
    plus = np.exp(point + steps)
    minus = np.exp(point - steps)
    approximations = {
        'forward': (plus-base)/steps,
        'backward': (base-minus)/steps,
        'central': (plus-minus)/(2*steps),
    }
    def measure(digits):
        with mp.workdps(digits):
            reference = mp.exp(mp.mpf(float(point)))
            return {name:[float(abs(mp.mpf(float(value))-reference)) for value in values]
                    for name,values in approximations.items()}
    errors = measure(100)
    repeated = measure(160)
    for name in errors:
        assert np.array_equal(errors[name], repeated[name])
    with mp.workdps(100):
        reference_text = mp.nstr(mp.exp(mp.mpf(float(point))), 95)
    return {'a':float(point),'h':steps.tolist(),'f_a':base,
            'f_plus':plus.tolist(),'f_minus':minus.tolist(),
            'approximations':{name:values.tolist() for name,values in approximations.items()},
            'errors':errors,'derivative_reference':reference_text}

results = {'function':'exp','cases':[finite_difference_experiment(1.),finite_difference_experiment(10.)],
           'reference_digits':[100,160], 'step_grid':'10**arange(-16,0.25,0.25)',
           'error':'absolute error against the analytic derivative of exp at the stored point'}
summary_rows = []
for case in results['cases']:
    h = np.asarray(case['h'])
    for method, errors in case['errors'].items():
        errors = np.asarray(errors)
        index = int(np.argmin(errors))
        window = (h>=1e-4)&(h<=1e-1)&(errors>0)
        slope = float(np.polyfit(np.log10(h[window]),np.log10(errors[window]),1)[0])
        summary_rows.append({'a':case['a'],'formula':method,'step_at_grid_minimum':float(h[index]),
                             'minimum_absolute_error':float(errors[index]),'truncation_slope':slope})
results['summary'] = summary_rows
helper.save_results('finite-difference-error',results,
    notebook='notebooks/6-dev/Math-Primer-2.ipynb',
    source_cells=[('notebooks/6-dev/Math-Primer-2.ipynb','results:finite-difference-error')],
    description='Binary64 exponential differences at 1 and 10 with 100/160-digit analytic derivative references',
    solver='NumPy exp and arithmetic; mpmath analytic references',quiet=True)
display(pd.DataFrame(summary_rows))

Scalars and scalar components are plain, vectors are bold lower case, and matrices are bold upper case: \alpha, x_i, \mathbf{x}, A_{ij}, and \mathbf{A}. The matrix \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} represents the linear map T:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n, T(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{Ax}. Linearity meansT(\alpha\mathbf{x}+\beta\mathbf{y})=\alpha T(\mathbf{x})+\beta T(\mathbf{y})

for every \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^m and \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}. The columns of \mathbf{A} are the images of the coordinate vectors: \mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_j=\mathbf{a}_j.

For \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}, \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{AB}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p} has entriesC_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}A_{ik}B_{kj}.

The inner dimensions must match. Multiplication composes maps: first apply \mathbf{B}, then \mathbf{A}. If \mathbf{A} is 4\times3 and \mathbf{B} is 3\times7, \mathbf{AB} is 4\times7; \mathbf{BA} is undefined because its inner dimensions are 7 and 4.

The transpose interchanges rows and columns, (\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T})_{ij}=A_{ji}. A square matrix is symmetric when \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} and diagonal when A_{ij}=0 for i\ne j. The identity has I_{ii}=1 and all off-diagonal entries zero.

For the illustrated \mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1.5&.5\\.5&1\end{smallmatrix}\right], the area changes by \det\mathbf{A}=1.25. A negative determinant reverses orientation; a zero determinant collapses area to zero.

For a square matrix \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, expansion along any row i gives\det(\mathbf{A})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(-1)^{i+j}A_{ij}\,\bar A_{ij},

where A_{ij} is the entry in row i and column j, and \bar A_{ij} is the determinant of the (n-1)\times(n-1) matrix obtained by deleting row i and column j from \mathbf{A}. Useful properties are\begin{aligned}
\det(\mathbf{AB})&=\det(\mathbf{A})\det(\mathbf{B}),&\det(\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T})&=\det(\mathbf{A}),\\
\det(\alpha\mathbf{A})&=\alpha^n\det(\mathbf{A}),&\det(\mathbf{I})&=1.
\end{aligned}

The exponent n in the scaling law matters: multiplying the whole matrix by \alpha scales each of its n rows. A square matrix is singular exactly when \det(\mathbf{A})=0.

records.content:
A linear combination of \mathbf{a}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{a}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n is \sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_j\mathbf{a}_j, with real coefficients. Their span is the set of all such combinations. They are linearly independent if \sum_j\alpha_j\mathbf{a}_j=\mathbf{0} implies \alpha_j=0 for every j; otherwise they are dependent.

A subspace S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n contains \mathbf{0} and is closed under linear combinations: \alpha\mathbf{x}+\beta\mathbf{y}\in S for all \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S and all real \alpha,\beta. A basis of S is a linearly independent spanning set. Its number of vectors is \dim S. The zero subspace has the empty basis and dimension zero.

For \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, the range or column space is\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf{A})=\{\mathbf{Ax}:\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^m\}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{a}_m\}.

The null space is \operatorname{Null}(\mathbf{A})=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^m:\mathbf{Ax}=\mathbf{0}\}. Both are subspaces, but they belong to different spaces: range in \mathbb{R}^n, null space in \mathbb{R}^m.

The rank r(\mathbf{A}) is the dimension of the column space, equivalently the row space or the size of the largest square submatrix with nonzero determinant. Full column rank means r=m; full row rank means r=n. Full rank means r=\min(n,m); otherwise the matrix is rank deficient.

records.content:
Let \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k be a basis of the null space, and extend it to a basis \mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_m of the domain. Every \mathbf{Ax} is a linear combination of \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_{k+1},\ldots,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_m, because the first k vectors map to zero. These remaining images are independent: any combination mapping to zero would be both a combination of the last basis vectors and a member of the span of the first k. Independence of the whole basis forces every coefficient to vanish. Thusr(\mathbf{A})+\dim\operatorname{Null}(\mathbf{A})=m.

For the illustrated matrix \left[\begin{smallmatrix}.5&1\\.5&1\end{smallmatrix}\right], the range is \operatorname{span}\{(1,1)^\mathsf{T}\} and the null space is \operatorname{span}\{(2,-1)^\mathsf{T}\}. Both have dimension one. If \mathbf{x}_0 solves \mathbf{Ax}=\mathbf{b}, every solution is \mathbf{x}_0+\mathbf{z} with \mathbf{z}\in\operatorname{Null}(\mathbf{A}). If \mathbf{b} is outside the range, there is no solution.

A square matrix \mathbf{A} is invertible when there is a matrix \mathbf{A}^{-1} satisfying \mathbf{AA}^{-1}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}. Then \mathbf{Ax}=\mathbf{b} has the unique solution \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}, although numerical software should solve the system directly rather than form the inverse. Also, \det(\mathbf{A}^{-1})=1/\det(\mathbf{A}). An orthogonal matrix \mathbf{Q} satisfies \mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^\mathsf{T}.

If \det\mathbf{A}=0 and an inverse existed, multiplicativity of the determinant would give 1=\det\mathbf{I}=\det(\mathbf{AA}^{-1})=\det\mathbf{A}\det\mathbf{A}^{-1}=0, a contradiction. The 

Invertible Matrix Theorem collects the converse and equivalent conditions.

For dense unstructured matrices, factorizing and solving usually takes less work than explicitly forming an inverse and multiplying. Leading operation counts for a single right-hand side are approximately 2n^3/3 for elimination versus 2n^3 for an inverse. Accuracy also depends on the algorithm and data; avoid treating a computed inverse as a universal cure for a difficult solve. See Higham (2002), §14.1, p.260.

A sparse matrix can have a dense inverse, increasing storage as well as arithmetic. For an explicit example, let \mathbf N have ones immediately above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Then \mathbf N^n=\mathbf0 and(\mathbf I-\mathbf N)^{-1}=\mathbf I+\mathbf N+\cdots+\mathbf N^{n-1}.

Multiplication telescopes to \mathbf I. The original matrix has 2n-1 nonzeros, while its inverse has n(n+1)/2 nonzeros. This example explains the storage risk; sparse factorization can also create fill and needs an appropriate ordering.

For a dense n\times n system, factorization costs approximately 2n^3/3 operations, and the two triangular solves cost approximately 2n^2 per right-hand side. With q right-hand sides, refactorizing each time costs q(2n^3/3+2n^2); reusing the factors costs 2n^3/3+2qn^2. For n=1000 and q=200, these are 1.3373\cdot10^{11} and 1.0667\cdot10^9, a ratio of about 125.4. These leading arithmetic counts omit lower-order work and do not predict an exact wall-clock speedup.

Doolittle elimination chooses unit diagonal entries in \mathbf{L}. See Higham (2002), §9.2, pp.162–163, and §9.4, pp.166–167 for growth and backward error. The

records.content:
For a square n\times n matrix \mathbf{A}, the following statements are equivalent:

\mathbf{A} is invertible; its row-reduced form is \mathbf{I}; and it has n pivots.

\mathbf{Ax}=\mathbf{0} has only the trivial solution, so \operatorname{Nul}(\mathbf{A})=\{\mathbf{0}\} and \dim\operatorname{Nul}(\mathbf{A})=0.

The columns of \mathbf{A} are linearly independent, form a basis of \mathbb{R}^n, and span \mathbb{R}^n; equivalently \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})=n.

The map \mathbf{x}\mapsto \mathbf{Ax} is both one-to-one and onto; therefore \mathbf{Ax}=\mathbf{b} has a solution for every \mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n.

A left or right inverse exists; \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} is invertible; \det(\mathbf{A})\ne0; and zero is not an eigenvalue.

The row space is \mathbb{R}^n, (\operatorname{Col}\mathbf{A})^\perp=\{\mathbf{0}\}, (\operatorname{Nul}\mathbf{A})^\perp=\mathbb{R}^n, and \mathbf{A} has n nonzero singular values.

These equivalences consolidate Lay’s Invertible Matrix Theorem into one searchable list.

For square \mathbf{A}, a nonzero vector \mathbf{v} is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \lambda when \mathbf{Av}=\lambda \mathbf{v}. Thus \mathbf{A}-\lambda \mathbf{I} is singular and eigenvalues are roots of \det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda \mathbf{I})=0. Counting algebraic multiplicity, \det(\mathbf{A})=\prod_i\lambda_i.

If \mathbf{A} is real and symmetric, the spectral theorem gives \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T} with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors. Only under this symmetry assumption can definiteness be read directly from eigenvalue signs: all positive means positive definite, all nonnegative means positive semidefinite, and mixed signs mean indefinite.

A nonsymmetric real matrix may have complex eigenvalues, and its eigenvalues do not in general classify the quadratic form \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{Ax}. That form is governed by the symmetric part (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T})/2. For rectangular matrices, singular values \sigma_i\ge0—the square roots of the eigenvalues of \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}—play the analogous role.

For \mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-2&-3\end{smallmatrix}\right],\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=\lambda(3+\lambda)+2=(\lambda+1)(\lambda+2).

For \lambda_1=-1, the equations in (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0} are multiples of v_1+v_2=0. The matrix has rank one, and eigenvectors are k(1,-1)^\mathsf{T} with k\ne0. For \lambda_2=-2 the eigenvectors are k(1,-2)^\mathsf{T} with k\ne0. These eigendirections are not orthogonal; symmetry is the hypothesis that guarantees an orthonormal eigenbasis. Counting algebraic multiplicity, \operatorname{tr}\mathbf{A}=\sum_i\lambda_i and \det\mathbf{A}=\prod_i\lambda_i. For nonsingular \mathbf{A}, the eigenpairs of \mathbf{A}^{-1} are (1/\lambda_i,\mathbf{v}_i).

records.content:
For real symmetric \mathbf{A} and every nonzero real \mathbf{x}, positive definite means \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{Ax}>0; positive semidefinite means \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{Ax}\ge0. Reverse the signs for negative definite or negative semidefinite. Indefinite means the form takes both positive and negative values. Singular means the matrix is not invertible; it is a different property from definiteness.

Write \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T} with orthogonal \mathbf{V} and set \mathbf{z}=\mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}. Then\mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{Ax}=\sum_i\lambda_i z_i^2,\qquad \mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}\iff\mathbf{z}\ne\mathbf{0}.

This proves the eigenvalue sign tests. Choosing \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{v}_i proves necessity; summing nonnegative squared coordinates proves sufficiency. A symmetric semidefinite matrix can be singular: \left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right] has eigenpairs (2,(1,1)^\mathsf{T}) and (0,(1,-1)^\mathsf{T}). Its quadratic form is (x_1+x_2)^2, so it is positive semidefinite and has a nontrivial null space.

For symmetric nonsingular \mathbf A=\mathbf V\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^{\mathsf T},\mathbf A^{-1}=\mathbf V\boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf V^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/\lambda_1,\ldots,1/\lambda_n).

Multiplying the two factorizations gives \mathbf I. Thus inversion preserves each eigenvector and reciprocates its eigenvalue. Keep each eigenvalue paired with its direction when reading a quadratic form or its inverse.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix have a picture: they are the principal
axes of the level sets of q(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12 \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}. In the rotated coordinates

large eigenvalue means steep, hence short.

For \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with m\ge n, a thin SVD is\mathbf{A}=\underbrace{\mathbf{U}}_{m\times n}\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{n\times n}\underbrace{\mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}}_{n\times n},

where \mathbf{U}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}_n, \mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{VV}^\mathsf{T}=\mathbf{I}_n, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n) with \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n\ge0. The columns of \mathbf{U} and \mathbf{V} are left and right singular vectors. For a rectangular thin \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{UU}^\mathsf{T} is a projection, not the identity on \mathbb{R}^m. For m<n, apply the construction to \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} or use a full SVD with rectangular \boldsymbol{\Sigma}.

Orthogonal factors preserve 2-norm lengths. Along \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i=\sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i; a zero singular value sends that direction to zero. The number of positive singular values is the exact rank. Numerical rank requires a scale-dependent tolerance: compare each singular value with a tolerance relative to \sigma_1, taking data accuracy into account.

records.content:
Substitute the factorization and use \mathbf{U}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}:\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}
&=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{U}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}\\
&=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^2\mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T},\\
\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i&=\sigma_i^2\mathbf{v}_i.
\end{aligned}

Conversely, diagonalize the positive semidefinite \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A} and set \mathbf{u}_i=\mathbf{Av}_i/\sigma_i for each positive \sigma_i. Then\mathbf{u}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{u}_j=\frac{\mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}=\delta_{ij}.

Complete these left singular vectors to n orthonormal columns if the rank is less than n; never divide by a zero singular value. The remaining right singular vectors lie in the null space. For full column rank, the compact formula is \mathbf{U}=\mathbf{AV}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}.

This is an algebraic connection, not a recommendation to compute an SVD by forming \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}. For full column rank, its 2-norm condition number is K_2(\mathbf{A})^2, which can lose information about small singular values. Use scipy.linalg.svd directly. It returns Vh, meaning \mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T} for real data; full_matrices=False requests the thin factors.

The pseudoinverse is \mathbf{A}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\dagger}\mathbf{U}^\mathsf{T}, replacing positive singular values by their reciprocals and zero ones by zero. It is a two-sided inverse only for a square nonsingular matrix. Small positive singular values amplify perturbations in the corresponding directions.

See Nocedal & Wright (2006), Appendix A, p.604, Eq.(A.15), for SVD. Activity: compute the SVD of \mathbf{A}_l and \mathbf{C}_d, reconstruct each matrix, and use the singular values to discuss its rank.

records.content:
A vector norm ||\mathbf{x}|| measures the length of a vector. It maps \mathbb{R}^n into the nonnegative reals and satisfies three properties:||\mathbf{x}|| = 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}, \qquad ||\alpha \mathbf{x}|| = |\alpha| \cdot ||\mathbf{x}||, \qquad ||\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}|| \leq ||\mathbf{x}|| + ||\mathbf{y}||

The last one is the triangle inequality. The p-norm is ||\mathbf{x}||_p = \left( \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p \right)^{1/p} for p \geq 1, and three cases matter here:

||\mathbf{x}||_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i| --- the 1-norm

||\mathbf{x}||_2 = \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 \right)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}} --- the Euclidean norm

||\mathbf{x}||_{\infty} = \max_i |x_i| --- the max norm

Also |\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{y}| \leq ||\mathbf{x}||_p \cdot ||\mathbf{y}||_q for p,q\in[1,\infty] with 1/p + 1/q = 1 (using 1/\infty=0); the case p = q = 2 is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

Induced matrix norms are defined by vector norms:||\mathbf{A}|| = \max_{\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}} \frac{||\mathbf{Ax}||}{||\mathbf{x}||} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad ||\mathbf{Ax}|| \leq ||\mathbf{A}|| \cdot ||\mathbf{x}||

The rules for the three induced norms are

||\mathbf{A}||_1 = \max_j \sum_i |A_{ij}| --- largest column sum

||\mathbf{A}||_{\infty} = \max_i \sum_j |A_{ij}| --- largest row sum

||A||_2 =  the largest singular value of \mathbf{A}

Finally, the induced norms and the Frobenius norm ||\mathbf{A}||_F = \left( \sum_i \sum_j A_{ij}^2 \right)^{1/2} all satisfy||\mathbf{AB}|| \leq ||\mathbf{A}|| \cdot ||\mathbf{B}||

for any two compatible matrices \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{B}. This is submultiplicativity, and it is what the condition number in the next section rests on.

Definition 2.7, pp. 21-22 in Biegler (2010).

The induced 2-norm is \sigma_1 because \|\mathbf{Ax}\|_2^2=\sum_i\sigma_i^2z_i^2\le\sigma_1^2\|\mathbf{z}\|_2^2 for \mathbf{z}=\mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}; equality holds along a leading right singular vector. Submultiplicativity follows by applying the defining inequality twice: \|\mathbf{ABx}\|\le\|\mathbf{A}\|\|\mathbf{Bx}\|\le\|\mathbf{A}\|\|\mathbf{B}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|, then taking the maximum over unit vectors.

For continuous finite-dimensional vector- or matrix-valued \mathbf{F} on [a,b] with a\le b,\left\|\int_a^b\mathbf{F}(t)\,dt\right\|\le\int_a^b\|\mathbf{F}(t)\|\,dt.

Apply the triangle inequality and homogeneity to each Riemann sum, then pass to the limit. Continuity ensures the sums and their norms converge. Combined with submultiplicativity, this bounds expressions such as \|\mathbf{A}(\int\mathbf{F})\mathbf{v}\| by \|\mathbf{A}\|\int\|\mathbf{F}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|.

For nonsingular square \mathbf{A} and an induced norm,K(\mathbf{A})=\|\mathbf{A}\|\,\|\mathbf{A}^{-1}\|\ge1.

In the 2-norm, K_2(\mathbf{A})=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}. For real symmetric nonsingular matrices this is \max_i|\lambda_i|/\min_i|\lambda_i|; eigenvalue magnitudes matter. Eigenvalues 2,-4,8 give K_2=4. For rectangular full-column-rank matrices the singular-value ratio measures sensitivity of the map on its domain, but there is no square two-sided inverse.

Let \mathbf{Ax}=\mathbf{b}\ne\mathbf{0} and \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}+\Delta\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{b}+\Delta\mathbf{b}. Subtract to get \Delta\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{b}. Also \|\mathbf{b}\|\le\|\mathbf{A}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|. Therefore\frac{\|\Delta\mathbf{x}\|}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}\le K(\mathbf{A})\frac{\|\Delta\mathbf{b}\|}{\|\mathbf{b}\|}.

The condition number is a worst-case amplification, not a prediction for every perturbation. With \mathbf{A}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon) and \mathbf{b}=(1,0)^\mathsf{T}, a perturbation (0,\delta)^\mathsf{T} gives \Delta\mathbf{x}=(0,\delta/\varepsilon)^\mathsf{T} and attains K_2=1/\varepsilon for 0<\varepsilon\le1. Perturbing along the first coordinate is amplified only by one.

For an approximate solution \hat{\mathbf{x}}, define the exact residual of the stored data \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}. Then \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}})=\mathbf{r} and the same argument gives\frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}\le K(\mathbf{A})\frac{\|\mathbf{r}\|}{\|\mathbf{b}\|}.

A relative residual 

10-12 and condition number 4.5\cdot10^{14} give the bound 450. This bound does not certify an accurate solution; it also does not establish that the actual forward error is large. Computing the residual in floating point introduces another error. The 

Numerical Errors experiment evaluates the residual and reference solution in high precision and separates rounding of the input data from error in the solve.

records.content:
In the 2-norm, allowing perturbations only in \mathbf{A} gives\eta_A=\min\left\{\frac{\|\Delta\mathbf{A}\|_2}{\|\mathbf{A}\|_2}:(\mathbf{A}+\Delta\mathbf{A})\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{b}\right\}=\frac{\|\mathbf{r}\|_2}{\|\mathbf{A}\|_2\|\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2}

for nonzero \hat{\mathbf{x}}. The lower bound follows from \mathbf{r}=\Delta\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}; equality is attained by \Delta\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{r}\hat{\mathbf{x}}^\mathsf{T}/\|\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2. If K_2\eta_A<1, the finite perturbation bound is\frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_2}\le\frac{K_2\eta_A}{1-K_2\eta_A}.

Indeed, \|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|\le K_2\eta_A\|\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|\le K_2\eta_A(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|); rearrange. The simpler K_2\eta_A expression is a first-order rule when that product is small. If perturbations are allowed in both \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{b}, the normwise backward error instead has denominator \|\mathbf{A}\|\|\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|. State which model is used. See Higham (2002), Theorems 7.1–7.2, pp.120–121.

Conditioning describes sensitivity of a problem. Backward stability describes an algorithm’s error over its intended class of inputs. A small measured backward error on one solve is evidence about that solve; it does not prove that the algorithm is backward stable for all inputs.

records.content:
Wilkinson’s matrix has 1 on the diagonal, -1 below it, and a final column of ones. With the pivot tie choices used here, partial pivoting makes no interchanges, and entries grow as 2^{n-1} during elimination. The table checks the permutation and growth against this exact-arithmetic pattern. Its reported 2-norm condition numbers stay moderate, while the error can become substantial.

The reference vector x_true is chosen first, and b = A @ x_true is rounded. Consequently the reported error includes that assembly error as well as error in the solve. The residual column is normalized by the Frobenius norm of the matrix and the 2-norm of the computed solution, as shown in the code. It is not \|\mathbf{r}\|_2/\|\mathbf{b}\|_2.

# D1: LU with partial pivoting on Wilkinson's matrix.
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)


def wilkinson(n):
    """1 on the diagonal, -1 below it, last column all ones."""
    A = np.eye(n) - np.tril(np.ones((n, n)), -1)
    A[:, -1] = 1.0
    return A


print("A for n = 5:")
print(wilkinson(5).astype(int), "\n")

header = "{:>4} {:>8} {:>14} {:>14} {:>14} {:>9} {:>9}"
row = "{:>4d} {:>8.1f} {:>14.1e} {:>14.1e} {:>14.1e} {:>9.1e} {:>9}"
print(header.format("n", "K(A)", "growth", "2^(n-1)", "rel. resid",
                    "rel. err", "P == I ?"))

for n in [20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]:
    A = wilkinson(n)
    x_true = rng.standard_normal(n)
    b = A @ x_true

    P, L, U = linalg.lu(A)
    growth = np.abs(U).max() / np.abs(A).max()

    x_hat = linalg.solve(A, b)
    rel_resid = np.linalg.norm(A @ x_hat - b) / (np.linalg.norm(A)
                                                 * np.linalg.norm(x_hat))
    rel_err = np.linalg.norm(x_hat - x_true) / np.linalg.norm(x_true)

    print(row.format(n, np.linalg.cond(A), growth, 2.0 ** (n - 1),
                     rel_resid, rel_err,
                     str(np.array_equal(P, np.eye(n)))))




For this run, inspect P == I ? and compare measured growth with 2^{n-1}. Ties are relevant: being a largest-magnitude candidate does not force every pivoting implementation to make the same choice. Large element growth weakens the usual backward-error guarantee for elimination; see Higham (2002), §9.4, pp.166–167.

Activity. Compare the error, growth, and condition number columns. Which column identifies a sensitive problem, and which identifies the risk of rounding amplification during elimination? Change the random seed and identify which quantities change.

To use a forward-error bound with this table, first match both the reference problem and the normalization. Its printed residual measure \rho_F converts to the matrix-only 2-norm backward error by \eta_A=\rho_F\|\mathbf{A}\|_F/\|\mathbf{A}\|_2, ignoring error in evaluating the residual. The finite bound K_2\eta_A/(1-K_2\eta_A) requires K_2\eta_A<1 and compares with the exact solution of the stored system, not automatically with x_true. The high-precision experiment on 

Numerical Errors makes those distinctions explicitly.

records.content:
The exact Hilbert matrix H_{ij}=1/(i+j-1) is symmetric positive definite for every n. For any nonzero \mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{z}=\int_0^1\left(\sum_{i=1}^nz_it^{i-1}\right)^2dt>0,

because a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish throughout the interval. A matrix stored in binary floating point has rounded entries and need not retain this property when the smallest eigenvalues are comparable to roundoff. Computing eigenvalues or a Cholesky factor introduces further rounding. The cell catches breakdown and prints it as a result.

# D2: Cholesky on the Hilbert matrix, which is SPD for every n in exact arithmetic.
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg

print("{:>4} {:>14} {:>16} {:>24}".format(
    "n", "reported K(A)", "smallest comp. e.v.", "scipy.linalg.cholesky"))

for n in [12, 13, 14, 15]:
    A = linalg.hilbert(n)
    smallest = np.linalg.eigvalsh(A).min()

    try:
        linalg.cholesky(A)
        status = "succeeds"
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
        status = "LinAlgError (expected)"
    except linalg.LinAlgError:
        status = "LinAlgError (expected)"

    print("{:>4d} {:>14.1e} {:>16.1e} {:>24}".format(
        n, np.linalg.cond(A), smallest, status))




Read the smallest computed eigenvalue and Cholesky status on each row. A negative computed eigenvalue or a Cholesky breakdown does not refute the proof for the exact rational Hilbert matrix. It concerns the stored matrix and floating-point calculation. Conversely, a successful factorization is not a high-accuracy certificate for the exact mathematical data. The numerical condition-number estimate can itself be unreliable near the precision limit.

10-8. Classical Gram–Schmidt, modified Gram–Schmidt, and Householder QR can all give small reconstruction errors \|\mathbf{QR}-\mathbf{A}\|_2. A QR factorization also requires \mathbf{Q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{I}. The table measures both properties.

# D3: three ways to compute QR, and how orthogonal Q really is.
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg


def classical_gram_schmidt(A):
    m, n = A.shape
    Q = np.zeros((m, n))
    R = np.zeros((n, n))
    for j in range(n):
        v = A[:, j].copy()
        for i in range(j):
            # Classical: every projection is taken against the ORIGINAL column.
            R[i, j] = Q[:, i] @ A[:, j]
            v = v - R[i, j] * Q[:, i]
        R[j, j] = np.linalg.norm(v)
        Q[:, j] = v / R[j, j]
    return Q, R


def modified_gram_schmidt(A):
    m, n = A.shape
    Q = np.zeros((m, n))
    R = np.zeros((n, n))
    V = A.copy()
    for j in range(n):
        R[j, j] = np.linalg.norm(V[:, j])
        Q[:, j] = V[:, j] / R[j, j]
        for i in range(j + 1, n):
            # Modified: project against the RUNNING remainder, not the original.
            R[j, i] = Q[:, j] @ V[:, i]
            V[:, i] = V[:, i] - R[j, i] * Q[:, j]
    return Q, R


eps = 1e-8
A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0, 1.0],
              [eps, 0.0, 0.0],
              [0.0, eps, 0.0],
              [0.0, 0.0, eps]])

print("A =\n", A)
print("\nK_2(A) = {:.1e}\n".format(np.linalg.cond(A)))

methods = [
    ("classical Gram-Schmidt", classical_gram_schmidt),
    ("modified Gram-Schmidt", modified_gram_schmidt),
    ("Householder (scipy.linalg.qr)", lambda M: linalg.qr(M, mode="economic")),
]

print("{:<32} {:>14} {:>14}".format("method", "||Q'Q - I||_2", "||QR - A||_2"))
for name, factorize in methods:
    Q, R = factorize(A)
    orth = np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ Q - np.eye(A.shape[1]), 2)
    recon = np.linalg.norm(Q @ R - A, 2)
    print("{:<32} {:>14.1e} {:>14.1e}".format(name, orth, recon))

A 4\times4 KKT matrix, with a positive definite Hessian block \mathbf{H}=2\mathbf{I} and two constraint rows that nearly duplicate each other:\mathbf{K}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{H} & \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{H}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\varepsilon\end{bmatrix}.

\mathbf{A} is nonsingular for every \varepsilon\neq0, so the inertia of \mathbf{K} - the counts of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues - is (2,2,0) exactly, on every row below. The exact column is not an assertion typed in by hand: it is recomputed symbolically with sympy, over the rationals, from the actual double precision entries of \mathbf{K}.

The wrong answers printed below are the demonstration. They are what this cell exists to show.

# D4: inertia of a nearly degenerate KKT matrix, three ways.
import numpy as np
import sympy
from scipy import linalg


def inertia_exact(K):
    """Exact inertia of the double precision entries, over the rationals."""
    M = sympy.Matrix(K.shape[0], K.shape[1],
                     lambda i, j: sympy.Rational(K[i, j]))
    pos = neg = zero = 0
    for value, multiplicity in M.eigenvals().items():
        v = sympy.N(value, 50)
        if v > 0:
            pos += multiplicity
        elif v < 0:
            neg += multiplicity
        else:
            zero += multiplicity
    return (pos, neg, zero)


def inertia_from_block_diagonal(D):
    """Inertia read off the block diagonal D returned by scipy.linalg.ldl."""
    pos = neg = zero = 0
    i, N = 0, D.shape[0]
    while i < N:
        if i + 1 < N and D[i, i + 1] != 0.0:
            ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(D[i:i + 2, i:i + 2])
            i += 2
        else:
            ev = np.array([D[i, i]])
            i += 1
        pos += int((ev > 0).sum())
        neg += int((ev < 0).sum())
        zero += int((ev == 0).sum())
    return (pos, neg, zero)


print("{:>10} {:>14} {:>12} {:>12} {:>12}".format(
    "epsilon", "reported K(K)", "exact", "ldl", "eigvalsh"))

for eps in [1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8, 1e-9, 1e-10]:
    H = 2.0 * np.eye(2)
    A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0 + eps]])
    K = np.block([[H, A.T], [A, np.zeros((2, 2))]])

    _, D, _ = linalg.ldl(K)
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(K)
    from_eig = (int((ev > 0).sum()), int((ev < 0).sum()), int((ev == 0).sum()))

    print("{:>10.0e} {:>14.1e} {:>12} {:>12} {:>12}".format(
        eps, np.linalg.cond(K), str(inertia_exact(K)),
        str(inertia_from_block_diagonal(D)), str(from_eig)))




No solver, no barrier parameter, no iteration - just a matrix, a factorization, and a wrong answer about it.

Find the row where the two computed columns disagree with each other, so at least one of them is wrong, and use the exact column to see which. On the machine the handout was written on that is \varepsilon=10^{-9}, where ldl is wrong and eigvalsh is right; on yours it may be a different row, or there may be more than one. That variability is itself the lesson: two routines in the same library, asked the same question about the same matrix, return different answers, and which one is wrong where depends on the LAPACK build underneath.

Activity

An interior point solver reads the inertia of the KKT matrix at every iteration to decide whether to correct the Hessian. What does this table do to that sentence?

A solver that reads (3,1,0) here concludes the reduced Hessian has the wrong curvature and adds a correction it does not need. Describe the mirror case, where the measurement error points the other way. Which is worse?

Where did the ill conditioning come from? Note that it is not a scaling accident: it is two constraints that nearly say the same thing, which approaches a constraint-qualification failure as the rows become identical. Each represented matrix in this table still has independent rows: near dependence is not an exact LICQ failure.

For \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, m\ge n, with independent columns, the thin QR factorization is \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{QR} with \mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, \mathbf{Q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{I}_n, and nonsingular upper-triangular \mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. For square \mathbf{A}, solve \mathbf{Rx}=\mathbf{Q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{b}. For a tall matrix, the same equation solves the full-column-rank least-squares problem, since the residual decomposes into components in the range of \mathbf{Q} and its orthogonal complement.

Take \mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}3&1\\4&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]=[\mathbf{a}_1\ \mathbf{a}_2] and \mathbf{b}=(4,6)^\mathsf{T}.

Normalize the first column: r_{11}=\|\mathbf{a}_1\|_2=5, \mathbf{q}_1=(3/5,4/5)^\mathsf{T}.

Project the second column: r_{12}=\mathbf{q}_1^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{a}_2=11/5. Subtract this component: \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{a}_2-r_{12}\mathbf{q}_1=(-8/25,6/25)^\mathsf{T}.

Normalize the orthogonal remainder: r_{22}=\|\mathbf{v}\|_2=2/5, \mathbf{q}_2=(-4/5,3/5)^\mathsf{T}. Orthogonality follows from \mathbf{q}_1^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{q}_1^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{a}_2-r_{12}=0.

Assemble \mathbf{Q}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}3/5&-4/5\\4/5&3/5\end{smallmatrix}\right] and \mathbf{R}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}5&11/5\\0&2/5\end{smallmatrix}\right]. The dot product of the two columns of \mathbf{Q} is zero.

Check the first row of \mathbf{QR}: ((3/5)5,\ (3/5)(11/5)-(4/5)(2/5))=(3,1), the first row of \mathbf{A}.

Compute \mathbf{Q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{b}=(36/5,2/5)^\mathsf{T}. Back substitution gives x_2=1, x_1=1.

The decomposition \mathbf{a}_2=r_{12}\mathbf{q}_1+r_{22}\mathbf{q}_2 is the geometric mechanism: a projection along the first unit direction plus a perpendicular remainder. This two-column Gram–Schmidt calculation explains the factors. Library QR uses Householder transformations; sign choices can change columns of \mathbf{Q} and matching rows of \mathbf{R} while leaving the product unchanged. See Nocedal & Wright (2006), Appendix A, pp.608–609, and Higham (2002), Chapter 19 for numerical analysis.

A real symmetric positive definite \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} has a unique factorization \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{LL}^\mathsf{T} with \mathbf{L} lower triangular and L_{jj}>0. The leading cost is n^3/3 operations. Matching column j givesL_{jj}=\sqrt{B_{jj}-\sum_{k<j}L_{jk}^2},\qquad L_{ij}=\frac{B_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}L_{ik}L_{jk}}{L_{jj}}\quad(i>j).

The radicands are positive under the positive-definite hypothesis in exact arithmetic. Nonpositive pivots can instead occur for singular semidefinite or indefinite matrices; rounding can also cause breakdown near the precision limit. A negative square root is one possible failure, not the only one.

For \mathbf{B}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}4&2\\2&5\end{smallmatrix}\right],\begin{bmatrix}L_{11}^2&L_{11}L_{21}\\L_{11}L_{21}&L_{21}^2+L_{22}^2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\2&5\end{bmatrix}.

Thus L_{11}=2, L_{21}=2/2=1, and L_{22}=\sqrt{5-1}=2. With \mathbf{b}=(6,7)^\mathsf{T}, solve \mathbf{Ly}=\mathbf{b} to get \mathbf{y}=(3,2)^\mathsf{T}; then solve \mathbf{L}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y} to get \mathbf{x}=(1,1)^\mathsf{T}.

For the indefinite \mathbf{B}'=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right], the same recurrence reaches L_{22}=\sqrt{1-4}=\sqrt{-3}. Its eigenvalues are 3 and -1. For the positive semidefinite matrix of all ones, it instead reaches a zero second diagonal entry, so the strictly positive-diagonal nonsingular factorization is unavailable.

Positive definiteness also follows directly from a nonsingular triangular factor: \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{LL}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}=\|\mathbf{L}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}\|_2^2>0 for nonzero \mathbf{x}. See Higham (2002), §10.1, pp.196–197.

x_worked = linalg.solve_triangular(U_worked, y_worked)

records.content:
This example is used in the closing 

Optimization for Decision Support lecture. It changes the numerical representation of a linear equality system, while preserving its original solution. Use the induced 2-norm condition number; it is a worst-case perturbation measure, not a prediction of the error in every solve.

For \mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf b, multiplying equality row i by a nonzero constant must multiply b_i as well. With positive diagonal row matrix \mathbf R, the equivalent system is \mathbf R\mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf R\mathbf b. For inequalities, a negative row multiplier reverses the inequality, so positive residual scales are the usual convention.

When dividing column j by d_j>0, define z_j=d_jx_j. Then \mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf z=\mathbf b and \mathbf x=\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf z. Bounds and any other occurrences of that variable must transform too. Combined row/column scaling gives \mathbf R\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf z=\mathbf R\mathbf b.

The example has\mathbf A=\begin{bmatrix}10^{-5}&500&.2\\3\cdot10^{-6}&1000&.4\\10^{-6}&200&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf b=\begin{bmatrix}1.7\\1.7\\1.3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf x=\begin{bmatrix}10^5\\10^{-3}\\1\end{bmatrix}.

The following calculation compares no scaling, row division by the largest absolute row entry, column division by the largest absolute column entry, and row-then-column scaling. Each solution is mapped back and checked in the original equations. The unequal improvement is a result for this example; row scaling can help other matrices, and neither scheme guarantees a small condition number for every problem.

import sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
if "google.colab" in sys.modules:
    import urllib.request
    urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndcbe/optimization/main/notebooks/helper.py", "helper.py")
else:
    sys.path.insert(0, "../")
import helper
helper.set_plotting_style()

scale_A = np.array([[1e-5, 500., .2], [3e-6, 1000., .4], [1e-6, 200., 1.]])
scale_b = np.array([1.7, 1.7, 1.3])
row_div = np.max(np.abs(scale_A), axis=1)
row_A, row_b = scale_A/row_div[:, None], scale_b/row_div
col_div = np.max(np.abs(scale_A), axis=0)
both_div = np.max(np.abs(row_A), axis=0)
scale_cases = [
    ("original", scale_A, scale_b, np.ones(3)),
    ("rows", row_A, row_b, np.ones(3)),
    ("columns", scale_A/col_div, scale_b, col_div),
    ("rows then columns", row_A/both_div, row_b, both_div),
]
scale_rows = []
for name, matrix, rhs, divisors in scale_cases:
    z = np.linalg.solve(matrix, rhs)
    recovered = z/divisors
    residual = float(np.linalg.norm(scale_A@recovered-scale_b, np.inf))
    assert residual < 1e-13
    scale_rows.append({"case":name, "condition_2":float(np.linalg.cond(matrix,2)),
                       "scaled_solution":z.tolist(), "recovered_solution":recovered.tolist(),
                       "original_residual_inf":residual})
display(pd.DataFrame(scale_rows).set_index("case"))



results = {"A":scale_A.tolist(), "b":scale_b.tolist(), "cases":scale_rows,
           "row_divisors":row_div.tolist(), "column_divisors":col_div.tolist(),
           "both_column_divisors":both_div.tolist()}
helper.save_results("ctx-scaling-actual", results,
    notebook="notebooks/6-dev/Math-Primer.ipynb",
    source_cells=[("notebooks/6-dev/Math-Primer.ipynb", "results:ctx-scaling-model"),
                  ("notebooks/6-dev/Math-Primer.ipynb", "results:ctx-scaling-archive")],
    description="Approved L27 row/column scaling example, with solutions recovered in original units",
    solver="NumPy linear solve and singular values", quiet=True)



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6,2.8))
rows = results["cases"]
for i,row in enumerate(rows):
    ax.plot([i,i],[1,row["condition_2"]],color="black",linestyle="-",linewidth=2)
    ax.plot(i,row["condition_2"],marker="s" if i<2 else "o",color="#0072B2",linestyle="none",ms=7)
    ax.annotate(f'{row["condition_2"]:.2g}', (i,row["condition_2"]),
                xytext=(0,8),textcoords="offset points",ha="center",fontsize=11)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set(xticks=range(4),xticklabels=["original","rows","columns","rows then\ncolumns"],
       ylabel="2-norm condition number",ylim=(1,2e9),xlim=(-.4,3.4))
ax.tick_params(axis="x",labelsize=12)
ax.grid(axis="y",which="major",alpha=.25)
fig.tight_layout()
helper.save_figure(fig,"ctx-scaling-actual",quiet=True)
plt.show()



The original and recovered solution is (10^5,10^{-3},1)^\mathsf T. Column scaling gives coordinates (1,1,1)^\mathsf T; row-then-column scaling gives approximately (.002,.001,.005)^\mathsf T. The much smaller coordinates in the combined case are not different physical decisions. The 2-norm condition numbers are approximately 1.49\cdot10^8, 1.44\cdot10^8, 2.79, and 4.50. They compare conditioning of four represented systems; check the original residual after reversing the transformation. Choosing scales needs characteristic units and model knowledge, not only a blind largest-entry rule. Near dependent equations can remain ill conditioned after unit scaling.

Let D\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and \mathbf F:D\to\mathbb R^n differentiable. Define (\mathbf J_F(\mathbf x))_{ij}=\partial F_i(\mathbf x)/\partial x_j for i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. Linearizing at fixed \mathbf x^k gives\mathbf F(\mathbf x^k+\mathbf p)=\mathbf F(\mathbf x^k)+\mathbf J_F(\mathbf x^k)\mathbf p+O(\|\mathbf p\|^2),

with the quadratic remainder when the Jacobian is locally Lipschitz. Newton sets the linear model to zero and solves\mathbf J_F(\mathbf x^k)\mathbf p^k=-\mathbf F(\mathbf x^k),\qquad
\mathbf x^{k+1}=\mathbf x^k+\mathbf p^k.

The actual residual at the update need not be zero. The row-oriented Jacobian requires no extra transpose. An inverse is useful in analysis, but a numerical implementation solves the linear system.

For f\in C^2(D) on an open D, write \mathbf g^k=\nabla f(\mathbf x^k) and \mathbf G^k=\nabla^2f(\mathbf x^k). With \mathbf x^k fixed,m_k(\mathbf p)=f(\mathbf x^k)+(\mathbf g^k)^T\mathbf p+\tfrac12\mathbf p^T\mathbf G^k\mathbf p.

Differentiating the model with respect to the chosen displacement gives\nabla_{\mathbf p}m_k=\mathbf g^k+\mathbf G^k\mathbf p,\qquad
\mathbf G^k\mathbf p^k=-\mathbf g^k.

This computes a model stationary point. It is the model minimum if \mathbf G^k\succ0. The model equals a quadratic objective exactly; for a nonlinear objective with locally Lipschitz Hessian its value remainder is O(\|\mathbf p\|^3).

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eqs. (2.37)–(2.39), pp. 34–35; Nocedal and Wright (2006), §11.1, pp. 274–277. The gradient in the numerical examples below is a column vector.

The existing nonlinear-model sketch uses f(x)=e^x-2x at x^k=1.8. The Newton displacement is approximately -0.6694, giving x^{k+1}=1.1306; the exact minimizer is the natural logarithm of 2. The objective drops from approximately 2.45 to 0.84, but the model stationary point still differs from the true minimizer.

import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg

x0 = np.array([3.0, 0.0])
g0 = np.array([4.0, 16.0])
H0 = np.diag([2.0, 8.0])
# Solve H0 @ p0 = -g0, then update the iterate.
p0 = linalg.solve(H0, -g0)
x1 = x0 + p0
print(p0, x1)




The step is [-2,-2]^T and the updated point is [1,-2]^T. A quadratic objective equals its quadratic model everywhere, so one exact Newton step reaches its stationary point when the Hessian is nonsingular.
