Explain the geometry. The overlap of both hatches is feasible. Why is the origin optimal even though the objective gradient is nonzero? The constraints restrict x_1 to be nonnegative and permit only x_2=0 when x_1=0.

With L=x_1+u_1(x_2-x_1^3)+u_2(-x_1^3-x_2), stationarity is\nabla_x L=\begin{bmatrix}1-3(u_1+u_2)x_1^2\\u_1-u_2\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf0.

The remaining conditions are g_1,g_2\le0, u_1,u_2\ge0, u_1g_1=u_2g_2=0. At the origin the first stationarity component is 1 for every finite multiplier vector.

Neither multiplier positive: u_1=u_2=0 gives gradient (1,0)^T, so stationarity fails. Zero multipliers do not remove the constraints or make this feasible problem unbounded.

Only u_1>0: the second stationarity row forces u_1=0, a contradiction.

Only u_2>0: the second row forces u_2=0, again a contradiction.

Both positive: the second row gives u_1=u_2=u; the first gives x_1^2=1/(6u). Complementarity requires both constraints active, which forces x_1=x_2=0, contradicting the first row. The algebraic relation has both square-root signs; feasibility selects x_1\ge0, but no finite feasible KKT point results.

An approximate stationarity path illustrates the difficulty: for t>0, choose (x_1,x_2)=(t,0), u_1=u_2=1/(6t^2). Stationarity holds and the point is feasible, but both inequalities are slack and u_i g_i=-t/6\ne0. As t\downarrow0, complementarity residuals vanish while multipliers diverge. This is not a family of exact KKT points. The original scan’s 3u denominator is replaced by the verified 6u relation.

hierarchy.lvl3: Actual and linearized directions at the cusp
Actual and linearized directions at the cusp

records.content:
At the origin the active row Jacobian is\mathbf J_g=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}.

Its inequalities impose d_2\le0 and -d_2\le0, hence L_S=\{(d_1,0):d_1\in\mathbb R\}. In contrast, |x_2|\le x_1^3 and x_1\ge0 imply every normalized nonzero feasible chord tends to (1,0)^T: |x_2|/x_1\le x_1^2\to0. Therefore T_S=\{(d_1,0):d_1\ge0\}.

Biegler calls (1,0)^T \mathbf d_1 and (-1,0)^T \mathbf d_2. The left-pointing \mathbf d_2 has \nabla f^T\mathbf d_2=-1 but cannot be realized by a feasible sequence. Two handwritten sketches reverse these names; the algebra and geometry fix the labels. A constraint qualification eliminates this extra first-order direction.

LICQ holds at a feasible point when all equality gradients and all active inequality gradients are jointly independent: \operatorname{rank}\mathbf J_{\mathcal A}=m+|\mathcal A_I|. It is a property of the constraint representation at a point, not a requirement that the point already be optimal. Equalities, weakly active inequalities, and active bounds all count. If there are more active rows than variables, LICQ cannot hold. Biegler, Definition 4.12 at the foot of p. 77; Nocedal and Wright, Definition 12.4, p. 320.

The cusp has two antiparallel nonzero rows, rank 1 rather than 2, so LICQ fails. Nonzero individual gradients are not enough.

Reverse inclusion under LICQ. Let c_{\mathcal A}(\mathbf z) stack all equalities and active inequalities in the tagged row order, and let Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m-|\mathcal A_I|)} have basis columns for \ker \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}. For any \mathbf d\in L_S, considerR(\mathbf z,t)=\begin{bmatrix}c_{\mathcal A}(\mathbf z)-tJ_{\mathcal A}\mathbf d\\Z^T(\mathbf z-\bar{\mathbf x}-t\mathbf d)\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf0.

At (\bar{\mathbf x},0) its derivative with respect to \mathbf z is [\mathbf J_{\mathcal A};\mathbf Z^T], a square nonsingular matrix: a vector in its null space belongs to \ker \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{range}\mathbf Z and is orthogonal to that space, hence is zero. The C1 implicit function theorem requires a C1 residual map, a zero residual at the base point and an invertible derivative with respect to the unknowns; these follow from the stated neighborhood data, feasibility and the displayed null-space argument. It yields a C^1 path \mathbf z(t), and differentiation at zero gives \mathbf z'(0)=\mathbf d. Thus \mathbf z(t)=\bar{\mathbf x}+t\mathbf d+o(t).

The construction gives exactly h_j(\mathbf z(t))=t\nabla h_j^T\mathbf d=0 and g_i(\mathbf z(t))=t\nabla g_i^T\mathbf d\le0 for active inequalities; continuity preserves the inactive inequalities for small positive t. These exact identities come from solving R=0, not merely truncating a Taylor expansion. Consequently L_S=T_S. This adapts Nocedal and Wright, Lemma 12.2, pp. 323–325, to g\le0 and row Jacobians; Biegler, Lemma 4.13, p. 78, requires the errata’s h_j subscript.

For the circle equality h=(x_1-1)^2+x_2^2-1=0 at (0,0), \mathbf d=(0,1)^T is tangent. The straight step (0,t) has h=t^2>0. The corrected path (1-\sqrt{1-t^2},t) is feasible and differs from the straight step by (t^2/2+O(t^4),0). LICQ promises a nearby feasible path, not feasibility of the straight step.

hierarchy.lvl2: From no feasible descent to KKT
From no feasible descent to KKT

records.content:
At a C^1 local minimum with LICQ, T_S=L_S, so no direction satisfies\nabla f^T\mathbf d<0,\qquad \mathbf J_h\mathbf d=0,\qquad \mathbf J_{g,\mathcal A_I}\mathbf d\le0.

The finite-dimensional linear alternative says that absence of a direction satisfying that system is equivalent to existence of a nonnegative active inequality multiplier and unrestricted equality multiplier balancing the objective gradient. Thus it gives \mathbf u_{\mathcal A_I}\ge0, unrestricted \mathbf v, with \nabla f+\mathbf J_{g,\mathcal A_I}^T\mathbf u_{\mathcal A_I}+\mathbf J_h^T\mathbf v=0. Inactive multipliers are zero, yielding dual feasibility and complementarity. Feasibility is already a hypothesis. This proves KKT necessity (Biegler, Theorem 4.14, p. 78; Nocedal and Wright, Theorem 12.1, p. 321, and proof pp. 323–329).

Conversely, a KKT vector implies \nabla f^T\mathbf d=-\mathbf u_{\mathcal A_I}^TJ_{g,\mathcal A_I}\mathbf d\ge0 for every \mathbf d\in L_S. This algebra needs no CQ. It is still a first-order necessary test, not general sufficiency. The separate convex certificate is at the 

Local Optimality reference.

At a fixed KKT point, stack active multipliers in the same order as \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}, with equality components unrestricted and inequality components nonnegative. If \boldsymbol\lambda^a and \boldsymbol\lambda^b both satisfy stationarity, then\mathbf J_{\mathcal A}^T(\boldsymbol\lambda^a-\boldsymbol\lambda^b)=0.

Full row rank makes \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}^T injective, so the difference is zero. Equivalently, multiply by \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}: the row Gram matrix \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}\mathbf J_{\mathcal A}^T is positive definite. This is the row-oriented version of Biegler’s Theorem 4.15 proof, p. 79; his column-oriented Gram matrix has the factors in the opposite order.

Failure of LICQ does not force multiple KKT multipliers. For \min0 subject to -x\le0, -2x\le0, at x=0 stationarity and nonnegativity require u_1+2u_2=0, hence (u_1,u_2)=(0,0) uniquely despite dependent rows. Without LICQ the unconstrained linear stationarity system has a null direction, but the multiplier sign restrictions may remove all nonzero displacements.

For redundant equalities the situation differs: if \mathbf J_h^T\boldsymbol\nu=0, equality multipliers can move freely as \mathbf v+t\boldsymbol\nu without sign restrictions. The active equality KKT matrix has null vector (\mathbf0,\boldsymbol\nu)^T, whatever the Hessian.

Uniqueness alone does not establish a differentiable solution branch or a shadow price. The 

sensitivity reference states the branch, sign, and second-order conditions and gives examples of nonsmooth values.

MFCQ holds when \mathbf J_h has full row rank and \exists\mathbf d\in\mathbb R^n:\ \mathbf J_h\mathbf d=\mathbf0 and \nabla g_i(\bar{\mathbf x})^T\mathbf d<0 for every i\in\mathcal A_I. With no active inequalities the strict condition is vacuous; equality independence still matters. This tests a feasible point, not just a solution. Biegler, Definition 4.16, p. 79; Nocedal and Wright, Definition 12.6, p. 339.

LICQ implies MFCQ: full row rank allows solving \mathbf J_{\mathcal A}\mathbf d=(\mathbf0,-\mathbf1)^T. The equality part is zero and every active inequality decreases strictly.

Strictly weaker: take h=x_2=0, g_1=-x_1\le0, g_2=-2x_1\le0 at the origin. The three active rows have rank 2, so LICQ fails; \mathbf d=(1,0)^T satisfies MFCQ. For f=x_1, stationarity gives v=0, u_1+2u_2=1, u_1,u_2\ge0. The multiplier set is the closed line segment from (1,0) to (0,1/2): bounded, nonunique.

At the cusp, MFCQ would require d_2<0 and -d_2<0, which is impossible. No finite KKT multiplier exists there.

Why MFCQ bounds a nonempty KKT multiplier set. If a sequence of KKT multipliers were unbounded, omit its identically zero inactive components, normalize it by its diverging norm, and take a convergent subsequence on the compact unit sphere in \mathbb R^{m+|\mathcal A_I|}. Dividing stationarity by that norm gives\mathbf J_{g,\mathcal A_I}^T\widehat{\mathbf u}+\mathbf J_h^T\widehat{\mathbf v}=\mathbf0,\quad\widehat{\mathbf u}\ge0,\quad\|(\widehat{\mathbf u},\widehat{\mathbf v})\|=1.

Dot with the MFCQ direction. Each active inequality derivative is strictly negative, so a zero sum forces \widehat{\mathbf u}=\mathbf0. Equality independence then forces \widehat{\mathbf v}=\mathbf0, contradicting unit norm. The fixed-point KKT multiplier set is closed, so it is compact if nonempty. MFCQ also ensures KKT existence at a C^1 local minimum.

Conversely, failure of MFCQ yields a nonzero homogeneous multiplier (\widehat{\mathbf u}\ge\mathbf0,\widehat{\mathbf v}) with \mathbf J_{g,\mathcal A_I}^T\widehat{\mathbf u}+\mathbf J_h^T\widehat{\mathbf v}=\mathbf0: equality dependence gives one immediately; otherwise the strict-direction theorem of alternatives gives one. Add its nonnegative ray to any existing KKT vector to obtain an unbounded multiplier set. Thus at a fixed KKT point with a nonempty multiplier set, MFCQ is equivalent to boundedness. The nonempty condition matters: \min x subject to x^2\le0 has sole feasible point 0, fails MFCQ, and has no KKT vector; the empty set is bounded in the set-theoretic sense. See Nocedal and Wright, p. 339, with this scope made explicit.

For C^1 data at a local minimum:

Condition

Geometry

KKT multipliers

LICQ

T_S=L_S; all active rows independent

Exist and are unique

MFCQ

T_S=L_S; common strict inward direction with equality tangency

Exist; nonempty compact set, possibly nonunique

All active constraints affine

T_S=L_S without independence

Exist, possibly unbounded

Abadie’s CQ

The statement T_S=L_S itself

Existence by the same alternative argument; no general uniqueness or boundedness

These are sufficient hypotheses; their failure is not proof that KKT fails. Example: \min x^2 subject to x^2\le0 has a KKT vector at zero although LICQ and MFCQ fail. Its multiplier set is [0,\infty).

MFCQ gives T_S=L_S: for any \mathbf d\in L_S, add \delta\mathbf w with a strict MFCQ direction \mathbf w. All active inequalities then decrease strictly. Full row rank of \mathbf J_h gives, by the implicit function theorem, an equality-feasible path \bar{\mathbf x}+t(\mathbf d+\delta\mathbf w)+o(t); strict inequality derivatives make it feasible for small t>0. Thus \mathbf d+\delta\mathbf w\in T_S. Let \delta\downarrow0 and use closedness of the tangent cone to get \mathbf d\in T_S.

Peterson (1973), SIAM Review 15, pp. 639–654, 

DOI, Table 1 pp. 643–644 and Figure 4 p. 645, maps a broader CQ hierarchy. Table 1 puts MFCQ on p. 643 and LICQ on the continuation p. 644. His principal formulation uses inequalities and a general set X; do not encode equalities as two opposite inequalities when translating MFCQ. His arrows point toward weaker conditions. The equality-aware definitions here follow the textbooks.

The following original experiment intentionally approaches the degenerate cusp with Ipopt. Keep its iterates and reported termination distinct from an exact KKT certificate: there is no finite multiplier vector at the true solution. Solver versions and tolerances can change the numerical output.

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.environ import (
    ConcreteModel,
    Var,
    Objective,
    Constraint,
    SolverFactory,
    Suffix,
    minimize,
    value,
)

## Create concrete Pyomo model
m = ConcreteModel()

## Set up to extract dual variables after model solve.
m.dual = Suffix(direction=Suffix.IMPORT)

## Declare variables with initial values
m.x1 = Var(initialize=1)
m.x2 = Var(initialize=1)

## Declare objective
m.OBJ = Objective(expr=m.x1, sense=minimize)

m.g1 = Constraint(expr=m.x2 <= m.x1**3)

m.g2 = Constraint(expr=-m.x1**3 <= m.x2)

## Specify IPOPT as solver
solver = SolverFactory("ipopt")

## Solve the model
results = solver.solve(m, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)

## Return the solution
print("x1 = ", value(m.x1))
print("x2 = ", value(m.x2))
print("\n")

## Inspect dual variables
m.dual.display()





Discussion. Inspect the iteration count, final primal residuals, point, and imported duals. Why is the point only approximately zero? Compare the growth of multiplier magnitudes with 1/(6t^2), rather than treating the solver’s output as a finite limiting KKT vector.

The raw Pyomo dual suffix uses the solver interface’s constraint orientation. It is not automatically the nonnegative u_i of the canonical g_i\le0 form. For this pair of upper/lower constraints, check the mapping against stationarity before interpreting the signs; the 

worked suffix checks illustrate this procedure. A large negative imported value does not by itself violate canonical dual feasibility.

For diagnosing larger models, continue to 

NLP Diagnostics with Degeneracy Hunter: full row-dependence theory, QR/MILP workflow, scaling and case-study context accompany the executable diagnostic example.

The current default run reports an optimal termination at a slightly negative x_1. Exact cusp feasibility requires x_1\ge0. Re-evaluate the original inequalities and multiplier products below. Both imported suffixes convert as u_i=-\texttt{m.dual[m.gi]} for this model; the stationarity residual checks that mapping.

Ipopt’s 

options reference describes bound relaxation and its limits. In an inequality formulation with slack variables, the internal feasibility and complementarity report can differ from evaluation of the original inequality. The numerical output here establishes that difference directly: small primal violation multiplied by a very large multiplier need not produce a small original-model complementarity residual. Keep the original experiment unchanged; an optimal solver status is not a proof of exact feasibility or KKT satisfaction at the cusp.

x = np.array([value(m.x1), value(m.x2)])
g = np.array([x[1] - x[0]**3, -x[0]**3 - x[1]])
u = -np.array([m.dual[m.g1], m.dual[m.g2]])
stationarity = np.array([1 - 3 * (u[0] + u[1]) * x[0]**2, u[0] - u[1]])
print(f"Original-model primal violation: {max(0.0, float(g.max())):.6e}")
print(f"Canonical multipliers: {u[0]:.6e}, {u[1]:.6e}")
print(f"Stationarity infinity norm: {np.linalg.norm(stationarity, np.inf):.6e}")
print(f"Original complementarity infinity norm: {np.linalg.norm(u * g, np.inf):.6e}")
assert np.all(u >= 0) and np.linalg.norm(stationarity, np.inf) < 1e-6

Reference: Beginning of Chapter 4 in Biegler (2010)

All four definitions compare feasible points and require \mathbf{x}^*\in\mathcal F.

Global: f(\mathbf{x}^*)\le f(\mathbf{x}) for every \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal F.

Local: for some \epsilon>0, the same inequality holds for every \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal N_\epsilon(\mathbf{x}^*)\cap\mathcal F, where \mathcal N_\epsilon=\{\mathbf{x}:\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^*\|<\epsilon\}.

Strict local: there exists \epsilon>0 such that f(\mathbf{x}^*)<f(\mathbf{x}) for every \mathbf{x}\in(\mathcal N_\epsilon(\mathbf{x}^*)\cap\mathcal F)\setminus\{\mathbf{x}^*\}.

Isolated local: \mathbf{x}^* is local and there exists \epsilon>0 such that no distinct local minimizer belongs to \mathcal N_\epsilon(\mathbf{x}^*)\cap\mathcal F.

The intersection is essential. For f=x_1, \mathcal F=\{x_1\ge0\}, the origin is a global minimum although its objective gradient is nonzero. It is not strict because feasible points on x_1=0 tie. For f=x^2, \mathcal F=[1,\infty), the point 1 is strict, isolated and global. For \mathcal F=\{0\}, the unique point is strict vacuously: there are no distinct feasible comparisons. For f=0 on \mathbb R, every point is global/local but none is strict or isolated.

The existing 

optimality reference gives the isolated-implies-strict argument and the strict-but-not-isolated counterexample; those proofs are not repeated here. Source: Biegler (2010), Definition 4.1, pp. 63–64, with the distinct-point qualification supplied.

As with unconstrained optimization, the following questions need to be considered:

If a solution \mathbf{x}^* exists, is it a global solution in \mathcal{F} or is it only a local solution?

What conditions characterize the optimal solutions?

Are there special problem classes of the NLP whose solutions have stronger properties and are easier to solve?

Are there efficient and reliable methods to solve the NLP?

A convex optimization problem has a convex feasible set and a convex objective on that set. Use a common convex domain X when applying the function test:f(\theta\mathbf{x}_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf{x}_b)\le
\theta f(\mathbf{x}_a)+(1-\theta)f(\mathbf{x}_b),\qquad
\mathbf{x}_a,\mathbf{x}_b\in X,\quad0<\theta<1.

Strict convexity makes this strict for distinct endpoints. We reserve \theta for this mixture and \alpha for a line-search length; the latter can exceed one.

For (x^2-1)^2, the second derivative is 12x^2-4: it is positive on [0.7,1.5], but the larger [-0.7,1.5] interval contains the comparison f(0)=1>f(\pm0.7)=0.2601. The midpoint violates the chord bound. The second pictured function is (\max\{0,1-x\})^2 for x\le2, then 1 for x>2. On [0,1.8] it is convex but not strict because it has a flat part. Across the jump, endpoints 2 and 2.5 have values 0 and 1, while their midpoint has value 1, greater than the chord value 1/2.

For the first interval of panel (b), the positive-part function q(x)=\max\{0,1-x\} is convex and nonnegative. Thus, with 0<\theta<1,q(\theta a+(1-\theta)b)^2\le[\theta q(a)+(1-\theta)q(b)]^2
\le\theta q(a)^2+(1-\theta)q(b)^2.

The first inequality uses monotonicity of squaring on nonnegative values; the second is convexity of the scalar square. This proves convexity of the squared positive part without differentiating at the join. It is not strictly convex because it is constant on [1,1.8]. For the quartic restricted to [0.7,1.5], f''(x)\ge12(0.7)^2-4=1.88>0 supplies the positive-curvature criterion from the Mathematics Primer.

A set is convex when it contains every segment between its points. Intersections preserve this property: endpoints in every set have their entire segment in every set. Unions need not preserve it; a midpoint between separated disks belongs to neither disk. The empty set is convex, but supplies no feasible solution.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eq. (4.2) and Theorem 4.2, pp. 64–65; the explicit function examples are prepared versions of the handwritten domain concept test. The first-use definitions are in the 

Mathematics Primer.

Convex feasible-region certificate. On a common convex domain X, suppose every scalar g_i is convex and every equality is affine, \mathbf h(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf b. Then\mathcal F=\{\mathbf{x}\in X:\mathbf g(\mathbf{x})\le0,\ \mathbf h(\mathbf{x})=0\}

is convex.

Take feasible endpoints and \bar{\mathbf{x}}=\theta\mathbf{x}_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf{x}_b, with 0<\theta<1. Convexity of X keeps \bar{\mathbf{x}} in the domain. For each component,g_i(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\le\theta g_i(\mathbf{x}_a)+(1-\theta)g_i(\mathbf{x}_b)\le0.

The affine equality gives\mathbf h(\bar{\mathbf{x}})=\theta\mathbf h(\mathbf{x}_a)+(1-\theta)\mathbf h(\mathbf{x}_b)=0.

The constant is preserved because the weights sum to one. Thus the combination is feasible. In a contradiction proof, infeasibility means some g_i(\bar{\mathbf{x}})>0 or some equality fails; a vector expression \mathbf g>0 would incorrectly require every inequality component to be positive.

The equivalent set proof uses convex sublevel sets \{g_i\le0\} and affine hyperplanes \{h_j=0\}, intersecting all of them with X.

Affine equalities are sufficient because they preserve both sides of an equality. Convexity alone gives only h(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\le0. For h=x_1^2+x_2^2-1, the endpoints (-1,0),(1,0) satisfy h=0, but their midpoint has h=-1 and is not on the circle.

Source: Biegler (2010), Theorem 4.2, pp. 64–65; the componentwise form follows the p.64 erratum. The affine extension follows directly from the displayed identity.

Local-to-global certificate. If \mathcal F is convex and f is convex on it, every local minimizer is global. If f is strictly convex, a minimizer, when it exists, is unique.

Suppose \mathbf{x}_a is local but not global. Then some feasible point \mathbf{x}_b has f(\mathbf{x}_b)<f(\mathbf{x}_a). It need not itself be a local minimizer. Let \epsilon define the local neighborhood. For\bar{\mathbf{x}}=\theta\mathbf{x}_a+(1-\theta)\mathbf{x}_b,

the segment is feasible and\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}-\mathbf{x}_a\|=(1-\theta)\|\mathbf{x}_b-\mathbf{x}_a\|.

Choose \theta sufficiently close to one to make this distance less than \epsilon. Convexity givesf(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\le f(\mathbf{x}_a)+(1-\theta)
[f(\mathbf{x}_b)-f(\mathbf{x}_a)]<f(\mathbf{x}_a),

contradicting local minimality at a feasible neighbor.

For uniqueness, suppose two distinct global minimizers tie at value m. Their feasible midpoint has value strictly less than their average m, a contradiction. Existence is separate: strictly convex e^x on \mathbb R has no minimizer.

These are applications of the existing first-use 

optimality lecture/reference argument to feasible comparisons. Sources: Biegler (2010), Theorem 4.3, p.65, correcting the proof’s two-local-minima assumption; Nocedal and Wright (2006), Theorem 2.5 proof, p.16.

For a nonempty bounded polytope, a linear objective attains an optimum at a vertex. An optimal face can contain other minimizers. This describes the bounded polygon pictures, not every LP: an LP can be infeasible, have an unbounded objective, or have a finite optimum on an unbounded polyhedron. A feasible polyhedron containing a line need not have vertices.

Strictly convex objectives can instead attain the unique minimum at a vertex, on an edge, or in the interior. Convexity certifies a value, not a universal boundary location.

A nonconvex feasible region can supply separated local minima even when the objective is convex; a nonconvex objective can supply multiple local minima on a convex region. Prove a nonconvex-set claim by giving feasible endpoints and a segment point outside it.

In panel (1), the two local minima are at the inner-arc endpoints. In panel (2), they are at the centers of the three interior contour wells.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Figures 4.1–4.3, pp.66–67.

Reference: Section 4.1 in Biegler (2010)

Motivating Question: Is this problem convex?

What is the smallest rectangle you can use to enclose three given circles? Reference: Example 4.4 in Biegler (2010).

The following optimization model is given in Biegler (2010) and 

adapted to use set notation.\begin{align*}
\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},A,B} \quad & 2(A + B) \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & A \geq 0, \quad B \geq 0 \\
& x_i, y_i \geq R_i, \quad x_i \leq B - R_i, \quad y_i \leq A - R_i, \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{C} \\
& (x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2 \geq (R_i + R_j)^2, \quad \forall i,j \in \{i \in \mathcal{C}, j \in \mathcal{C}: i < j\}
\end{align*}

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches


def create_circle_model(circle_radii):
    """Create circle optimization model in Pyomo

    Arguments:
        circle_radii: dictionary with keys=circle name and value=radius (float)

    Returns:
        model: Pyomo model
    """

    # Create a concrete Pyomo model.
    model = pyo.ConcreteModel()

    # Initialize index for circles
    model.CIRCLES = pyo.Set(initialize=circle_radii.keys())

    # Create parameter
    model.R = pyo.Param(
        model.CIRCLES, domain=pyo.PositiveReals, initialize=circle_radii
    )

    # Create variables for box
    model.a = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.PositiveReals)
    model.b = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.PositiveReals)

    # Set objective
    model.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=2 * (model.a + model.b), sense=pyo.minimize)

    # Create variables for circle centers
    model.x = pyo.Var(model.CIRCLES, domain=pyo.PositiveReals)
    model.y = pyo.Var(model.CIRCLES, domain=pyo.PositiveReals)

    # "In the box" constraints
    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def left_x_con(m, c):
        return m.x[c] >= m.R[c]

    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def left_y_con(m, c):
        return m.y[c] >= m.R[c]

    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def right_x_con(m, c):
        return m.x[c] <= m.b - m.R[c]

    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES)
    def right_y_con(m, c):
        return m.y[c] <= m.a - m.R[c]

    # No overlap constraints
    @model.Constraint(model.CIRCLES, model.CIRCLES)
    def no_overlap_con(m, c1, c2):
        if c1 < c2:
            return (m.x[c1] - m.x[c2]) ** 2 + (m.y[c1] - m.y[c2]) ** 2 >= (
                m.R[c1] + m.R[c2]
            ) ** 2
        else:
            return pyo.Constraint.Skip

    return model


def initialize_circle_model(model, a_init=25, b_init=25):
    """Initialize the x and y coordinates using uniform distribution

    Arguments:
        model: Pyomo concrete model (modified in place)
        a_init: initial value for a (default=25)
        b_init: initial value for b (default=25)

    Returns:
        Nothing. But per Pyomo scoping rules, the input argument `model`
        can be modified in this function.

    """
    # Initialize
    model.a = a_init
    model.b = b_init

    for i in model.CIRCLES:
        # Adding circle radii ensures the remains in the >0, >0 quadrant
        model.x[i] = random.uniform(0, 10) + model.R[i]
        model.y[i] = random.uniform(0, 10) + model.R[i]



Next, we will create a dictionary containing the circle names and radii values.

# Create dictionary with circle data
circle_data = {"A": 10.0, "B": 5.0, "C": 3.0}
circle_data



# Access the keys
circle_data.keys()



Now let’s create the model.

# Create model
model = create_circle_model(circle_data)



And let’s initialize the model.

# Initialize model
initialize_circle_model(model)
model.pprint()

Next, we’ll define a function to plot the solution (or initial point)

# Plot initial point


def plot_circles(m):
    """Plot circles using data in Pyomo model

    Arguments:
        m: Pyomo concrete model

    Returns:
        Nothing (but makes a figure)

    """

    # Create figure
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 6))

    # Adjust axes
    l = max(m.a.value, m.b.value) + 1
    ax.set_xlim(0, l)
    ax.set_ylim(0, l)

    # Draw box
    art = mpatches.Rectangle((0, 0), width=m.b.value, height=m.a.value, fill=False)
    ax.add_patch(art)

    # Draw circles and mark center
    for i in m.CIRCLES:
        art2 = mpatches.Circle(
            (m.x[i].value, m.y[i].value), radius=m.R[i], fill=True, alpha=0.25
        )
        ax.add_patch(art2)

        plt.scatter(m.x[i].value, m.y[i].value, color="black")

    # Show plot
    plt.show()


plot_circles(model)

# Specify the solver
solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")

# Use the MA27 linear solver from HSL. The IDAES binaries
# (`idaes get-extensions`) are statically linked against HSL, so MA27 is
# available both here and on Colab. Pinning it keeps the iteration log in
# this notebook reproducible -- the default differs between Ipopt builds.

# Solve the model

assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"

Next, we can inspect the solution. Because Pyomo is a Python extension, we can use Python (for loops, etc.) to programmatically inspect the solution.

print("Name\tValue")
for c in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var):

    )

The usual structural test checks a convex objective, convex scalar inequalities in g_i\le0 form, and affine equalities on a common convex domain. It is a sufficient certificate. A failed representation test does not alone prove the feasible set nonconvex.

For \min x^2 subject to x^3\le0, the constraint function is not convex on \mathbb R, since its second derivative 6x is negative for x<0. Yet its feasible set is (-\infty,0], identical to the affine representation x\le0. The problem has a convex objective and a convex feasible set. Similarly x^3=0 defines the singleton \{0\} although that equality representation is nonlinear.

The circle-packing no-overlap set is outside a disk in relative-center coordinates. Opposite boundary points have an infeasible midpoint. The indexed model, two numerical arrangements and multistart experiment already have their home in 

Continuous Optimization: Nonlinear Programming; they are not copied into this reference. The existing numerical example above remains an introduction to the model.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Figures 4.1–4.3, pp.66–67, and Example 4.4, pp.67–68. The equivalent representations are directly verified by their signs/zero sets.

For C^2 maps f:D\to\mathbb R, \mathbf h:D\to\mathbb R^m on open D\subset\mathbb R^n, consider \min f(\mathbf x) subject to h(\mathbf x)=0, use L=f+\mathbf v^Th, row Jacobian \mathbf{J}_h, and residual F(\mathbf x,\mathbf v)=(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}L,h)^T. Its Jacobian is\mathbf{K}=F'=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{W}&\mathbf{J}_h^T\\\mathbf{J}_h&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{W}=\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2L.

The Newton step solves \mathbf{K}(\mathbf d_x,\mathbf d_v)^T=-F and updates both variables. Equivalently, set \bar{\mathbf v}=\mathbf v^k+\mathbf d_v and solve\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{W}&\mathbf{J}_h^T\\\mathbf{J}_h&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf d_x\\\bar{\mathbf v}\end{bmatrix}
=-\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f\\h\end{bmatrix}.

These are the stationarity equations of \min_{\mathbf d}\nabla f^T\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf d^T\mathbf{W}\mathbf d subject to h+\mathbf{J}_h\mathbf d=\mathbf{0}. With full-row-rank \mathbf{J}_h and \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}\succ0, they give the unique constrained-QP minimum even when \mathbf{W} is indefinite in full space. Without this curvature condition a Newton root is not automatically a QP minimizer. Biegler (5.4)–(5.6), p. 93; Nocedal–Wright (18.2)–(18.9), pp. 530–532.

The existing teaching code below uses a column gradient matrix A, so \mathbf{J}_h = A.T when comparing formulas. Its finite-difference helpers and intentional singular solves and starts near different stationary points remain unchanged.

# Load required Python libraries.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg


## Check if element of array is NaN
def check_nan(A):
    return np.sum(np.isnan(A))


## Calculate gradient with central finite difference
def my_grad_approx(x, f, eps1, verbose=False):
    """
    Calculate gradient of function f using central difference formula

    Inputs:
        x - point for which to evaluate gradient
        f - function to consider
        eps1 - perturbation size

    Outputs:
        grad - gradient (vector)
    """

    n = len(x)
    grad = np.zeros(n)

    if verbose:
        print("***** my_grad_approx at x = ", x, "*****")

    for i in range(0, n):

        # Create vector of zeros except eps in position i
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[i] = eps1

        # Finite difference formula
        my_f_plus = f(x + e)
        my_f_minus = f(x - e)

        # Diagnostics
        if verbose:
            print("e[", i, "] = ", e)
            print("f(x + e[", i, "]) = ", my_f_plus)
            print("f(x - e[", i, "]) = ", my_f_minus)

        grad[i] = (my_f_plus - my_f_minus) / (2 * eps1)

    if verbose:
        print("***** Done. ***** \n")

    return grad


def my_jac_approx(x, h, eps1, verbose=False):
    """
    Calculate Jacobian of function h(x) using central difference formula

    Inputs:
        x - point for which to evaluate gradient
        h - vector-valued function to consider. h(x): R^n --> R^m
        eps1 - perturbation size

    Outputs:
        A - Jacobian (n x m matrix)
    """

    # Check h(x) at x
    h_x0 = h(x)

    # Extract dimensions
    n = len(x)
    m = len(h_x0)

    # Initialize Jacobian matrix
    A = np.zeros((n, m))

    # Calculate Jacobian by row
    for i in range(0, n):

        # Create vector of zeros except eps in position i
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[i] = eps1

        # Finite difference formula
        my_h_plus = h(x + e)
        my_h_minus = h(x - e)

        # Diagnostics
        if verbose:
            print("e[", i, "] = ", e)
            print("h(x + e[", i, "]) = ", my_h_plus)
            print("h(x - e[", i, "]) = ", my_h_minus)

        A[i, :] = (my_h_plus - my_h_minus) / (2 * eps1)

    if verbose:
        print("***** Done. ***** \n")

    return A


## Calculate gradient using central finite difference and my_hes_approx
def my_hes_approx(x, grad, eps2):
    """
    Calculate gradient of function my_f using central difference formula and my_grad

    Inputs:
        x - point for which to evaluate gradient
        grad - function to calculate the gradient
        eps2 - perturbation size (for Hessian NOT gradient approximation)

    Outputs:
        H - Hessian (matrix)
    """

    n = len(x)
    H = np.zeros([n, n])

    for i in range(0, n):
        # Create vector of zeros except eps in position i
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[i] = eps2

        # Evaluate gradient twice
        grad_plus = grad(x + e)
        grad_minus = grad(x - e)

        # Notice we are building the Hessian by column (or row)
        H[:, i] = (grad_plus - grad_minus) / (2 * eps2)

    return H


## Linear algebra calculation
def xxT(u):
    """
    Calculates u*u.T to circumvent limitation with SciPy

    Arguments:
    u - numpy 1D array

    Returns:
    u*u.T

    Assume u is a nx1 vector.
    Recall: NumPy does not distinguish between row or column vectors

    u.dot(u) returns a scalar. This function returns an nxn matrix.
    """

    n = len(u)
    A = np.zeros([n, n])
    for i in range(0, n):
        for j in range(0, n):
            A[i, j] = u[i] * u[j]

    return A


## Analyze Hessian
def analyze_hes(B):
    print(B, "\n")

    l = linalg.eigvals(B)
    print("Eigenvalues: ", l, "\n")

def alg51(x0, calc_f, calc_h, eps1=1e-6, eps2=1e-6, max_iter=50, verbose=False):
    """
    Basic Full Space Newton Method for Equality Constrained NLP

    Input:
        x0 - starting point (vector)
        calc_f - function to calculate objective (returns scalar)
        calc_h - function to calculate constraints (returns vector)
        eps1 - tolerance for primal and dual steps
        eps2 - tolerance for gradient of L1

    Outputs:
        x - history of steps (primal variables)
        v - history of steps (dual variables)
        f - history of objective evaluations
        h - history of constraint evaluations
        df - history of objective gradients
        dL - history of Lagrange function gradients
        A - history of constraint Jacobians
        W - history of Lagrange Hessians

    Notes:
        1. For simplicity, central finite difference is used
           for all gradient calculations.
    """

    # Declare iteration histories as empty lists
    x = []
    v = []
    f = []
    L = []
    h = []
    df = []
    dL = []
    A = []
    W = []

    # Flag for iterations
    flag = True

    # Iteration counter
    k = 0

    # Copy initial point to primal variable history
    n = len(x0)
    x.append(x0)

    # Evaluate objective and constraints at initial point
    f.append(calc_f(x0))
    h.append(calc_h(x0))

    # Determine number of equality constraints
    m = len(h[0])

    # Initial dual variables with vector of ones
    v.append(np.ones(m))

    # Print header for iteration information
    print("Iter. \tf(x) \t\t||h(x)|| \t||grad_L(x)|| \t||dx|| \t\t||dv||")

    while flag and k < max_iter:

        # STEP 1. Construct KKT matrix

        if k > 0:
            # Evaluate objective function
            f.append(calc_f(x[k]))

            # Evaluate constraint function
            h.append(calc_h(x[k]))

        # Evaluate objective gradient
        df.append(my_grad_approx(x[k], calc_f, 1e-6))

        # Evaluate constraint Jacobian
        A.append(my_jac_approx(x[k], calc_h, 1e-6))

        # Evaluate gradient of Lagrange function
        L_func = lambda x_: calc_f(x_) + (calc_h(x_)).dot(v[k])
        L_grad = lambda x_: my_grad_approx(x_, L_func, 1e-6)
        dL.append(L_grad(x[k]))
        norm_dL = linalg.norm(dL[k])

        # Evaluate Hessian of Lagrange function
        W.append(my_hes_approx(x[k], L_grad, 1e-6))

        if verbose:
            print("*** k =", k, " ***")
            print("x_k =", x[k])
            print("v_k =", v[k])
            print("f_k =", f[k])
            print("df_k =", df[k])
            print("h_k =", h[k])
            print("A_k =\n", A[k])
            print("W_k =\n", W[k])
            print("\n")

        # Assemble KKT matrix
        KKT_top = np.concatenate((W[k], A[k]), axis=1)
        KKT_bot = np.concatenate((A[k].T, np.zeros((m, m))), axis=1)
        KKT = np.concatenate((KKT_top, KKT_bot), axis=0)

        if verbose:
            print("KKT matrix =\n", KKT, "\n")

        # Check if KKT matrix is singular
        l, eigvec = linalg.eig(KKT)

        if verbose:
            print("KKT matrix eigenvalues:")
            print(l)

        zero_eigenvalues = sum(np.abs(l) <= 1e-8)

        if zero_eigenvalues > 0:
            flag = False
            print("KKT matrix is singular. Eigenvalues:\n")
            print(l, "\n")

        ## STEP 2. Solve linear system.

        if flag:
            b = -np.concatenate((dL[k], h[k]), axis=0)
            z = linalg.solve(KKT, b)
        else:
            z = []

        ## STEP 3. Take step
        if flag:
            dx = z[0:n]
            dv = z[n : n + m]

            x.append(x[k] + dx)
            v.append(v[k] + dv)

            norm_dx = linalg.norm(dx)
            norm_dv = linalg.norm(dv)

        ## Print iteration information
        print(
            k,
            "  \t{0: 1.4e} \t{1:1.4e} \t{2:1.4e}".format(
                f[k], linalg.norm(h[k]), norm_dL
            ),
            end="",
        )

        if flag:
            print(" \t{0: 1.4e} \t{1: 1.4e}".format(norm_dx, norm_dv), end="\n")
        else:
            print(" \t -------  \t -------", end="\n")

        # Increment counter
        k = k + 1

        ## Check convergence criteria
        if flag:
            flag = norm_dx > eps1 and norm_dv > eps1 and norm_dL > eps2

    if flag and k >= max_iter:
        print("Reached maximum number of iterations.")

    return x, v, f, h, df, dL, A, W

def my_f(x):
    return x[0] ** 2 + 2 * x[1] ** 2 - 1 * x[2]


def my_h(x):
    h = np.zeros(2)

    h[0] = x[0] + x[1] - 1
    h[1] = x[0] + x[1] - x[2] - 5

    return h

def visualize(xk=[]):
    n1 = 101
    n2 = 101
    x1eval = np.linspace(-2, 2, n1)
    x2eval = np.linspace(-2, 2, n2)

    X, Y = np.meshgrid(x1eval, x2eval)

    Z = np.zeros([n2, n1])

    for i in range(0, n1):
        for j in range(0, n2):
            Z[j, i] = my_f3((X[j, i], Y[j, i]))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
    CS = ax.contour(X, Y, Z)
    ax.clabel(CS, inline=1, fontsize=12)

    # Add unit circle
    # Okabe-Ito blue (figures/dowling.mplstyle), was matplotlib's "b".
    circ = plt.Circle((0, 0), radius=1, edgecolor="#0072B2", facecolor="None")
    ax.add_patch(circ)

    # Plot iteration history
    if len(xk) > 0:
        for i in range(0, len(xk)):
            if i == len(xk) - 1:
                c = "#D55E00"  # Okabe-Ito vermillion: the final iterate
            else:
                c = "black"
            plt.scatter(
                (xk[i][0]),
                (xk[i][1]),
                marker="*" if i == len(xk) - 1 else "o",
                s=90 if i == len(xk) - 1 else 30,
                color=c,
            )

    plt.xlim([-2, 2])
    plt.ylim([-2, 2])


visualize()

records.content:
Nonlinear equalities do not automatically imply a nonconvex feasible set. A circle is nonconvex: the chord between two distinct feasible points leaves its boundary. The nonlinear equation x_2+x_2^3=0 defines the affine line x_2=0 and has nonzero gradient there. The structural convex-NLP definition uses affine equalities, while the actual set must be checked from its representation. See the 

convexity reference for the first-use domain/set proof.

For C^2 data, a local equality-constrained minimum satisfying LICQ has \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}\succeq0; a feasible KKT point with \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}\succ0 is a strict local minimum. These are the equality-only specializations of the 

second-order reference, rather than different theorems to memorize.

Assume \mathbf{J}=\mathbf{J}_h has full row rank and the step uses the unregularized equality row \mathbf{J}\mathbf d=-h. Let \mathbf{Y} have \mathbf{JY} nonsingular, and let \mathbf{Z} span \ker \mathbf{J} so [\mathbf{Y}\ \mathbf{Z}] is nonsingular. Write \mathbf d=\mathbf{Y}\mathbf p_Y+\mathbf{Z}\mathbf p_Z:\mathbf p_Y=-(\mathbf{JY})^{-1}h,\qquad
\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}\mathbf p_Z=-\mathbf{Z}^T\nabla f-\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WY}\mathbf p_Y.

The first equation restores the linearized constraint. Multiplying the stationarity row by \mathbf{Z}^T eliminates the multiplier, yielding the second equation. Once the full step is known,\bar{\mathbf v}=-(\mathbf{JY})^{-T}\mathbf{Y}^T(\nabla f+\mathbf{W}\mathbf d),\qquad
\mathbf d_v=\bar{\mathbf v}-\mathbf v^k.

This is algebraically equivalent to the full KKT solve when the matrices are nonsingular. Tangential optimization contains the coupling \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WY}\mathbf p_Y; it is not an independent minimization that ignores the normal step.

An orthonormal QR choice has \mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{Q}_R, \mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{Q}_N. For one constraint a^T, the minimum-length normal displacement is -h\,a/\|a\|^2. A coordinate choice \mathbf{Y}=e_i gives -h\,e_i/a_i when a_i\ne0; its length relative to the orthogonal normal step is \|a\|/|a_i|, which grows as that basic coefficient approaches zero. The total unregularized Newton step is basis invariant; its decomposition and conditioning are not.

The prepared example has h=x_1^2+x_2^2-1, \mathbf x^k=(0.70,1.07), h=0.6349 and \mathbf{J}=(1.40,2.14). The orthogonal normal length is 0.2483; the x1-coordinate normal length is 0.4535, ratio 1.8266. Both hit the linearized constraint; neither alone promises exact nonlinear feasibility. Its complete objective is f=\tfrac12(\mathbf x-\mathbf c)^T\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf x-\mathbf c), \mathbf c=(0.95,0.62)^T, \mathbf{Q}=\operatorname{diag}(2,1.2). With a=\mathbf{J}^T, choose \mathbf{Y}=a/\|a\|, \mathbf{Z}=(-\mathbf{Y}_2,\mathbf{Y}_1)^T, estimate v=-(\mathbf{Y}^T\nabla f)/(\mathbf{JY}), and form \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{Q}+2v\mathbf{I}. The displayed tangential equation gives \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}=1.621 and \|\mathbf{Z}\mathbf p_Z\|=0.4967. These inputs reproduce every displacement in the illustration; it is a distinct toy model, not the nonlinear notebook experiment.

Full-space sparse symmetric factorizations can exploit a sparse KKT matrix. Reduced space is attractive when the effective dimension n-\operatorname{rank}\mathbf{J} is small and the basis/projection can be formed or applied efficiently. Dense data alone is not a universal rule. Gould, Hribar and Nocedal (2001), Section 3, pp. 1380–1381, give a projection method that avoids explicitly forming \mathbf{Z}; Biegler, Sections 5.3.1–5.3.2, pp. 96–102, develops coordinate and orthogonal alternatives.

Permute the variables so \mathbf{J}=[\mathbf{J}_B\ \mathbf{J}_S] with a nonsingular m\times m basic block. Then\mathbf{Z}=\begin{bmatrix}-\mathbf{J}_B^{-1}\mathbf{J}_S\\\mathbf{I}\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{Y}_c=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf p_{Y_c}=-\mathbf{J}_B^{-1}h.

Apply \mathbf{Z} through sparse solves with \mathbf{J}_B rather than forming its dense inverse. The first-order multiplier estimate \bar{\mathbf v}\approx-\mathbf{J}_B^{-T}\mathbf{Y}_c^T\nabla f drops the step-dependent term from the exact formula above; it is asymptotically consistent when the step tends to zero, but is not algebraically identical away from the solution.

The alternative \mathbf{Y}_o=[\mathbf{I};\mathbf{J}_S^T\mathbf{J}_B^{-T}] obeys \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Y}_o=\mathbf{0}. Write \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{J}_B^{-1}\mathbf{J}_S. Then\mathbf{JY}_o=\mathbf{J}_B(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{BB}^T),\qquad \mathbf p_{Y_o}=-(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{BB}^T)^{-1}\mathbf{J}_B^{-1}h.

One may apply (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{BB}^T)^{-1}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{B})^{-1}\mathbf{B}^T to exchange an m-dimensional solve for an (n-m)-dimensional solve when that is favorable. Neither \mathbf{Y}_o nor \mathbf{Z} is generally normalized. Biegler, (5.22)–(5.27), p. 101. The minimum-length normal displacement is orthogonal to \ker \mathbf{J}; a coordinate normal step can be longer and need not be perpendicular to the tangential component.

Gould et al., (3.3)–(3.8), p. 1380, apply the orthogonal projector without forming a basis:P=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{JJ}^T)^{-1}\mathbf{J},\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}&\mathbf{J}^T\\\mathbf{J}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P\mathbf r\\\mathbf w\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf r\\0\end{bmatrix}.

Their generalized preconditioned system (3.11), p. 1381, replaces \mathbf{I} by \mathbf{G} with positive curvature on \ker \mathbf{J}. The paper also warns that projected residuals can lose relative accuracy through cancellation; avoiding an explicit basis does not remove numerical error. Factorization structure, fill, conditioning, and residual checks govern the implementation choice.

Let an equality KKT solution (\mathbf x^*,\mathbf v^*) satisfy LICQ and SOSC. If f,h_j have locally Lipschitz Hessians, and both starting components are sufficiently close, the exact full-step Newton method has \|\mathbf e_{k+1}\|\le C\|\mathbf e_k\|^2 for the combined primal/dual error \mathbf e_k=(\mathbf x^k-\mathbf x^*,\mathbf v^k-\mathbf v^*). There exist \rho,C>0 for which every start within the \rho-ball has well-defined exact steps obeying this bound for all k\ge0. Merely assuming C^2 data does not supply this quadratic rate. Biegler, Theorem 5.1, p. 93; Nocedal–Wright, equality-Newton/QP discussion, pp. 530–532.

Its nonsingular KKT Jacobian follows from full row rank and positive reduced Hessian; the 

inertia reference proves the signature identity. Apply the existing 

Newton error proof to \mathbf F: \mathbf e_{k+1}=\mathbf F'(\mathbf z_k)^{-1}\int_0^1[\mathbf F'(\mathbf z_k)-\mathbf F'(\mathbf z^*+t \mathbf e_k)]\mathbf e_k\,\mathbf{d}t. A bounded inverse and a Lipschitz derivative bound give \|\mathbf e_{k+1}\|\le ML\|\mathbf e_k\|^2/2. This specializes the canonical proof without copying its full integral/norm lesson.

Newton can converge to a maximum or saddle because it seeks a stationarity root. For f=-x_1^2, h=x_2=0, starting at (a,0) gives \mathbf d=(-a,0) and reaches the maximum at zero, raising the objective from -a^2 to zero.

records.content: The existing algorithms use finite differences, an iteration cap, and step/gradient stopping logic. They are demonstrations, not production convergence certificates. Their loop can stop when one tested quantity becomes small; it does not require every feasibility/stationarity residual to be small. Re-evaluate h and \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}L at the last appended point, rather than using an older history entry. A small dual step alone is not optimality, and a finite-difference Newton run is not a proof of the exact-derivative quadratic rate. Keep the singular solves and different starting-point outcomes as intentional experiments. At the circle point (-1,0) the correct multiplier is v=1.5 and the unit-tangent curvature is 1, a local minimum. The original start uses v=1, which makes the initial KKT matrix singular even though the primal point is a minimum. The new analytic residual cells distinguish that failed start from a solved KKT point. Use atan2 to distinguish angle branches; arcsin alone can report an angle near zero for a point near (-1,0).

An exact Newton iteration evaluates F=(
abla_{\mathbf{x}}L,h) and its Jacobian at the current primal/dual point, solves \mathbf{K}\mathbf d=-F, then updates both components. Biegler’s Algorithm 5.1, p. 93, errata lines 18–19 adds the feasibility term to the residual test: \max(\|
abla_{\mathbf{x}}L\|,\|h\|)>\varepsilon_2, and evaluates h in the iteration. A small update can signal stagnation; it does not substitute for a small residual.

The preserved teaching loop uses its original conjunction of separate step and gradient conditions, so a single small tested quantity can end the loop. For an implementation intended to certify a candidate, require both \|h\|_\infty\le	au_{m feas} and \|
abla_{\mathbf{x}}L\|_\infty\le	au_{m stat} at the same final point, and report a stalled or capped run separately. The analytic cells above evaluate those two quantities after each original experiment, including the singular starts. They supply evidence for interpreting an outcome without hiding the original failure behavior.

# Load required Python libraries.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg


## Check if element of array is NaN
def check_nan(A):
    """Count NaN entries in an array."""
    return np.sum(np.isnan(A))


## Calculate gradient with central finite difference
def my_grad_approx(x, f, eps1, verbose=False):
    """
    Calculate gradient of function f using central difference formula

    Inputs:
        x - point for which to evaluate gradient
        f - function to consider
        eps1 - perturbation size

    Outputs:
        grad - gradient (vector)
    """

    n = len(x)
    grad = np.zeros(n)

    if verbose:
        print("***** my_grad_approx at x = ", x, "*****")

    for i in range(0, n):

        # Create vector of zeros except eps in position i
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[i] = eps1

        # Finite difference formula
        my_f_plus = f(x + e)
        my_f_minus = f(x - e)

        # Diagnostics
        if verbose:
            print("e[", i, "] = ", e)
            print("f(x + e[", i, "]) = ", my_f_plus)
            print("f(x - e[", i, "]) = ", my_f_minus)

        grad[i] = (my_f_plus - my_f_minus) / (2 * eps1)

    if verbose:
        print("***** Done. ***** \n")

    return grad


def my_jac_approx(x, h, eps1, verbose=False):
    """
    Calculate Jacobian of function h(x) using central difference formula

    Inputs:
        x - point for which to evaluate gradient
        h - vector-valued function to consider. h(x): R^n --> R^m
        eps1 - perturbation size

    Outputs:
        A - Jacobian (n x m matrix)
    """

    # Check h(x) at x
    h_x0 = h(x)

    # Extract dimensions
    n = len(x)
    m = len(h_x0)

    # Initialize Jacobian matrix
    A = np.zeros((n, m))

    # Calculate Jacobian by row
    for i in range(0, n):

        # Create vector of zeros except eps in position i
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[i] = eps1

        # Finite difference formula
        my_h_plus = h(x + e)
        my_h_minus = h(x - e)

        # Diagnostics
        if verbose:
            print("e[", i, "] = ", e)
            print("h(x + e[", i, "]) = ", my_h_plus)
            print("h(x - e[", i, "]) = ", my_h_minus)

        A[i, :] = (my_h_plus - my_h_minus) / (2 * eps1)

    if verbose:
        print("***** Done. ***** \n")

    return A


## Calculate gradient using central finite difference and my_hes_approx
def my_hes_approx(x, grad, eps2):
    """
    Calculate gradient of function my_f using central difference formula and my_grad

    Inputs:
        x - point for which to evaluate gradient
        grad - function to calculate the gradient
        eps2 - perturbation size (for Hessian NOT gradient approximation)

    Outputs:
        H - Hessian (matrix)
    """

    n = len(x)
    H = np.zeros([n, n])

    for i in range(0, n):
        # Create vector of zeros except eps in position i
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[i] = eps2

        # Evaluate gradient twice
        grad_plus = grad(x + e)
        grad_minus = grad(x - e)

        # Notice we are building the Hessian by column (or row)
        H[:, i] = (grad_plus - grad_minus) / (2 * eps2)

    return H


## Linear algebra calculation
def xxT(u):
    """
    Calculates u*u.T to circumvent limitation with SciPy

    Arguments:
    u - numpy 1D array

    Returns:
    u*u.T

    Assume u is a nx1 vector.
    Recall: NumPy does not distinguish between row or column vectors

    u.dot(u) returns a scalar. This function returns an nxn matrix.
    """

    n = len(u)
    A = np.zeros([n, n])
    for i in range(0, n):
        for j in range(0, n):
            A[i, j] = u[i] * u[j]

    return A


## Analyze Hessian
def analyze_hes(B):
    """Print a Hessian and its eigenvalues."""
    print(B, "\n")

    l = linalg.eigvals(B)
    print("Eigenvalues: ", l, "\n")

def assemble_check_KKT(W, A, deltaA, deltaW, verbose):
    """Assemble a regularized KKT matrix and check its inertia."""

    n = np.size(W, 0)

    if np.size(W, 1) != n:
        print("WARNING: W is not square. Something is broken.")

    rA = np.size(A, 0)
    m = np.size(A, 1)

    if rA != n:
        print("WARNING: A does not have the correct number of rows.")

    # Assemble KKT matrix
    KKT_top = np.concatenate((W + deltaW * np.eye(n), A), axis=1)
    KKT_bot = np.concatenate((A.T, -deltaA * np.eye(m)), axis=1)
    KKT = np.concatenate((KKT_top, KKT_bot), axis=0)

    # Check inertia of KKT matrix.
    # Out of simplicity, we will just calculate the eigenvalues.
    # Biegler, 2010 explains a more sophisticated (and computationally efficient)
    # strategy
    l, eigvec = linalg.eig(KKT)

    zero_tol = 1e-12

    # Count number of positive eigenvalues
    pos_ev = sum(l >= zero_tol)

    # Count number of eigenvalues close to zero
    zero_ev = sum(np.abs(l) < zero_tol)

    # Count number of negative eigenvalues
    neg_ev = sum(l <= -zero_tol)

    inertia_correct = n == pos_ev and m == neg_ev

    if verbose:
        print(
            "deltaA = ",
            deltaA,
            "  deltaW = ",
            deltaW,
            "inertia =(",
            pos_ev,
            ",",
            neg_ev,
            ",",
            zero_ev,
            ")\n",
        )

    return KKT, inertia_correct, pos_ev, neg_ev, zero_ev


def alg52(x0, calc_f, calc_h, eps1=1e-6, eps2=1e-6, max_iter=10, verbose=False):
    """
    Basic Full Space Newton Method for Equality Constrained NLP

    Input:
        x0 - starting point (vector)
        calc_f - function to calculate objective (returns scalar)
        calc_h - function to calculate constraints (returns vector)
        eps1 - tolerance for primal and dual steps
        eps2 - tolerance for gradient of L1

    Outputs:
        x - history of steps (primal variables)
        v - history of steps (dual variables)
        f - history of objective evaluations
        h - history of constraint evaluations
        df - history of objective gradients
        dL - history of Lagrange function gradients
        A - history of constraint Jacobians
        W - history of Lagrange Hessians

    Notes:
        1. For simplicity, central finite difference is used
           for all gradient calculations.
    """

    ### Specifics for Algorithm 5.2
    # Tuning parameters
    delta_bar_W_min = 1e-20
    delta_bar_W_0 = 1e-4
    delta_bar_W_max = 1e40
    delta_bar_A = 1e-8
    kappa_u = 8
    kappa_l = 1 / 3

    # Declare iteration histories as empty lists
    x = []
    v = []
    f = []
    L = []
    h = []
    df = []
    dL = []
    A = []
    W = []

    # Set for first iteration
    delta_A = 0.0
    delta_W = 0.0
    delta_W_last = 0.0

    # Flag for iterations
    flag = True

    # Iteration counter
    k = 0

    # Copy initial point to primal variable history
    n = len(x0)
    x.append(x0)

    # Evaluate objective and constraints at initial point
    f.append(calc_f(x0))
    h.append(calc_h(x0))

    # Determine number of equality constraints
    m = len(h[0])

    # Initial dual variables with vector of ones
    v.append(np.ones(m))

    # Print header for iteration information
    print(
        "Iter. \tf(x) \t\t||h(x)|| \t||grad_L(x)|| \t||dx|| \t\t||dv|| \t\tdelta_A \tdelta_W"
    )

    while flag and k < max_iter:

        # STEP 1. Construct KKT matrix

        if k > 0:
            # Evaluate objective function
            f.append(calc_f(x[k]))

            # Evaluate constraint function
            h.append(calc_h(x[k]))

        # Evaluate objective gradient
        df.append(my_grad_approx(x[k], calc_f, 1e-6))

        # Evaluate constraint Jacobian
        A.append(my_jac_approx(x[k], calc_h, 1e-6))

        # Evaluate gradient of Lagrange function
        L_func = lambda x_: calc_f(x_) + (calc_h(x_)).dot(v[k])
        L_grad = lambda x_: my_grad_approx(x_, L_func, 1e-6)
        dL.append(L_grad(x[k]))
        norm_dL = linalg.norm(dL[k])

        # Evaluate Hessian of Lagrange function
        W.append(my_hes_approx(x[k], L_grad, 1e-6))

        if verbose:
            print("*** k =", k, " ***")
            print("x_k =", x[k])
            print("v_k =", v[k])
            print("f_k =", f[k])
            print("df_k =", df[k])
            print("h_k =", h[k])
            print("A_k =\n", A[k])
            print("W_k =\n", W[k])
            print("\n")

        ######
        # Algorithm 5.2: Add inertia correction to Algorithm 5.1

        ### ALG. 5.2, STEP 1
        delta_A = 0
        delta_W = 0

        KKT, inertia_correct, pos_ev, neg_ev, zero_ev = assemble_check_KKT(
            W[k], A[k], delta_A, delta_W, verbose
        )

        if not inertia_correct:
            ### ALG. 5.2, STEP 2
            # Assume zero eigenvalue is from rank-deficient Jacobian.
            # Set delta_A to non-zero value
            if zero_ev != 0:
                delta_A = delta_bar_A

            ### ALG. 5.2, STEP 3
            if delta_W_last == 0:
                delta_W = delta_bar_W_0
            else:
                delta_W = max(delta_bar_W_min, kappa_l * delta_W_last)

        while (not inertia_correct) and flag:
            ### ALG. 5.2, STEP 4
            KKT, inertia_correct, pos_ev, neg_ev, zero_ev = assemble_check_KKT(
                W[k], A[k], delta_A, delta_W, verbose
            )

            ### ALG. 5.2, STEP 5
            if not inertia_correct:
                delta_W = kappa_u * delta_W

            ### ALG. 5.2, STEP 6
            if delta_W > delta_bar_W_max:
                flag = False
                print("Abort step computation. KKT matrix is severely ill-conditioned.")

        delta_W_last = delta_W

        ## STEP 2. Solve linear system.

        if flag:
            b = -np.concatenate((dL[k], h[k]), axis=0)
            z = linalg.solve(KKT, b)
        else:
            z = []

        ## STEP 3. Take step
        if flag:
            dx = z[0:n]
            dv = z[n : n + m]

            x.append(x[k] + dx)
            v.append(v[k] + dv)

            norm_dx = linalg.norm(dx)
            norm_dv = linalg.norm(dv)

        ## Print iteration information
        print(
            k,
            "  \t{0: 1.4e} \t{1:1.4e} \t{2:1.4e}".format(
                f[k], linalg.norm(h[k]), norm_dL
            ),
            end="",
        )

        if flag:
            print(" \t{0: 1.4e} \t{1: 1.4e}".format(norm_dx, norm_dv), end="")
        else:
            print(" \t -------  \t -------", end="")

        print(" \t{0: 1.4e} \t{1: 1.4e}".format(delta_A, delta_W), end="\n")

        # Increment counter
        k = k + 1

        ## Check convergence criteria
        if flag:
            flag = norm_dx > eps1 and norm_dv > eps1 and norm_dL > eps2

    if flag and k >= max_iter:
        print("Reached maximum number of iterations.")

    return x, v, f, h, df, dL, A, W

Now consider a model whose constraint Jacobian has full row rank but whose objective has multiple stationary points on the feasible set.

Consider:\begin{align}\min_{\mathbf{x}} \quad & x_1^3 - x_2 -x_1 x_2 - x_2^2 \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)

    ax.clabel(CS, inline=1, fontsize=12)

    # Add unit circle

    circ = plt.Circle((0, 0), radius=1, edgecolor="#0072B2", facecolor="None")
    ax.add_patch(circ)

    # Plot iteration history
    if len(xk) > 0:

records.content:
The inertia of a real symmetric matrix is (n_+,n_-,n_0), counting positive, negative and zero eigenvalues. The spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis. For nonsingular \mathbf S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, \mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{BS} and \mathbf{B} have the same inertia. This congruence changes coordinates in the quadratic form; it need not preserve eigenvalue magnitudes. Biegler, Theorem 5.2, p. 94.

Proof mechanism. For subspaces U,V\subset\mathbb R^n, \dim(U\cap V)\ge\dim U+\dim V-n because \dim(U+V)\le n. The largest dimension of a subspace on which \mathbf q^T\mathbf{B}\mathbf q is positive definite is n_+: the spectral theorem supplies an n_+-dimensional positive space, and a larger subspace must intersect the nonpositive eigenspace. The invertible map \mathbf{S} preserves dimensions and positive quadratic forms, so that maximum dimension is unchanged. Apply the same argument to -\mathbf{B} for n_-; the remaining dimension is n_0. This also preserves nonsingularity.

records.content:
Let \mathbf{J} have full row rank and choose a null basis \mathbf{Z} and a right-inverse basis \mathbf{Y} with \mathbf{JY}=\mathbf{I}_m. Since [\mathbf{Z}\ \mathbf{Y}] is nonsingular, write \mathbf d=\mathbf{Z}\mathbf q+\mathbf{Y}\mathbf r. The KKT quadratic form is\mathbf q^T\mathbf{H}_R\mathbf q+2\mathbf q^T\mathbf{G}\mathbf r+\mathbf r^T\mathbf{H}_N\mathbf r+2\mathbf r^T\mathbf v,

where \mathbf{H}_R=\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ}, \mathbf{G}=\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WY} and \mathbf{H}_N=\mathbf{Y}^T\mathbf{WY}. Set \mathbf v=\widetilde{\mathbf v}-\mathbf{G}^T\mathbf q-\tfrac12\mathbf{H}_N\mathbf r; this is an invertible triangular coordinate change. The form becomes \mathbf q^T\mathbf{H}_R\mathbf q+2\mathbf r^T\widetilde{\mathbf v}. Each normal/multiplier pair has matrix \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right] with eigenvalues +1 and −1. Therefore\operatorname{In}\mathbf{K}=\operatorname{In}(\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{WZ})+(m,m,0).

This proves both nonsingularity when the reduced Hessian is nonsingular and the target (n,m,0) when it is positive definite. It includes the zero-dimensional reduced space when m=n. The formula requires full row rank and the unregularized zero dual block. Biegler (5.8)–(5.10), pp. 94–95.

For \mathbf{W}=\operatorname{diag}(2,-2) and \mathbf{J}=[0\ 1], \mathbf{Z}=(1,0)^T gives reduced Hessian 2. The full KKT eigenvalues are 2,-1+\sqrt2,-1-\sqrt2, so its inertia is (2,1,0) despite an indefinite primal Hessian.

For \delta_A>0, eliminate the negative-definite dual block by congruence. Its Schur complement is\widehat{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{W}+\delta_W\mathbf{I}+\delta_A^{-1}\mathbf{J}^T\mathbf{J}.

Consequently \operatorname{In}\mathbf K_\delta=\operatorname{In}(\widehat{\mathbf{W}})+(0,m,0). Since \mathbf{J}^T\mathbf{J}\succeq0, choosing \delta_W so \mathbf{W}+\delta_W\mathbf{I}\succ0 suffices for the target (n,m,0), even if \mathbf{J} is rank deficient. For a bounded sequence of \mathbf{W} matrices one uniform sufficiently large shift exists. This is a direct proof of Biegler’s Theorem 5.4, pp. 97–98, in row notation; it avoids requiring an impossible full-column-rank r×m matrix when r<m in the printed proof.

With full row rank, m<n and \delta_A=0, an orthonormal \mathbf{Z} gives \mathbf{Z}^T(\mathbf{W}+\delta_W\mathbf{I})\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{H}_R+\delta_W\mathbf{I}. Thus the threshold is \delta_W> -\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{H}_R) (with a nonnegative shift); the boundary is singular if the smallest reduced eigenvalue becomes zero. For m=n, the null space has zero dimension and no smallest reduced eigenvalue; the signature identity gives (n,n,0) for every primal shift with zero dual correction. For a nonorthonormal basis use the pair (\mathbf{H}_R,\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z}) rather than this simple eigenvalue shift.

The prepared n=3, m=1 example uses \mathbf{W}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&0\\1&-1&1\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right], \mathbf{J}=[1\ 1\ 1], \delta_A=0. Its threshold is approximately 1.5275: below it the inertia is (2,2,0), at it one eigenvalue is zero, and above it the inertia is (3,1,0). These are exact-arithmetic sign conclusions; sufficiently small eigenvalues still need a numerical tolerance.

Dual regularization changes the equality row to \mathbf{J}\mathbf d_x+h=\delta_A\mathbf d_v. It does not impose exact linearized feasibility when \delta_A\mathbf d_v\ne\mathbf{0}. A correct regularized signature does not prove the unregularized reduced Hessian is positive or the original constraints are independent. Check residuals and the physical model, and connect rank diagnosis to 

Degeneracy Hunter.

records.content:
A pivoted symmetric indefinite factorization has a block-diagonal middle factor with 1×1 or 2×2 blocks. Sylvester’s law lets us count its block eigenvalue signs; a 2×2 block’s two diagonal signs alone are insufficient. This often reuses the factorization needed for the solve, preserving sparse structure better than computing a dense full spectrum. Numerical pivoting, scaling and tolerances still matter. Biegler, p. 97.

The approved 

Math-Primer D4 experiment stays at that website home. For \mathbf{W}=2\mathbf{I}_2, \mathbf{J}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\varepsilon\end{smallmatrix}\right], every nonzero represented epsilon in the displayed experiment gives an exactly full-rank rational matrix and KKT inertia (2,2,0). Floating-point LDL and eigensolver counts can disagree. If epsilon is so tiny that 1+epsilon rounds to 1, that represented Jacobian really is rank deficient; the exact conclusion then changes.

For the ideal real matrix, a singular value \sigma of \mathbf{J} produces KKT eigenvalues 1\pm\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}. The small negative branch is equivalently -\sigma^2/(1+\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}). Since the small singular value is approximately |\varepsilon|/2, that eigenvalue is about -\varepsilon^2/8. Its scale can fall below roundoff in the large matrix even though exact LICQ holds. This explains why a signature measurement can spuriously request a correction, or miss negative curvature. Do not call near-degeneracy an exact CQ failure.

The original implementations are deliberately small teaching routines: dense finite differences, an eigenvalue tolerance and a correction cap. They do not certify a global optimum or enforce every residual in their stopping test. The original redundant-constraint and multiple-stationary-point experiments remain; inspect final feasibility, stationarity and reduced curvature in addition to the printed iteration status.

The handout’s former sweep uses distinct analytic toy inputs\mathbf{W}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\1&-1&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{J}=(1,1,1),\qquad\delta_A=0.

For an orthonormal null basis, the lowest reduced eigenvalue is approximately -1.52752523. Hence \delta_W^*=1.52752523 is the crossing: below it inertia is (2,2,0), at it (2,1,1), and above it (3,1,0). At shifts 0 and 3, the KKT eigenvalues are approximately (-1.7520,-0.8698,1.4467,3.1750) and (-0.5656,1.3946,4.3744,5.7966).

The original negative saddle contribution persists; the extra negative eigenvalue from tangent curvature crosses zero. This threshold needs full row rank, zero dual correction, and the orthonormal reduced-Hessian interpretation. With duplicate rows \mathbf{J}=(1,1,1;2,2,2), a primal correction alone leaves an exact multiplier-null direction for every shift. Positive dual regularization removes that forced null direction, but the curvature correction must still be chosen appropriately. The plot source applies only these toy inputs; it does not reproduce the notebook’s solver trajectory.

Some of the writing on this page was drafted or edited by an AI assistant and has not yet been reviewed: 9 rewritten and 3 added markdown cells, measured against the last version of this notebook predating AI editing (2026-08-17).

This notice is about the prose only. It says nothing either way about the code, the numbers or the figures, which are checked separately. It is removed once the page has been reviewed.

Reference: Biegler (2010), Chapter 4, §4.3, pp.72–74; Rockafellar (1993), Lagrange Multipliers and Optimality, §9, pp.224–225. The log-model and its nonlinear KKT system have their complete home in 

Local Optimality Conditions. 

Constraint Qualifications develops multiplier existence/uniqueness and the link to actual feasible directions.

Let D\subset\mathbb R^n be open, with f:D\to\mathbb R, \mathbf g:D\to\mathbb R^r, and \mathbf h:D\to\mathbb R^m. The inequalities are componentwise.

For \min f(\mathbf{x}) subject to \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})\le\mathbf{0} and \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}, define equality indices \mathcal{E}=\{1,\ldots,m\} and inequality indices \mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,r\}. The active inequality index set at a feasible point is\mathcal{A}_I(\mathbf{x})=\{i\in\mathcal{I}:g_i(\mathbf{x})=0\}.

If both types are collected into one set, use distinct constraint labels:\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{x})=\{(h,j):j\in\mathcal{E}\}\cup\{(g,i):i\in\mathcal{A}_I(\mathbf{x})\}.

Equality h_1 and inequality g_1 are different constraints, even though their component indices are both 1. The inactive inequality indices are \mathcal{I}\setminus\mathcal{A}_I, rather than a difference with untagged equality indices. All equalities belong to the combined active set at every feasible point.

Why an inactive constraint drops out locally. Suppose g_i(\mathbf{x}^*)<0 and g_i is continuous. There is \rho_i>0 such that g_i(\mathbf x)<0 for every \mathbf x\in\mathcal B(\mathbf x^*,\rho_i)\subset D, where \mathcal B(\mathbf x^*,\rho_i)=\{\mathbf x:\|\mathbf x-\mathbf x^*\|<\rho_i\}. For finitely many inactive inequalities, take the intersection of these neighborhoods. Removing them leaves exactly the same feasible comparisons in that neighborhood. Their KKT multipliers are zero by complementarity, so they contribute nothing to gradient balance either. This is a local argument, not permission to remove them from the optimization model.

The prepared example uses f(x)=(x^2-1)^2+0.1(3x-x^3) and g=-x\le0. Its derivative is (x^2-1)(4x-0.3). At x=1, f''=7.4>0, g=-1 and f=0.2. Every point in (0.7,1.3) satisfies the inequality, so it is irrelevant to that local test. Removing it globally admits the other strict local minimum x=-1, with value -0.2. A constraint that is inactive at the current solution can still exclude a better distant solution.

Source: Biegler p.72 for the active/local characterization; explicit index spaces, continuity proof and polynomial example are independently specified here.

records.content:
Choose \hat\imath\in\mathcal{A}_I(\mathbf{x}^*) and replace just one inequality byg_{\hat\imath}(\mathbf{x})+\epsilon\le0.

Positive \epsilon tightens the right-hand side to -\epsilon; negative \epsilon relaxes it. Let \mathbf{x}^{\epsilon} be a nearby local minimizer branch, with \mathbf{x}^0=\mathbf{x}^*, and put V(\epsilon)=f(\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon}). This is a local branch value. It need not select the global minimum for every perturbed problem.

The drawing uses f=x_1^2+x_2^2, g=b-x_1\le0, h=x_2-x_1=0, and b=1. The exact solution branch is \mathbf{x}^{\epsilon}=(b+\epsilon,b+\epsilon)^T for b+\epsilon>0. It has V(\epsilon)=2(b+\epsilon)^2, V'(0)=4b, inequality multiplier u^*=4b and equality multiplier v^*=-2b.

Hypotheses for the following Taylor proof. The data are continuously differentiable; \mathbf{x}^{\epsilon} is differentiable at zero; there exists \delta>0 such that the same inequalities remain active for every |\epsilon|<\delta. Thus\Delta\mathbf{x}:=\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}^*=\epsilon\mathbf{x}'(0)+o(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon).

Taylor remainders are therefore o(\epsilon), meaning their norm divided by |\epsilon| tends to zero. The active-set statement alone does not justify dividing an uncontrolled approximation by \epsilon.

Equalities are satisfied at both points:\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon})-\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}^*)=\mathbf{J}_h(\mathbf{x}^*)\Delta\mathbf{x}+o(\epsilon).

Every unperturbed active inequality is still zero:0=g_i(\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon})-g_i(\mathbf{x}^*)=\nabla g_i(\mathbf{x}^*)^T\Delta\mathbf{x}+o(\epsilon),\qquad i\in\mathcal{A}_I\setminus\{\hat\imath\}.

The selected one stays active at its changed bound:-\epsilon=g_{\hat\imath}(\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon})-g_{\hat\imath}(\mathbf{x}^*)=\nabla g_{\hat\imath}(\mathbf{x}^*)^T\Delta\mathbf{x}+o(\epsilon).

At the unperturbed KKT point,\nabla f=-\mathbf{J}_h^T\mathbf{v}^*-\mathbf{J}_g^T\mathbf{u}^*.

Use the objective expansion and substitute this identity:\begin{aligned}
V(\epsilon)-V(0)&=\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*)^T\Delta\mathbf{x}+o(\epsilon)\\
&=-\sum_{j\in\mathcal E}v_j^*\nabla h_j^T\Delta\mathbf{x}-\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}u_i^*\nabla g_i^T\Delta\mathbf{x}+o(\epsilon)\\
&=-\sum_{j\in\mathcal E}v_j^*\bigl(h_j(\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon})-h_j(\mathbf{x}^*)\bigr)
\\&\quad-\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}u_i^*\bigl(g_i(\mathbf{x}^{\epsilon})-g_i(\mathbf{x}^*)\bigr)+o(\epsilon)\\
&=u_{\hat\imath}^*\epsilon+o(\epsilon).
\end{aligned}

All equality differences vanish. Inactive inequalities have u_i^*=0. Untouched active inequalities have zero constraint difference. The selected constraint has difference -\epsilon, and its contribution is -u_{\hat\imath}^*(-\epsilon). HenceV'(0)=\lim_{\epsilon\to0}\frac{V(\epsilon)-V(0)}{\epsilon}=u_{\hat\imath}^*.

This is the sign convention for g+\epsilon\le0. If instead the constraint is written g\le b, increasing b relaxes it and the derivative with respect to b is -u^*. For an equality written h+\eta=0, the same substitution gives \partial V/\partial\eta=v^*. With a differentiable multi-parameter branch,dV=\mathbf{u}^{*T}d\boldsymbol\epsilon+\mathbf{v}^{*T}d\boldsymbol\eta.

Rescaling g to c g, c>0, changes the multiplier to u/c. Its units and numerical magnitude depend on the constraint’s scaling; the product of multiplier and the corresponding constraint perturbation is invariant. A large multiplier is not comparable across arbitrary scalings.

Source: Biegler p.73 for the Taylor argument. The branch/remainder scope and sign/scaling extensions are stated explicitly; Rockafellar Thm.9.1 p.224 distinguishes an ordinary derivative from a general subgradient interpretation.

Strict complementarity means every active inequality is strongly active, equivalently \mathcal A_w is empty. If there are no active inequalities it holds vacuously. Equality multipliers are unrestricted and are not classified by this inequality definition. Nonunique multiplier vectors can yield different strong/weak classifications for the same primal point; uniqueness is a separate regularity question.

For \min(x-a)^2 subject to -x\le0, x^*=\max(a,0) and stationarity is 2(x^*-a)-u^*=0. At a=-1, the bound is strongly active with u^*=2. At a=0, it is weakly active with u^*=0. At a=1, it is inactive with u^*=0. Zero multiplier does not imply slack.

Source: Biegler Def.4.6 and the preceding sets, p.73; the explicit prepared examples supply the distinctions.

Thus x^*=1/2, u_L^*=1, u_U^*=0. The lower bound is strongly active and strict complementarity holds. The objective and bounds are convex, so this candidate is the global minimum. Enumeration considers up to 2^r subsets; infeasible or sign-inconsistent branches are rejected, rather than accepted just because some stationarity equations have a root. Active-set and interior-point methods avoid exhaustive enumeration.

Perturb the lower bound to 1/2+\epsilon. For -1/2<\epsilon<1/2, it remains active:x^{\epsilon}=\tfrac12+\epsilon,\qquad V_s(\epsilon)=\tfrac14+\epsilon+\epsilon^2,\qquad V_s'(0)=1=u_L^*.

The exact full value function isV_s(\epsilon)=\begin{cases}0,&\epsilon\le-1/2,\\(1/2+\epsilon)^2,&-1/2<\epsilon\le1/2,\\+\infty,&\epsilon>1/2.\end{cases}

For \epsilon<-1/2, the lower bound is inactive; at \epsilon=1/2 both bounds coincide and the feasible set has one point. Beyond that the problem is infeasible. The original slope 1 predicts only the local linear term; for \epsilon=0.1 the true increase is 0.11, not 0.10. Continuing that old line far enough can even predict a negative value for a squared objective.
