Weak-activity variation: derive the zero multiplier

records.content:
Now use \min x^2 subject to 0\le x\le1. WriteL=x^2-u_Lx+u_U(x-1),\qquad 2x-u_L+u_U=0.

At x^*=0, the upper bound is slack, so complementarity gives u_U^*=0. The full stationarity equation then gives u_L^*=0. The lower bound is active but weak, and strict complementarity fails. This derives the result without assuming u_L=0 in advance. The 2018 scan’s case-ii premise states that value; keeping it in the reference as a source reading does not make it a necessary premise for the derivation.

Perturb the lower bound to x\ge\epsilon:x^{\epsilon}=\max(\epsilon,0),\qquad
V_w(\epsilon)=\begin{cases}0,&\epsilon\le0,\\\epsilon^2,&0<\epsilon\le1,\\+\infty,&\epsilon>1.\end{cases}

Tightening to \epsilon>0 changes the value by \epsilon^2; loosening keeps the unconstrained minimizer and changes the value by zero. Both one-sided first derivatives at zero are zero, matching the multiplier. Their second-order behavior differs.

An active-set change requires rechecking the smooth-branch interpretation; it does not automatically destroy the value derivative. Both value functions are continuously differentiable at the slack-to-active transitions shown in the plot (\epsilon=-1/2 and \epsilon=0), with a change in the second derivative. Their feasibility-domain endpoints are separate: perturbing beyond 1/2 or 1, respectively, makes the model infeasible. In the weak example the solution branch has different one-sided derivatives, but the value still has derivative zero. For a finite perturbation, recompute the relevant active state and multiplier rather than extrapolating the old slope indefinitely.

Source: Biegler Example 4.7 and variation, pp.73–74. Case enumeration, complete parameter domains and the two-sided qualifications are explicit here.

hierarchy.lvl3: Computing a branch derivative with the active KKT matrix
Computing a branch derivative with the active KKT matrix

records.content:
For twice continuously differentiable data, collect equalities and selected active inequalities into constraint rows \mathbf J_A, with multipliers \boldsymbol\lambda. A constant right-hand-side perturbation changes one active equation but not its gradient. Differentiating the active stationarity/equality equations of a smooth branch gives\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf W&\mathbf J_A^T\\\mathbf J_A&\mathbf0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf x'(0)\\\boldsymbol\lambda'(0)\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf0\\-\mathbf e_{\hat\imath}\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf W=\nabla^2_{xx}L(\mathbf x^*,\boldsymbol\lambda^*).

Here \mathbf e_{\hat\imath} is the unit vector in the stacked row corresponding to the perturbed inequality. Its row position includes the equality rows; it is not an unadjusted original inequality index.

This is a derivative of the active KKT equations, not an optimization algorithm. A nonsingular matrix gives one branch derivative. Nocedal & Wright (2006), Appendix A.2, Theorem A.2, p.631, gives the implicit function theorem used here: it supplies a nearby smooth root branch when this active KKT Jacobian is nonsingular; feasibility, multiplier signs and a local sufficiency test are still needed to identify it as the intended minimizer branch. Strictly positive active multipliers and strictly slack inactive constraints persist under small continuous changes; weak activity needs special care.

One sufficient nonsingularity test is full row rank of \mathbf J_A and positive definiteness of \mathbf W on its null space. To verify it, consider a homogeneous solution (\mathbf p,\mathbf q):\mathbf W\mathbf p+\mathbf J_A^T\mathbf q=\mathbf0,\qquad\mathbf J_A\mathbf p=\mathbf0.

Multiplying the first equation by \mathbf p^T gives \mathbf p^T\mathbf W\mathbf p=0. Positive curvature on the null space forces \mathbf p=\mathbf0. Then \mathbf J_A^T\mathbf q=\mathbf0, and full row rank forces \mathbf q=\mathbf0. If the active Jacobian is square and nonsingular, its null space is already zero. This explains why the moving-fence/rail toy problem has a well-defined branch even before a nonzero tangent-curvature direction is available.

The matrix construction and nonsingularity argument are independently derived from the displayed KKT equations; the extended reduced-Hessian treatment is in 

Second Order Optimality Conditions.

When the value has two one-sided slopes

records.content:
Consider the convex problem\min_x x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\epsilon-x\le0,\quad -x\le0.

Its exact value is V(\epsilon)=\max(\epsilon,0). At zero both constraints are active and stationarity is 1-u_1-u_2=0 with nonnegative multipliers. Every pair (u_1,u_2)=(t,1-t), 0\le t\le1, is valid. The same primal point therefore has nonunique multipliers. The right value derivative is 1, the left derivative is 0, and there is no ordinary two-sided derivative. The selected constraint multiplier u_1\in[0,1] is a subgradient, not an arbitrary choice of a common slope.

This example also shows why strong/weak labels can depend on the multiplier vector: (1,0) and (0,1) exchange which active constraint is weak. The two gradients are both -1, so LICQ fails, even though a direction d>0 strictly decreases both active inequality linearizations.

Rockafellar Thm.9.1 p.224 states a regular-subgradient interpretation under its hypotheses; ordinary partial derivatives follow when the relevant value function is differentiable. Thm.9.3 p.225 gives the convex directional/subgradient relation under its stated existence and lower-semicontinuity hypotheses. In that convex setting, the right and left coordinate slopes are the largest and smallest compatible coordinate multipliers. Those statements should not be read as a global smooth sensitivity theorem for arbitrary nonconvex problems.

The local Taylor proof, the weak squared-value example and this kink example serve different purposes: a smooth branch gives a derivative; a branch switch can leave the value differentiable; nonunique multipliers can describe a range of one-sided sensitivities.

Reference: 

Pyomo Suffix documentation, especially importing solver data and exporting warm-start information. IMPORT retrieves solver-supported suffixes, EXPORT sends them, and IMPORT_EXPORT does both. Names and support depend on the solver/interface. The existing example below uses the Ipopt NL interface: dual for constraint multipliers and ipopt_zL_out/ipopt_zU_out for variable-bound multipliers. The _in suffixes provide the bound-multiplier warm start. Check termination before interpreting any stored suffix, and check the model’s stationarity/sign convention when comparing it with g\le0 mathematics.

The warm start below solves the same model again, using the first primal/dual point. It is a demonstration of passing initialization, not a guarantee that warm starting always reduces iterations or selects a global minimum.

\begin{align} \min_{x_1,...,x_4} \quad & x_1 \cdot x_4 \cdot (x_1 + x_2 + x_3) + x_3 \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & x_1 \cdot x_2 \cdot x_3 \cdot x_4 \geq 25 \\
 & x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 + x_4^2 = 40
\end{align}

import pyomo.environ as pyo

# Example from
# https://pyomo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/pyomo_modeling_components/Suffixes.html#exporting-suffix-data

model = pyo.ConcreteModel()
model.x1 = pyo.Var(bounds=(1, 5), initialize=1.0)
model.x2 = pyo.Var(bounds=(1, 5), initialize=5.0)
model.x3 = pyo.Var(bounds=(1, 5), initialize=5.0)
model.x4 = pyo.Var(bounds=(1, 5), initialize=1.0)
model.obj = pyo.Objective(
    expr=model.x1 * model.x4 * (model.x1 + model.x2 + model.x3) + model.x3
)
model.inequality = pyo.Constraint(
    expr=model.x1 * model.x2 * model.x3 * model.x4 >= 25.0
)
model.equality = pyo.Constraint(
    expr=model.x1**2 + model.x2**2 + model.x3**2 + model.x4**2 == 40.0
)

### Declare all suffixes
# Ipopt bound multipliers (obtained from solution)
model.ipopt_zL_out = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.IMPORT)
model.ipopt_zU_out = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.IMPORT)
# Ipopt bound multipliers (sent to solver)
model.ipopt_zL_in = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.EXPORT)
model.ipopt_zU_in = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.EXPORT)
# Obtain dual solutions from first solve and send to warm start
model.dual = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.IMPORT_EXPORT)

ipopt = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")

results = ipopt.solve(model, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)



Inspect dual variables for lower bound

model.ipopt_zL_out.display()



Inspect dual variables for upper bound

model.ipopt_zU_out.display()

### Set Ipopt options for warm-start
# The current values on the ipopt_zU_out and ipopt_zL_out suffixes will
# be used as initial conditions for the bound multipliers to solve the
# new problem
model.ipopt_zL_in.update(model.ipopt_zL_out)
model.ipopt_zU_in.update(model.ipopt_zU_out)
ipopt.options["warm_start_init_point"] = "yes"
ipopt.options["warm_start_bound_push"] = 1e-6
ipopt.options["warm_start_mult_bound_push"] = 1e-6
ipopt.options["mu_init"] = 1e-6

results = ipopt.solve(model, tee=True)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
    f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
)

hierarchy.lvl3: Translate solver suffixes and check gradient balance
Translate solver suffixes and check gradient balance

records.content:
For this minimization model and Ipopt NL interface, use the canonical inequality g=25-x_1x_2x_3x_4\le0 and equality h=\sum_i x_i^2-40=0. The imported inequality dual is u, and the equality multiplier in L=f+u g+v h is the negative of the imported equality dual. The canonical lower-bound multiplier is ipopt_zL_out; the canonical upper-bound multiplier is the negative of the signed ipopt_zU_out suffix. Lower-bound multipliers enter stationarity with a minus sign, upper-bound multipliers with a plus sign. Keep the raw signed suffix values when passing a warm start back to the solver. The calculation below checks these signs against independently written analytic gradients, rather than assuming that every solver/interface uses the same suffix convention.

A small residual establishes approximate KKT consistency for this returned point, not a global-minimum certificate for the nonconvex model. The warm-start demonstration repeats the same problem; timing and iteration counts can change with the solver version.

The existing four-variable model has inactive upper bounds. A separate one-variable check, \min -x with 0\le x\le1, makes the upper bound strongly active and verifies its sign with a nonzero multiplier.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([pyo.value(model.x1), pyo.value(model.x2),
              pyo.value(model.x3), pyo.value(model.x4)])
variables = [model.x1, model.x2, model.x3, model.x4]
u = float(model.dual[model.inequality])
v = -float(model.dual[model.equality])
z_lower = np.array([float(model.ipopt_zL_out.get(var, 0.0)) for var in variables])
z_upper = -np.array([float(model.ipopt_zU_out.get(var, 0.0)) for var in variables])

# Analytic derivatives of the displayed objective and canonical constraints.
gradient_f = np.array([x[3] * (2*x[0] + x[1] + x[2]),
                       x[0]*x[3], x[0]*x[3] + 1,
                       x[0]*(x[0] + x[1] + x[2])])
gradient_g = -np.prod(x) / x
gradient_h = 2*x
stationarity = gradient_f + u*gradient_g + v*gradient_h - z_lower + z_upper
primal_residual = max(0.0, 25-np.prod(x), abs(np.dot(x, x)-40),
                      float(np.max(1-x)), float(np.max(x-5)))
complementarity = max(abs(u*(25-np.prod(x))),
                      float(np.max(np.abs(z_lower*(1-x)))),
                      float(np.max(np.abs(z_upper*(x-5)))))
assert np.max(np.abs(stationarity)) < 1e-5
assert primal_residual < 1e-5 and complementarity < 1e-5
assert u >= -1e-7 and np.min(z_lower) >= -1e-7 and np.min(z_upper) >= -1e-7

print("Primal point:", np.round(x, 8))
print(f"Objective: {pyo.value(model.obj):.8f}")
print(f"Canonical inequality multiplier u: {u:.8f}")
print(f"Canonical equality multiplier v: {v:.8f}")
print("Lower-bound multipliers:", np.round(z_lower, 8))
print("Upper-bound multipliers:", np.round(z_upper, 8))
print(f"Max stationarity residual: {np.max(np.abs(stationarity)):.3e}")
print(f"Max primal residual: {primal_residual:.3e}")
print(f"Max complementarity residual: {complementarity:.3e}")

# A nonzero upper-bound multiplier checks the signed suffix conversion.
probe = pyo.ConcreteModel()
probe.x = pyo.Var(bounds=(0, 1), initialize=0.5)
probe.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=-probe.x)
probe.ipopt_zL_out = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.IMPORT)
probe.ipopt_zU_out = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.IMPORT)
probe_result = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt").solve(probe)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(probe_result)
raw_upper = float(probe.ipopt_zU_out[probe.x])
canonical_upper = -raw_upper
canonical_lower = float(probe.ipopt_zL_out[probe.x])
probe_stationarity = -1 - canonical_lower + canonical_upper
assert raw_upper < -0.5 and canonical_upper > 0.5
assert abs(probe_stationarity) < 1e-6
assert abs(pyo.value(probe.x)-1) < 1e-6
print(f"Active-upper-bound raw suffix: {raw_upper:.8f}")
print(f"Active-upper-bound canonical multiplier: {canonical_upper:.8f}")
print(f"Active-upper-bound stationarity residual: {abs(probe_stationarity):.3e}")

Reference Section 4.2 in Biegler (2010)

For twice continuously differentiable objectives, a local unconstrained minimum has zero gradient and positive-semidefinite Hessian. These are necessary conditions; they do not classify every stationary point. The definitions, derivative tests and proofs have their existing home in 

Unconstrained Optimality Conditions. Here the feasible neighborhood and constraint reactions change the test.

Here is a 

helpful handout.

Consider \min f(\mathbf{x}) subject to g(\mathbf{x})\le0. The objective is a landscape; its downhill force is -\nabla f. The fence force is -u\nabla g, with u\ge0, pointing toward the feasible side.

The drawn arrows are gradients, pointing toward increasing values. At a regular constrained minimum with an active pushing fence,\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*)+u^*\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^*)=0.

The objective contour is tangent to the fence. Opposite gradient directions do not require equal lengths: the multiplier supplies the scale. Rescaling a constraint changes the numerical multiplier, so raw arrow lengths are not force magnitudes.

Source: Biegler (2010), Figures 4.5–4.6, pp.68–69. The handout and website use this same prepared drawing.

An equality h(\mathbf{x})=0 acts as a rail. Its force -v\nabla h can point either way, because v is unrestricted.

Balance is \nabla f+u\nabla g+v\nabla h=0. For this illustrative drawing the normalized gradients are approximately\nabla f=(0.9825,0.1861)^T,\quad
\nabla g=(-0.8587,-0.5125)^T,\quad
\nabla h=(-0.8480,0.5300)^T.

They give u\approx0.76265>0, v\approx0.38634. The direction \mathbf p=(0.5300,0.8480)^T is tangent to the rail, enters the feasible side of the fence, and raises the objective to first order. Its negative crosses the fence. Thus there is feasible motion, but no nonzero critical direction at this intersection. “No allowable directions” in a curvature discussion refers to the critical cone, not all feasible motion.

For the displayed rounded vectors, the equality tangent space is one-dimensional: every tangent vector is \mathbf p=t(0.5300,0.8480)^T, t\in\mathbb R. The exact dot products of these supplied decimals are\nabla h^T\mathbf p=0,\qquad
\nabla g^T\mathbf p=-0.889711t,\qquad
\nabla f^T\mathbf p=0.6785378t.

The linearized inequality therefore requires t\ge0, and zero first-order objective change then requires t=0. This establishes the whole critical cone \{0\} rather than testing only one direction. These conclusions describe the prepared drawing; the derivatives of the later log-model are calculated independently.

Removing the rail permits a downhill direction along the fence toward its tangency minimum. For example, \mathbf q=(-0.5125,0.8587)^T has \nabla g^T\mathbf q=0 and \nabla f^T\mathbf q=-0.34372718<0. But \nabla h^T\mathbf q=0.889711\ne0, so the rail excludes this descent direction. Source: Biegler (2010), Figure 4.7 and Eq. (4.9), pp.70–71. The later numerical example uses its own objective and gradients; these normalized drawing vectors are not substituted into that model.

Use row-oriented Jacobians \mathbf J_g\in\mathbb R^{r\times n} and \mathbf J_h\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} and\mathcal L(\mathbf x,\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=f(\mathbf x)+
\mathbf g(\mathbf x)^T\mathbf u+\mathbf h(\mathbf x)^T\mathbf v.

Assume C^1 data on an open neighborhood of a feasible local minimum. If LICQ holds there, the following necessary multiplier conditions apply:\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\mathbf x}\mathcal L&=\nabla f+\mathbf J_g^T\mathbf u+\mathbf J_h^T\mathbf v=0,\\
\mathbf g&\le0,\qquad\mathbf h=0,\qquad\mathbf u\ge0,\\
g_i u_i&=0\quad\text{for every }i.
\end{aligned}

Evaluate these at the candidate. Equality multipliers have no sign restriction. Dot-product complementarity \mathbf g^T\mathbf u=0 is equivalent to the component conditions because every summand is nonpositive. The prepared product-vector diagram compares nonpositive terms with a zero vector. If any term is strictly negative, no other nonpositive term can cancel it to make the sum zero.

Inactive constraints have g_i<0, hence u_i=0. Active constraints have g_i=0 and may have a positive multiplier (strongly active) or zero multiplier (weakly active).

Regularity is a hypothesis. LICQ means the equality gradients and active inequality gradients are linearly independent. It is one sufficient qualification for the first-order necessary conditions. For \min x subject to x^2=0, the only feasible point is a strict global minimum, but 1+v(2x)=0 cannot hold at zero for any multiplier. The constraint gradient is zero. See 

Constraint Qualifications for the full theory.

Feasible and critical directions differ. The linearized feasible cone imposes \mathbf J_h\mathbf p=0 and \nabla g_i^T\mathbf p\le0 on active inequalities. At a KKT point,\nabla f^T\mathbf p=-\sum_iu_i\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p\ge0.

Critical directions have zero first-order objective change. Since every term on the right is nonnegative, they are exactly the directions satisfying\begin{aligned}
\mathbf J_h\mathbf p&=0,\\
\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p&=0&&g_i=0,\ u_i>0,\\
\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p&\le0&&g_i=0,\ u_i=0.
\end{aligned}

A positive multiplier does not prevent every feasible inward move; it makes that move raise the objective to first order. Such a direction is not critical. These are first-order tangent tests; nonlinear constraints need not remain feasible along an entire straight step.

For g=-x_2 at the origin, f=x_1^2+x_2 has u=1 and critical directions p_2=0. Its feasible directions with p_2>0 already raise the objective. For f=x_1^2+x_2^2, u=0 and every linearized feasible direction p_2\ge0 is critical.

With C^2 data on an open neighborhood and LICQ at a local minimum, second-order necessity gives\mathbf p^T\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2\mathcal L\,\mathbf p\ge0
\quad\text{for every critical direction }\mathbf p.

Together with KKT, strict positivity on every nonzero critical direction is sufficient for a strict local minimum. The two examples satisfy it on their respective cones. If the critical cone is \{0\}, the strict condition is vacuous; feasible noncritical directions are controlled by their positive first-order change. Full theorem/proof material has its existing home in 

Second-Order Conditions.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eqs. (4.9)–(4.12), pp.70–71; Theorems 4.14–4.15, pp.77–78; critical cone in §4.3.3, p.79; Theorems 4.17–4.18, pp.80–81. The constraint-qualification counterexample follows directly from its singleton feasible set and zero constraint derivative.

Consider the following two dimensional optimization problem:\begin{align} \min_{x_1,x_2} \quad & f(\mathbf{x}) := x_1^2 - 4 x_1 + \frac{3}{2} x_2^2 -7x_2 + x_1 x_2 + 9 - \mathrm{ln}(x_1) - \mathrm{ln}(x_2) \\
\mathrm{s.t.} \quad & g(\mathbf{x}) := 4 - x_1 x_2 \leq 0 \\
 & h(\mathbf{x}) := 2 x_1 - x_2 = 0
\end{align}

def solve_opt(consider_g, consider_h):
    """Solve the example with the selected constraints enabled."""

    ## Create concrete Pyomo model
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

    ## Declare variables with initial values
    m.x1 = pyo.Var(bounds=(0, 100), initialize=10)
    m.x2 = pyo.Var(bounds=(0, 100), initialize=10)

    ## Declare objective
    m.OBJ = pyo.Objective(
        expr=m.x1**2
        - 4 * m.x1
        + 1.5 * m.x2**2
        - 7 * m.x2
        + m.x1 * m.x2
        + 9
        - pyo.log(m.x1)
        - pyo.log(m.x2),
        sense=pyo.minimize,
    )

    if consider_g:
        ## Add inequality constraint
        m.con1 = pyo.Constraint(expr=4 - m.x1 * m.x2 <= 0)

    if consider_h:
        ## Add equality constraint
        m.con2 = pyo.Constraint(expr=2 * m.x1 - m.x2 == 0)

    ## Specify IPOPT as solver
    solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")

    ## Solve the model
    results = solver.solve(m, tee=True)
    assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
        f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
        f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
    )

    ## Return the solution
    return [pyo.value(m.x1), pyo.value(m.x2)]

    ax.set_xlim(X1LO, X1HI)
    ax.set_ylim(X2LO, X2HI)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")


def _arrow(ax, base, vec, label, scale=1.0, offset=(0.1, 0.1), **kwargs):
    """One gradient, drawn AND named. The name is the greyscale-safe identity."""
    kwargs.setdefault("width", 0.045)
    kwargs.setdefault("length_includes_head", True)
    tip = base + scale * vec
    ax.arrow(base[0], base[1], scale * vec[0], scale * vec[1], zorder=5, **kwargs)
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(tip[0] + offset[0], tip[1] + offset[1]),
        fontsize=14,
        zorder=6,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0),
    )


def make_figure():
    x_a, x_b, x_c = [np.asarray(p["solution"]) for p in results["panels"]]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.9))
    x1 = np.linspace(X1LO, X1HI, 200)

    for ax in axes:
        _contours(ax)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("$x_2$")

    # --- Take 1: unconstrained -------------------------------------------
    axes[0].plot(*x_a, marker="*", markersize=18, color="black", linestyle="none")
    axes[0].set_title("1. unconstrained", fontsize=14)

    # --- Takes 2 and 3 share the inequality -------------------------------
    for ax in axes[1:]:
        g_boundary = 4.0 / x1
        ax.plot(x1, g_boundary, color="#0072B2", linestyle="--", linewidth=2.5)
        # Infeasible side: x1 x2 < 4, i.e. below the hyperbola.
        ax.fill_between(
            x1,
            X2LO,
            np.minimum(g_boundary, X2HI),
            facecolor="0.55",
            alpha=SHADE_ALPHA,
            hatch=HATCH_CYCLE[0],
            edgecolor=plt.rcParams["hatch.color"],
            linewidth=0.0,
            zorder=0,
        )
        ax.annotate(
            "$g(\\mathbf{x}) \\leq 0$",
            xy=(2.55, 0.72),
            fontsize=13,
            bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0),
        )

    axes[1].plot(*x_b, marker="*", markersize=18, color="black", linestyle="none")
    axes[1].set_title(r"2. add $g(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$", fontsize=14)
    _arrow(axes[1], x_b, np.asarray(results["panels"][1]["gradient_f"]), r"$\nabla f$", scale=SCALE, color="black")
    _arrow(
        axes[1],
        x_b,
        np.asarray(results["panels"][1]["gradient_g"]),
        r"$\nabla g$",
        scale=SCALE,
        color="#0072B2",
        offset=(-0.15, -0.42),
    )

    # --- Take 3: the full KKT picture -------------------------------------
    axes[2].plot(x1, 2 * x1, color="#E69F00", linestyle="-.", linewidth=2.5)
    axes[2].annotate(
        "$h(\\mathbf{x}) = 0$",
        xy=(2.52, 4.52),
        fontsize=13,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0),
    )
    axes[2].plot(*x_c, marker="*", markersize=18, color="black", linestyle="none")
    axes[2].set_title(r"3. add $h(\mathbf{x}) = 0$", fontsize=14)
    _arrow(axes[2], x_c, np.asarray(results["panels"][2]["gradient_f"]), r"$\nabla f$", scale=SCALE, color="black")
    _arrow(
        axes[2],
        x_c,
        np.asarray(results["panels"][2]["gradient_g"]),
        r"$\nabla g$",
        scale=SCALE,
        color="#0072B2",
        offset=(0.16, -0.40),
    )
    _arrow(
        axes[2],
        x_c,
        np.asarray(results["panels"][2]["gradient_h"]),
        r"$\nabla h$",
        scale=SCALE,
        color="#E69F00",
        offset=(0.08, -0.32),
    )

    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

fig = make_figure()
helper.save_figure(fig, "kkt-geometry", quiet=True)

For the unconstrained problem, stationarity requires\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) =
\begin{bmatrix}
2x_1-4+x_2-1/x_1 \\
3x_2-7+x_1-1/x_2
\end{bmatrix}_{\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*}=\mathbf{0}.

Numerically, \mathbf{x}^*=(1.3475,\,2.0470) and f(\mathbf{x}^*)=-0.8742. Moreover,\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^*) =
\begin{bmatrix}
2+1/(x_1^*)^2 & 1 \\
1 & 3+1/(x_2^*)^2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2.5507 & 1 \\
1 & 3.2387
\end{bmatrix}
\succ 0,

so \mathbf{x}^* is a strict local minimizer.

For the constrained problem, define\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x},u,v)=f(\mathbf{x})+u\,g(\mathbf{x})+v\,h(\mathbf{x}).

The concrete KKT system is\begin{aligned}
2x_1-4+x_2-1/x_1-u x_2+2v&=0,\\
3x_2-7+x_1-1/x_2-u x_1-v&=0,\\
4-x_1x_2&\le0,\qquad 2x_1-x_2=0,\\
u&\ge0,\qquad u(4-x_1x_2)=0,
\end{aligned}

with x_1,x_2>0 and v\in\mathbb R. Products and reciprocals make the stationarity equations nonlinear. Complementarity supplies separate active-state branches, while domain, primal feasibility and multiplier signs remain mandatory checks on every root.

The exact point is (\sqrt2,2\sqrt2)^T. Solving the KKT conditions gives the rounded values\mathbf{x}^*=(1.4142,\,2.8284),\qquad u^*=1.068,\qquad v^*=1.0355,

with g(\mathbf{x}^*)=0, h(\mathbf{x}^*)=0, and f(\mathbf{x}^*)=0.1579. The Lagrangian Hessian is\nabla^2_{\mathbf{xx}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*,u^*,v^*)=
\begin{bmatrix}
2+1/(x_1^*)^2 & 1-u^* \\
1-u^* & 3+1/(x_2^*)^2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2.5 & -0.068 \\
-0.068 & 3.125
\end{bmatrix}.

The exact multipliers are u^*=(17-9\sqrt2)/4>0 and v^*=(5/2)(\sqrt2-1). The active inequality and equality gradients are independent. Since the inequality multiplier is positive, a critical direction must be tangent to both constraints; the critical cone is \{0\}, so the second-order sufficient condition is satisfied vacuously. Feasible motion still exists: \mathbf p=(1,2)^T is tangent to the equality and enters the inequality interior, but raises the objective to first order.

This particular example also admits a global certificate. On its positive log domain, 4-x_1x_2\le0 is equivalent to 4/x_1-x_2\le0, a convex inequality; its second derivative in x_1 is 8/x_1^3>0. The equality is affine, and the objective Hessian is positive definite throughout the domain: its diagonal entries exceed 2 and 3, with off-diagonal entry 1, so its determinant exceeds 5. The problem therefore has a convex feasible set and a strictly convex objective even though the original product constraint function is not convex. The local minimum is the unique global minimum. This illustrates the representation distinction in 

Convexity Revisited, rather than applying a failed structural test as a converse.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eqs. (4.16)–(4.24), p.72; Theorem 4.3, p.65, and Theorem 4.18, p.81. The equivalent-constraint/global certificate and exact multipliers are independently derived from the displayed model.
Objective-value source correction: the displayed model has constant +9, yielding approximately -0.874224 without constraints and 0.157862 with both constraints. The book’s -2.8742 and -1.8421 are two units lower and correspond to replacing that constant by +7. The additive constant changes values but not gradients, minimizers, multipliers or curvature. We keep the displayed +9 model and its independently evaluated values.

If the equality is retained but the inequality is assumed slack, set u=0 and x_2=2x_1. The restricted objective isf(x_1,2x_1)=9x_1^2-18x_1+9-\ln2-2\ln x_1.

Stationarity gives 18x_1-18-2/x_1=0, or 9x_1^2-9x_1-1=0. Its positive root is (9+\sqrt{117})/18\approx1.100925, with x_2\approx2.201850. But g=4-2x_1^2\approx1.575927>0, so this branch is infeasible. The active branch instead enforces 4-2x_1^2=0, and the positive domain selects the exact point derived above. A root is accepted only after domain, primal feasibility, multiplier sign and complementarity checks.

The Lagrangian Hessian is a sum of scalar-component Hessians,\nabla^2_{xx}L=\nabla^2f+u\nabla^2g+v\nabla^2h
=\begin{bmatrix}2+1/x_1^2&1-u\\1-u&3+1/x_2^2\end{bmatrix}.

At the exact constrained point, the diagonal entries are 2.5 and 3.125, and the off-diagonal is 1-u^*=(9\sqrt2-13)/4\approx-0.068019. Biegler Eq.(4.24) p.72 prints a positive off-diagonal. The errata fixes the diagonal signs but leaves that further sign error. The critical-direction matrix\begin{bmatrix}-2\sqrt2&-\sqrt2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}

has determinant 4\sqrt2, so its null space is zero. It describes directions tangent to the equality and the positively weighted active inequality. It does not describe every feasible direction: (1,2)^T is an inward feasible rail direction and increases the objective to first order.

Printed orientation discrepancy. Biegler Eq.(4.9) p.70 uses transposed vector-constraint gradients, while Eqs.(4.17)–(4.18) p.72 use columns for the same stationarity components. The course consistently defines \mathbf J_g with constraint rows (r\times n), so \mathbf J_g\mathbf p is a constraint-change vector and \mathbf J_g^T\mathbf u is an n-component gradient contribution. A single scalar-constraint gradient is a column. This resolves the dimensions without adopting two definitions of the same symbol.

Sources: Biegler Eqs.(4.13), (4.16)–(4.25), pp.71–72, with the displayed positive-domain substitutions and exact derivatives independently checked. The complete multiplier-sensitivity and strong/weak reference is 

Analysis of KKT Conditions.

Reading: Biegler (2010), Nonlinear Programming, §6.2, pp. 135–151; Nocedal & Wright (2006), Numerical Optimization, Chapter 18, pp. 529–562.

This guide supplements Lecture 23 with complete QP certificates, elastic repairs, line-search and trust-region algorithms, reduced-space details and local-rate conditions. The implementation laboratory then exposes each dense QP/KKT solve and preserves successful runs and useful failure cases.

Start with the 

QP model, 

elastic repairs, 

trust-region families, or 

local rates. 

Constrained Globalization supplies the general acceptance proofs and Maratos correction. 

Equality Newton supplies the equality-QP bridge; 

Quasi-Newton Methods supplies the general BFGS derivation.

The prototype implements scalar-relaxed line-search SQP. The trust-region, SLQP and sparse methods are fully described here but require different computational machinery; they are not implemented by the prototype.

AI-drafted prose, not yet reviewed by Prof. Dowling.

Some of the writing on this page was drafted or edited by an AI assistant and has not yet been reviewed: 39 added markdown cells, measured against the last version of this notebook predating AI editing (2026-08-17).

This notice is about the prose only. It says nothing either way about the code, the numbers or the figures, which are checked separately. It is removed once the page has been reviewed.

On an open D\subset\mathbb R^n, take f:D\to\mathbb R, \mathbf h:D\to\mathbb R^{m_h} and \mathbf g:D\to\mathbb R^{m_g} of class C^2. Row Jacobians have dimensions m_h\times n and m_g\times n; the curvature model \mathbf B is symmetric n\times n. Use the course convention L=f+\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h+\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}\mathbf g, with equalities \mathbf h=\mathbf0, inequalities \mathbf g\le\mathbf0, and \mathbf u\ge\mathbf0. At iteration k, put \mathbf a_k=\nabla f(\mathbf x^k) and \mathbf B_k=\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2L(\mathbf x^k,\mathbf v^k,\mathbf u^k) or a chosen approximation. An IQP subproblem is\min_{\mathbf d}\ \mathbf a_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B_k\mathbf d\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\mathbf h_k+\mathbf J_h^k\mathbf d=\mathbf0,\qquad
\mathbf g_k+\mathbf J_g^k\mathbf d\le\mathbf0.

This uses a quadratic Lagrangian model and affine constraint models. Linearizing a nonlinear inequality does not certify feasibility of the nonlinear trial. The QP supplies a step and multiplier estimates; an acceptance procedure from 

Constrained Globalization selects the new point. 

Equality Newton owns the exact equality KKT/QP bridge and its local assumptions.

In the bound formulation used by the code, introduce nonnegative slacks with \mathbf g(\mathbf x)+\mathbf s=\mathbf0 and relabel the enlarged primal vector and equality vector. The equality Jacobian below is \mathbf J. Inequalities are now represented by these equalities and simple bounds. The subproblem is\min_{\mathbf d}\ \mathbf a_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B_k\mathbf d\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\mathbf h_k+\mathbf J_k\mathbf d=\mathbf0,\qquad
\mathbf x_L\le\mathbf x^k+\mathbf d\le\mathbf x_U.

Here the code’s argument g means the objective gradient, its J is a row Jacobian, and its lam means the course equality multiplier \mathbf v. Its bound-QP solver returns a signed gradient zeta: positive at a lower bound, negative at an upper bound. At a solved QP, \boldsymbol\zeta=\mathbf u_L-\mathbf u_U and stationarity is \mathbf a+\mathbf B\mathbf d+\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\bar{\mathbf v}-\mathbf u_L+\mathbf u_U=\mathbf0. Do not read this signed quantity as a nonnegative inequality multiplier.

Biegler §6.2, pp.135–136; Nocedal–Wright (18.11), p.533.

Nocedal–Wright writes L_{NW}=f-\boldsymbol\lambda_E^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h-\boldsymbol\lambda_I^{\mathsf T}\mathbf c_I with \mathbf c_I\ge\mathbf0. For the same equality function, \mathbf v=-\boldsymbol\lambda_E. When \mathbf g=-\mathbf c_I, however, \mathbf u=\boldsymbol\lambda_I. Thus equality multipliers reverse sign but inequality multipliers do not under this function conversion. For a lower bound, c_L=x-x_L and g_L=x_L-x; for an upper bound, c_U=x_U-x and g_U=x-x_U. Both nonnegative bound multipliers retain their values. State the constraint function and Lagrangian together when translating.

If a bound set were known, matrices \mathbf E_L,\mathbf E_U collect the corresponding unit columns. The QP would impose \mathbf E_L^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf x^k+\mathbf d)=\mathbf E_L^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_L and its upper-bound analogue. The general inequality QP keeps the bounds as inequalities and chooses which are active at its solution. Active bounds at the current point and at the QP endpoint need not be the same.

Flat QP minimizers span more than the selected endpoint face.

If a QP KKT solution has \mathbf d=\mathbf0, its affine residuals equal the original constraint values. QP stationarity becomes NLP stationarity, and dual feasibility/complementarity apply at the same point. Therefore a zero QP KKT step gives an NLP KKT point, without needing a separate uniqueness argument. It does not alone prove second-order optimality or a global minimum. In computation, verify the QP’s KKT residuals and solve status rather than assuming its returned step is exact.

A useful converse holds with sufficient strict convexity on the equality tangent. Suppose the current point is NLP KKT and \mathbf B is positive definite on \ker\mathbf J_h. Zero is a feasible QP step. For any other feasible \mathbf d, stationarity gives\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d=-\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}\mathbf J_h\mathbf d-\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}\mathbf J_g\mathbf d\ge0.

The equality term is zero. Positive multipliers only occur at active inequalities; there \mathbf J_{g,i}\mathbf d\le0, so each remaining term is nonnegative. Since \mathbf J_h\mathbf d=0 and \mathbf d\ne0, \frac12\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d>0. Hence the QP objective at every nonzero feasible step exceeds its value at zero, making zero the unique global QP minimum. Full positive definiteness is a convenient sufficient special case. This converse imposes more than curvature on one selected all-active face.

The distinction matters in Biegler Theorem 6.1, p.136. Consider f=x_2^2, no equalities, 0\le x_1\le1, current (0,0), and QP Hessian \operatorname{diag}(0,2). The QP may return (1,0) with zero upper-bound multiplier. At that endpoint the active row [1,0] is independent, the null curvature is2, and its KKT matrix is nonsingular. Yet all (d_1,0) with 0\le d_1\le1 minimize the QP. The original current point is NLP KKT with the same zero multipliers, despite the selected nonzero step. Positivity on the all-active null space misses the weak bound’s critical directions. In the book’s fixed-face proof, zero does not satisfy that endpoint’s upper-bound equality. Use the certificate/converse above rather than promoting active-face nonsingularity to global primal uniqueness. 

Second Order Conditions supplies the critical-cone distinction.

A sharper fixed-face converse can instead assume strict complementarity at the selected QP endpoint, the same multipliers satisfying NLP KKT at the current point, and positive curvature on that selected active null space. Every positively weighted bound/inequality is active at both points, so its affine row gives \mathbf J_A\mathbf d=\mathbf0. Subtracting the two stationarity equations gives \mathbf B\mathbf d=\mathbf0. Therefore \mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d=0 and active-null positivity forces \mathbf d=\mathbf0. The flat example fails this added strict-complementarity assumption. This is a different sufficient converse, not a reason to omit weakly active directions from the general theorem.

Strictly and weakly weighted bounds respond differently to center perturbations.

At a feasible \mathbf x^*, define \mathcal A^*=\{i:g_i(\mathbf x^*)=0\}. The active Jacobian stacks \mathbf J_h and the rows \nabla g_i^{\mathsf T} for i\in\mathcal A^*. LICQ means these rows are linearly independent; strict complementarity means u_i^*>0 for every i\in\mathcal A^*. Under strict complementarity, SOSC uses the true solution Hessian \mathbf W^*=\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2L(\mathbf x^*,\mathbf v^*,\mathbf u^*) and requires \mathbf p^{\mathsf T}\mathbf W^*\mathbf p>0 for every nonzero direction in the null space of this active Jacobian. L18/L21 supply the general critical-cone and second-order statements.

For the exact SQP curvature \mathbf B=\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2L(\mathbf x,\mathbf v,\mathbf u), Nocedal–Wright Theorem 18.1, p.533, assumes a local KKT solution, LICQ, strict complementarity and SOSC. There is a neighborhood of the solution and its relevant multiplier vector where a local QP solution branch has the same active set. A general Hessian approximation needs its own closeness/regularity conditions; the exact-Hessian theorem does not apply to an arbitrary symmetric model. Biegler Theorem 6.5, pp.141–142, gives the analogous eventual-set property for a converging SQP sequence. This stabilizes the active-set algebra; it does not prove global QP uniqueness far away or remove the need for accepted full steps and local smoothness/Hessian assumptions.

Strict complementarity is sufficient for this identification theorem, not necessary for every example to identify its set. For \min x^2 subject to x\ge0, the solution has zero multiplier, but the exact QP step from a positive start reaches zero immediately and its active set remains identifiable. Without strict complementarity, the theorem no longer excludes changing weakly active sets; it does not assert that all such problems fail.

Likewise, LICQ is a sufficient KKT factorization condition, not a necessary condition for unique primal optimization: \min x^2 with duplicate inequalities -x\le0,-2x\le0 has a unique minimum. A solver may select an independent working subset. It must still distinguish truly redundant rows from dependent gradients with inconsistent residuals: the equations d=0 and d=-1 have the same gradient but cannot both be satisfied. Discarding the latter merely because its gradient is dependent changes the problem. Preserve primal/dual residual checks when rank safeguards or least-squares solves are used.

Three separate questions govern the subproblem: is its feasible set nonempty, is its objective bounded below/attained, and which primal/dual solution is unique? Full indefiniteness need not make an equality QP unbounded when reduced curvature is positive. A compact inequality feasible set bounds a continuous quadratic objective even if it is indefinite. Independent active rows with positive curvature on that face make its KKT system nonsingular; they need not settle global minimization across other faces. These are distinct issues.

An IQP outer method solves an inequality QP and reads a working-set estimate from its solution. An EQP outer method estimates a working set first, then computes an equality-QP step on that set. An active-set QP subsolver can be used inside IQP; choosing it does not convert the outer algorithm to EQP. Nocedal–Wright §18.2, pp.533–534.

Warm starts reuse a previous QP working set or factorization when successive subproblems are related. They can reduce work near a stable solution; they do not guarantee that the next set is identical. Whether IQP or EQP is cheaper depends on derivative evaluation cost, sparsity, conditioning, degeneracy and the quality of the set estimate. Neither family requires exhaustive enumeration of every inequality subset.

SLQP uses an LP phase to estimate a working set, followed by an EQP phase. A hard-constraint LP can itself be infeasible, so the practical scheme uses a penalty LP on an infinity-norm trust box. Its objective is the linear objective model plus the piecewise-linear constraint violation. A basic optimal solution can identify a working set, but not every LP optimum returned by every solver is a vertex. Select independent active rows and retain feasibility/restoration safeguards.

The fuller Nocedal–Wright construction, pp.551–552, uses a Cauchy point \mathbf p^C=\alpha_{LP}\mathbf p^{LP} giving sufficient decrease in the merit model. It selects an independent subset of constraints active in the LP model. In the EQP objective, violated constraints contribute the derivative of their current penalty branch: equality residuals contribute \rho_{\rm pen}\operatorname{sign}(h_i^{lin})\nabla h_i, and violated course inequalities g_i^{lin}>0 contribute \rho_{\rm pen}\nabla g_i. Working-set rows are enforced at equality inside a Euclidean trust ball with its own radius. Let \mathbf p^Q be that candidate. The total step is\mathbf p=\mathbf p^C+\alpha_Q(\mathbf p^Q-\mathbf p^C),\qquad0\le\alpha_Q\le1,

chosen to improve the merit model. This is not simply discarding the LP point and taking an unconstrained equality-QP solution. LP and EQP radii serve different roles. The penalty update below also applies, with a zero-Hessian LP model.

A feasible nonlinear point can coexist with contradictory affine step requirements.

The constraints x\le1,x^2\ge4 are feasible at x=-2, but at x=1 their linearizations require d\le0 and d\ge3/2. A feasible NLP can have an empty local affine model inside its physical bounds.

Biegler Example 6.3, p.140, uses\min x_1+x_2,\quad h_1=1+x_1-x_2^2+x_3=0,\quad h_2=1-x_1-x_2^2+x_4=0,

with 0\le x_2\le2 and x_3,x_4\ge0. At (0,.1,0,0) both residuals are .99, not the printed first value 1.01. The affine rows are.99+d_1-.2d_2+d_3=0,\qquad .99-d_1-.2d_2+d_4=0,

with -.1\le d_2\le1.9 and d_3,d_4\ge0. Adding the rows gives .4d_2=1.98+d_3+d_4\ge1.98, hence d_2\ge4.95, contradicting its upper bound. The held errata restores the omitted starting-point components but does not repair the 1.01 arithmetic.

The global solution is (-3,2,6,0), with objective -1. A complete verification eliminates the equalities: nonnegative slacks imply 1-x_2^2\le x_1\le x_2^2-1, so 1\le x_2\le2. At a fixed x_2, minimize by x_1=1-x_2^2, giving f=1-x_2^2+x_2. Its derivative 1-2x_2<0 on [1,2], so the unique minimizing x_2 is2 and the remaining variables follow. Course equality multipliers (0,1), upper x_2 multiplier3 and lower x_4 multiplier1 satisfy KKT. This global calculation uses this example’s special structure; a generic SQP status is not a global certificate.

Residual slacks and their multiplier cap.

The \ell_1 elastic QP introduces \mathbf s,\mathbf t\ge\mathbf0:\min_{\mathbf d,\mathbf s,\mathbf t}\ \mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d+\rho_{\rm pen}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf s+\mathbf t),\quad
\mathbf h+\mathbf J\mathbf d=\mathbf s-\mathbf t,\quad\mathbf x_L\le\mathbf x+\mathbf d\le\mathbf x_U.

For a bound-feasible current point, zero step and component positive/negative parts of \mathbf h give a feasible lifted point. More generally, a nonempty physical box allows a bound-feasible step and appropriate residual slacks. Strict positive primal curvature gives a finite unique primal minimum; mere feasibility with an indefinite unbounded objective does not. At optimality with positive weight, the slacks represent the residual’s actual positive and negative parts. Their stationarity implies -\rho_{\rm pen}\le\bar v_j\le\rho_{\rm pen}; a positive s_j forces \bar v_j=\rho_{\rm pen} and a positive t_j forces \bar v_j=-\rho_{\rm pen}. This multiplier cap belongs to the l1 formulation, not the scalar formulation. Biegler6.13p138; Nocedal–Wright18.12p536.

The scalar repair implemented below minimizes\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d+M(\xi+\xi^2/2),\quad
(1-\xi)\mathbf h+\mathbf J\mathbf d=\mathbf0,

with the physical step bounds and 0\le\xi\le1. The book’s6.16only prints \xi\ge0; the notebook adds the upper bound. A zero step with \xi=1 is feasible when the current point satisfies the box. For \mathbf B\succ0,M>0, the lifted objective Hessian \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf B,M) is positive definite, giving a unique minimizer on the convex feasible set. The \xi^2 term alone does not make flat primal directions unique.

At \xi=0 the chosen step satisfies the original affine equalities. For 0<\xi<1 it contracts their residual by 1-\xi. A positive \xi does not prove that exact affine feasibility was impossible: for h=-1,J=1,a=0,B=1000,M=1, and physical x\in[0,2] at x=0, the exact step1is feasible but the weighted optimum chooses \xi=999/1001 and d=2/1001. A finite weight can prefer partial relaxation. With only the book’s lower bound on \xi, the data a=100,B=M=1,h=-1,J=1 and broad physical bounds produce \xi=50,d=-49. Thus a contraction interpretation needs an explicit domain/safeguard.

At \xi=1 the step is tangent to the affine equalities; it need not be zero. For h=x_1-x_1^2+1, current (0,0), lower bound x_1\ge0, \mathbf a=(0,-1) and \mathbf B=\mathbf I, the guarded scalar QP forces \xi=1,d_1=0 but selects d_2=1. A feasible nonlinear point exists at x_1=(1+\sqrt5)/2. Diagnose lost contraction/restoration needs; do not infer global infeasibility or zero tangent movement.

For Example 6.3, the relaxed row sum gives 1.98(1-\xi)\le.76, so the minimum feasible relaxation is 1-.76/1.98=.616161\ldots. The actual solver below computes its selected relaxation separately. At the all-zero start, \xi=1 is forced by the two rows and nonnegative slacks, but there remain feasible d_2 values in [0,2]. For this example’s gradient and positive Hessian, the minimizing primal step is zero. Preserve that specific failure; do not turn it into a universal statement about \xi=1.

Elastic merit descent: complete sign argument

records.content:
The elastic merit-descent argument uses the actual contraction and bound signs.

Assume a bound-feasible current point and an exact QP KKT solution, including nonnegative bound multipliers and endpoint complementarity. For the actual scalar step, \mathbf J\mathbf d=-(1-\xi)\mathbf h. The forward norm expansion from 

Constrained Globalization givesD\phi_p=\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d-\rho_{\rm pen}(1-\xi)\|\mathbf h\|_p.

At the QP endpoint, bound complementarity and a bound-feasible current point imply \bar{\mathbf u}_L^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d\le0 and \bar{\mathbf u}_U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d\ge0. Dot QP stationarity with \mathbf d and substitute its equality row:\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d=-\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d+(1-\xi)\bar{\mathbf v}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h+\bar{\mathbf u}_L^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d-\bar{\mathbf u}_U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d.

For 0\le\xi<1, 1\le p\le\infty, dual exponents 1/p+1/q=1 with 1/\infty=0, and \rho_{\rm pen}\ge\|\bar{\mathbf v}\|_q+\epsilon_{\rm pen} with \epsilon_{\rm pen}>0 giveD\phi_p\le-\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d-\epsilon_{\rm pen}(1-\xi)\|\mathbf h\|_p.

With \mathbf B\succ0, a nonzero step is strictly descending; at zero residual/zero step it is stationary, not a strict-descent exception. Biegler6.21p140prints a positive quadratic sign followed by a strict-negative claim; the preceding stationarity calculation requires the negative sign above. Full positive curvature is used here. The weaker reduced-curvature variants require the appropriate coupling-aware analysis from L22, not this unchanged multiplier rule.

A complete scalar-relaxed line-search outline is:

Start inside a consistent physical box and the differentiability domain D; evaluate every trial inside D. Evaluate f,\mathbf a,\mathbf h,\mathbf J and the chosen curvature model.

Solve the guarded scalar QP, checking its primal/dual residuals and inner solve status. If it produces no adequate contraction or progress, diagnose restoration or a stall rather than declaring the entire NLP infeasible.

Compute the actual forward merit derivative. For the full-positive model and \xi<1, use the multiplier bound above; alternatively use a properly safeguarded direct slope rule. Compare all trials with the same current weight.

Backtrack from a full step with 0<\eta<1/2 until \phi_p(\mathbf x+\alpha\mathbf d)\le\phi_p(\mathbf x)+\eta\alpha D\phi_p. Use L22’s correction safeguard near the solution. If a correction fails, discard it; if the line search exhausts its limit, report failure/restoration rather than unconditionally accepting its last trial.

Update the primal and specified dual estimates. Re-evaluate actual new-point feasibility, stationarity, dual signs and complementarity; a small step alone is not convergence. Then form the fixed-multiplier secant pair when updating curvature.

Biegler Algorithm 6.1p141takes full QP multiplier updates independently of primal \alpha. Nocedal–Wright Algorithm 18.3p545damps both: \boldsymbol\lambda^{k+1}=\boldsymbol\lambda^k+\alpha(\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}-\boldsymbol\lambda^k). They are different algorithm choices. Neither implies intermediate complementarity automatically.

Nocedal–Wright’s model-based rule uses V(\mathbf d)=\|\mathbf h+\mathbf J\mathbf d\|_1 and q_\rho=f+\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+(\sigma/2)\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d+\rho V(\mathbf d). Require q_\rho(\mathbf0)-q_\rho(\mathbf d)\ge\kappa\rho[V(\mathbf0)-V(\mathbf d)], 0<\kappa<1. If the violation decrease \Delta V>0, this gives\rho\ge\frac{\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+(\sigma/2)\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d}{(1-\kappa)\Delta V}.

For an exact affine-feasibility step \Delta V=\|\mathbf h\|_1, this is18.36p542. For a relaxed step use its actual \Delta V; do not divide by zero at an already feasible tangent step. Algorithm 18.3uses \sigma=1. This rule measures predicted progress without relying directly on the multipliers; its behavior depends on the problem and model, not an unconditional superiority claim.

The existing code adds its own hybrid weight safeguard when relaxation is large. It is not literally either textbook algorithm in every branch. Its original stopping/failure behavior remains below, with separate diagnostic interpretation.

What the global argument must establish

records.content:
Uniform decrease, summability and limit transfer are separate proof steps.

The term global convergence refers to approach to first-order stationary/KKT points from a larger class of starts, under algorithmic assumptions. It does not mean the globally best solution of a nonconvex NLP.

A transparent sufficient argument assumes bound-feasible primal iterates in a compact subset of D, QP solutions satisfying the scalar model’s KKT equations, bounded QP multipliers (including bound multipliers), an eventually fixed weight satisfying \rho_{\rm pen}\ge\|\bar{\mathbf v}^k\|_q+\epsilon_{\rm pen} with one fixed \epsilon_{\rm pen}>0, accepted step lengths \alpha_k\ge\underline\alpha>0, \mathbf B_k\succeq b\mathbf I with b>0 and uniformly bounded norm, and contraction \xi_k\le1-\gamma with \gamma>0. Continuity on that compact set gives a merit lower bound by Weierstrass. The derivative bound above and accepted Armijo steps with one fixed \eta>0 yield\phi_k-\phi_{k+1}\ge\eta\underline\alpha\big[b\|\mathbf d_k\|_2^2+\epsilon_{\rm pen}\gamma\|\mathbf h_k\|_p\big].

Summing against the merit lower bound gives finite sums of squared steps and violations, hence \mathbf d_k\to\mathbf0 and \mathbf h_k\to\mathbf0. Bounded curvature makes the QP stationarity defect -\mathbf B_k\mathbf d_k vanish. Compactness and bounded duals allow subsequences with convergent primal/dual values; continuity gives stationarity and dual signs. QP complementarity at \mathbf x^k+\mathbf d_k transfers to \mathbf x^k because the difference in each product is a bounded multiplier times a vanishing step. Thus the limit is NLP KKT. This proof does not establish one convergent whole sequence, SOSC or a global minimum.

Biegler Theorem 6.4p141states a related KKT limit-point result for compact primal/trial sequences, uniform continuity, positive bounded curvature, LICQ, solvable QPs with \xi<1 and a sufficiently large weight. Its precedingp140discussion separately emphasizes contraction bounded away from1. Pointwise \xi<1 or pointwise positivity is not a uniform constant; an implementation must establish the safeguards its proof uses. Nocedal–Wright18.3p557explicitlyincludes bounded steps/dual values, a fixed sufficiently large penalty and its particular model-decrease line search. The prototype’s status string does not verify those global hypotheses. The finite-update issue for a bounded monotone weight is explained fully at the L22 reference.

Use \mathbf s_k=\mathbf x^{k+1}-\mathbf x^k and\mathbf y_k=\nabla_{\mathbf x}L(\mathbf x^{k+1},\mathbf v^{k+1},\mathbf u^{k+1})-\nabla_{\mathbf x}L(\mathbf x^k,\mathbf v^{k+1},\mathbf u^{k+1}).

Both gradients fix the same updated multipliers. For linear physical bounds, the bound-gradient contributions cancel; the code therefore uses objective and equality-gradient terms. Changing the multiplier in the second term instead introduces an unwanted dual-step contribution. The general BFGS and damping derivations remain at 

Quasi-Newton Methods; this section applies them to constrained curvature.

For \mathbf B\succ0,\mathbf s\ne\mathbf0, put a=\mathbf s^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf s>0 and b=\mathbf s^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y. Powell’s rule takes \theta=1 if b\ge.2a, otherwise \theta=.8a/(a-b), and \mathbf r=\theta\mathbf y+(1-\theta)\mathbf B\mathbf s. The actual rule chooses 0<\theta\le1; zero is a limiting conceptual case, not a finite selected value. If it selects1, the positive-curvature test has passed, so that actual ordinary update preserves definiteness. Forcing1while ignoring the test can produce an indefinite update. The convex combination is in secant vectors; updated matrices are not generally their affine mixture.

A constrained family makes negative measured curvature concrete. Let f=-2x_1^2+\frac12(x_2-2)^2, h=x_1, with solution (0,2). Its true full Hessian is \operatorname{diag}(-4,1) but its tangent curvature is1. At (-\epsilon,2-3\epsilon) with \mathbf B=\operatorname{diag}(2,3), the equality-QP step is (\epsilon,\epsilon) and the fixed-multiplier secant is (-4\epsilon,\epsilon). Thus \mathbf s^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y=-3\epsilon^2 even arbitrarily close to the strict constrained minimum. At \epsilon=1, a=5,b=-3,\theta=.5,\mathbf r=(-1,2) and the actual existing damping routine yields \left[\begin{smallmatrix}2.2&-3.2\\-3.2&5.2\end{smallmatrix}\right] with positive eigenvalues. A full positive approximation cannot converge to this specifically indefinite true Hessian; SOSC does not imply every problem has an indefinite full Hessian.

For full-row-rank \mathbf J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} and a null basis \mathbf Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}, use \mathbf d=\mathbf n+\mathbf Z\mathbf q, with \mathbf J\mathbf n=-\mathbf h and \mathbf J\mathbf Z=\mathbf0. The unrelaxed reduced objective is(\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf a+\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf n)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf q+\tfrac12\mathbf q^{\mathsf T}\mathbf H_R\mathbf q,

where \mathbf H_R=\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf Z. Its bounds are \mathbf x_L\le\mathbf x+\mathbf n+\mathbf Z\mathbf q\le\mathbf x_U. An arbitrary null basis does not turn these into independent coordinate bounds on \mathbf q. With \mathbf J=[1,1], \mathbf Z=(1,-1) and current (.5,.5) inside [0,1]^2, the true tangent coordinate interval is [-.5,.5]; q=1 violates both physical bounds.

For scalar relaxation, the reconstructed step must be \mathbf d=(1-\xi)\mathbf n+\mathbf Z\mathbf q. Exact substitution into the full lifted objective retains(1-\xi)\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf n+\tfrac12(1-\xi)^2\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf n+
\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Z\mathbf q+(1-\xi)\mathbf q^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf n+
\tfrac12\mathbf q^{\mathsf T}\mathbf H_R\mathbf q+M(\xi+\xi^2/2).

The normal and coupling terms depend on \xi and cannot be dropped as constants. Biegler6.33p145is a reduced approximate model with frozen/dropped terms, not this exact substitution. Its subsequent Algorithm 6.3Step 4prints an unscaled normal reconstruction. Use the actual relaxed normal in a bound-feasible implementation and test its actual merit derivative.

The difference can survive line search: for h=x_1+20x_1^2-1, current (0,0) and 0\le x_1\le.25, the normal is (1,0). A reduced elastic candidate q=0,\xi=.75 has valid scaled step (.25,0). The unscaled (1,0) violates the upper bound, although the NLP has feasible x_1=.2. A backtracked \alpha=.275 trial has violation .7875, below the weight1Armijo bound .9725 with \eta=.1, but still violates the physical bound by .025. Merit acceptance cannot substitute for preserving hard bounds. The original full lifted notebook solver already returns its actual primal step and is kept unchanged.

The exact multiplier from a full QP obeys\bar{\mathbf v}=-(\mathbf J\mathbf Y)^{-\mathsf T}\mathbf Y^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf a+\mathbf B\mathbf d-\bar{\mathbf u}_L+\bar{\mathbf u}_U).

Dropping \mathbf B\mathbf d produces a first-order/least-squares estimate, not the exact QP multiplier. With \mathbf Y=\mathbf J^{\mathsf T} it uses -(\mathbf J\mathbf J^{\mathsf T})^{-1}\mathbf J(\mathbf a-\mathbf u_L+\mathbf u_U). Nocedal–Wright pp. 539–540 also analyzes dropping the normal/tangent coupling term near a solution; it is an approximation justified by normal-step behavior and the rate conditions below, not an algebraic identity. Reduced BFGS uses \mathbf s_R=\alpha\mathbf q and the projected fixed-multiplier gradient change. If the basis changes, its curvature coordinates need consistent transport/interpretation. L21’s equality reference owns the full normal/coupling derivation.

Large sparse factorization and active-set updates

records.content:
Reduced-space methods can be economical when n-m is small, but basis construction, dense fill, the number of active bounds and conditioning also matter. Many degrees of freedom can favor sparse full KKT/Hessian operations or limited-memory updates rather than a dense full BFGS matrix. Biegler pp. 144–147 uses examples and approximate dimension thresholds; these are design heuristics, not universal cutoffs or a claim that every QP implementation is dense.

An active-set solver can reuse a factorization when adding a row. Let \mathbf K\mathbf z=\mathbf r be the current nonsingular KKT system and append \mathbf e^{\mathsf T}\mathbf z=b with multiplier u. Solve \mathbf K\mathbf z_0=\mathbf r and \mathbf K\mathbf w=\mathbf e. If \mathbf e^{\mathsf T}\mathbf w\ne0,u=\frac{\mathbf e^{\mathsf T}\mathbf z_0-b}{\mathbf e^{\mathsf T}\mathbf w},\qquad\mathbf z=\mathbf z_0-\mathbf w u.

This is the Schur update in6.36p147; it uses solves, not explicitly forming an inverse. A zero or small denominator warns about dependence/conditioning and requires a consistency/rank safeguard. To drop an active row, permit a slack in that row and impose zero on its multiplier, yielding the analogous augmented6.37system. These operations update the working system, not a proof of global primal uniqueness. The prototype below deliberately recomputes dense systems rather than implementing these sparse updates.

Independent coordinate bounds need not enforce the total physical trust radius.

For \Delta>0, define \|\mathbf d\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le n}|d_i|. Its closed radius-\Delta ball is the coordinate box [-\Delta,\Delta]^n. A hard SQP trust model adds \|\mathbf d\|_\infty\le\Delta to the affine constraints and physical bounds. Its feasible set can be empty even for a feasible NLP. For the line d_1+d_2=2.04, its distance is 1.443 in Euclidean norm and 1.02 in infinity norm; both miss radius1, but the ball and box are different sets. State the chosen norm when interpreting a circle illustration. A finite trust radius makes a feasible quadratic model bounded, including indefinite curvature; it does not automatically cure rank deficiency, infeasibility or inaccurate inner solves.

Composite relaxation. The generic normal/tangent proof and acceptance mechanism remain at 

Constrained Globalization. For bounds, retain \mathbf x_L\le\mathbf x+\mathbf n+\mathbf Z\mathbf q\le\mathbf x_U in the tangent model and coordinate the total trust radius. Biegler6.39–6.45p149–150restricts the problem to dependent variables \mathbf y without bounds and independent variables \mathbf z with simple bounds. With \mathbf J=[\mathbf J_y,\mathbf J_z] and invertible \mathbf J_y, it uses \mathbf Y=[\mathbf I;\mathbf0] and \mathbf Z=[-\mathbf J_y^{-1}\mathbf J_z;\mathbf I]. Independent coordinate bounds on \mathbf z+\mathbf q then have their stated meaning. These bases are not generally orthogonal, so the independent coordinate radius must be coordinated with \|\mathbf Y\mathbf p_Y+\mathbf Z\mathbf q\|\le\Delta.

For h=y+2z-1, current (1.3,0), normal (-.3,0) and \mathbf Z=(-2,1), q=.2 gives total step (-.7,.2) with length .7280. It satisfies an independent z bound |q|\le.25 but violates a total step radius .6. The true squared length is .09+1.2q+5q^2, including coupling. This special-coordinate lesson extends the L22 composite model; it does not repeat its generic proof. Projected/truncated CG can exploit negative curvature in a bounded tangent subproblem, but step-quality and constraint safeguards still apply.

S-l1QP. Set V(\mathbf d)=\sum_j|h_j+\mathbf J_{h,j}\mathbf d|+\sum_i\max(g_i+\mathbf J_{g,i}\mathbf d,0). Minimize \mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d+\frac12\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\mathbf d+\rho_{\rm pen}V(\mathbf d) on the trust box. If physical bounds are hard, retain their intersection with that box; otherwise include their violations consistently in V. A bound-feasible current point makes zero belong to the hard domain. Softened constraint rows cannot make it empty. The nonempty hard domain is closed and bounded in finite-dimensional space, hence compact. By Weierstrass, a continuous model attains a global minimum there even if curvature is indefinite; uniqueness and cheap solution do not follow. Slack lifting makes the piecewise formulation a smooth QP with linear constraints, but it can still be nonconvex. Nocedal–Wright18.49–18.50pp549–550.

Here the penalty changes the computed step, not only its acceptance. The complete18.5update procedure onpp553–554first solves with the previous weight. If the selected step is exactly affine-feasible, retain the weight subject to the model-decrease safeguard. Otherwise solve a minimum-violation model on the same trust domain to obtain \mathbf p_\infty. If that reference reaches zero violation, increase the weight and resolve until the penalty-model step does so; if it cannot, require a prescribed fraction of its achievable violation reduction. Finally increase/resolve as needed so model reduction exceeds a fixed fraction of weight times the actual predicted violation reduction. If that reduction is zero, use the appropriate stationary/restoration branch; do not divide by it. With SLQP, the analogous LP stage uses zero quadratic curvature. These extra solves trade inner work against better penalty selection; they are not a universal efficiency guarantee.

Filters. A hard filter trust method solves the bounded affine QP when feasible and invokes restoration when its model cannot be solved/accepted. Historical acceptance and near-feasibility objective switching remain necessary. Biegler p. 148 separately describes an elastic filter line-search extension with projected-curvature, bounded-dual and sufficient-consistency assumptions; the next page gives the hard filter trust model. An elastic problem’s lifted feasibility does not guarantee that its residual is sufficiently small or that its numerical solve succeeds. Fletcher–Leyffer–Toint Theorem7contains method-specific restoration/KKT/regularity alternatives; see the complete L22 filter reference. Do not assign that theorem unchanged to every penalty/elastic/filter variant.

Local rates: what the hypotheses actually guarantee

records.content:
A constructed sequence has two-step superlinearity and persistent one-step ratios.

Exact equality/SQP Newton steps have a quadratic local primal-dual rate under LICQ, SOSC, locally Lipschitz second derivatives, close primal/dual starts and accepted full steps. Stable active sets allow the inequality problem to use that local model; they do not supply every hypothesis by themselves. L21 owns the equality proof and L22 owns the Maratos safeguard.

Let \mathbf P_k be an orthogonal projector onto the locally fixed active tangent and \mathbf s_k=\mathbf x^{k+1}-\mathbf x^k. A one-sided projected Dennis–Moré condition controls \|\mathbf P_k(\mathbf B_k-\mathbf W^*)\mathbf s_k\|/\|\mathbf s_k\|\to0. A two-sided condition controls only \|\mathbf P_k(\mathbf B_k-\mathbf W^*)\mathbf P_k\mathbf s_k\|/\|\mathbf s_k\|\to0. The missing normal/tangent coupling is a real difference: with \mathbf P=\operatorname{diag}(0,1), \mathbf B=2\mathbf I, \mathbf W=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right] and \mathbf s=(1,1), the two-sided numerator is0but the one-sided numerator is1.

Biegler6.24–6.27p142summarizes exact, one-sided superlinear and two-sided two-step conditions. Nocedal–Wright18.6p559gives ordinary full BFGS Q-superlinearity with strong full-Hessian positivity, close initial data and its regularity assumptions. Its printed parenthetical r_k=s_k is a typo: ordinary BFGS uses r_k=y_k. The same page distinguishes damped BFGS R-superlinearity from one-step Q-superlinearity. Theorem 18.7assumes the sequence already converges, bounded approximations, its smoothness hypothesis and the two-sided projected condition to establish two-step superlinearity. The latter assumes \mathbf x^k\to\mathbf x^* and nonzero errors e_k=\|\mathbf x^k-\mathbf x^*\| and means: for every \varepsilon>0, there is K such that e_{k+2}/e_k<\varepsilon for all k\ge K. Equivalently,\frac{\|\mathbf x^{k+2}-\mathbf x^*\|}{\|\mathbf x^k-\mathbf x^*\|}\longrightarrow0.

It need not force every one-step ratio to zero. Let a_0=.5, a_{j+1}=a_j^2, e_{2j}=a_j and e_{2j+1}=a_j/2. Both two-step ratios equal a_j\to0, while every even-to-odd ratio is .5. This is an error-sequence illustration, not a claimed trajectory of the prototype. Finite run tables can illustrate a rate but cannot prove asymptotic conditions. Nor is “quadratic if exact, two-step otherwise” a universal classification of every SQP method.

The original computational cells below are retained. They implement a dense active-set bound-QP solver, scalar-relaxed line-search SQP, damped BFGS and an optional reoptimized correction. They do not implement the trust-region/SLQP/sparse variants explained above.

hessian='exact' uses the actual Lagrangian Hessian followed by full-space convexification. It does not necessarily take the unmodified exact Newton step. hessian='bfgs' uses the safeguarded update.

The inner solver can fall back to least squares on singular KKT systems and has a finite iteration cap; its return does not itself prove an exact feasible QP optimum. It does not warm-start working sets across outer iterations.

The scalar upper bound \xi\le1 and hybrid penalty logic are explicit prototype safeguards. A relaxation near1causes the original code’s stall status, not a proof of global infeasibility.

The stopping test uses small primal step and equality violation rather than every original-model KKT residual. The original outer result does not return bound multipliers. Diagnostics identify any reconstructed final-bound multipliers separately from solver-returned equality values.

The line search has a finite retry loop, and its current prototype path does not return a separate failure if that loop exhausts. The generic correction is equality-based and clips to bounds; the bounded example’s acceptance is empirical, and a general local-rate proof needs a bound-aware correction. The Maratos circle has no active physical bounds.

Fresh actual runs give near-roundoff original-point feasibility/stationarity for the circle and active-bound examples with both modes. On Biegler6.3from (0,.1,0,0), BFGS reaches (-3,2,6,0); the convexified-exact mode hits the100-iteration limit with violation 2.5148\times10^{-5} and stationarity defect .21557. From the all-zero start both keep the \xi=1 failure with violation1. Those outcomes are useful teaching evidence. They remain visible rather than being removed or “repaired” to make a comparison look successful. Decisions between full/reduced curvature, line search/trust methods and alternative solvers should use actual derivative cost, sparsity, residuals and failure traces rather than categorical method rankings.

records.content:
The code uses L=f+\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h with a row Jacobian and hard bounds \mathbf x_L\le\mathbf x\le\mathbf x_U. The 

bound QP and sign table define the model. lam stores the course equality multiplier \mathbf v; the objective-gradient argument g is not a vector of inequality functions. Nocedal–Wright equality multipliers reverse sign for the same equality function, while their nonnegative inequality multipliers retain their values when \mathbf g=-\mathbf c_I.

For equality-only subproblems, solve_kkt solves\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf B&\mathbf J^{\mathsf T}\\\mathbf J&\mathbf0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf d\\\bar{\mathbf v}\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f\\\mathbf h\end{bmatrix}.

A singular-system least-squares fallback is a numerical safeguard; inspect residuals before treating the returned values as a QP KKT solution.

def solve_kkt(H, g, A, r):
    """
    Solve the equality constrained QP

        min_p   g' p + 1/2 p' H p    s.t.   A p + r = 0

    by solving its first order KKT system

        [ H   A' ] [ p  ]     [ g ]
        [ A   0  ] [ mu ]  = -[ r ].

    This is Eq. (5.5) of Biegler (2010), p. 93 -- the same linear system
    the equality constrained Newton method solved -- and it is the only
    linear algebra in the whole method.

    Inputs:
        H : Hessian of the QP objective, (n, n)
        g : gradient of the QP objective, (n,)
        A : constraint Jacobian, (m, n). Our row convention: A = J_h.
        r : constraint residual, (m,)

    Outputs:
        p  : QP step, (n,)
        mu : multipliers for A p + r = 0, (m,)
    """
    n = H.shape[0]
    m = A.shape[0]

    # Assemble the (n + m) x (n + m) KKT matrix.
    K = np.zeros((n + m, n + m))
    K[:n, :n] = H
    if m > 0:
        K[:n, n:] = A.T
        K[n:, :n] = A

    # Right-hand side.
    rhs = np.concatenate([-g, -r])

    # Solve. Fall back to least squares if the KKT matrix is singular,
    # which happens when A does not have full row rank (LICQ fails).
    try:
        sol = linalg.solve(K, rhs)
        if not np.all(np.isfinite(sol)):
            raise linalg.LinAlgError("non-finite KKT solution")
    except linalg.LinAlgError:
        sol = linalg.lstsq(K, rhs)[0]

    return sol[:n], sol[n:]

records.content:
The QP chooses the active set, and re-chooses it every iteration -- that is what we bought by relaxing the known-active-set problem (6.9)--(6.10). The price is that a QP with inequalities is not a linear solve. We pay it with a textbook primal active set method: fix a working set of bounds, solve the resulting equality QP with solve_kkt, then add a blocking bound or release one whose multiplier has the wrong sign.

def solve_bound_qp(H, c, A, b, lo, hi, z0, max_iter=200, tol=1e-9):
    """
    Primal active set method for the bound constrained QP

        min_z   1/2 z' H z + c' z
        s.t.    A z = b
                lo <= z <= hi

    started from a *feasible* point z0.

    The working set W holds the indices currently fixed at a bound. On
    every pass we fix those variables, solve the resulting equality
    constrained QP with `solve_kkt`, and then either

      * move along the step, adding whichever bound blocks first, or
      * if the step is zero, inspect the bound multipliers and release
        the bound whose multiplier has the wrong sign.

    This is Algorithm 16.3 of Nocedal & Wright (2006), specialized to
    bounds. It is deliberately simple: no warm start, no cycling
    safeguard beyond `max_iter`, dense factorizations throughout.

    Inputs:
        H, c    : QP objective, (n, n) and (n,). H must be positive definite.
        A, b    : equality constraints A z = b, (m, n) and (m,)
        lo, hi  : bounds, (n,) each
        z0      : feasible starting point, (n,)

    Outputs:
        z    : QP solution, (n,)
        mu   : multipliers for A z = b, (m,)
        zeta : multipliers for the bounds, (n,).
               zeta_i > 0 at a lower bound, zeta_i < 0 at an upper bound.
        nit  : number of active set passes
    """
    n = len(z0)
    m = A.shape[0]
    z = np.array(z0, dtype=float)

    # Working set: indices sitting on a bound at the starting point.
    W = set(i for i in range(n) if abs(z[i] - lo[i]) <= tol or abs(z[i] - hi[i]) <= tol)
    mu = np.zeros(m)

    for it in range(max_iter):
        free = sorted(set(range(n)) - W)
        g = H @ z + c

        # Step in the free variables only; fixed variables do not move.
        p = np.zeros(n)
        if free:
            p_free, mu = solve_kkt(
                H[np.ix_(free, free)], g[free], A[:, free], np.zeros(m)
            )
            p[free] = p_free
        else:
            mu = np.zeros(m)

        if linalg.norm(p, np.inf) <= tol:
            # Stationary for the current working set. Check the bound
            # multipliers and release one if its sign is wrong.
            zeta = H @ z + c + A.T @ mu
            worst, worst_val = None, tol
            for i in W:
                if hi[i] - lo[i] <= tol:
                    continue  # genuinely fixed variable, never released
                at_lo = abs(z[i] - lo[i]) <= tol
                at_hi = abs(z[i] - hi[i]) <= tol
                if at_lo and -zeta[i] > worst_val:
                    worst, worst_val = i, -zeta[i]
                elif at_hi and zeta[i] > worst_val:
                    worst, worst_val = i, zeta[i]
            if worst is None:
                return z, mu, zeta, it
            W.discard(worst)
        else:
            # Ratio test: how far can we move before hitting a bound?
            alpha, blocking = 1.0, None
            for i in free:
                if p[i] > tol and hi[i] < BIG:
                    a = (hi[i] - z[i]) / p[i]
                elif p[i] < -tol and lo[i] > -BIG:
                    a = (lo[i] - z[i]) / p[i]
                else:
                    continue
                if a < alpha:
                    alpha, blocking = a, i
            z = z + alpha * p
            if blocking is not None:
                W.add(blocking)

    zeta = H @ z + c + A.T @ mu
    return z, mu, zeta, max_iter

The original function below implements the 

guarded scalar QP, with 0\le\xi\le1. A bound-feasible current point makes (\mathbf d,\xi)=(\mathbf0,1) feasible. Positive full primal curvature and M>0 make its convex objective strictly convex. The upper bound on \xi is an explicit addition to the book’s printed domain.

Selected relaxation

What follows

\xi=0

The selected step satisfies the original affine equalities.

0<\xi<1

The selected step contracts the residual; merit descent requires the 

curvature and weight conditions.

\xi=1

Contraction is lost; diagnose a stall/restoration need. A tangent step may still be nonzero.

Positive relaxation can be preferred even when the original affine model is feasible. The original function’s short docstring should be read with these precise distinctions. Stack \mathbf z=[\mathbf d;\xi] to obtain one more variable, Jacobian column -\mathbf h, and Hessian diagonal entry M.

def solve_sqp_subproblem(g, B, h, J, d_lo, d_hi, M=1.0e4):
    """
    Assemble and solve the relaxed SQP subproblem, Biegler (6.15)-(6.16),
    pp. 138-139:

        min_{d, xi}   g' d + 1/2 d' B d + M (xi + xi^2 / 2)
        s.t.          h (1 - xi) + J d = 0
                      d_lo <= d <= d_hi,   0 <= xi <= 1

    Stacking z = [d; xi] turns this into exactly the bound constrained QP
    `solve_bound_qp` already handles: one extra variable, one extra
    column -h in the Jacobian, and one extra diagonal entry M.

    Inputs:
        g, B         : objective gradient and Hessian (approximation) at x^k
        h, J         : equality constraint residual and Jacobian at x^k
        d_lo, d_hi   : x_L - x^k and x_U - x^k
        M            : elastic penalty weight

    Outputs:
        d       : primal step, (n,)
        xi      : relaxation, scalar in [0, 1]. xi = 0 means the
                  linearization was consistent; xi = 1 means it could
                  only be satisfied by giving up entirely.
        lam_bar : equality multipliers from the QP, (m,)
        zeta    : bound multipliers for d, (n,)
        nit     : active set passes
    """
    n = len(g)
    m = len(h)

    # Objective: 1/2 [d; xi]' H_qp [d; xi] + c_qp' [d; xi]
    #          = g'd + 1/2 d'B d + M (xi + xi^2/2)
    H_qp = np.zeros((n + 1, n + 1))
    H_qp[:n, :n] = B
    H_qp[n, n] = M
    c_qp = np.concatenate([g, [M]])

    # Constraint: h (1 - xi) + J d = 0   <=>   [J | -h] [d; xi] = -h
    A_qp = np.zeros((m, n + 1))
    A_qp[:, :n] = J
    A_qp[:, n] = -h
    b_qp = -h

    # Bounds, including 0 <= xi <= 1.
    lo = np.concatenate([d_lo, [0.0]])
    hi = np.concatenate([d_hi, [1.0]])

    # d = 0, xi = 1 is always feasible: it satisfies the equality row
    # exactly. This is what makes the relaxed subproblem well posed.
    z0 = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n), [1.0]])

    z, lam_bar, zeta, nit = solve_bound_qp(H_qp, c_qp, A_qp, b_qp, lo, hi, z0)
    return z[:n], z[n], lam_bar, zeta[:n], nit
